Praise for The Emerald Handbook of Blockchain for Business:

Maximizing the potential of any technology to create value requires both vision and execution. Knowledge is a key to success in both. This book delivers in-depth coverage of both public and permissioned (business focus) types of Blockchains. The authors’ exploration of the advantages/limitations, risks/rewards, and futures/realities is a door opener to the potential awaiting anyone serious about understanding or using blockchain technologies to impact the world.

– Francis D. Poeta, Serial Entrepreneur, CTO, IBM

The Emerald Handbook of Blockchain for Business is a must-own book for anyone interested in blockchain. It offers readers an in-depth journey starting from the origins of blockchain technology and cryptoassets, to the evolution of the technology into multiple industries including global finance, real estate, healthcare, and more. It also discusses innovative, cutting-edge developments in this ecosystem, including token economics, interoperability, and blockchain's impact on other emerging technologies.

– Ron Quaranta, Chairman of the Board, Wall Street Blockchain Alliance

The Emerald Handbook of Blockchain for Business sheds light on blockchain with 22 chapters deploying an easy-to-understand style. The book starts with fundamental concepts and extends to intricate cases. It blends the know-how and experience of academics and practitioners into the blockchain domain. This book is a candidate to be a worldwide handbook of blockchain for academics, students, practitioners, entrepreneurs, business people, consultants, researchers, policymakers, and all technology-lovers.

– Professor Ibrahim E. Sancak, PhD, ZWIRN-Research Center, Ostfalia University of Applied Sciences, Germany, Founding (E) Director, Market Oversight and Enforcement Division, Capital Markets Board of Turkey

In this book, the team of experts delivers a balanced introduction to the world of blockchain and its diverse applications. The authors first explain the theoretical fundamentals of blockchains and the different components and then cover a spectrum of industry and business applications of this transformational technology. With the wide topic coverage, this book presents a comprehensive must-read primer for anyone interested in the study of blockchain.

– Petr Novotny, PhD, Research Staff Member & Master Inventor, IBM Research

When you're editing, you want to be the perfect appreciator, not another writer.

–Joseph Kanon

The path leading to publishing a book is long and sometimes bumpy with some unexpected detours along the way. For example, a global pandemic occurred during this project. To get to the end of our journey required the contributions of many people along the way. As editors, we are mindful of the important role that each plays. Although all the roles differ, each contributed meaningfully to completing this book. We greatly appreciate everyone's contributions, but particularly want to recognize the following individuals.

The chapter authors are at the heart of an edited book. Writing is hard work. We gratefully acknowledge the countless hours they invested in writing and revising their chapters thereby sharing their knowledge and experience about blockchain. As editors, our role was not to change their ideas, but to help craft and polish them to bring out their brilliance. We thank the highly talented staff at Emerald Publishing, especially Charlotte Maiorana, Senior Editor for Business, Economics, and Finance. We also recognize the support provided by our respective institutions: Kogod School of Business at American University, Frank G. Zarb School of Business at Hofstra University, and Lehman College at City University of New York. Finally, we are grateful for our families, who were largely silent partners in this process. We dedicate this book to Linda and Rory Baker; Parvin, Auzin, and Daniel Nikbakht; Frederick Smith and Kathleen Stein Smith as well as Patrick and Frederick Stein Smith.

About the Editors

H. Kent Baker, CFA, CMA, is University Professor of Finance in the Kogod School of Business at American University. Professor Baker is an award-winning author/editor of 38 books including Debt Markets and Investments, Investment Traps Exposed: Navigating Investor Mistakes and Behavioral Biases, Financial Behavior: Players, Services, Products, and Markets; Investor Behavior: The Psychology of Financial Planning and Investing, and Survey Research in Corporate Finance. He is also the editor of two book series: Financial Markets and Investments (Oxford University Press) and the H. Kent Baker Investments Series (Emerald Publishing). As one of the most prolific finance academics, he has published more than 190 refereed academic journal articles and 125 practitioner-oriented articles appearing in such outlets as the Journal of Finance, Journal of Financial and Quantitative Analysis, Financial Management, Journal of Corporate Finance, Financial Analysts Journal, Journal of Portfolio Management, and Harvard Business Review. He has consulting and training experience with more than 100 organizations and has conducted more than 800 training programs in North America and Europe. Professor Baker holds a BSBA from Georgetown University; an MEd, MBA, and DBA from the University of Maryland; and an MA, MS, and two PhDs from American University.

Ehsan Nikbakht, CFA, FRM, PRM, is C.V. Starr Distinguished Professor of Finance in the Frank G. Zarb School of Business at Hofstra University. His latest research focused on volatility transmission across different markets. Among his recent publications are blockchain and distributed financial data (Managerial Finance 2019), the external monitoring of private firms (Global Finance Journal 2017), and the international perspective of spillover effects on REITs (International Journal of Business 2016.) His book Foreign Loans and Economic Performance received a Stessin Prize for outstanding scholarly publication. Professor Nikbakht has delivered numerous educational presentations at major financial institutions including Bank of America, Goldman Sachs, Morgan Stanley, S&P, PNC, Royal Bank of Canada, Merrill Lynch, Legg Mason, State Street, and Deutsche Bank. He received an MBA from the Iran Center for Management Studies and a DBA in finance from George Washington University.

Sean Stein Smith, CPA, CMA, CGMA, CFE, is an Assistant Professor of Business and Economics in Lehman College at City University of New York. He serves on the Advisory Board of the Wall Street Blockchain Alliance, where he chairs the Accounting Work Group. Professor Smith has published numerous articles and several books focusing on the intersection of accounting, financial services, and emerging technologies. He also is the chairperson of the NJCPA's Emerging Technologies Interest Group (#NJCPATech). Professor Smith is on the Advisory Board of Gilded, a TechStars '19 company and AICPA-CPA.com Startup Accelerator participant. He was a Visiting Research Fellow at the American Institute of Economic Research in 2019 continuing his research on blockchain, crypto assets, and financial services. He is a frequent guest on television, radio, and other multimedia discussing emerging technologies and financial services. Professor Smith received a B.S, M.S, and MBA from Fairleigh Dickinson University and a DBA from Capella University.

Part I
Blockchain: History and Background

Chapter 1

Blockchain: An Overview

H. Kent Baker, Ehsan Nikbakht and Sean Stein Smith

Abstract

Blockchain is an emerging technology that started in the cryptocurrency sphere with bitcoin but expanded to include numerous applications. This chapter provides an overview of the book. It begins by identifying the three main components of a blockchain. Next, it discusses the book's purpose, distinguishing features, and its intended audience. The chapter then outlines the book's structure, consisting of 22 chapters divided into four main parts. It offers a brief synopsis of each section and chapter. Finally, it ends with a summary and conclusions.

Keywords: Blockchain; cryptocurrency; distributed ledger; business applications; regulatory issues; consensus mechanisms

Introduction

The blockchain cannot be described just as a revolution. It is a tsunami-like phenomenon, slowly advancing and gradually enveloping everything along its way by the force of its progression.William Mougayar, advisor, investor, and author of The Business Blockchain

Although an emerging technology, blockchain is here to stay. It combines three main components: (1) a distributed network, (2) digital transactions, and (3) a stored ledger. As Blythe Masters, an experienced financial services and technology executive, notes, “Blockchain technology, or distributed ledger technology, is just a way of using the modern sciences of encryption to enable entities to share a common infrastructure for database retention” (Johnson 2016). However, the buzzwords blockchain and distributed ledger can be confusing. A common misconception is that blockchain and distributed ledger are the same. A distributed ledger refers to a decentralized database existing across several locations or among multiple participants. A blockchain is just one type of distributed ledger. A blockchain is basically a shared database filled with entries that must be confirmed and encrypted. Each document entry is dependent on a logical relationship to all its predecessors. The term blockchain refers to the “blocks” that get added to the chain of transaction records. Unlike blockchain, a distributed ledger does not necessarily require having a data structure in blocks (Belin 2020). One way to view blockchain and distributed ledger is similar to thinking of Coke and soft drinks. The former is a type of the latter.

Cryptocurrency bitcoin was the first mainstream manifestation of blockchain's potential. Satoshi Nakamoto, a pseudonymous person or group, first outlined bitcoin in a 2008 white paper (Nakamoto 2008). In early 2009, Nakamoto released bitcoin to the public resulting in enthusiastic supporters starting to exchange and mine this virtual currency (Martucci 2020). Although bitcoin was the first established cryptocurrency, previous attempts tried to create online currencies with ledgers secured by encryption such as b-money and bit-gold, but they were never fully developed (Marr 2017).

Since its inception, blockchain has stretched its wings beyond the crypto sphere. Imaginative thinkers have identified new ways for this powerful technology to bring innovative solutions to different problems that result in clear benefits for individuals and institutions. Blockchain offers the potential of creating a safer world. Today, blockchain provides an abundant and diverse set of use cases across society. Every so often, new technology has the promise to change the world in ways that are currently unimagined. Blockchain is such an innovation. Not surprisingly, many companies, governments, financial institutions, and entrepreneurs are engaging with blockchain. Yet, because blockchain can be an extreme and disruptive change, its infiltration into business and society has been uneasy and sometimes met with resistance.

About This Book

This section discusses the book's purpose, distinguishing features, and its intended audience.

Purpose

The book's main purpose is to provide academics, practitioners, students, and others with a broad understanding of some current issues in the emerging blockchain technology and its applications. The coverage extends from discussing basic concepts and their application to increasingly intricate and real-world situations. This volume spans the gamut from theoretical to practical while offering a useful balance of detailed and user-friendly coverage. A discussion of relevant research permeates the books.

Another objective of this book is to provide an overview and understanding of two distinct areas. First, integral to any advanced or industry-specific analysis is the need for practitioners and academics to understand and articulate the core components of how blockchain technology functions. Specifically, questions addressed within this book include what differentiates blockchain from existing data management options and what business problems can be solved via its implementation. Second, the book explains how different industry sectors are using blockchain technology. Upon completing this book, readers should know how blockchain functions and some business applications of increased blockchain integration. The book is not intended to provide solutions to every question blockchain poses, but rather to offer the actionable business intelligence required to make effective decisions. The Emerald Handbook of Blockchain for Business provides a fresh look at this intriguing and dynamic but often complex subject.

Distinguishing Features

Several features distinguish The Emerald Handbook of Blockchain for Business from others.

  • Focuses on business applications and challenges: The book provides a detailed examination of some of the most important aspects of blockchain. It focuses on the opportunities and challenges facing blockchain adoption and implementation across different industries.
  • Offers insights from a diverse set of authors: The book skillfully blends the contributions of scholars and practitioners into a single review of critical topics about blockchain. The varied backgrounds of the contributors assure different perspectives and a rich interplay of ideas.
  • Provides an internally consistent approach: While retaining the content and perspectives of the many contributors, the book follows an internally consistent approach in format and style. Like a choir that contains many voices, this book has many chapter authors with their separate voices. A goal of both a choir and this book is to have the many voices sing together harmoniously. Accomplishing this task requires skilled editing by the coeditors to create a seamless flow when moving from chapter to chapter. Hence, the book is much more than merely a collection of chapters from an array of different authors.
  • Reflects current trends and research on blockchain: When discussing the results of empirical studies that connect theory and practice, the objective is to distill them to their essential content so they are understandable to a wide array of readers with different backgrounds.
  • Contains end-of-chapter discussion questions: The end of Chapters 2–22 contains between four and six discussion questions that reinforce key concepts with guideline answers presented at the end of the book. This feature should be especially important to faculty and students using the book in courses.
  • Offers a glossary of blockchain terms: The book contains a glossary of key terms related to blockchain for easy reference.

Intended Audience

Given its broad scope, this practical and comprehensive book should be relevant to academics, practitioners, students, and others interested in blockchain. For academics, the book provides the basis for a better understanding of various aspects of blockchain and as a springboard for future research. Academics can also use the book as a stand-alone or supplementary resource for courses in blockchain or related areas. Since this book covers both the technological underpinnings of blockchain and related applications, it should be of interest to practitioners seeking to become more knowledgeable about this fast-moving subject area. Students and others wanting to improve their knowledge of blockchain should find this book essential reading.

Structure of the Book

The remainder of this book consists of 21 chapters divided into four main parts. A brief synopsis of each section and chapter follows.

Part I – Blockchain: History and Background

Besides the current chapter, this part consists of three other chapters (Chapters 2–4) that provide important background information that sets the stage for the remaining parts.

Chapter 2 – History of Distributed Ledgers and Blockchain (Joey Ryan and Sean Stein Smith)

This chapter examines one of the most innovative and disruptive technologies in the modern era ‒ blockchain and its various applications. Although blockchain is commonly associated with bitcoin, a cryptocurrency developed to serve as a replacement for existing fiat currencies, the landscape continues to experience rapid change. New cryptocurrency options, specifically an array of stablecoins that private sector actors or even government agencies may issue, continue to accelerate adoption by individuals and institutions. Stablecoins are cryptocurrencies pegged or otherwise connected to an external asset such as fiat currencies or commodities. Their initial purpose was to reduce price volatility commonly associated with bitcoin and other traditional cryptocurrencies. The chapter also discusses blockchain's opportunities and challenges, including interoperability, cybersecurity, and other technical considerations. It introduces blockchain, crypto assets, and different industry applications.

Chapter 3 – Review of Blockchain and Emerging Applications (Timothy Grief and Ehsan Nikbakht)

The purpose of this chapter is to review the main emerging applications in blockchain technology. The major areas are examined through different stages ‒ some established and some new. The chapter discusses credit scoring, water usage and climate change, supply chain management, health industry, smart cities, accounting and credit models, sustainable developments, business process improvements, fraud detection, predicting default in e-commerce, and breaking the poverty chain. Although blockchain has both risks and limitations, its potential opportunities and rewards are substantial. Although an application of blockchain started with a public platform for creating and trading cryptocurrencies, blockchain is now going through numerous forms of public (permissionless), private (permissioned), and hybrid systems to improve transparency, efficiency, data sharing, and reduce transaction costs.

Chapter 4 – Technical Aspects of Blockchain (Hak J. Kim)

Blockchain has gained much attention in business and society as a new way to provide trust and security in the public internet. It promises reliable data transmission by using cryptography and distributed ledger technologies. Despite substantial interest, businesses and other organizations have not widely adopted blockchain because of its complex technical nature. However, blockchain is growing quickly as it extends its usage from finance to many other sectors. Several challenges face blockchain adopters including scalability in size and speed, interoperability among networks, and legal and regulatory issues. This chapter provides a technical foundation of blockchain including concepts, key properties, architecture and components, technical algorithms, operational procedures, and technical challenges.

Part II – Types of Blockchain

This part contains five chapters (Chapters 5‒9) that examine public, private, and hybrid blockchains as well as consensus mechanisms, token economies, and modifications needed to spur consumer adoption of blockchain.

Chapter 5 – Public Blockchains and Applications (Hugo Benedetti)

Public blockchains are permissionless blockchains, allowing universal access to read, write, and validate information stored in the network. This permissionless nature also implies a lack of a central coordinating authority. Instead, coordination of the blockchain's users and management is embedded in the software protocol and complemented by incentive mechanisms, together commonly referred to as cryptoeconomics. A relevant feature of public blockchains is censorship resistance, which is the inability of an adversarial user to deny access to read, write, and validate functions. It enables the decentralization, disintermediation of business processes, institutions, and networks. Censorship resistance also poses challenges, such as the inability to block ethically questionable information, transactions, and markets. Examples of public blockchain applications include monetary and financial networks (Bitcoin and Zcash), distributed virtual machines (Ethereum and EOS), and distributed data storage (Sia).

Chapter 6 – Private and Hybrid Blockchains and Applications (Gina Pieters and Sean Stein Smith)

This chapter discusses and analyzes private and hybrid blockchains and the various implications of such blockchains for enterprise adoption. It also examines stablecoins, central bank digital currencies, and central bank cryptocurrencies regarding blockchain implementation and crypto-asset development. The chapter frames technical explanations and their associated practical implications in the context of blockchain technology developments, with a focus on various kinds of hybrid blockchains such as private and private permissioned models. Finally, the chapter discusses key considerations and questions that enterprises should address before implementing and developing a private or hybrid blockchain.

Chapter 7 – Consensus Mechanisms and Related Issues (Deniz Appelbaum)

Consensus mechanisms are essential to blockchains. Any business considering blockchain technology should acquire base knowledge of these algorithms. Consensus algorithms provide blockchains with the business-friendly features of immutability, tracking, and prevention of double-spending. This chapter provides a basis for understanding how the predominant consensus mechanism proof-of-work operates via hashing and its underlying issues such as whether they are scalable for a specific application. It also covers proof-of-stake and other consensus mechanism proposals.

Chapter 8 – Token Economies (Alim Khamisa)

Decentralized peer-to-peer (P2P) blockchain networks are ushering in a new wave of open source business model innovation. Central to this innovation is the cryptographic token – a blockchain-native asset that facilitates new value creation and exchange models. Tokens enable, for the first time, web-native business models that are a driving force behind the web's evolution into a more decentralized and fairer public utility – Web 3.0. At its core, Web 3.0 disintermediates economic transactions, enables individuals to have greater control and privacy of their data, and creates a more balanced system based on the principles of shared economics that levels the playing field between individuals and businesses. It is giving rise to decentralized applications (dApps) powered by token economies and accompanying on-chain governance mechanisms. The purpose of this chapter is to provide an overview of the various types of token models and delve into token economy design. Token engineering and cryptoeconomics are emerging fields within this domain that draw on a diverse set of disciplines – economics, cryptography, distributed systems, and engineering – to design sustainable and valuable token economies.

Chapter 9 – Proposed Modifications to Spur Consumer Adoption of Blockchain (Katherine McKechnie, Alexandra M. Dunn, and Sayan Sarkar)

Data theft and fraud is a growing concern in the modern era. Protection of data conflicts with the ease of accessing data. Blockchain, which reduces the need for a third-party intermediary, offers a solution that can be applied on large and small scales for government, business, and individual consumers. This chapter examines the functions and benefits of blockchain on all of these levels. Using hash codes and other security features such as smart contracts, cryptographic signatures, and verified identity, blockchain improves efficiency and security of data. The chapter also explains how blockchain can function in specific industries such as healthcare, real estate, and personal identity. Finally, the chapter explains why consumers on each level should adopt blockchain to improve the current standing of data security and data availability.

Part III – The Frontier of Blockchain Technology

This part has six chapters (Chapters 10–15) that deal with issues affecting the frontier of blockchain technology.

Chapter 10 – Blockchain: Speed, Efficiency, Decreased Cost, and Technical Challenges (Amanda Wilke and Sean Stein Smith)

This chapter explores blockchain's five key elements ‒ distribution, encryption, immutability, tokenization, and decentralization. It also examines blockchain's potential to revolutionize today's businesses by looking at the efficiency and transparency blockchain brings to business processes. Additionally, the chapter discusses the added benefits of traceability and potentially decreasing long-term costs before reviewing some of the known technical challenges blockchains face today especially pertaining to commercial and enterprise adoption. Limited block size and low transaction rates potentially inhibit blockchain's ability to scale to meet the needs of current and future enterprises. The lack of blockchain standards and creating multiple blockchains, complicate interoperability between the various blockchain platforms. The chapter concludes by offering potential solutions to blockchain's current technical challenges and how enterprises might adapt blockchain in the future.

Chapter 11 – The Importance of Interoperability, Decentralization, and Choice (Kirk Phillips)

Blockchains offer some amazing value propositions like immutability, P2P value transfer, monetary sovereignty, and programmable money. Yet, blockchains emerged without the ability to talk with one another and exchange information between chains. Developers focused on outperforming the competition with the most secure and fastest transaction throughput blockchains, but interoperability was an afterthought. Information gatekeepers seeking profit and commercialization circumvented the organic development of a decentralized internet, and blockchains could suffer the same fate unless interoperability wins the race this time. Fortunately, the composability of blockchains and smart contracts is leading to a wave of product innovation, and crosschain compatibility is becoming a more central focus. The internet of blockchains is well on its way to delivering decentralization, the power of choice, and a level playing field for humankind. This chapter examines the development of blockchain interoperability, how it relates to the growth of the early internet, the different approaches to achieving interoperability, and why interoperability is such a critical value proposition.

Chapter 12 – Convergence with Artificial Intelligence and Other Related Concepts (Lian Duan)

Artificial intelligence (AI) is computer science techniques that make computers work and react like humans. Despite being in an early development stage, these techniques are mature enough to have many meaningful applications such as voice recognition, automatic driving, and financial robo-advising. For these AI techniques to learn from experience, it requires them to collect, save, and analyze big data using as sensors, a Spark system, and deep learning algorithms. Blockchain is another emerging technology designed to help collect, share, and update data across multipeer organizations. This chapter provides a discussion of the convergence between AI and blockchain for potentially useful AI applications across multipeer organizations.

Chapter 13 – Risk Management and Transference Issues in Blockchain Technologies (Joseph Brunsman)

This chapter analyzes how business insurance policies may or may not act as insuring mechanisms for losses related to blockchains data breaches and cryptocurrency losses. Addressing this issue involves comparing various policy language found within popular commercial crime, general liability, and cyber insurance policies as they may relate to blockchain and cryptocurrency losses in a general scenario. Fundamental definitional issues arose within each type of policy. Commercial crime policies are unlikely to provide coverage for blockchain-related losses but might provide coverage for certain cryptocurrency losses. General liability insurance is unlikely to provide coverage for either loss. Cyber insurance policies may circumstantially provide coverage for cryptocurrencies, such as bitcoin, but are unlikely to insure for blockchain losses. Businesses must wait for the insurance market to catch up to these technologies or use more unique insurance mechanisms as a risk management and risk transference mechanism.

Chapter 14 – Legal and Regulatory Issues in the Temporary Regime (J. Scott Colesanti)

The Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) has expediently regulated blockchain, like its lifeline cryptocurrency. To reach such transactions, the agency employs a four-part common law test defining “investment contract.” Once within the jurisdiction of securities laws, such business premised upon alt-currency is subject to antifraud provisions that can be used by government and private plaintiffs alike. Thus, since 2013, the SEC has proven a formidable regulator of blockchain technology, even as some officials question the broad scope. The states have enacted varied approaches, ranging from tax benefits to daunting licensing requirements. The Internal Revenue Service (IRS) has simply warned that cryptocurrency gains can be taxed, while the Treasury Department has reiterated that money transmitter limitations apply to all entities exchanging currency. This chapter provides the fundamentals of the present regulatory scheme for virtual currency along with the caveat that this crudely drawn mosaic may soon be supplanted by statute or rule.

Chapter 15 – Regulator Ambiguity and Its Impact on Blockchain (Shehan Chandrasekera)

Virtual currencies such as bitcoin have gained in popularity depending on their underlying blockchain. Over the past decade, various regulatory agencies such the IRS, Commodities Futures and Trading Commission (CFTC), SEC, Financial Crimes Enforcement Network (FinCen), and Financial Industry Regulatory Authority (FINRA) have attempted to regulate various aspects of this space. Lack of communication between these agencies coupled with slow policymaking after the release of the first guidance in 2014, procedures have created a fragmented and incohesive set of rules. The chapter primarily focuses on the IRS efforts on regulating virtual currency–related transactions. It also discusses several virtual currency–related tax guidance issued by the IRS such as Notice 2014–2021, Frequently Asked Questions (FAQs), Revenue Ruling 2019–2024, and Schedule 1. Next, the chapter examines how those generic rulings have failed to provide clarity at the granular level, causing ambiguity involving applying those rules.

Part IV – Blockchain Applications in Business

This part consists of seven chapters (Chapters 16–22). It begins by examining considerations for blockchain adoption and integration and then highlights blockchain applications in finance, healthcare, real estate, supply chain, accounting, and auditing.

Chapter 16 – Considerations for Blockchain Adoption and Integration (Michael Nizich and Michael Campisi)

This chapter discusses the value of blockchain technology and its unique attributes that make it so attractive for organizations to consider implementing and adopting into different business areas and processes. It uses a traditional system development life-cycle model to drive the discussion and challenge readers to consider various factors when deciding to implement blockchain solutions into their organizations. These factors include establishing a legitimate need, identifying the total cost of ownership, estimating the return on investment, evaluating an organization's technical ability to achieve implementation, and its ability to support and maintain the blockchain for extended periods during its life cycle. The chapter aims to deliver a realistic and practical framework for blockchain implementation into an organization and to guide organizational leaders who are considering implementing blockchain solutions. The chapter addresses such issues as: Does an organization need blockchain technology? Can it afford this technology? Who is responsible for implementing and keeping the blockchain running? Is adopting blockchain worthwhile?

Chapter 17 – Blockchain Applications in Finance (Steven Cosares, Kristin Kalish, Thomas Maciura, and Andrew C. Spieler)

This chapter discusses examples of financial services facilitated by implementing blockchains. These examples provide a sample of novel approaches to integrating blockchains with a more traditional information systems approach that institutions use to obtain, maintain, and deliver information to those who need it. The chapter summarizes various blockchain applications, including shareholder voting, real estate transactions, dividend payments, insurance, and foreign exchange (FX) transactions. Shareholder voting has advanced from paper voting but still has major inefficiencies. Similarly, the FX market is fractured with little regulatory oversight. The distributed ledger technology of blockchains can improve the efficacy of the FX post-trade processes. Similar benefits are available for insurance products, where contracts are relatively simple. The decision to migrate to a blockchain solution is often coupled with decisions about how a company may need to cooperate with its competitors.

Chapter 18 – Blockchain Applications in Healthcare (Alevtina Dubovitskaya)

A person's medical information evolves and is usually stored and processed by multiple entities in various formats, substantial volumes, and for different purposes. Emerging blockchain technology provides an opportunity to enable transparent data sharing and integration for patient-centered treatment, verifiable data provenance, and optimization of healthcare processes. This chapter provides an overview of applications of blockchain technology in healthcare. First, domain-specific requirements for compliant healthcare data management are summarized. Next, the chapter describes how blockchain can fulfill such requirements and presents different approaches for healthcare data storage and management using blockchain. A discussion of the current barriers for adopting blockchain technology and potential future directions toward developing blockchain-based healthcare systems concludes the chapter.

Chapter 19 – Blockchain Applications in Real Estate (Joshua Harris and Ehsan Nikbakht)

Real estate is an exceedingly vast, important asset class that nearly every household, business, and investor are exposed to in some fashion. Real property records remain highly fractured, and transactions are extremely complex and costly despite improvements in technology and finance. As such, the real estate industry presents many opportunities for improvement via blockchain applications. This chapter discusses the nature of real estate parcel location and data management, which is a unique opportunity unto itself that is partially a prerequisite for commercially viable blockchain applications. It then focuses on key areas of practical use cases for blockchain in the real estate industry. Areas for application development include real estate transactions, closings, title insurance, real estate finance, mortgage processes, and real estate operations including investment management. Given the size of the asset class and continuous volume of transactions, blockchain technology has huge potential for use in different real estate sectors.

Chapter 20 – Blockchain Applications in Supply Chain (Kaushik Sengupta)

The emerging use of blockchain technology in the supply chain space has generated a growing interest among companies regarding how this technology could improve supply chain practices and reduce costs. Besides the key benefits of a tracking mechanism for the entire supply chain, companies are looking at associated benefits to improve current practices. This chapter addresses issues related to technology, trust, and benefits to all partners in the supply chain. It also discusses the roles of new technologies such as smart contracts and existing technologies such as radio-frequency identification (RFID) in the context of blockchain. Additionally, the chapter provides details about specific blockchain examples such as TradeLens and Food Trust. Most of the current applications are based on permissioned blockchains with specific companies like IBM and Ethereum taking a lead in developing the underlying ledger system. Challenges in adopting a new technology always exist. Companies can address these challenges by objectively analyzing the benefits, gaining top management support, leveraging existing technologies, and identifying key benefits that allow an end-end improvement in the supply chain.

Chapter 21 – Crypto Accounting Valuation, Reporting, and Disclosure (Sean Stein Smith)

The dialog around the accounting for, reporting, and disclosing information linked to cryptocurrencies, blockchain, and crypto assets is likely to evolve and take different forms as the information and context change moving forward. These considerations and debates are likely to further develop and mature as applications such as smart contracts and stablecoins move from the periphery to the mainstream. Yet, a few core considerations need to be addressed as this conversation advances, specifically related to the accounting and reporting of crypto assets. The purpose of this chapter is to provide an analysis and discussion of several issues that connect blockchain and crypto assets focusing on valuation, reporting, and disclosure. Examples of these issues include how to report and disclose the valuation of various crypto assets, what should be disclosed in terms of internal controls, and what information needs to be reported in terms of smart contracts from an operational and financial perspective.

Chapter 22 – Auditing and Examining Blockchain Information (John “Jack” Castonguay)

This chapter discusses the understanding that external auditors and assurance professionals need to possess and use when providing assurance services to companies implementing blockchain for financial reporting purposes or holding digital assets on their balance sheets. The chapter discusses financial statement audit activities and internal controls (i.e., integrated audits) over financial reporting activities in detail using practice examples within the confines of what is allowable under existing regulations and industry standards. It also presents differences from audits of accounting information on legacy accounting information systems, and discusses the limitations imposed by current regulation and auditing standards, and reviews industry-accepted best practices. Finally, the chapter presents blockchain’s potential to improve audit and assurance services alongside existing applications and use cases.

Summary and Conclusions

Blockchain is an emerging and growing technology with applications in numerous business fields including finance, healthcare, real estate, supply chain, accounting, and auditing. Unlike a traditional database, blockchain extensively uses cryptography (i.e., writing security codes) and permanently maintains the data. The Emerald Handbook of Blockchain for Business consists of 22 chapters discussing fundamental concepts and their application to increasingly complicated real-world situations.

The book's main purpose is to provide academics, practitioners, students, and others with a solid and broad understanding of the current issues involving emerging blockchain technology. The book focuses on blockchain's practical aspects while maintaining a reasonable balance of conceptual and applied coverage. Contributors to this book, who are academics and practitioners, are involved in this new technology’s research and practice. This carefully prepared handbook should help readers develop a fundamental knowledge of blockchain and the growing business applications of blockchain integration.

Chapter 2

History of Blockchain

Joseph “Joey” Ryan and Sean Stein Smith

Keywords: Blockchain; fiat; stablecoins; cryptocurrency; interoperability; money; cybersecurity

Introduction

Some call blockchain, among other things, a trustless internet system, the Internet 2.0, and an opportunity to democratize access to information and financial resources, specifically providing options outside of traditional fiat currencies. This chapter focuses on the background and history of blockchain and specific blockchain-based applications for different economic sectors. Before that discussion, the chapter examines blockchain's evolution. Like any technological tool, the current form of blockchain technology is the result of previous iterations, prior failures, and iterative steps that jointly led to its current state. Although originally designed as an alternative to the current financial infrastructure, blockchain technology has accelerated rapidly as evidenced by current developments including stablecoins and central bank options. The purpose of this chapter is threefold: (1) to outline the foundations of blockchain technology, (2) to discuss influential trends and topics in this space, and (3) to examine how blockchain technology may influence the broader economy moving forward.

Blockchain Components

This section begins by introducing the core components of blockchain (Singh 2020). Below are key components of any blockchain system.

  • Tamper resistant ledger. Any blockchain comprises a tamper-resistant or immutable ledger containing information about transactions that have previously occurred between network members. This tamper-resistant nature forms the core of the value proposition of blockchain across industry lines.
  • Consensus methodology. To add information to the tamper-resistant ledger, some group must approve this information. Thus, multiple network members review and approve any added information regardless of the specifics involved.
  • Encryption. The bitcoin blockchain uses the SHA-256 bit encryption methodology, which has proven resistant to hacking attempts to date. Ironically, the National Security Agency (NSA) initially developed this encryption and not a member of the original cyberpunk community. Every blockchain has some sort of encryption technology and platform embedded at the core of the network system.
  • Peer-to-peer transfers (P2P). At the center of any blockchain is the ability of individuals or organizations to conduct transactions and share information directly with other network members without having to rely on intermediaries or a third party to perform confirmations or other verification processes. These processes serve a role but also add cost, time, and complexity to the transactional process. The initial intent of blockchain technology was to enable individuals and institutions to conduct transactions without needing third party intermediaries.
  • Node. Every computer that is a member of a blockchain network is referred to as a node. Although full and partial nodes exist, every network member can be correctly called a node. Full nodes are involved in the approving and verifying of transactions, and ultimately, blocks. Operating a partial node is also an option. The capabilities and rights of partial nodes vary depending on the specific blockchain implementation. Generally speaking, partial nodes operate in more of a read-only mode and do not play an active role in approving transactions.
  • Miners. As part of the blockchain network, miners are the nodes that are actively involved in the consensus process used to verify transactions before these transactions are batched in blocks. Miners are incentivized to participate in this process with the ability to earn compensation from either confirming blocks as they are added to the blockchain or processing transactions.
  • Real-time transmission of information between network members. A core differentiating factor between blockchain and other data management systems is that information is disseminated on a nearly continuous basis among network members. Thus, although data are handled in a decentralized and distributed manner, only a single source of truth exists. In other words, any network member or external firm granted access to network information can rely on any single record maintained on the blockchain.

Cryptocurrency Terminology

Many blockchain connected mediums of exchange have entered the marketplace since bitcoin entered the space between 2008 and 2009. In general terms, crypto consists of several specific categories. Nakamoto (2008) offers an authoritative whitepaper on the subject.

  • Decentralized cryptocurrencies. The most well-known and highly traded cryptocurrencies fall into this category, such as bitcoin and ether. These cryptocurrencies are neither issued nor governed by any centralized entity or third party. A decentralized model was a direct result of blockchain's origins as a libertarian-inspired development. Yet, alongside the lack of support and regulatory clarity, this model has also led to numerous questions and obstacles to adoption. Simply put, the lack of centralized support services, backstop or support of a governmental agency, and subsequent price volatility seem to have formed central characteristics of how people perceive decentralized cryptocurrencies.
  • Asset-backed coins (stablecoins). Price volatility may form a primary, or even defining, characteristic of decentralized cryptocurrencies, but this same characteristic is also a major obstacle to usage as a legitimate fiat alternative. Asset-backed coins or stablecoins are primarily defined by the reduced price volatility that comes from pegging, tethering, or otherwise connecting a crypto asset to an external asset. A common use case for stablecoins is the increased ability of individuals and merchants to use stablecoins as a medium of exchange rather than as an investment.
  • Central bank digital currencies (CBDCs). CBDCs represent the most recent iteration and addition to the crypto asset space, signaling an important shift in the blockchain and crypto asset ecosystem. Specifically, since a central bank or central government manage and govern CBDCs, these crypto assets operate and are, by default, almost completely opposite in nature of a decentralized cryptocurrency such as bitcoin. Many contend that the Libra Association model actually laid the ground work for CBDC development that has accelerated in the aftermath of that specific project (Massad 2020). The underlying premise of the Libra Association was (1) to develop a form of private money not issued or governed by a central bank or other governmental entity, and (2) to have this form of private money (crypto asset) not specifically connected to any one existing fiat currency. This approach resulted in a non-governmental medium of exchange that could be used on an international basis, potentially undermining the role of fiat currencies the world over. The primary use case and driving force of CBDC development is two-fold: (1) the increased usage of cryptocurrencies and blockchain as a legitimate fiat alternative and (2) increased clarity pertaining to the accounting and reporting aspects surrounding blockchain and crypto. Both of these upsides are connected to the implicit backstop generated by association with a central government or entity.

Blockchain and the History of Money

The history of money is a long and tumultuous one that has several major phases and time periods that have defined how money is used as well as how individuals and institutions interact with financial resources (Beattie 2020). According to Ammous (2018), the quintessential function that defines money is being a medium of exchange. That is, money's primary function is to be exchanged for other goods and services. For any item to be treated and categorized as money, it must effectively function as a medium of exchange and possess several specific traits.

  • Be easily divisible. A medium of exchange must be easily divisible, or at least have the ability to have a proxy divisible. Gold bullion, for example, may be labeled by some as a legitimate alternative to fiat currency, but the lack of divisibility serves as a headwind to its mainstream use.
  • Function as a unit of account. Any proposed medium of exchange must be able to function as a unit of account, which means that the price or relative value of this medium of exchange must have a consistent price level when compared to other assets.
  • Be portable. A medium of exchange has to be portable; it has to be able to be carried and stored by individuals and merchants without causing undue complications.

The traits of money, serving as a medium of exchange, are characteristics that are neither unique to any one specific fiat currency nor specific to any one currency unit.

Fiat currency can be understood as any medium of exchange that is issued ‘by fiat’, or by government order, rather than being tethered, connected, or consistent of precious metals or other hard assets (Merriam-Webster 2020). In other words, the functionality of money is not so much dependent on any one institution or issuing entity, but on the faith and confidence that individuals have in the medium itself. What this means for the future of blockchain and crypto assets remains unclear, but it does seem relatively self-evident that the future of money is more digital than analog. Virtual currencies and the digital representation of money may not be a particularly new or innovative idea, but they do seem to be one that is more conducive to the increasingly online and digital economy. Specific to an online environment and way of conducting transactions, the double-spend problem results from the digital nature of financial resources in such an environment. Double-spending is a potential flaw in a digital cash scheme in which spending the same single digital token can occur more than once. Instead of physically trading currency for goods and services, these currencies are digitized and are represented as code. This digitization is, of course, essential for online commerce, but can also lead to the code potentially being copied and reused by unethical actors. This undermining of the value of virtual currency is the core of the double-spend problem. Besides solving the double-spend problem that previously stymied attempts at a virtual or digital currency, blockchain and different crypto assets appear to offer a protection or hedge against inflation or other market moves.

Money is not inherently connected to any governmental entity or agency, but that does seem to be the direction in which money as a medium of exchange has evolved. All that is required of money to serve a legitimate medium of exchange and way to conduct transactions is to be accepted, redeemable, and readily exchangeable for goods and services. Especially in an online environment or a business landscape that is increasingly dominated by e-commerce or other transactions conducted in a digital environment, the potential for a legitimate alternative to fiat currency is not an abstract idea. In fact, digital currencies, virtual currencies, and the continued growth of online transactions seem only poised to accelerate as a side effect of both technology and other bigger picture events. Specifically, COVID-19, despite the terrible health and various economic ripple effects that the pandemic has had on the economy at large, seems well positioned to accelerate the technology and digitization trends that already existed. Automation, digitization, and the trend toward remote working already existed in the economy, but as a matter of necessity to combat the pandemic, these trends have moved from optional to mandatory in nature. That said, and taking into account the appetite for a durable and robust digital currency, the underlying difficulties with actually getting a digital currency to work will only be addressed with an option that is both available to the public and possesses the characteristics of crypto assets that are appealing to investors worldwide.

Borderless Money

One of the largest and most prominent potentials associated with blockchain and crypto asset technology is the fact that these tools allow the development and maintenance of private money, which serve as an alternative to traditional fiat currencies. Comprehending the differences between blockchain-based or enabled-money and current fiat currencies is critical to understanding the initial appeal and functionality of this technology. In the modern era, especially since the formation of nation states that have replaced prior arrangements of empires and historical arrangements, these nation states have come to the forefront in terms of issuing and controlling currency. Nothing is inherently wrong with a centrally managed medium of exchange in theory. In fact, many of the recent crypto asset developments are trending toward increased centralization, but the historical track record is not particularly positive.

The Weimar Republic of Germany and more recently Zimbabwe may be the two most familiar examples of the mismanagement of public finances and currencies, but are far from the only instances. The fact that many of the largest emerging economies had large debts payable in currencies that were not their own exacerbated the global financial currency crisis sparked by the failure of Long Term Capital Management (LTCM). An additional concern that has emerged as a second order effect of the COVID-19 pandemic, as governments around the globe allocated trillions to stimulus and recovery efforts, is that these efforts will ultimately lead to a debasement of the currencies involved. Inflation, interest rates, and the connections that are supported to exist between these two factors continue to be broken down as a result of negative interest rates, outsized government spending, and geo-political tensions. Blockchain, no matter what additional applications and use cases are discussed, was developed to support the development and proliferation of bitcoin.

Bitcoin is the antithesis to any existing fiat currency in that no central government or governmental agency issue or print it. For any new unit of bitcoin to enter the marketplace requires network members (miners) expending effort and other network members confirming those efforts and associated results. Thus, bitcoin and other crypto assets developed in a similar manner and exist outside of normal political influence channels. The idea that private money exists outside of the reach of political leaders is revolutionary and a key reason that regulatory authorities have not given bitcoin and other crypto assets a warm reception.

This less than welcoming embrace is not as bizarre as it might initially appear. After all, nations and private sector organizations are continuously competing to develop the next stage in technology tools and applications (Business Insider Intelligence 2020). When currency is involved, however, controlling the currency used within a nation is the key to the governing power of the political leaders in charge. Additionally, the power of a centralized governmental entity to impose and collect taxes, and in turn fund different programs and initiatives, is a crucial component of how a governing party maintains authority and legitimacy. In other words, the idea of blockchain and crypto asset technology strikes at the heart of how a country sustains itself, funds programs, and maintains the support of the governed. In that context, the fact that initial efforts to use crypto assets resulted in less than enthusiastic responses is not surprising.

The development of blockchain occurred to disrupt, disintermediate, and topple the current financial infrastructure. Specifically, a few different components of blockchain technology are connected and integral to every iteration of blockchain. Regardless of the version of blockchain being implemented or the use case that is being examined, the following components need to be part of the dialog and conversation.

Blockchain Consensus

Although the blockchain space may have initially been created as a permissionless model allowing individuals and institutions to conduct financial transactions, many other use cases have since been developed (Ahmadifar, Dahiya, Williams, and Williamson 2019). Yet, regardless of the specific blockchain being analyzed, several core components are associated with blockchain technology.

The tamper resistant nature of any information stored on the blockchain platform lies at the core of why organizations have sought to develop and implement blockchain-based applications. This tamper resistance is directly related to the consensus methodologies that are central to blockchain implementation, which is how information is added to previous blocks that are already on the blockchain.

Although many consensus methodologies exist, two of the most common methodologies are proof of work (PoW) and proof-of-state (PoS) (Wang, Thai, Hu, and Wang 2019).

  • PoW is a race between different full nodes that are attempting to verify transactions and blocks as they are added to the existing blockchain. After a full node obtains the solution to the math puzzle, other miners post this solution for verification. The most complex of consensus methodologies involving the completely random nature of which node is involved and the immutable nature of this methodology result in the PoW methodology being the safest way of securing blockchain-based information.
  • PoS consensus methodology represents a contrasting platform for how network members approve and subsequently add data to a blockchain platform. Instead of randomizing the validation of transactions and blocks based on computer processing power, the PoS process seeks to reward network members who are larger stakeholders in the network. Usually judged or evaluated based on the ownership percentage of a native token or coin, the higher percentage ownership controlled by a certain member correlates to the likelihood of that member being assigned the block validation process.

Although some experts and thought leaders may label this characteristic of blockchain as an immutable record of information, this characterization is not only incorrect but also can mislead participants seeking to benefit from an implementation. No system is completely immutable including blockchain-based systems. Furthermore, every blockchain is based around a consensus methodology through which information and data are added to the blockchain. Although specifics vary between blockchains, some sort of group-based requirement always exists to add information to a blockchain (Sharma 2018).

Besides the consensus methodology, every type of blockchain uses an encryption process to secure the information as it is added and stored from the blockchain. For example, the bitcoin blockchain uses the SHA-256 encryption methodology, which to date has proven to be immutable. No matter the encryption methodology used by a specific blockchain, any technology can be hacked.

After encrypting, securing, and storing information on the blockchain, another core component of blockchain technology is the near real-time distribution of information to network participants. Specifically, as network members add different blocks of information to the network, the newly updated record of blockchain is distributed to all of these different network members. Although the speed with which these transactions or blocks are added to the existing record varies depending on the blockchain itself and the consensus methodology employed, every network member is kept as up-to-date as any other network member.

Such variability in speed coupled with other technical issues related to developing and maintaining the blockchain has led some market participants to question the business use case of the technology. In essence, the question around the viability of blockchain platforms is usually centered around the complexity involving interoperability and the slower speed around transaction processing versus incumbent platforms. Besides these issues, the relatively straight forward considerations around cost can also lead many institutions to ask:Why use blockchain?

Why Blockchain

A common question involving blockchain is why this technology was necessary in the first place. To comprehend the answer requires understanding the initial use case of blockchain. The entire crypto asset ecosystem depends on the functionality of blockchain, whereas blockchain platforms need not use a cryptocurrency. Although this situation might seem similar to current database applications, understanding that blockchains and databases represent two distinct technologies is important (Schlapkohl 2019). Blockchain applications and platforms often use tokens or crypto assets, but can also be used to manage the storage and sharing of information among network members. Blockchain solves the current need of handling, storing, and transferring sensitive information among different entities without requiring an external third party. An examination of any industry reveals a similar structure no matter what industry or geographic region is analyzed. Data pass through a centralized and external third party before being stored or distributed to the intended recipients. The fact that a trusted third party has lied, and continued to lie, is at the core of virtually every data management system.

The centralization of information and data processing can be thought of as an inconvenience or nuisance in some markets, but in other areas of the world, this centralization can have devastating economic and societal consequences. Individuals, institutions, and entire sections of nations can be summarily removed or banned from engaging with a nation's financial infrastructure or even the global financial markets. This situation is something that any crypto asset would in theory be able to protect against. However, for any crypto asset to effectively operate on a global basis in a consistent manner requires some confidence that all can access these crypto assets. Despite various parties developing and issuing different crypto assets, different stakeholders require access to these assets. Centralizing the development and access to crypto assets may or may not improve the user experience, but it could lead to opportunities for abuse and other restrictive measures being enacted.

Regardless of the level of centralization or decentralization of a specific blockchain implementation, a blockchain seems to present a halfway point between existing options. Centralized data processes, platforms, and methodologies may be able to process data and transactions more rapidly than blockchains, but have fallen victim to hacks and breaches across numerous economic sectors. Despite that, having a single source of truth, and the ability to trust counterparties, via an intermediary, removes compliance and other mundane work performed by organizations. Decentralized data processing platforms, such as file sharing platforms, allow access by numerous parties that increases the flexibility of these platforms, but can also result in data integrity issues. Additionally, these copies can be located offline and online, resulting in no single source of truth. Blockchain seems to represent the best of both by combining the single record of truth created by a centralized system, while also distributing and decentralizing the data management process. This decentralization also means that addressing the issues connected to interoperability is critical to the continued growth of the sector (Macheel 2016). Understanding where blockchain fits among the spectrum of technology and data management options that currently exist and are used in the marketplace is key to comprehending the potential opportunities and challenges created by this technology.

Distilling the benefits of blockchain technology for business applications and the transfer of information between organizations brings several benefits to the forefront. The following discussion summarizes the benefits that are evident to business owners or entrepreneurs seeking to leverage crypto or blockchain for payments, or investors seeking to maximize returns.

  • Speed of transactions. The speed with which transactions, payments, and other transfers of information occur can be seen as a bit of a paradox. In traditional payment systems, the upfront transaction, purchase, or transfer happens much more quickly than on a blockchain-based platform. Conversely, blockchain-based or settled payments may take slightly longer to finalize at initial transfer/communication, but are finalized on a more timely basis.
  • Transparency. As digital information and data become more prevalent, whether connected to underlying blockchains or not, transparency and access to information on a continuous basis become increasingly important. In terms of individual and institutional adoption of blockchain/crypto, transparency can bring benefits to financial reporting, non-profit projects, governmental data, and the usage around intellectual property.
  • Cost. Improving transaction speed and transparency should lower costs for the organizations involved in the individual transfer of information. Savings related to blockchain initiatives are likely to vary among organizations, but can be connected to having access to information on a continuous basis, lower the amount of funds needed to be held in a correspondent banking institution, and result in fewer instances of rework, corrections, and other corrective actions.

Blockchains Importance in the Internet Age

The internet is arguably one of the most important innovations of the modern era. A major impact of this innovation is on the growth of e-commerce that affects virtually every aspect of the global economy. Alongside this rapid development and expansion of e-commerce was a retrenchment and reinforcement of the centralized or external third party model that has dominated the financial services space. Specific to the online or e-commerce environment is a concern over the so-called double-spending problem, which does not exist to the same extent for a physical currency. Double-spending is a potential flaw in a digital cash scheme enabling someone to spend the same single digital token more than once.

Here is a brief summary of the double-spending problem. In an online or digital environment, no physical custody or control exists over the equivalent of cash that is used to fuel the e-commerce sector. Without such a physical control or custody procedure in place around the digital version of currency, the following scenario can occur. An individual or merchant could simply copy the code that represents the financial value being transferred between individuals and merchants and use that same code repeatedly in a series of virtual transactions. Since no physical cash or currency units change hands, the virtual currency could soon become worthless without some sort of clearinghouse or equivalent to verify this value is only being exchanged once. Consider another example: if anyone could simply photocopy US currency on a copy machine, the currency's value would soon diminish dramatically.

After several attempts by major financial institutions in the United States and on an international basis, this underlying problem remained unresolved. Without some check and balance on the transfer of virtual currency, even the most promising virtual currency concept would not succeed. At the heart of the bitcoin blockchain was a mathematical proof that ensured that no unit of crypto (i.e., the native token and medium of exchange linked to the bitcoin blockchain) would be spent or used more than once. This breakthrough, detailed below, allowed individuals and/or merchants, to exchange value directly with one another without reliance on a third party or centralized clearinghouse. Separating the approval of transactions from the transactions themselves represented a breaking away from the traditional underpinnings of the financial system.

Of particular interest connecting blockchain and crypto assets to the online shopping and e-commerce space is the rise of stablecoins. The value of this marketplace in 2020 was over $10 billion (Di Maggio and Platias 2020). Organizations that have sought to facilitate P2P virtual transactions or the ability of individuals to conduct business with small and medium enterprises (SMEs), such as Venmo, Zelle, and Square, have experienced dramatic growth since introduction. The primary benefits associated with these applications are their lower costs, ease of use, mobile compatibility, and importantly for blockchain applications, a lack of trust and comfort among millennials and Gen-Z individuals with incumbent financial institutions. As blockchain and crypto continue to develop and mature alongside other P2P platforms, they stand to benefit over the medium to long term.

Different Models of Blockchain

Depending on the use case and application being discussed, differing types of blockchain may be more or less appropriate. A public/permissionless blockchain is a decentralized network that is not governed by any single entity or group of entities and is open to any individual or institution to join. The borderless and open source nature of such a blockchain is consistent with the ethos of many early blockchain proponents and serves as a potential democratizing force across industry lines. Such a model, however, also necessitates a more robust data approval and recording process, which can slow processing times. Due to these slower data and approval times, this original model of blockchain is not particularly suited to enterprise or commercial use. The bitcoin blockchain can be used as a relevant example of such a blockchain.

A private/permissioned blockchain is a hybrid between a public/permissionless model and a more traditional centralized data processing structure. Oftentimes organized and led by a single entity or a small group of entities, a private/permissioned blockchain can institute higher levels of controls and barriers to initial entry as well as what roles different members can exercise. The higher barriers to entry, increased controls that can be implemented, and greater degree of trust that results can lead to faster processing speeds that are more well suited to enterprise and commercial adoption. For contextual purposes, many of the largest enterprise adoptions to date have leveraged a private/permissioned model to launch blockchain initiatives.

A consortium blockchain represents a halfway point between a public/permissionless blockchain and a private/permissioned blockchain. Organized and governed by a group of entities, the controls, roles, and permissions granted to various network members can vary according to existing governance protocols. Implementing this type of blockchain model can benefit the organizing firms by enabling them to spread risk, cost, and potential liability. However, this joint governance model can raise issues linked to how the network and its members are managed on an operational basis. Specifically, these issues involve the processes by which members are added, how roles and obligations are assigned, and how members are potentially removed.

A consortium blockchain model, especially one composed of industry leading or large players in the specific economic sector, may generate an affiliated benefit. One factor limiting wider adoption is the lack of consistent and standardized regulatory frameworks in the blockchain and broader crypto asset space, specifically as they are connected to how these networks are governed and managed (Rikken, Janssen, Kwee, Bolívar, and Scholl 2019). A blockchain platform or framework that has the backing of large and influential organizations in the economic sector may be better able to have comprehensive conversations around regulatory standard setting that are necessary for wider adoption. Ironically, the regulators and incumbents that blockchain and crypto assets were intended to disrupt invariably play an important role in the maturation of blockchain and crypto assets.

The Promise of Blockchain

Blockchain has numerous applications and use cases that extend far beyond the bitcoin blockchain or only use cases connected to financial services. The idea of democratizing information, resources, and financial transactions away from centralized authorities or institutions is the realization of a longtime goal of libertarians and other fans of more limited government. The power of this democratizing process of information is difficult to overstate. Allowing any individual or institution to transact and exchange value with counterparties on a global basis represents a true paradigm shift.

Many different industry applications are potentially possible. Any industry or economic sector relying on the transfer of information among a large number of economic parties and organizations is a potential fit for implementing blockchain. Insurance, real estate, financial services and markets, accounting, logistics, food safety and transportation, and intellectual property are just a few of the economic sectors that can potentially benefit from increased blockchain integration. The publication of the Forbes Top 50 list, documenting the 50 largest organizations in the world that have integrated blockchain into business operations, is indicative at just how far ranging blockchain implementation has become. This listing, with associated commentary, is freely available and widely published on Forbes.com on an ongoing basis.

Like any other technology tool, blockchain is simply an amalgamation of technology tools and platforms that have been combined together. Blockchain is an evolving and fast moving space. Developing, implementing, and integrating technology tools within organizations is always a process, and the success or failure of any implementation depends on the education, training, and buy-in among the employees.

Obstacles to Blockchain Adoption

With every promise or opportunity invariably lies challenges to adoption that need to be addressed before mainstream adoption. Here are some obstacles to adopting blockchain and crypto. Cost and education routinely rank among the highest or most prominent reasons as to why blockchain implementation has stalled. Additional obstacles to wider adoption are interoperability and cybersecurity. These obstacles remain relevant for any iteration of blockchain, including permissionless, permissioned, consortium, or hybrid models.

Interoperability

Interoperability is the method by which technology systems communicate and interact with each other. The ability to communicate and interact among different technology systems is an imperative for any platform to achieve mass market adoption. Blockchain is not any different. Until a blockchain platform and its applications can communicate easily and seamlessly with other technology systems, the chance of achieving mass adoption is unlikely.

Any technology tool or application must be able to interoperate, or exchange information and data among the blockchain and existing technology platforms. Data uploaded or stored on a blockchain platform are unable to assist with the decision-making process if other existing technology systems cannot extract, analyze or otherwise used this information. Interoperability may seem like an abstract or technical topic, but the functional side of the interoperability conversation cannot be ignored. Specifically, any network members with appropriate levels of designated access must be able to access the data. Even with the continued investment and development of blockchain and blockchain-based applications, the ability of blockchain information to seamlessly interact with non-blockchain information remains a work in progress.

Cybersecurity

Cybersecurity must play an important role in the blockchain and crypto asset conversation. If individuals and institutions are to achieve mass utilization and adoption of blockchain technology, it must be safeguarded by some sort of backstop. Although some type of security platform or otherwise security-oriented platform is unnecessary, need exists for security, privacy, and the realization that both individuals and institutions want to use blockchain and crypto assets without the undue risk of losing financial assets (Tashea 2018). Although blockchain specific policies have yet to emerge in the marketplace, the ecosystem must evolve to satisfy customer and merchant needs. Given the lack of established blockchain and crypto asset specific insurance policies, this is not an idle risk. Some of the largest crypto asset exchanges in the world have been breached, and have either had to self-insure these losses to reimburse users (Binance) or to file for bankruptcy and close up shop. The continued lack of clarity and guidance around the cybersecurity and insurance provisions for blockchain and crypto assets represents an obstacle to adoption from either an institutional level or retail perspective.

Blockchain Implementation

A blockchain platform or service may provide a valuable service to specific individuals or organizations. Yet, to achieve mass market adoption, any blockchain application requires that a blockchain organization develop and implement protocols appropriate for that organization (Marsh 2019). Specifically, the organization must successfully address the interoperability issues that arise whenever introducing blockchain to the organization. Assessing the specific control and implementation issues is critical especially considering the wide array of blockchain iterations available. For example, if an entity wants to be paid in a cryptocurrency running on a specific blockchain, the entity should determine the risks associated with custody and liquidity of the digital asset, as well as specific controls around access and authorization to the crypto assets used within the transaction.

Depending on the specific type of information to be stored and shared on this blockchain, additional privacy and data management issues may need to be considered. For example, and even though the blockchain and crypto asset dialog had originally emerged and developed in the financial services space, applications and use cases continue to expand far beyond this original space. Healthcare, intellectual property, insurance claims, real estate information, and other types of personally identifiable information are increasingly becoming integrated with blockchain platforms. Internal controls, establishing appropriate workflows, and processes might not always be associated with blockchain and crypto assets, but they are integral to the continued development and expansion of blockchain applications and implementation.

Summary and Conclusions

Blockchain and crypto assets have increasingly moved from a fringe topic to the mainstream. A first step toward institutional adoption is for banks to offer crypto custodian services. In turn, taking this step is likely to push crypto assets into the spotlight, highlighting their benefits of speed, transparency, and low cost and leading to mass adoption. Yet, the applications and possibilities for blockchain technology far exceed simple banking or financial transactions. With each opportunity comes an array of challenges and obstacles that need to be addressed by incumbent actors and new entrants to the space.
