Chapter 3

Review of Blockchain and Emerging Applications

Timothy Grief and Ehsan Nikbakht

Keywords: Blockchain; supply chain; credit scoring; smart cities; cryptocurrencies; hybrid systems

Introduction

A blockchain is a decentralized public ledger that uses cryptography to record transactions among a network's participating agents. A network using public (permissionless) blockchain consists of specific agents, and each transaction must be verified by an agreement, in most cases, among the majority of the agents. Once the transaction is entered into the system, the data on the chain are permanently stored and cannot be erased. Additionally, the information should be accessed using private and public keys held by the agents of a specific network. Each agent is assigned a private key, which is the equivalent of a password, for the agent's own information. An agent is also assigned a public key, which is an address that enables the agent to access specific information, comparable to an access code. A fundamental concept of the technology is that a transaction within a marketplace where participating members verify the transactions is more secure as well as time- and cost-efficient than any alternative. Because blockchain can be used across multiple applications, its flexibility is a major feature and an advantage of this prominent platform.

Blockchain became an emerging technology in 2008, starting with the digital currency bitcoin. Although the technology is widely known for its association with cryptocurrency, various applications have the potential to change the business landscape. Blockchain technology is now revolutionizing the way that data are shared and how transactions are completed. This revolution is due to the technology's versatility and efficiency. Blockchains allow transactions to be traceable but also anonymous. Additionally, the technology can eliminate transaction costs while also increasing the accuracy of transactions. Not every blockchain including bitcoin transactions can be traced via IP addresses connected with computers running the nodes.

Nordgren and Weckstrom (2019) discuss the limitations of this technology and the challenges that private sectors, governments, and research centers face when implementing this technology. Yet, they conclude that as limitations including speed and computer power-intensive difficulties are overcome and more support comes from policymakers, no limits exist to the list of innovative applications for this technology. The purpose of this chapter is to review selected applications of blockchain.

Review of Blockchain and Emerging Applications

This section provides an overview of blockchain and the difference between permissionless versus permissioned platforms followed by a review of major emerging blockchain applications. To understand blockchain requires familiarity with its origins. Blockchain emerged with the creation of bitcoin, which started with SatoshiNakamoto's paper on a peer-to-peer (P2P) electronic system of payments (Nakamoto 2008). The basic premise of the P2P system is that it allows payments of coins to be sent between two parties without having a third party verify and mediate the transactions. A coin is defined as a chain of digital signatures with each coin being transferred from person to person in a transaction by signing a hash of another transaction as well as using a public key. By using a hash, words and numbers input are encrypted to improve security. The recipient verifies the signatures to receive the funds. A major issue with this premise is that it does not eliminate the common risk of the payer “double-spending.” Double-spending is a potential flaw in digital cash systems where the same coins can be spent twice, resulting in one party not receiving the coins.

A proposed solution to double-spending is using a timestamp server. The public private key functionality and hash IDs help to solve the double-spent issues and track the quantity in process. A timestamp server works by widely publishing a hash so that the data are verified to exist. A server does not publish a hash if no data exist because data are required to prove the need of the hash. The new hash contains the previous timestamp, which creates a chain verifying and proving each timestamp. Afterward, a proof-of-work (PoW) process, which is the authentication of the original algorithm, is applied to solve any concerns over fair majority decisions for transaction verifications. A majority decision (verification) is needed to ensure the PoW that the algorithm used is valid.

The technology is highly secure, as demonstrated by the fact that the probability of an attacker catching up to the chain exponentially diminishes upon each additional block being added. Therefore, attackers only have the potential to affect their own recent transactions; merely a self-transaction hack, which should not affect the rest of the chain. Majority decisions are represented by the longest chain, also meaning that they have the greatest PoW. Proof-of-work is a protective process that demands a high level of system accuracy and requires having participating agents in the network. Network agents are incentivized to participate by the fact that the initial transaction in a block creates new coins in a predetermined quantity as outlined in the original bitcoin whitepaper that decreases over time as the total quantity of bitcoin that has been mined increases. In the case of a public (permissionless) blockchain, a transaction fee might be included in the verification and posting of a new block. The creator owns the new coin, which is beneficial to the creator because it has value. This benefit (reward) is the economic rationale for the possible value for a bitcoin.

The need for blockchain may derive from the inefficiencies of the current systems, which primarily use financial institutions as the third party. Using financial institutions not only creates high transaction costs but also is subject to human error and limitations. Additionally, the blockchain can be more private despite being a public ledger: Privacy is achieved by keeping certain public keys anonymous. If the key is anonymous, the transaction can be seen by all except the sender and the recipient. The main reason blockchain technology has such potential is that it eliminates privacy concerns and transaction costs.

Understanding the main steps of a blockchain's functioning is critical. For example, in the case of funds transfer, a six-step process is required to get information or money from a first to a second party. The process begins with one party wanting to send money to someone else. The transaction is represented by a block and is broadcast to every party in the network; namely, creating a block and broadcasting to all parties constitute the second and third steps. During the fourth step, those within the network approve the transaction to validate it. The fifth step consists of adding the block to the chain, which provides an inexpugnable and transparent record of transactions. Lastly, during the sixth step, the second party receives the information or money.

The original purpose of the blockchain was to ensure credibility and avoid double-spending. A blockchain orders transactions in groups, which are called blocks, and these blocks are placed in chronological order. This system ensures credibility by enforcing a verification process where transactions must be verified by the majority of the network. A more complex process is in place to avoid double-spending. The blockchain eliminates the risk of double-spending by using onerous mathematical puzzles. A unique puzzle is assigned to each block. Each block is accepted into the blockchain as long as it contains the correct answer to the corresponding mathematical puzzle. Nodes complete these puzzles in roughly 10 minutes on the bitcoin blockchain to prove that they are using enough computing resources. This process is also known as PoW. Blockchain is becoming increasingly accepted because of the importance and speed of these processes in applications across different sectors, in particular in the financial and supply chain management. Yet, in some cases, certain permissionless networks such as bitcoins may suffer from speed in process and executions. Within industries such as financial services, infrastructure security, healthcare, and supply chain management, PoW and transaction verification could diminish costs while increasing speed and accuracy. The impact can be valuable enough to affect the success of companies and industries (Crosby, Nachiappan, Pattanayak, Verma, and Kalyanaraman 2016).

Since its introduction, blockchain technology has expanded far beyond payment transactions into corporate governance, agriculture, capital markets, and other disciplines. Many applications, in particular for trades, health care, and procurements, exist because of blockchain's many benefits and versatility. Benefits ranging from payment finality to timestamps with permanent data are part of the economic justification for this technology to be used across different industries and for different purposes.

Aside from the historical background, understanding the main principles of the technology is also important. Four common principles of blockchain are (1) payment finality, (2) computational problem solving, (3) hash functions, and (4) proof-of-work (PoW)/proof-of-stake (PoS).

  • Payment finality is a feature of the technology that demands transactions to be final and disallows for transactions to be reverted.
  • Computational problem solving is the process completed by a node that must be done in order to create a new block. In the case of blockchains that rely on coins, creating a block also creates a coin (asset), and whoever created the block owns the new asset. This creates competition within crypto-economies because it allows money to be created and earned by a mining (verification algorithm) process. Although the blockchain is widely known for its application to cryptocurrencies, the true essence of the technology is informational.
  • Hashes are an integral part of blockchain because they represent all of the information entered during all transactions. The common functions of blockchain, such as recording data and verifying transactions, are used to accelerate data lookup, and the blockchain achieves the lookup by using a mathematical algorithm to convert an input into an output.
  • PoW is needed to create new blocks, and a well-known alternative to it is PoS. PoS has major advantages because the protocols divide the stake blocks proportionally to the miner's wealth. This process decreases the likelihood of the block being attacked and can lead to faster blockchains.

Besides knowing the principles of blockchain, recognizing the differences among public, private, and hybrid blockchains is also important. A public blockchain is a decentralized ledger that is accessible to any user. These chains rely on a PoW/PoS mechanism for validation purposes. Private ledgers, on the other hand, are much more complex. Private ledgers' security depends on permissions, which are monitored and restricted by “write-permissions” and “read-permissions.” Private ledgers are not decentralized and are invitation-only networks that are governed by a single entity. Organizations can use private blockchains to employ distributed ledger technology while keeping the data private. Examples of public and private blockchains are bitcoins and electronic funds transfer (EFT), respectively. A blockchain can also be partially private by only displaying certain information to the public and requiring a private key to access the other information. This type of blockchain is referred to as a hybrid blockchain (Pilkington 2016). Table 3.1 provides a summary comparison between the two main types of blockchain: public and private.

Table 3.1. Differences between Public and Private Blockchains.

Characteristic Public Private
Access Open read/write Pre-approved members only
Transaction creation Anyone Members only
Transaction speed Slower due to scalability Faster
Security PoW/PoS Pre-approved participants
Identity Anonymous/pseudonymous Known identities
Asset Native assets Any asset
Energy High consumption Low consumption

Note: This table displays the main differences for each characteristic between public and private blockchains.

Credit Scoring

Since 2019, an emerging application of blockchain has focused on in the restructuring of the credit reporting industry. In the United States, three major credit bureaus are available ‒ Equifax, Experian, and TransUnion. In 2018, they earned more than $10 billion in revenue (IBISWorld 2019). Although millions of end users and customers use these three bureaus, many issues and risks are associated with them. Legal regulators have improved some of the issues, but limitations still exist. The bureaus collect and store vast amounts of sensitive data, but they do not update records immediately and occasionally have records that appear for the wrong individuals, have differing information, have no access to foreign credit information, and can be breached as publicly reported for the Equifax in 2017. These daunting issues can be solved or minimized with blockchain. For example, a possible solution for the problems with credit bureaus is eliminating the current bureaus altogether. Instead of relying on these agencies, blockchains that depend on smart contracts, which are self-executing between the parties, could be used throughout the lending process and replace the bureaus. This approach may eliminate all the costs and could protect the sensitive data using cryptography.

For credit scoring and credit reporting, using smart contracts to dictate the information in a blockchain and eliminate the third parties could enhance efficiency. Specifically, hash functions update information instantaneously, and the information is guaranteed to be correct because it needs to be verified by the entire network and proved valid by sequentially computed nodes (Goharshady, Behrouz, and Chatterjee 2018).

Credit scoring and financial reporting rely heavily on the data received. As data continue to increase both in frequency and volume, these data become a pivotal asset for business operations. Companies buy and sell data because they can use the information to learn about their targets, existing and potential customers, and interests. A way to maximize data sharing is to use blockchain and artificial intelligence (AI) to create a protected platform that can provide information instantaneously often called just-in-time (JIT) data. JIT data sharing involves considerable opportunities and potential risks across multiple sectors, including financial services healthcare and public sectors. The opportunities are the attractive aspect of data sharing in trusted data marketplaces. Trusted data marketplaces are essential for a safe and protected ecosystem among data consumers and providers. Otherwise, the ecosystems depend on a centralized system, a trusted third party, and various sets of terms and conditions including privacy policies. A trusted data marketplace must ensure full control over data with strong and implemented policies (Roman and Stefano 2016). Blockchain and smart contracts can be used to create a trusted ecosystem because of the wide-ranging data sharing that stakeholders control. Additionally, integrating this technology protects and guarantees data by eliminating a “middle man” and verifying the transactions of data. In this use of data sharing and collecting data, blockchain and smart contracts can provide specifically requested information and use analytic algorithms to sort and retrieve the data. The analytic algorithms give credit providers a holistic picture of a borrower's background. The development of various analytic algorithms to comprehensively and permanently store the data is a major transformation, considering that present-day credit risk assessments do not consider a borrower's entire background, primarily because gathering the data would be too costly and time-consuming. Having a more comprehensive system of credit scoring using blockchains when combined with logistic regressions or expert systems is of economic value added because it allows more borrowers to have access to credit. It also reduces the gap between borrowers with a well-established versus little credit history, increases information flow, and decreases the information asymmetry for credit, which ultimately enhances financial inclusion.

As credit scoring has become increasingly prevalent with expeditious improvements, AI technologies have been used to mitigate preeminent risks with sharing information among all parties both at individual and institutional levels. The emergence of AI in the credit scoring industry was the result of rapid growth and the need for progress within the credit industry. Various advanced technologies use algorithms that can enhance performance, including support vector machines (SVMs), artificial neural networks (ANNs), genetic algorithms (GA), and genetic programming (GP).

The SVMs are among the most useful AI technologies because they have been widely adopted and helped solve classification issues along with high-dimensional problems. Algorithms that solve issues, such as SVMs, ensure optimized results by categorizing data in a high-dimensional feature space. Once data are categorized, these data can easily be accessed and used. The ANN is a concept that was built off of the structure and functioning of the human brain. An ANN system has many interconnected processing elements, which allow the system to solve complex problems. Other technologies, such as the GA and GP, work to optimize systems by reducing redundancies, which increase the accuracy and quality of the decisions made (Chen, Zen, and Lin 2014).

Blockchain and AI have revolutionized credit scoring. Along with other statistical methods such as discriminant analysis and logistic regressions, they are now among the most commonly used techniques for credit scoring. Credit scoring uses historical data, but how the data are gathered and used to modify the end result. The concept of hybridizing AI with logistic regression emerged in an attempt to maintain a much-needed high level of accuracy. The first use of logistic regression model was to analyze the probability of bankruptcy, and it eventually became common practice for credit scoring. This approach, however, is limiting because it fails to incorporate appropriate assumptions such as the normal distribution of the data. Logistic regressions suffer from unrealistic assumptions, which prompted a need for improvement and led to using AI. AI techniques combined with logistic regressions relaxed the assumptions and substantially improved the interpretability of variables. A known source of risk is “dimensional interference” because additional data dimensions increase the potential of inaccuracies and difficult interpretability. Hybridizing AI and logistic regression when used together reduce the data dimensions and thus increase accuracy (Lu, Liyan, and Hongwei 2013).

Managing Water Usage during Climate Change

Climate change is one of the major pressing issues in the world today. As often reported through various public media, both the temperature levels and the frequency of precipitation and heat-trapping gas emissions are increasing. More droughts, heat waves, and natural disasters are occurring and sea levels are rising. Researchers attempt to combat climate change using many methods. Identifying the root problem is a first step in helping to solve the existing and potential problems and verifying the information used to assure that it is correct and disseminated accurately. Blockchain can be used to ensure the fidelity of data collection and the security and verification of data. AI can also be used to accelerate the discovery of complex patterns. Once the data are correct and organized, and researchers are aware of complex patterns, they can try to combat the issues in a more focused and systematic manner. At the very least, integrating these technologies for the efficient optimization and verification of data on water use can allow scientists to identify and define issues quicker.

Verified and organized data can better represent the impact that climate change has on multi-scale water availability and provide more accurate reports on global water scarcity. Once complex patterns and problems are discovered, scientists can begin to understand the patterns and help solve concerning issues. Optimizing data are critical, especially regarding the environment (Lin, Petway, Lien, and Settele 2018).

Managing Food Supply

Supply chains ‒ the flow of goods and services ‒ are complex systems with numerous stakeholders. A major issue among supply chains is information asymmetry. This issue is particularly important for food supply chains due to the fact that it could lead to food fraud, which can place people, farmers, and retailers at risk.

Using blockchain in supply chain systems ensures all data are symmetrical and provide food safety. Specifically, blockchain-based evaluation systems can improve the effectiveness of supervision and management in the food supply chain. All data are gathered using smart contracts and are then used in the decision-making process. Since the data are in a cumulative blockchain sequence, no omissions, redundancies, or inaccuracies exist. All stakeholders in the food supply chain are aware of the currently limited traceability, supervision, and management regarding traders, which is why the notion of implementing a blockchain is both feasible and necessary (Mao, Wang, Hao, and Li 2018).

Another revolutionary process for supply chains that blockchain technology can introduce is using support vector machines, which are learning models using machine learning, for sentiment analysis. Sentiment analysis identifies, organizes, and extracts sentiments from texts, which is particularly beneficial for food supply chains because it can verify the consumers and producers who must be trusted. Machine learning such as a long short-term memory (LSTM) network can be used for sentiment analysis because of the numerous advantages it provides. LSTM is a unique architecture for a neural network and provides a high accuracy rate. These networks are machine learning and are used to act as an artificial brain using data to make intelligent decisions. Sentiment analysis aids with decision-making regarding food supply chains because it provides a more complete background of the customer. Such backgrounds are imperative in the case of food supply chains because food can be damaged, harmed, or poisoned. Thus, awareness by both buyers and sellers can mitigate the overall risk.

Sharing Services: Contributing to Smart Cities

As the global population, especially the urban population, has increased, living conditions have become more challenging including communication and access to resources. This change has brought about the emergence of smart cities. A smart city relies on innovation and technology to have something unique to offer, such as introducing smart parking or blockchain and AI into city life including the healthcare industry. Integrating technology across entire cities may improve performance simply by providing immediate and accurate information. The concept of sharing services and resources is an opportunity for blockchain technology to be implemented and for blockchain experts and policymakers to consider.

A triangle framework including humans, technologies, and organizations identifies the attributes of the sharing economy of a smart city, which may create a synergistic value added in terms of reducing costs and better access to resources. Blockchain increases the accessibility and availability of technology, which makes people willing to accept access over ownership and to trust organizations and technology.

Blockchain-based sharing services in smart cities are unique in that they relate mostly to the relations between technologies. The first step of implementing the triangular framework consists of eliminating intermediaries, which reduces trust issues between individuals and organizations. This step not only alleviates, if not eliminates, the common problem of trust throughout business, but also contributes to minimizing the cost of intermediaries (Sun, Yan, and Zhang 2016).

Real-time Accounting and Credit-risk Modeling

Accounting is a robust and systematic industry upon which many individuals, investors, and companies rely. Trusting a systematic approach can often be troublesome due to manipulated financial data, required reporting times, and different accounting practices such as “first-in, first out” (FIFO) and “last-in, first out” (LIFO) inventory valuation. Historically, companies have manipulated certain methods of reporting financial data to make the company ostensibly appear more attractive or profitable. Such manipulation, such as using a valuation method to artificially inflate the net income and earnings per share, may create a moral hazard and mislead stakeholders including employees, investors, and consumers. Aside from the potential for fraud, the mandatory reporting of publicly held corporations gives a three-month lag on information because of the quarterly reporting requirement. Additionally, FIFO and LIFO practices determine the cost of goods sold per unit and cost of inventory based on a firm's operations, which appear on the income statement and potentially sway the views of investors.

These issues, however, can be solved or managed with the integration of blockchain technology. Once integrated, accounting happens in real time. Because it requires a higher level of accuracy, the impacts of different practices may not be as harsh, and each entity's current financial standing can be seen at all times. Also, for financial accounting reports and corporate governance, an opportunity exists for blockchain to facilitate the process and communication among stakeholders (Yermack 2017).

The basic premise of real-time accounting is that the entirety of a company's financial profile can be public or private and automatically be recalculated after each transaction. This sequential automatic recalculation allows investors and businesspeople to have immediate access to this important information, which can be reason enough for adopting it. This improvement may also help asset valuation including both equity and fixed income, which heavily relies on the accuracy and availability of data. A blockchain system, if implemented properly, ensures accuracy and data protection, which is appealing to the accounting industry.

Using blockchain could increase efficiency not only in the accounting industry but also in capital markets. The volatility of publicly traded stocks might not be artificially influenced if people always had access to a company's current financial standing. Facilitating access to data may lead to a reduction in speculative short sales, stock price manipulation, and sell-outs.

Blockchain technology could also drastically improve credit-risk modeling. The reason is that most credit-risk modeling heavily relies on accounting information contained in financial statements. Once blockchain is integrated and those statements are all updated in real time, an increase in transparency and accuracy should occur. Since public companies are required to report quarterly, risk measures currently cannot be observed more than once every three months. Although quarterly reporting in itself is not a problem, credit-risk modeling could still be improved with more frequent risk measures.

Even the common credit-risk models including the Merton model and the Altman Z-score can be improved through blockchain technology. In their simplest forms, these models use variables taken directly from financial statements and are run to predict a company's probability of insolvency (Altman 1968; Merton 1974). Up-to-date income statements and balance sheets would ensure that the credit-risk model provides the most accurate answer since the models can use current variables and provide predictions with the data with greater certainty. If the variables lag behind or the data are improperly collected, the results become biased (Bystrom 2016). For future research, the authors believe a potential for using blockchain in extending the above classic credit models.

Blockchain for Sustainable Development

Since the financial crisis of 2007–2008, the financial industry has required both regulation and reform, specifically Dodd-Frank and Basel Agreements. Many investors, consumers, and banks were left in disarray due to banks having too much freedom including the use of their internally developed models to measure capital adequacy and liquidity requirements. After the market collapsed and the crisis ended in 2009, the markets gradually recovered with each passing year. The crisis is a reason consumers and investors felt uneasy and unprotected and became skeptical of banks. Because of its potential for efficiency and transparency, blockchain has the ability to benefit all stakeholders and society at large. Blockchain can be pivotal in this application because it can protect consumers and banks more efficiently than regulations can. Blockchain can help to reshape the economy by providing faster and cheaper financial services while offering greater transparency for consumers. Additionally, the digitization and verification of data and transactions reduce the number of procedures and guarantee correct transactions. Lastly, information is recorded automatically and instantly, which benefits both consumers and the financial services industry (Nguyen 2016).

Business Process Improvement

Many governments, major banks, and other Fortune 500 companies have begun to research how to implement blockchain technology in their operations, examples of which appear in the annual Forbes Blockchain 50 listing. Blockchain can be used in many different ways because of smart contracts. For example, some companies may use blockchain for simpler purposes such as data sharing while others may use it for more complex purposes such as payment systems with custom payouts.

Companies across all industries have been actively seeking blockchain-based systems to adopt in order to improve their business processes. The best way to evaluate a business process is to analyze the value that the process adds to the company because systems that only increase speed are not always as beneficial as expected. However, blockchain can increase speed, lower costs, and enable companies to focus on growth with the capital saved from integrating blockchain technology.

In the case of supply chains using blockchain-based technology, the technology tracks goods and materials to prevent both counterfeit and low-quality products. Other industries could experience similar benefits preventing erroneous and outdated information. With the accuracy of data ensured, the next concern is the flexibility of the technology and how the data can be used. Blockchain technology uses smart contracts that execute specific activities as defined in the conditions of the contract. This feature allows the technology to conduct most processes and secure them regardless of the requested activities (Milani, Garcia-Banulos, and Dumas 2018).

Blockchain and the Healthcare Industry

Healthcare is the fifth largest industry in the United States worth $124.4 trillion in 2019, shortly behind financial services at $126.1 trillion in 2019 (Largest.org 2019). The industry includes the generalization and commercialization of goods and services to treat all types of patients. Healthcare is also one of the most regulated industries since it directly relates to human well-being. Regulation is not the only challenge in the healthcare industry. Other challenges include intellectual property, patient data privacy, data sharing between hospitals, multiple intermediaries, and a lack of transparency to consumers. The healthcare industry is progressive, with high-level technology and was among the first to adopt blockchain-based systems. An example includes the delivery and tracking medicine delivery through blockchain. The technology is under consideration by a various online pharmacy companies including some start-ups in different phases such as Capsule with an ambition of becoming the Amazon of the pharmacy industry. Post COVID-19 crisis, this trend is expected to accelerate to help alleviate the delivery problem of medicine especially during a crisis.

The management of healthcare data also includes other aspects such as storage, access, and sharing information. Additionally, data in the healthcare industry are held to a high standard of privacy, as confidentiality is integral to the industry. If data are managed well and properly, patients should receive more accurate and comprehensive treatment. A way to maintain well-managed healthcare data is possibly to integrate blockchain into healthcare companies' systems, such as health information exchanges (HIE).

Vital projects in healthcare today are blockchain-based systems called HIE. The HIE projects focus on electronic health records (EHR) and various medical specialties. Some projects already use a verifiable data exchange process. The HIE initiatives being used for exchanging data show that the technology can serve multiple purposes in the healthcare industry. With systems that increase speed and data quality, companies may discover and develop new drugs faster and cheaper. Intellectual property management, clinical trials, and supply chains can also be improved. Intellectual property management can benefit from digital process with timestamps, which keep track of patents. Innovations based on blockchain may improve clinical trials by providing data integrity and enabling quick advances in the development process. Therefore, integrating blockchain technology into supply chains is imperative for maintaining optimal and intended usage of the drugs produced. Blockchain corrects and expedites all of the major processes within the industry. Besides these benefits, blockchain-as-a-service (BaaS), which allows businesses to use cloud-based solutions to build apps, contracts, and functions, can maximize competence in prescription management, billing claims management, telemedicine, and analytics consulting (Katuwal, Pandey, Hennessey, and Lamichhane 2018).

Blockchain technology and AI are both robust and, when converged, facilitate progress, and create a synergetic effect. A major progression of the technology is transfer learning, which is especially beneficial to healthcare because it is a time-sensitive industry. Many relevant algorithms require vast amounts of data for inter-domain training/learning, which is why companies use transfer learning. Transfer learning is a process of transferring information learned from one domain or dataset to another. This method of learning is implemented to mitigate the time required to build a system capable of mastering the activities demanded and to achieve high accuracy. For example, an important use of converging the technologies is to improve biomedical research. Decentralizing and accelerating research in healthcare can be transformative because of the rapid improvements it brings and the control it gives to patients. Currently, patients do not have full control over their medical records and may not be aware of the value that the data hold. By decentralizing healthcare, patients would have access to privileges about their own records, which they could then monetize if they choose to do so. Such monetization can be done by patients selling their own personal medical records the way the hospitals currently do.

Advanced technologies such as blockchain and AI have generated developments in deep learning, which imitates the functions of the human brain to process data and creates patterns for decision-making. This has resulted in more clear and accurate image/text generation in the medical field. More accurate imaging can result in better treatments for patients. Additionally, the convergence of the two technologies gives clinicians a better perception of a patient's clinical history due to all the data gathered. With a better understanding of clinical history, clinicians can help identify an individual risk profile of developing chronic conditions (Mamoshina et al. 2017).

Currently, major limitations exist in supply chain management in the healthcare industry. The limitations are obstacles and risks, which must be accounted for to prevent delays, fraud, and inefficiencies. A reasonable means to identify these obstacles and to advance security, integrity, and functionality is to conduct a feasibility study for using blockchain technology in the healthcare industry. Implementing the technology can prevent and decrease the risk of wrong and/or inefficient delivery of medicines to consumers both at domestic and global levels. Such implementation is done by ensuring that the data from each transaction is correct and not altered in any way.

The most pressing reason for adopting blockchain technology in the health supply chain is the intrusion of subpar and falsified medicines, which affects organizations and patients alike. The US Food and Drug Administration notes and tracks where subpar medicines are sent, and reports that falsified medicines occur in both high- and low-income areas.

Implementing blockchain for supply chain management in healthcare can be achieved by having key requirements such as identification, tracing, and verification. The technology would function similarly to how it does elsewhere by having unique identifiers, allowing manufacturers and distributors to provide tracing information, and creating an open solution system to verify products. This process may directly result in better medicines and data being passed between buyers and suppliers (Clauson, Breeden, Davidson, and Mackey 2018).

Electronic medical sharing is an aspect of blockchain that may improve the quality of the healthcare industry. Medical record sharing is highly sensitive and demands security and trust, which is why blockchain could be a viable solution for it. Using blockchain allows hospitals and doctors to maintain sequential cumulative histories of treatment processes for every patient permanently and accurately. The medical histories of patients may play an instrumental role in the treatment process because they allow for a more holistic process as clinicians can make decisions based on a patient's background. Also, data can be protected in a private blockchain that contains a patient's entire file. This file can then be shared between doctors and hospitals by including the different users in the network and providing them with the appropriate keys for access. Additionally, the data may be shared by way of a cloud server to patients, specialists, hospitals, pharmacies, insurance companies, or biobanks. Sharing data among these stakeholders reduces costs, time requirements, and the risk of possible omission and commission errors (Dubovitskaya, Xu, Ryu, Schumacher, and Wang 2017).

Fraud Detection Using Blockchain Technology

The internet poses many risks to users, especially during transactions with anonymous users. These risks include, but are not limited to, identity theft, data loss, hacking, and credit card fraud. This situation creates a need for reputation systems, which are systems that aggregate and distribute feedback on different entities. The systems evaluate the users' reputation based on past transactions and behaviors. The evaluations consist of two types of measurements: computational and non-computational. A non-computational rating is assigned based on the user's activities, whereas a computational rating is assigned numerically. This assignment is done to have a holistic evaluation of users. Additionally, the computational ratings include a content analysis of the aggregated information.

Since rating systems rely heavily on aggregated historical information from many users, blockchain could potentially increase the speed and accuracy of these systems. A particular benefit of integrating blockchain into rating systems is the prevalence of privacy. When rating systems have more privacy, users are more inclined to provide information. Having greater privacy results in more information being available to analyze a user, which in turn could prevent fraud. The information in and the accuracy of these systems is imperative in preventing fraudulent users on the internet. Thus, these systems protect consumers, mitigate losses, bolster consumer confidence, and boost sales (Cai and Zhu 2016).

Predicating Customer Default in E-commerce

E-commerce has been growing year after year. In 2018, e-commerce sales grew by 13.6%, and in 2019 they grew by 14.9% (Digital Commerce 360 2020). With the rapid growth of the industry, a need exists for customer default prevention. Without prevention, the volume of defaulted payments would likely surge, and the system's integrity would be in jeopardy. A potential solution is to apply blockchain technology and AI to facilitate risk management for e-commerce. Although preventing retail defaults can be challenging, a system that predicts payment defaults based on a framework using AI as a secondary verification in the system could greatly improve the process. The framework suggests that a system called genetic programming (GP) is intuitive enough to automatically focus on specific features while continuing to learn the model. GP is a technique that uses a population of computer programs to create a new and improved program. The population consists of a stochastic variation, which along with specified criteria for solutions is how the program constantly improves. This ability gives the model a predictive power that can more accurately classify customers or applicants rather than simply classify them as “good” or “bad.” The model creates a complete ranking of all customers and generates a GP score for each. The score, however, is not a probability, so to be useful in mitigating risk, it must be converted to a probability through a process called “calibration.” GP provides the most competitive classificatory accuracy, which it achieves using logistic regression and support vector machines. In practice, using these machine-learning methods can more accurately determine which customers are reliable. Using systems to increase readiness for defaults and dealing with defaults with default prevention are important because of the rapid growth of e-commerce and the difficulty of maintaining the scalability of payment defaults (Vanneschi, Horn, Castelli, and Popovic 2018).

Blockchain as a Tool to Break the Poverty Chain

As a distributed ledger technology, blockchain may be able to reshape the world in the near future because of the drastic impacts the technology can have on politics, society, and the economy. All three areas can benefit from crucial improvements with speed and accuracy. The high expectations for how blockchains can specifically affect society at large raise questions about their potential to solve political, societal, and economic issues at various levels. The emerging technology has the potential to break poverty chains and improve the socioeconomic status of the countries using the technology.

Blockchain offers countries the potential of using the technology as a tool to help break the poverty chain and contribute to improving the Global South, which is a term used by the World Bank to refer to relatively lower- and middle-income countries located in Asia, Africa, Latin America, and the Caribbean due to the region's underdevelopment and poor political climate. The most interesting potential for integrating blockchain-based platforms involves the ability to reduce corruption and fraud. This issue is particularly relevant for the Global South because of the impact that corruption and fraud can have on the donors. Currently, donations to the Global South are often stolen or lost, which diminish the prospective donors' trust and the ability of the authorities in the Global South to use the funds for improvement. In the absence of corruption and fraud, donors are more likely to trust that their funds are being received and thus may donate and allocate more funds to the good causes. Additionally, increasing the speed and decreasing the costs for transactions, many enable the Global South to have better international relations. Blockchain-based platforms are expected to have a distinct impact, encouraging premier technology companies to devote more time and effort to creating platforms that can improve their systems including holding and organizing property records through blockchain. These possible but far reaching and challenging blockchain applications could break poverty chains and improve economies across the globe (Kshetri 2017).

Summary and Conclusions

This chapter reviews some applications of blockchain technology that currently are in different phases of development. Some are more established as they have passed the pilot tests for application of blockchain in their businesses including companies in the financial sector, accounting and auditing, and supply management. Although promising, other sectors are still relatively new to this emerging technology including smart cities, healthcare, sustainable developments, fraud prevention, JIT public data sharing, poverty chain management, water distribution, and waste management. For full-blown implementation in public and private blockchain platforms, obstacles are numerous; yet the potential reward is substantial. Researchers in academia and industry have great opportunities to explore and conduct various analysis of the strengths, weaknesses, opportunities and threats (SWOT analysis) for various industries as potential domains of innovative blockchain application both at domestic and global levels.

Chapter 4

Technical Aspects of Blockchain

Hak J. Kim

Keywords: Blockchain cryptography; distributed ledger; technical algorithms; Proof of Work; Proof of Stake; block; immutability; cryptographic hashing

Introduction

The creation of the internet with an open network architecture occurred in 1972 allowing the public to access all the interconnected networks (Leiner et al. 1997). The number of internet users has grown dramatically during the past several decades (Warf 2013). However, the internet today has become a playground for hackers to steal data and breach systems ( The Economist 2019). Internet users are worried about data breaches by cyberattacks because of its unreliable network architecture and security. Securing the internet is not optional, but necessary for communication and sharing data (Abbosh and Bissel 2019).

Many people know bitcoin as a cryptocurrency, but are unfamiliar with blockchain. Some market participants mistakenly believe that any blockchain is simply a kind of bitcoin. Blockchain is a distributed ledger to store transactions data on distributed computers (Brakeville and Perepa 2019). It collects transactions into blocks, records cryptographically secured blocks in the ledger in chronological order, and allows participants to access the resulting ledger (i.e., nodes).

Blockchain networks are primarily decentralized in nature to prevent a single point of failure and create a more resilient network (Anderson 2019). For secure data transmission, the blockchain network introduces cryptographic algorithm which is a technique to alter data from plaintext to ciphertext in a peer-to-peer (P2P) network (Li, Jiang, and Bertino 2019). The network relies on many discrete computers to provide trust or security. These computers are anonymous entities. They cannot alter data stored within the blockchain systems. For example, if one entity attempts to change the content of a block, all of the following blocks would need to be changed as well. Thus, no single entity can tamper with the records because transparency keeps all participants honest. However, if a certain amount of them (i.e., the 51% rule in bitcoin) are compromised, data stored in a blockchain system become mutable.

This chapter consists of the following sections. The first section presents a technical overview of blockchain, including concepts and key properties such as decentralization and immutability. The second section explains the architecture of blockchain with its integral elements, such as a block, node, and miner. The third section introduces key blockchain technologies: cryptographic hashing, Merkle hash tree and root, distributed ledger, and consensus algorithms, such as Proof of Work (PoW) and Proof of Stake (PoS). The fourth section describes the blockchain mechanism and technical challenges. The fifth section provides a summary and conclusions.

Overview of Blockchain

Blockchain has received much attention in technology and business over the last several years. However, some organizations are reluctant to introduce blockchain technology because of its technical complexity and disruptive nature. So, a comprehensive technical understanding of blockchain is needed for its broad acceptance in business. Before jumping into the depths of blockchain technologies, this section offers an overview its concepts, types, and properties.

Concepts

According to Crosby, Nachiappan, Pattanayak, Verma, and Kalyanaraman (2016), blockchain is a distributed ledger that records everything happening in a chronological timeline. The information stored in the ledger is distributed through a P2P (Brakeville and Perepa 2019). Each network participant has a copy of the ledger's data that is distributed through a network. All participants in a transaction have access to the same real-time ledger. Any member can track the history of all transactions that are maintained by many nodes permanently (Deloitte 2016). The blockchain network is dynamic and keeps growing with the increasing number of transactions. Blockchain effectively removes the step of establishing trust between each party through a distributed ledger and cryptographic encryption. It also allows transparency between all participants in the transactions. Blockchain uses cryptographic hashes to create a sequential chain of permanent records that are all linked. Since the ledgers are distributed across a network and are dependent upon cryptographic hashes, the integrity of the transactions is secure (Brakeville and Perepa 2019).

Fig. 4.1 shows an example of the blockchain process. Each block maintains a hash, which is copied from the previous block as shown in the bold black box. It is a kind of chain from past blocks to the most current blocks. Modification in the blockchain is cumbersome and impractical because one change in a block requires changing each subsequent block.

Fig. 4.1. An Example of a Blockchain Process. Note: This figure shows a basic blockchain process about how to build a chain between blocks using hashes. Source: Brownworth 2019 (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=_160oMzblY8).

Types of Blockchain Networks

The two general categories of blockchain networks are public (permissionless) and private (permissioned) (Sharma 2019). As its name implies, a public blockchain network is open to the public, meaning anyone can join and validate transactions. Participants can be traced through network analysis, but tracking asset ownership is difficult. The public blockchain network is generally considered to be trustless, which means that participants need not trust each other, so it requires consensus (e.g., PoW) within the network and gives some incentives to participate (e.g., cryptocurrency). A preagreed upon methodology determines consensus. Since a public blockchain is permissionless, anyone with access to the ledger can see any transaction on it (Jayachandran 2017). The ledger is encrypted, so only participants can see it. Each transaction is also encrypted, so only those with a need to know can decrypt.

A private blockchain network is limited to a defined set of participants. For example, it may be only for specific people in a business network who have a membership. So, a private blockchain network is a permissioned blockchain. For example, a private blockchain requires an invitation to join, and a single entity or consortium must validate new members (Jayachandran 2017). The organizing firm or firms determine the consensus methodology to be used. Since the ledger is partitioned into isolated subsets of participants, a few selected participants can access the ledger and send transactions.

Key Properties of Blockchain

Blockchain provides trust in transactions through distributed databases and cryptographic algorithms to ensure data integrity in the network. It is composed of the chain of data blocks by cryptographic hashing and consensus algorithm. So, the two key properties of blockchain are decentralization and immutability.

Decentralization

A blockchain network is designed as a decentralized system (Anderson 2019), where computers on the network maintain a distributed database to share with all participants. Anyone can join as a node and then have a ledger for storing blocks of information, which is the validated record of all transactions. Hence, a blockchain is also referred to as a distributed ledger.

Since a blockchain network is distributed in nature (Rosic 2017), no single hardware infrastructure or master computer is available to manage the entire network. Each computer contains some blocks in the distributed database, but these blocks are grouped together in a P2P network. Thus, no single authority approves transactions or sets a rule to have transactions accepted in the blockchain network (Banafa 2019). Consequently, all participants are mandated to reach a consensus to approve transactions and create blocks. The decentralization property of blockchain makes blocks recovery easier and faster because blocks are stored at multiple locations. Decentralization also enables a participant to have access to information even when a system on the network shuts down.

Immutability

A blockchain network is designed to be immutable (Tasca and Tessone 2019). It helps to prevent unauthorized access of data because an attacker has to manipulate every single piece of the information on the blockchain (Patel 2018). Immutability is similar to tamper resistance in that blockchain data are difficult to alter or modify due to every chain being different. When transactions are entered in the blockchain network, they are automatically saved in chronological order, which makes tracing historical transactions for auditing or investigations easier, and the blockchain network is maintained through a P2P network. Every node can have different privileges and rights on the network, but the ability to read past information is available to every network node.

Architecture of Blockchain Network

Fig. 4.2 shows the architecture of blockchain network. The three key elements of blockchain network are a block, node, and miner.

Fig. 4.2. Architecture of a Blockchain Network. Note: This figure shows the structure of a blockchain network and its key components such as nodes, blocks, and miners.

Block

A block is the basis of the blockchain network (Frankenfield 2020a), which contains a set of transactions created during a period of time. Once a block is completed and approved, it is permanently recorded in the ledger. Fig. 4.3 shows the structure of a block, which consists of a header and data.

Fig. 4.3. Structure of a Block. Note: This figure shows the elements of a block's header such as version, timestamp, nonce, difficulty target, previous hash, and Merkle root.

The elements of header are version, timestamp, difficulty target, nonce, previous hash, and Merkle root (Ghosh, Gupta, Dua, and Kumar 2020).

  • Version is used to read the contents of each block correctly. It helps when updating a block protocol.
  • Timestamp is the time the block is built. It shows when and what has happened in the block.
  • Difficulty target is a value set to regulate how quickly a block is solved. For example, the difficulty target is adjusted every 2016 blocks and created an average of 10 minutes between blocks.
  • Nonce is a dummy number that miners use to get a block hash less than or equal to the target threshold. Once the nonce is discovered, then all transactions in the block are added to the blockchain.
  • P revious hash is a hash root of the previous block. It is used for connecting with other blocks as a chain.
  • Merkle root is the hash of all the hashes of all the transactions to form a single line of text. It is used for the chain to next block.

As Fig. 4.4 shows, different types of blocks are possible in blockchain, such as a genesis block, stale block, and orphan block (Li et al. 2019).

  • A genesis block is the first block in a blockchain network. On the bitcoin blockchain, the genesis block was created in 2009. It contains the following message: “The Times 03/Jan/2009 Chancellor on brink of second bailout for banks.” The genesis block becomes the universal parent of all the blocks in the blockchain. Any block in every node is ultimately connected to this genesis block.
  • A stale block is a validated block, but is not a part of the current best chain block, which is the longest chain in several chains.
  • An orphan block is also validated but is not accepted into the blockchain network because of a time lag in the block's acceptance. For example, two blocks are validated at a similar time. Once one block gets accepted into the blockchain, then the other block is discarded from getting added to the blockchain as an orphan block.

Fig. 4.4. Types of Block. Note: This figure shows the types of blocks including genesis block, best chain of blocks, stale block, and orphan block.

Node and Miner

A node is a communication point in the blockchain network. Any computer or server can be a node. All nodes are connected to each other in a P2P network (Jimi 2018). A node's responsibilities are maintaining the ledger, receiving transactions from other nodes, and validating transactions. A node can be set to either online or offline. Online nodes are receiving, saving, and broadcasting all the latest blocks of transactions from and to other nodes, while offline nodes do not. A master node requires much more resources, including electricity, storage space, and memory because it is hosting a very large server on the network (Brega 2018).

A miner is a specific node to participate in performing the block verification process. It determines whether each transaction is legitimate. For example, if the block including the encrypted transaction is broadcasted, miners perform the tasks necessary to confirm and validate the block itself. Once the validation process has been completed, the original miner who performed the initial validation broadcasts this block and associated validation information to the rest of the network. Then, other miners participate in verifying this PoW to establish the legitimacy of the transaction in that particular block.

A miner always needs to run a full node to select valid transactions to form a new block (Jimi 2018). A full node contains a complete history of transactions that have been recorded on that specific blockchain on any device. Without a full node, users cannot determine what proposed transactions are valid according to the current blockchain's transaction history. However, a node is not necessarily simultaneously a miner. A device can run a full node by receiving, storing, and broadcasting all transaction data, like a server, without actually creating new blocks of transactions. In this case, a node functions more like a pass point with a directory, whereas a miner is the same but simultaneously tries to create new blocks of transactions as well.

Blockchain Technologies

A blockchain network contains several key technologies: cryptographic hashing (chain), Merkle hash tree and root (block validation), a distributed ledger (decentralized records), and consensus protocols (PoW).

Cryptographic Hashing

Cryptographic hashing is a method used to generate a code by using a mathematical function to a set of data (Tasca and Tessone 2019). It is used for proving that the data have not been forged or modified. This hashing is one-way process, so it cannot derive the input from the output. In other words, reverse engineering a cryptographic hash to discover the initial entry is virtually impossible. Bitcoin uses cryptographic hashing to find a solution as a PoW to validate. For example, a random string of digits, which is called nonce, is repeatedly inserted into a hashing formula until finding a desirable hash code, which is six zeroes (0s).

Blockchain typically uses SHA256, which is a hashing algorithm with a 256-bit text long output. For example, entering the following text “The purchase amount of the goods is $1,000” generates the following SHA256 hash:

63B96BC65067A1374482DC009B51B38C5A0BFFA88785EBD010F9EA4-A2901258B.

Any change of this text results in the different code. For example, changing the amount $100 results in the value:

475DD78A89790841952D351C09FF6E5F7D522EC95FF1110A13D724-57C6217642.

The created code from cryptographic hashing can be a chain to connect two blocks in the blockchain network. This statement means that a current block is linked to the previous block by the previous hash. Fig. 4.5 shows a diagram of block hashing. Assuming that block 1's data are “abc,” block 2's data are “def,” and block 3's data are “ghi,” each block creates a hash code, like “234,” “657,” and “735.” Each code is a chain between two blocks.

Fig. 4.5. Block Hashing (I). Note: This figure shows a simple hashing algorithm to connect two blocks as a chain in blockchain network.

As Fig. 4.6 shows, any modification to a data creates a different value, so the hashes do not match up. In that case, the previous hash in the downstream chain has to be recreated.

Fig. 4.6. Block Hashing (II). Note: This figure shows how any modification breaks the chain between blocks by creating a different hash value.

Mining is a PoW to confirm a transaction and adding transactions to the existing blockchain ledger of transactions distributed among all users of a blockchain (Crosset 2018). By creating a hash of a block of transactions that cannot be easily forged, mining protects the integrity of the entire blockchain without needing a central system. Mining uses cryptographic hashing as a PoW algorithm. If a miner wants to solve the mathematical problem for adding a block to the blockchain, the miner has to find a hash value for the data in its block. When a miner attempts to add a new block of transactions to the blockchain, the miner broadcasts the block to all the nodes on the network. Based on the block's legitimacy, nodes can accept or reject the block. When a node accepts a new block of transactions, the node saves and stores the new block on top of the rest of the blocks, which have already stored in the node. Also, nodes broadcast and spread this transaction history to other nodes that may need to synchronize with the blockchain. Miners repeat this process of changing the nonce indefinitely until they randomly hit an output string that meets the signature requirements (i.e., seven zeroes (0s) in bitcoin). This newly created hash becomes a chain that connects between two blocks, meaning that each block is connected by a hash code as a chain.

Merkle Hash Tree and Root

In 1979, Ralph Merkle developed a hash tree to make better digital signatures. This hash tree is used for one-time signatures and authenticated public key distribution to provide authenticated responses as to the validity of a certificate (Merkle 1980). Today, Merkle Hash Tree (MHT) is extended to verify whether the received data are altered in a P2P network and to efficiently arrange large sets of data in computer science and cryptography.

MHT is a technique to optimize data structure as a tree-like arrangement, which consists of a “root” as the hash at the top, “leaves” in the intermediate hashes, and “data” on the bottom. Fig. 4.7 shows a diagram of MHT. Each piece of raw data (i.e., D1, D2, D3, and D4) on the bottom is individually hashed. It creates the corresponding hash value, such as H1, H2, H3, and H4. Now H1 and H2 are concatenated as the same group and then hashed to create a new hash value (H12). The same is done with H3 and H4 to create H34. Finally, H12 and H34 are concatenated and hashed to create a root (H1234).

Fig. 4.7. Merkle Hash Tree and Root. Note: This figure shows a basic Merkle tree structure, which is a way of organizing large amounts of data using hashes.

In blockchain, MHT serves to encode the transaction data more efficiently and securely in a block through hashing. For example, it creates a blockchain signature (i.e., a root hash), which is a chain to connect blocks in a blockchain network. Each signature is combined with other signatures to create a new, overarching signature. This process can be seen as the mechanism used to chain blocks together. As Fig. 4.8 shows, MHT creates a root hash, which is the hash of all the hashes of all the transaction data in a block and then puts it in a block header.

Fig. 4.8. Merkle Hash Tree and Root in Blockchain. Note: This figure shows how a Merkle hash tree is used to a blockchain network to verify the integrity of transactions efficiently and quickly.

Distributed Ledger

A distributed ledger in blockchain is a database that is distributed across nodes (Brakeville and Perepa 2016). A centralized ledger has multiple ledgers, but only a master ledger (i.e., clearing house) keeps the true records. Unlike the centralized ledger, a distributed ledger has a single ledger that is shared by all nodes. All nodes have some level of access to that ledger and determine the true state of the ledger.

In blockchain, the distributed ledger records all transactions that have occurred in a chronological timeline within a network. All nodes agree to a rule (i.e., protocol) that determines the ledger's true state at any point. Blockchain can hold an undisputable record through this distributed ledger technology. No central authority is needed, but individuals or entities compromise each other for the trust of transactions in the blockchain network.

The distributed ledger tracks the history of all events and maintains their records. The information stored in the ledger is distributed through a P2P network. This network is dynamic and keeps growing with the increasing number of transactions. Since each participant in the network has a copy of the ledger's data that is distributed through the network, all participants in a transaction have the same real-time ledger.

Consensus Algorithms

In computer science, a consensus algorithm is a way to get agreement among a number of processes for a single data value ( Wikipedia 2020). Similarly, blockchain uses a consensus algorithm to settle discrepancies within the same data sets that are stored on different nodes. All participating entities in a specific blockchain must adhere to and follow the same consensus algorithm to participate on the blockchain.

Another role of the consensus algorithm is to maintain a consistent ledger. Given that a blockchain network has no centralized authority, consensus algorithms describe which network members can validate blocks of data and how others can verify their legitimacy. Transactions require validation to ensure ledger integrity. This validation can prevent double spending, which is a potential flaw in a digital cash scheme in which the same digital token can be spent more than once. Different blockchains have different algorithms for doing this validation, which often depends on the level of inherent trust in the participants. So, each validation by different blockchains has different tolerances for malicious activity, redundancy, and performance.

Several techniques are available to validate transactions such as PoW (Krawisz 2013), PoS (Rosic 2017), Proof of Elapsed Time (PoET) (Frankenfield 2020b), and Byzantine Fault Tolerance (BFT) (Vukolić 2016).

Proof of Work

PoW is the most common consensus algorithm in the blockchain network. Since PoW requires miners to solve difficult cryptographic puzzles, it relies on high energy use and is also slow to confirm transactions for the approval of their validation. Once a transaction is broadcasted, miners start decrypting it by adding a random strings of digits (i.e., nonce) into a hashing formula until finding a desirable outcome. The first miner to publish the verified PoW gets a reward. Other miners verify it by taking the alleged input string and applying it to the same formula to see if the outcome is indeed that what was presented. When a participant wants to add this validated transaction to a block, all participants in the blockchain network attempt to approve it. They do this by applying a consensus algorithm to the transaction to verify its validity. If a majority of the participants (i.e., the 51% rule in bitcoin) agree, then this transaction is validated. After a set of approved transactions is bundled in a block, this block is sent to all nodes in the blockchain network. Bitcoin and Ethereum use PoW as a consensus algorithm.

Proof of Stake

PoS is an alternative to PoW. Unlike PoW, PoS gives the miners who hold coins (e.g., bitcoin) the ability to mine or validate transactions. In other words, the power of mining is proportional to the amount of coins a miner owns. For example, a miner who holds 1% of the coins available can mine or validate only 1% of the blocks. So, PoS can provide advantages to attackers seeking to launch a 51% stake of mining by pooling resources. Nxt is the first to implement a PoS consensus algorithm in 2013 (Kuo, Lee, and Low 2018).

Proof of Elapsed Time

Intel developed PoET in 2016 as an alternative of PoW, which requires high resource consumption such as electricity. PoET uses a random timer system in the blockchain network. Each node generates a random waiting time and goes to sleep for that specific duration. The first node with the shortest wait time wakes up and commits a new block to the blockchain, broadcasting the necessary information to the whole peer network. The same process then repeats for the discovery of the next block, much like how a lottery system might operate. PoET is implemented in Hyperledger Sawtooth's framework, which is an enterprise blockchain platform for building distributed ledger applications and networks.

Byzantine Fault Tolerance

The derivation of BFT is from the Byzantine Generals' Problem, which is generals' dilemma to decide whether to attack or retreat when communicating through untrusted messengers (Lamport, Shostak, and Pease 1982). BFT is a protocol to reach consensus in a distributed network even though some of the nodes fail to respond or respond with incorrect information. It provides a safeguard against system failures by employing collective decision-making aimed at reducing the influence of the faulty nodes. BFT is reasonably efficient and tolerant against malicious participants. The typical example of BFT-enabled blockchain is Hyperledger IROHA, which is a permission-based blockchain.

Operational Procedure and Technical Challenges

The key procedure of operation in blockchain is to build a chain of blocks, which links blocks using cryptographic hashes. Although the task of building and operating blockchain network appears simple and straightforward, several technical challenges exist such as network scalability, interoperability between nodes, and legal and compliance issues. The following discussion is a step-by-step operational procedure of blockchain and its technical challenges.

Operational Procedure

Fig. 4.9 shows the procedure of blockchain. Users create transactions and broadcast them to all the participants in the network for validation. When transactions are sent, they are encrypted by cryptographic methods (i.e., digital signatures and/or public keys). The validated transactions are accepted in a block. This block is broadcasted to all network participants for the approval of validation. Once approved, this block is connected into the existing blocks and then this new block is broadcasted to nodes for the approval using a consensus protocol. After its approval, this block is now chained to prior blocks and becomes the true state in the blockchain network.

Fig. 4.9. Operational Process of Blockchain. Note: This figure shows the procedure of a blockchain operation from transaction activities to block validation (PoW).

Technical Challenges

Although blockchain has many benefits such as providing trust and security, the blockchain system has several technical issues ‒ scalability, interoperation, and legal and compliance (Crosby, Nachiappan, Pattanayak, Verma, and Kalyanaraman 2016).

  • Scalability. The first technical challenge is the scalability of a blockchain network. Since the block is small (i.e., 1 MB in bitcoin), it cannot contain a large number of transactions. Additionally, a distributed ledger may create a bottleneck in data flow. Theoretically, the distribution of blocks should be well balanced, but this situation does not happen in practice. More often, a ledger is centralized to a specific ledger as it grows over time. For example, a larger node requires high computational power and large storage, so it validates much faster and contains more blocks. As a result, only a few large nodes can process a block and lead to the centralization of a blockchain network.
  • Interoperation. The second technical challenge is interoperation between the different types of blockchain networks. Currently, thousands of blockchain projects use various platforms and solutions. However, no standards are available to build blockchain networks. As a result of using different protocols, consensus algorithms, and coding languages, these multiple standalone blockchain networks cannot communicate each other.
  • Legal and compliance issues. The third technical challenge is legal and compliance issues. No globally consistent or applicable regulations are available for blockchain because it is a new territory. Since some current legislators do not foresee the blockchain revolution, several legal issues remain unresolved. For example, no regulations cover a smart contract in blockchain. When transactions occur in a blockchain network, limited regulation exists on how to report, disclose, and value these transactions. Thus, blockchain users face a risk without any specific regulation.

Summary and Conclusions

This chapter covered some technical concepts of blockchain and its architecture focusing on three key elements ‒ a block, node, and miner. These elements include four blockchain technology components: cryptographic hashing, Merkle hash tree and root, distributed ledger, and consensus algorithms. Other issues connected to blockchain implementation discussed include scalability of blocks and a distributed ledger, processing power of nodes, and storage.

Blockchain has become a reality and can rapidly change how business in many industries operates such as finance, healthcare, energy, and retail. It is revolutionary that transactions in a public network are transparent and secure. Although blockchain is still far from being a mature technology, it has tremendous potential. Thus, a technical understanding of blockchain is essential to the success of businesses in the future.
