Part II
Types of Blockchain and Related Issues

Chapter 5

Public Blockchains and Applications

Hugo Benedetti

Keywords: Permissionless blockchains; censorship resistance; consensus mechanisms; cryptoeconomics; decentralized ledger; Proof-of-work (PoW); Proof-of-stake (PoS)

Introduction

Public blockchains are permissionless blockchains, allowing universal access to read, write, and validate information stored in the network. More specifically, public access grants the ability to access relevant information stored in the blockchain; create user handles (e.g., accounts, addresses, contracts, or private-public key combinations) and interact with the blockchain by receiving, retrieving, transforming, and posting information; and participate in the information storage and validation process. Private blockchains, also referred to as permissioned blockchains, incorporate mechanisms to restrict some or all these three key functions ‒ read, write, and validate.

To ensure their permissionless nature, public blockchains lack a central coordinating authority by design. Sets of rules and incentive mechanisms that aim to generate a self-governing ecosystem replace the authority figure. Rules are explicitly embedded in the software protocols to guarantee the correctness of stored information (i.e., previous blocks), correctness of new information to be included in the blockchain and correctness of the process followed to write each block on the blockchain (i.e., consensus process). These rules provide incentives for users to interact and participate in the storage and validation of individual data, block data, and the complete blockchain as well as to reduce the incentives to engage in adversarial behavior.

The set of rules and incentive mechanisms that replace the central authority are commonly referred to as cryptoeconomics. Although no formal consensus exists on the term's scope, the core concepts relate to the combination of cryptography and mechanism design to coordinate networks. Virtually all public blockchains enforce their cryptoeconomies through the issuance of cryptocurrencies, which are native digital monetary units that reward participation in the validation process and allow users to receive compensation for services provided. These cryptocurrencies are intrinsic to each blockchain and their issuance dynamics vary according to each project's specific needs.

A key element within cryptoeconomics is the consensus protocol, which is the set of rules and mechanisms implemented in a blockchain protocol to determine which block is added to the blockchain and in most implementations, and which validator is rewarded for such work. Just as with cryptoeconomics, the consensus process goes beyond the rules that are written in the blockchain code and involves incentive mechanisms to ensure proper functioning of the validator network. Nearly all blockchains also use the consensus protocol to issue and distribute tokens into the blockchain network.

Consensus protocols can be grouped into categories according to their block-writer selection mechanism. The most implemented protocols are Proof of Work (PoW), Proof of Stake (PoS), and Delegated Proof of Stake (DPoS). PoW protocols assign block-writing according to validator's resource contribution to the blockchain network, while PoS protocols consider validator's cryptocurrency commitments guaranteeing the validity of inputted transactions. The DPoS function similarly to PoS, with the added option of granting any user to delegate her cryptocurrency commitments to a validator of her choice, allowing indirect participation in the block-writing process. Less commonly implemented protocols include hybrid protocols, which combine PoW and PoS; and non-standard protocols, which use alternative processes that do not fit in the previous categories.

Some attributes of public blockchains are decentralization, censorship resistance, tamper resistance, transparency, and anonymity. All of these attributes have a high probability of attainment, but none is guaranteed, as they depend on the correct coding and functioning of the blockchain protocol, cryptoeconomic design, behavior of all blockchain participants, and external factors that cannot be encompassed in the contracts.

The choice between public and private blockchain protocols has no clear answer, ever-changing as technology progresses and new use cases are brought forward. Public blockchains' promise of universal user access brings forward the possibility of greater network scale, and therefore greater network effects and positive externalities, compared to their private blockchain counterparts. In the opposite direction, universal validator access potentially leads to data propagation and confirmation delays. Consensus protocols and mechanisms have led to validator cartel formation and market concentration.

The purpose of this chapter is to provide an overview of public blockchains as well as examples of current implementations. The chapter is organized as follows. The next section provides a background on public blockchains, introduces their key elements and commonly attributed features, and presents current challenges. Subsequently, the chapter provides a review of the leading projects on three types of public blockchains use cases ‒ (1) monetary and financial networks, (2) distributed computing and virtual machines, and (3) decentralized markets. Lastly, the chapter concludes with a summary and closing questions.

Background on Public Blockchains

Blockchain is a public decentralized ledger platform (Evans 2014) or public ledger of all transactions or digital events that have been executed and shared among participating parties (Crosby, Nachiappan, Pattanayak, Verma, and Kalyanaraman 2016). These definitions explicitly refer to blockchains as “public.” Nakamoto (2008) envisioned bitcoin, the first implementation of blockchain technology, as a means to remove the central authority in financial networks and replace it by a peer-to-peer (P2P), publicly auditable ledger of transactions.

Public blockchains are more than a public decentralized ledger. In fact, they could be viewed more as a general-purpose technology(Breshnahan and Trajtenberg 1995) to create, store, and manage decentralized databases (Lipsey, Carlaw, and Bekhar 2005; Wright and De Filippi 2015). From a complementary perspective, Davidson, De Filippi, and Potts (2016) contextualize public blockchains as the evolution of polycentric and the governance of common pool resources.

The focal element of public blockchains is their permissionless nature, allowing universal access to read, write, and validate information stored in the network. Private blockchains, also referred to as permissioned blockchains, incorporate mechanisms to restrict some or all these three key functions ‒ read, write, and validate. To ensure this permissionless characteristic, public blockchains lack a central coordinating authority, replacing it with sets of rules and incentive mechanisms that aim to generate a self-governing ecosystem. Lacking a central authority is a necessary condition for public blockchains to ensure their permissionless attributes. However, the opposite does not hold true for their private blockchain counterparts. Private blockchains do not need to have a central authority to enforce their permissioned nature, as permissions can be enforced by a decentralized authority.

Cryptoeconomics and Consensus Protocol

As previously noted, cryptoeconomics refers to the set of rules and incentive mechanisms that replace the central authority. Kaal (2018) explicitly considers cryptoeconomics as the convergence of multiple disciplines other than cryptography and economics, such as finance, law and regulation, governance, mechanism design, and distributed systems. Berg, Davidson, and Potts (2019) introduce the concept of institutional cryptoeconomics, as the study of how blockchains interact with existing and future social institutions.

An important element within cryptoeconomics is the consensus protocol. Irresberger, John, and Saleh (2020) group the consensus protocols into five categories: (1) PoW, (2) PoS, (3) hybrid, (4) DPoS, and (5) non-standard. According to their analysis, PoW was the most commonly used consensus mechanism before 2015, being implemented in nearly 50% of public blockchains. From 2015 forward, PoW lost its dominance and is currently being implemented in about 20% of newly launched blockchain protocols. Bach, Mihaljevic, and Zagar (2018) as well as Chaudhry and Yousaf (2018) provide a qualitative comparison of the alternative consensus models.

The PoW protocols require validators to solve a pseudo-random and resource intensive calculation. The pseudo-random process allows the probability of receiving validation (block-writing) rights to be related to the amount of resources committed to the network. Some PoW protocols target a linear relation, while others prefer a positive but marginally decreasing one to reduce the potential allocation of block-writing rights in few users with larger resources. Although most protocols have implemented energy intense calculations as means to measure resource contribution, others have introduced variations to incorporate energy efficient calculations, incorporating the use of scarce resources such as hard drive memory space and elapsed time. In all the variations of PoW algorithms, the increasing usage of limited resources constrains the long-term growth of the blockchain.

PoS pseudo-randomly assigns validation rights to agents according to their committed token wealth (“staked” tokens) to guarantee the correctness of transactions included in a block. Users with greater wealth commitments have higher probabilities of validating a block. Users writing blocks that contain incorrect transaction are penalized by a reduction of their committed token wealth. PoS protocols reduce validator's incentives to enter a computational arms race, as computational power is not directly related to the probability of being assigned block-writing rights. Therefore, the direct cost of the block-writing process is severely reduced. In turn, the direct cost is mainly the opportunity cost of staked tokens, which remain unusable during the staking process.

Hybrid mechanisms combine PoW and PoS, either sequentially or simultaneously. In the sequential mechanism, PoW is used to launch the block-writing assignment, providing incentives for validators of competing blockchains to transfer their computing power and accelerate the validator network growth. Once a certain network size is achieved, the consensus protocol is modified to PoS, reducing the block-writing process cost. In the simultaneous mechanism, PoW is used for block-writing assignment and PoS for blockchain governance. This model potentially allows non-validator users to participate in the blockchain's decision-making process.

In DPoS, validators are pseudo-randomly assigned from a group of delegate users, who in turn are selected by all users willing to commit part of their token wealth. DPoS protocols allow users to directly affect the level of block-writing concentration by pooling or splitting their wealth into fewer/greater number of validators.

Lastly, non-standard consensus protocols do not fit in any of the previous categories, such as those based on user reputation or non-token voting. For example, some blockchain protocols rely on validators to approve transactions by voting. If a certain proportion of validators ‒ majority or super majority ‒ vote to approve a transaction, the transaction is added to the blockchain. Validators can be chosen by users through token voting or token staking; performance parameters such as network up-time, voting participation or validator age, or others such as reputation and voting consistency.

In most blockchains, the consensus protocols also determine the creation and distribution of their cryptocurrency. Some blockchains such as Bitcoin only create new units of their cryptocurrency when a new block is written on the blockchain, as a reward to the block-writing validator (“block reward” or “mining”). In this case, the blockchain's first block (“genesis block”) contains only one transaction, the block reward assigned to the genesis validator. If no other validator joins the network, the sole validator is the recipient of all newly created cryptocurrencies. Some blockchain developers have used this mechanism to accumulate large amounts of cryptocurrencies (“pre-mine”) before the network's official launch to external users. Other blockchains launch with a predetermined amount of cryptocurrency assigned to certain users, hence their genesis block already contains a set of accounts and cryptocurrency balances, and also creates new cryptocurrency as block rewards. In all cases, the distribution and concentration of validators directly affect the distribution and concentration of block rewards and therefore, the distribution of cryptocurrency wealth in the network. Critics of PoS and DPoS consensus protocols point to the observed concentration of wealth as one the main risks of such protocols, since a reduced number of users could easily control the majority of the block-writing rights of the network. According to the website www.arewedecentralizedyet.com, during mid-2020, the percentage of cryptocurrency held by the top 100 accounts of major PoS blockchains (e.g., Ardor and QTUM) and DPoS (Nano) reached 67%, 73%, and 62%, respectively. During the same period, the top 100 accounts of PoW blockchains (e.g., Bitcoin and Ethereum) held 19% and 34% of their respective cryptocurrency issuance.

Common Attributes of Public Blockchains

Public blockchains frequently expose a set of attributes or features to emphasize the potential benefits of the technology. These attributes are decentralization, censorship resistance, tamper resistance, transparency, and anonymity (Lin and Liao 2017). However, these attributes are not inherent to the general technology, but features can be inserted in the blockchain protocol and incentivized through behavioral mechanisms, according to the nature and needs of each specific project.

Decentralization is perhaps the most touted characteristic of public blockchains, and yet potentially the most debated. The concept of centralization is simple to understand as an activity's concentration of control under a single authority. By contrast, decentralization consists of the distribution of control over multiple participants. The debate stems from the reduced number of users participating in the consensus process of leading blockchains and the high concentration of cryptocurrency balances in a limited number of accounts. The following website provides a real-time update on several measures of blockchain decentralization (www.arewedecentralizedyet.com). For instance, during mid-2020, three and four entities controlled more than 50% of Ethereum and Bitcoin's validating power, respectively. According to Chu and Wang (2018), validator decentralization is limited by the industry dynamics in block mining.

Censorship resistance refers to the inability of blocking blockchain interactions to read, write, or validate by a third party. In theory, any user with the ability to connect to the network can read the blockchain's contents, post transactions, and participate in the validation process. In practice, all these interactions can be limited either by factors internal or external to the blockchain ecosystem. Examples of internal factors include users rejecting/returning transaction from specific addresses (blacklisting and whitelisting) (Möser, Böhme, and Breuker 2014; Conti, Gangwal, and Ruj 2018); users blocking certain nodes (eclipse attack) (Marcus, Heilman, and Goldberg 2018) or users (distributed denial of service attacks (DDoS)) (Vasek, Thornton, and Moore 2014); and validators creating a hard fork in the blockchain to remove certain transactions (DuPont 2018; Mehar et al. 2019). External factors include network blocking by internet service providers and governments (Leonard 2016).

Although the assumption is that data stored on a public blockchain are immutable, a better description is to refer to such data as highly expensive and difficult to modify, hence referred to as tamper resistant. The consensus process itself allows for natural block adjustment and rewriting as new valid blocks propagate through the network. Valid blocks that are propagated but excluded in the longest chain of blocks are termed orphan-blocks. Because of this process, blockchain protocols suggest that users consider a transaction as valid only after a certain number of blocks have been written on top of the block containing the transaction (Nakamoto 2008; Buterin 2014, Wood 2014). A more graphic example of data modification corresponds to hard forks to remove certain transactions (DuPont 2018; Mehar et al. 2019) and block re-organizations (Bissias, Levine, Ozisik, and Andresen 2016).

Public blockchains provide public ledgers, which depending on the disclosure policies, potentially allow any user to reconstruct and trace the entire history of any transaction, including all the addresses or accounts with which it has ever interacted. This feature is described as transparency. In most blockchain protocols, ledger transparency is essential to audit a blockchain's integrity. This feature, however, is not omnipresent across protocols. In fact, privacy preservation is a major challenge in public blockchains (Halpin and Piekarska 2017; Mödinger, Kopp, Kargl, and Hauck 2018). Cryptographic solutions such as those implemented by the Zcash blockchain (Sasson et al. 2014) or zkLedger (Narula, Vasquez, and Virza 2018) allow any user to access and validate the integrity of the blockchain and any transaction without revealing information other than its validity.

Since public blockchains neither require users to identify themselves nor limit the number of addresses a user can create, a common assumption is that public blockchains provide anonymity to users. This fact has been contested in part by the ability to trace the full transaction history in most public blockchains (Reid and Harrigan 2013; Herrera-Joancomartí 2014; Halpin and Piekarska, 2017; Goldfeder, Kalodner, Reisman, and Narayanan 2018; Mödinger et al. 2018; Feng, He, Zeadally, Khan, and Kumar, 2019). Moreover, some anonymizing procedures, such as those used on illicit markets (Möser, Böhme, and Breuker 2013), P2P networks (Koshy, Koshy, and McDaniel 2017), darknets (Kanemura, Toyoda, and Ohtsuki 2019), and Tor (Biryukov and Pustogarov 2015) are also limited by the public ledger transparency. Lastly, even privacy-oriented blockchain protocols such as Monero (Van Saberhagen 2013) have had their anonymizing features breached (Kumar, Fischer, Tople, and Saxena 2017).

Potential Benefits and Challenges of Public Blockchains

The open and permissionless access environment of public blockchains allows universal user participation, unleashing the highest potential for network effects in the platform. These network externalities affect the speed of adoption of the technology, growth of the network itself, and native cryptocurrency pricing dynamics (Catalini and Gans 2016; Halaburda and Gandal 2016; Biais, Bisiere, Bouvard, Casamatta, and Menkveld 2018; Cong, Li, and Wang 2019; Benedetti and Nikbakht 2020; Sockin and Xiong 2020). But as a network grows, the issue of scalability and congestion arises. As Hinzen, Kose, and Saleh (2019a, 2019b) discuss for the case of bitcoin and PoW blockchains, respectively, transaction rates are bounded even if block rates are made arbitrarily fast, leading to transaction congestion and limiting the overall usage of the blockchain. The same permissionless environment permits universal validator participation potentially propelling data propagation and block confirmation delays, affecting transaction speed (Hinzen et al. 2019a, 2019b).

Builders of consensus protocols and mechanisms aim to decentralize validator power. Nakamoto (2008) proposed a P2P validation protocol and included an algorithm to adjust PoW's difficulty to account for technological improvement and to reduce the potential benefits of scale. The goal was to pursue the permanent presence of individual users as validators creating effectively a network of peers. However, the real magnitude of technological improvement was impossible to foresee as the introduction of hardware developed with the sole purpose of solving the PoW algorithm with application specific integrated circuits (ASICs), which improved upon household central processing unit calculation abilities over 100 million times (Taylor 2017). This disruption removed the possibility of validators using any hardware other than ASICs.

Wood (2014) explicitly states the two goals of Ethereum on its PoW protocol: (1) wide accessibility to individual users to participate as validators and (2) limit the ability of well-funded adversaries to control large part of the network. Because ASICs threatened those goals, Ethereum developed a PoW algorithm incompatible with coexistent ASIC technology. The situation changed in 2018 with the introduction of Ethereum specific ASICs, forcing validators to transition to the new technology. The arms race for processing power has led to the emergence of validator conglomerates that accumulate a large proportion of validating power (Alsabah and Agostino 2020). Despite the massive efficiencies of ASICs, the competition for processing power and the PoW difficulty adjustment results in a permanently increasing demand for energy, raising awareness on the potential socio-political environmental effects of the process (Vranken 2017). Even as other consensus protocols, such as PoS (Saleh 2020), do not involve high energy usage, the widespread notion that public blockchains are heavily energy intensive cannot easily be changed.

Examples of Public Blockchains

This section presents some relevant examples of public blockchains. Rather than providing a historical reference on the evolution of public blockchains, focusing on the most widely advertised or those with higher market capitalization, the examples provided highlight key use cases and emphasize unique features. The section starts with Bitcoin, as the first public blockchain and a decentralized financial network, followed by Zcash, a privacy preserving financial network. Next, the chapter presents two distributed virtual machine projects: Ethereum, which is the first Turing complete blockchain protocol; and EOSIO, also a Turing complete protocol with a DPoS protocol that improves transaction throughput and confirmation times. Lastly, the chapter presents Sia, a public blockchain powering a decentralized data storage market.

Bitcoin

Nakamoto (2008), who created the first public blockchain (Bitcoin), developed a financial network based on using its native cryptocurrency, also called bitcoin. Originally envisioned to create a digital cash system, allowing P2P transfers of bitcoins, the protocol proved flexible enough to accommodate additional uses, such as data storage and time stamping, custom cryptocurrencies or tokens, simple financial instruments, decentralized lotteries, and P2P gambling.

In Bitcoin, validators are called “miners” and are compensated pseudo-randomly according to their processing power. Compensation is provided by the creation of new bitcoins assigned to the block-writer, in addition to transaction fees self-determined by users. The block reward was set at 50 bitcoins per block and scheduled to reduce by half every 210,000 blocks, approximately four years (“halving”). The most recent halving occurred on May 11, 2020, setting the block reward at 6.25 bitcoins. The PoW protocol is calibrated to allow the introduction of a new block every 10 minutes and each block contains about 3,500 transactions. Each transaction can have multiple input and output addresses, effectively multiplying the potential address-to-address transactions per block.

Software upgrades are proposed by the community to the community through the submission of bitcoin improvement proposals. This technical document is presented to the community in open forums, discussed by Bitcoin core developers and relevant stakeholders, such as miners, crypto exchanges, and relevant bitcoin holders. After a period of discussion, the proposal is voted by miners. Each block-writing miner can cast a vote by including a segment of code in the written block. As block-writing rights are pseudo-randomly distributed according to computing power, a miner that controls 20% of the computing power should be able to cast close to 20% of the votes. BIPs on backward compatible upgrades (“soft forks”) are approved by supermajority (55%), while backward incompatible upgrades (“hard forks”) must be implemented by the totally of miners. An opposing miner is effectively removed from the network, as its version of the protocol would be incompatible with the upgraded protocol.

The Bitcoin protocol has since been updated multiple times, including fixes and upgrades such as doubling the transaction capacity per block. Nevertheless, scalability of transactions is a major challenge and developers focused on creating applications that work on top of the blockchain (“second layer” solutions). During 2019, the Bitcoin blockchain processed over 120 million transactions.

As open source software, Bitcoin's source code served as inspiration for over a 1000 different public blockchains, with different degrees of similarity. Although some only took the general concept of blockchain and expanded its functionalities, others merely adjusted parameters in the code, such as block generation time or block size.

A major second layer solution has been the Omni layer, previously called Mastercoin, a software protocol that builds on top of the Bitcoin blockchain, using it as a reference point for transaction settlement. The Omni layer allows the issuance of custom cryptocurrencies and blockchain enabled assets, which can be transferred on the Bitcoin blockchain.

In 2014, the founders of Omni layer launched the first US dollar-backed digital asset, named Tether. Asset backed tokens provide the opportunity to combine attributes of blockchain assets (low-transaction costs, international borderless transferability, trustless ownership, pseudo-anonymity, real-time ledger transparency, and independence from banking systems) with the underlaying price dynamics of the backing asset. Digital tokens backed by fiat currency are commonly referred to as “fiat backed stable coins.” Cryptocurrency trading platforms, also called crypto exchanges, quickly adopted Tether to provide their users with a digital asset having pricing characteristics closely related to the US dollar, without using actual US dollars. Tether has broadened its scope to include additional currencies and assets (EUR, CNH, and gold), as well as token issuances in other blockchains (Ethereum, Tron, EOSIO, Liquid, and Algorand). Tether publishes a real-time balance of its unaudited reserves in the website https://wallet.tether.to/transparency. As of May 2020, Tether's published US dollar reserves reached little over $9 billion. Academics have questioned the correlation of Tether with bitcoin pricing and trading, finding conflicting results (Wei 2018; Griffin and Shams 2019).

Ethereum

The Ethereum blockchain provides a Turing complete programming language allowing users to create complex self-executing contracts (Buterin 2014; Wood 2014). Its native cryptocurrency called ether is used as means of payment for code execution. Ethereum's most relevant use case to date, at least in terms of impact on the blockchain ecosystem, has been the issuance, sale, and distribution of alternative tokens to be used as the exclusive means of payment in decentralized applications, a process commonly referred to as initial coin offerings (ICOs).

The Ethereum blockchain hosts various decentralized applications such as decentralized autonomous organizations (DAOs); decentralized cryptocurrency exchanges (DEXs); advanced financial services such as crypto loans, fixed income instruments, financial derivatives, and pooled investment vehicles; and decentralized game platforms.

In 2016, a flaw in the code of a smart contract named “The DAO,” an acronym for decentralized autonomous organization, allowed a hacker to transfer ether with an approximate value of $60 million. Given the project's relevance and the need to isolate the incident, the Ethereum community decided to generate an alternate blockchain ledger called a hard-fork, which only removed the attacker's transaction and recognized the new chain as the official Ethereum blockchain.

This event led to the questioning of the real decentralization and immutability of public blockchains, as well as the role of the founder, Vitalik Butering as the de-facto leader of the decentralized project. The initial Ethereum blockchain is now called Ethereum Classic and is currently maintained by those who decided to continue using the original ledger that contained the DAO transaction.

The flexibility provided by a Turing complete protocol has allowed for several ground-breaking innovations. Until the end of 2018, the most common application of Ethereum was the issuance of crypto-tokens and crowdfunding through ICOs, evolving in 2019 to decentralized applications such as crypto-marketplaces, which allow trading any token issued on the Ethereum protocol. The end of 2019 saw the irruption of a new application ‒ decentralized finance (DeFi), which offers financial products such as collateralized loans, income earning deposits, and financial derivatives.

Zcash

The Zcash blockchain also created a financial network for its native cryptocurrency called Zcash (Sasson et al. 2014). Unlike Bitcoin and most public blockchains, Zcash is a “privacy” cryptocurrency including additional cryptography elements to shield transactions. This process allows user addresses, transactions, and balances to remain encrypted but still be verifiable. As a result, while most public blockchains allow users to reconstruct, validate, and audit the entire history of any user address, transaction, and balance, Zcash allows users to audit the correctness of any transaction, but without disclosing any information on the user address, transaction, or balance. In addition, Zcash allows users to choose “transparent” addresses, which are publicly traceable on the blockchain. Another relevant feature is compensation. As most protocols, Zcash rewards miners with block rewards and transaction fees. However, 20% of the block rewards is distributed among founders, vested employees, founding company, steering foundation, and developers. This compensation mechanism provides a direct flow of resources to support the blockchain's further development.

EOSIO

The EOSIO blockchain is a Turing complete programming language with key differencing features (Grigg 2017). Its consensus protocol is based on DPoS, resulting in only 21 elected users performing validations and writing blocks, allowing for a transaction throughput 1,000 times higher than Bitcoin. Validators use an asynchronous byzantine fault tolerant (aBFT) process to agree on the contents of each block, after which it becomes final and irreversible. Its native cryptocurrency called EOS is not used as a means of payment, but as a deposit to perform transactions. Unlike most public blockchains, EOSIO does not require users to pay for code execution. Instead, EOS is locked into an account while the code is executed and freed upon code termination. Its validators are only compensated by token issuance. The largest ICO performed up to 2019, raising over $4.2 billion, funded EOSIO (Fisch 2019).

Sia

The Sia blockchain is tailored to a special case of a smart contract called a file contract (Champine and Vorick 2014). The contract is an agreement between an uploader and several hosts to store certain data for a specific amount of time. The uploaded data are divided, encrypted, distributed, and stored on the unused hard drive space of redundant hosts. The blockchain is not used to store the uploaded data, but to issue the file contract, place payment in escrow, and release payment as proof of file storage is provided. The native monetary unit of the Sia blockchain is SiaCoin. Hosting prices are set freely by users and hosts, and as of mid-2020 lies at around 10% of the price of leading cloud storage solutions such as AWS, Dropbox, or Box. A second layer application called Skynet allows users to provide P2P access to their files stored on Sia network. This creates a decentralized file sharing market for hosted data.

Summary and Conclusions

Public blockchains are permissionless blockchains, allowing universal access to read, write, and validate information stored in the network. This permissionless nature also implies the intentional absence of a central coordinating authority. Instead, the coordination of users and management of the blockchain is embedded in the software protocol and complemented by incentive mechanisms, together commonly referred to as cryptoeconomics.

Some common features of public blockchains are decentralization, censorship resistance, tamper resistance, transparency, and anonymity. All of these features have a high probability of attainment, but none are guaranteed, as they depend on the correct coding and functioning of the blockchain protocol, cryptoeconomic design, behavior of all blockchain participants, and external factors that cannot be encompassed in the contracts.

Foreseeing a universal, one-size-fits-all blockchain protocol, whether it is a public, private, or hybrid, is difficult to imagine. What is more realistic, and in line with the evolution observed in the market, is the specialization and customization of blockchain protocols to the specific needs of certain types of data and use cases, additional protocols allowing the interoperability of blockchains, and the development of applications and interfaces that operate on top of blockchains. Lastly, developments are likely to allow blockchains to permeate and eventually disrupt brick and mortar businesses and institutions, much like the internet disrupted traditional business.

Discussion Questions

(1)Describe public blockchains and mention three current applications.

(2)Explain how public blockchains ensure the adherence of transaction and block-writing rules.

(3)Discuss the need for predefined mechanisms and rules to modify a public blockchain's protocols.

(4)PoW consensus protocols have been criticized because of their high and continuously increasing mining cost. Discuss how mining cost affects the tamper resistance attribute of public blockchains.

(5)Discuss whether a public blockchain requires issuing its own native cryptocurrency to provide incentives to its validator network.

Chapter 6

Private and Hybrid Blockchains and Applications

Gina Pieters and Sean Stein Smith

Keywords: Hybrid blockchains; central bank digital currencies; central bank cryptocurrencies; enterprise implementation; privacy; interoperability; stablecoins

Introduction

This chapter focuses on blockchains that are not fully public, specifically hybrid and private blockchain models and applications. It begins by reviewing a general framework of blockchain technology used to define and differentiate the two types of blockchain from each other and from a public blockchain. The chapter then discusses several applications as illustrative examples of the differences.

Defining Blockchain Layers

This chapter does not distinguish between distributed ledger technology (DLT) and blockchain, despite the fact that all blockchains are DLTs, but not all DLTs are blockchains. Any system based on DLT consists of three layers ‒ (1) protocol, (2) network, and (3) data ‒as represented in Fig. 6.1 and adapted from Rauchs et al. (2018). The protocol layer is tasked with providing and updating the set of software-defined rules to determine how the system operates. Next, the network layer connects actors, data, and processes according to the implemented protocol layer. Finally, the data layer comprises the information flowing through the system and the relation of the data to the protocol and network layer.

Fig. 6.1. The Layer–component–process Configuration of a Distributed Ledger Technology (DLT) System. Note: Any blockchain system can be analyzed using the following framework, which consists of three layers, with each layer containing two to three components with subprocesses. In a public blockchain, all the processes are permissionless, but in a private blockchain, all processes are permissioned. In a hybrid blockchain, some processes are permissioned and others are permissionless. Source: Adapted from Rauchs et al. (2018).

Each layer consists of components, and each component consists of processes. For example, the protocol layer consists of the alteration component containing the protocol change processes, which are the rules that determine who and how the underlying software code changes. The network layer contains the validation component that in turn includes the transaction validation process, which determines how individual transactions are validated, and a record validation process, which determines how a record (i.e., a combination of transactions) is validated. The data layer has the input component, which determines the source or method of data input, as well as any programmatically executable transactions (PETs) or smart contracts components.

Every process can be either permissionless (i.e., accessible to anyone) or permissioned (i.e., accessible to only those with appropriate clearance or permission). If all processes within a component are permissionless, then the component is permissionless; if all components are permissionless, the layer is permissionless. If all layers are permissionless, then the system is permissionless and fully decentralized: a public blockchain. Bitcoin is an example of a fully decentralized system.

In contrast, if all processes are permissioned, then the distributed ledger is similar to a standard enterprise database: a private blockchain. A hybrid blockchain falls between these two extremes: at least one layer has a permissioned component and at least one layer has a permissionless component. Choosing which components are permissioned and permissionless is part of the decisions made when designing a blockchain, as discussed later in this chapter.

A private process might be the simplest place to begin analysis because its essence is most similar to existing technology applications. In a private process, only a selected and approved number of network members can engage with a process. An example of a private process could be a large organization engaging the data broadcast process (network layer) to share information with selected entities having access to the network layer.

A permissioned process is an outgrowth and iteration of private processes, but comes equipped with flexibility not inherent to a private process. In a permissioned blockchain, permissioned members have differing levels of access or interaction to any process. Such an arrangement can lead to a more flexible and business appropriate type of blockchain if the organizing entities want to invite external regulator or auditor organizations. For example, a permissioned process could allow an external audit firm, bank examiner, or other regulator to gain view-only access to a subset of records, not to all network data. A consortium blockchain is a private or permissioned blockchain where permission is granted to a user group such as employees from a group of companies, rather than other individuals.

Finally, a public process, sometimes called a permissionless process, places no external restrictions on who is allowed access to the process. This kind of process might be most commonly associated with blockchains via applications such as bitcoin and ether. For example, anyone who downloads the correct software can be a miner engaging in transaction verification for bitcoin or can view the entire history of transactions. A hybrid blockchain, for example, may combine the data accessibility as a public process, but retain control of transaction verification as a private process. Or it could do the opposite: the data layer could be readable only on a permissioned or private basis, while the transaction handling and verification processes may be a public process.

Private Blockchains

Public blockchains, most famously associated with bitcoin, were the first type of blockchain to come to market. Private blockchains are a newer iteration of blockchain technology, developed in large part as a response to issues associated with public blockchains linked to technical complexity, scalability, and costs associated with implementation. A private blockchain is potentially most appropriate for implementations when a limited number of network members would like to share information openly with each other. Examples of where a private blockchain network might represent the most applicable and logical iteration of a hybrid blockchain would be if a larger organization would like to share information with its primary suppliers. Conversely, if suppliers have a single large customer accounting for a substantial percentage of its total business, this option might seem reasonable. Such an open information sharing arrangement necessitates stricter protocols for adding and removing members, differing levels of access to network information, and a higher level of centralization of the management of blockchain compared with public/permissionless blockchains.

Consortium blockchains represent a subset of private blockchains. In a private blockchain, a single point of authority typically determines permissions and member access. In a consortium model, this power is spread throughout a group, or consortium, of organizations. The Libra Association, which is discussed in more depth later in this chapter, is a high-profile example of a consortium blockchain with which the investing public and market actors are familiar. Some primary benefits of a consortium blockchain are its ability to spread costs associated with blockchain implementation and to pool technical and personnel resources. It also offers the potential for creating and lobbying for industry standard setting protocols. Rather than having various private blockchains purporting to represent industry best practices, a consortium blockchain organized by leading firms with a broad membership can make that claim. The fact that a consortium blockchain provides industry actors with a stronger and more consistent voice with regulators might be the greatest benefit of this type of private blockchain. The lack of consistent regulatory approaches for blockchains continues to be a major obstacle to broader adoption; a consortium blockchain approach might present a viable solution.

Comparing Private and Public Blockchains

The processes of private blockchains are all permissioned, while the processes of public blockchains are all permissionless. How does this difference affect the functions of private and public blockchains? The comparison between public and private blockchains can focus on various differentiating factors that exist between these two general categories of blockchain, but they are primarily linked to the cost, complexity, and controls differences.

The comparison begins by examining how members are added to the network itself. Public blockchains generally have few to no restrictions of which individuals or institutions can become part of the network. A private blockchain is permissioned: a new actor can join the private blockchain only if some external authority approves that actor. In a previous example, if an organization with a private supply blockchain contracted with another supplier, the organization would choose whether to add that supplier to its blockchain. The organization would also remove any supplier from the blockchain with whom it had ceased doing business. Members may also have different levels of access to the blockchain based upon their permissioned status.

Next, the comparison turns to how data are added to the blockchain. Due to its open membership access, a public blockchain must have a rigorous consensus methodology to approve any data to be added to the record. Various consensus methodologies exist, but the most common one for a public blockchain is the proof-of-work (PoW) system, wherein network members known as full nodes compete to solve a mathematical puzzle. These full nodes are incentivized to participate, and make the required investments to do so, due to the compensation in the form of coins or tokens earned by the full node that correctly solves the problem first. They can earn additional compensation by validating individual transactions and blocks, which assists in keeping full nodes engaged and active.

Conversely, private blockchains do not require such a complex consensus or compensation system because they are organized and managed by either a single or small group of organizations. The permissioned members may also have different levels of access to the network and data layers. For example, a relatively small group of network members may have the ability to add information to the blockchain, with a much larger pool of participants being able to participate in a read-only mode. An analogy is internet search engines. Anyone with an internet connection can search and view stored information, but only a selected small group has the ability to edit either how that information is presented or what results appear in certain order. A use case for a private permissioned blockchain data layer would be for organizations or agencies that might be required to disclose additional information, such as nonprofits or governmental agencies. A private permissioned blockchain would allow the entity to report financial information, disclose nonfinancial information, but to control the ability of how to update these data.

More broadly, the issue of scalability differentiates public and private blockchains. Inherent in a private blockchain is a higher level of trust between members since members need to be actively admitted to this private network, unlike a public blockchain where anyone can join. This higher implied trust also means that the consensus methodologies to approve data, changes to the protocol, or other decisions requiring agreement can be simpler and therefore more scalable. Reducing the complexity of consensus also means that a wider range of organizations, across a spectrum of technical expertise and personnel, can be members of the network. Limiting participation to approved or vetted members only means that the size of the blockchain record is more or less controllable and modified as business needs dictate.

In contrast, the trustless consensus methodologies often used by public blockchains for transaction or record validation, such as Nakamoto consensus PoW models, intentionally slow down transaction validation as a means to maintain data integrity and accuracy. This transaction validation rate (a minimum of 10 minutes for bitcoin) is incompatible with required speeds for commercial enterprises, while also potentially requiring vast amounts of computational power. While developers of a “trustless” public blockchain must focus on data integrity and accuracy, developers of private blockchains with “trusted” members can focus relatively more on transaction processing and posting speed.

Consequently, private blockchains can more often achieve enterprise level speed and capacity since the process for adding transactions is not as complex or as time-consuming. This characteristic of private blockchains helps to explain the rationale for their initial development. Although management teams recognized the benefits of blockchain technology, the lack of enterprise level processing speed rendered them only marginally useful. Implementing blockchain in the private sector has not been connected to public blockchains, but instead has consisted almost entirely of different types of private blockchains.

Cost is also an area differentiating implementing public versus private blockchains. The development and implementation costs of blockchains such as personnel, software, hardware, and employee training are similar to other large-scale technology projects. A private blockchain also enables allocating these costs among network members. Thus, if an entity wants to join a private blockchain, that entity can more accurately forecast and budget for these costs since the development of a private blockchain involves a specific purpose. Public blockchains, notably the bitcoin and Ethereum blockchain, are not designed for institutional or commercial adoption, which in turn leads to the large-scale customization. By contrast, private blockchains are developed and built for enterprise adoption and can be designed as an expansion or reinterpretation of current enterprise database systems. As a result of this deliberate design, executives can better understand the cost structure of implementation.

Both types of blockchains can add value to particular use cases, but these use cases vary. Hybrid blockchains blend the benefits and costs of private and public blockchains attempting to combine some qualities of both.

Motivating Hybrid Blockchains

Why would any enterprise choose a hybrid blockchain instead of a public or private blockchain? As previously noted, the decentralized design of public blockchains was not designed for enterprise use. Bitcoin's original idea was to disrupt and disintermediate traditional financial structures by engaging in pure peer-to-peer digital transfers with no singular entity in control or holding any influence. That is, anyone could join or use the blockchain. The lack of a coordinating responsible entity, while key for the original cypherpunk method of bitcoin, poses legal and profit-claiming problems when moved to a business or enterprise context.

But why not simply adopt a private blockchain? The fully permissioned nature of a private blockchain imposes a cost of exclusion. Because everyone cannot join or use the network, the enterprise cannot reach its full market or engage in all the processes or data activities desired by its business model. A hybrid blockchain allows an enterprise to retain a blockchain's decentralized aspect for the permissionless part of its business model, while retaining control over parts that could be used to generate profits or to meet a legal liability or adherence perspective such as transaction information of users. Of course, enterprises could opportunistically use the terminology of “hybrid blockchain” as a marketing ploy, leaving only nonessential or superficial aspects of their blockchain decentralized while maintaining control over key functions. A hybrid blockchain contains several processes or components that an enterprise maintains under both a permissioned and a permissionless setting, which is a hybrid of the private and public blockchain.

A hybrid blockchain could allow network access only to those users with desirable identities such as users with no criminal history or corroborated financial documentation. Or, it could allow any users who carry the appropriate token issued by a separate “identity-checking” blockchain. Alternatively, a hybrid blockchain could allow anyone network access, but restrict who is allowed to make modifications to the underlying code (protocol), instead of using the anarchic system embedded within a permissionless system, allowing it to retain control of any updates to its product or project.

A hybrid blockchain with a centralized decision-maker model may be able to implement decisions more quickly and flexibly than a public blockchain that must wait for consensus. This scaling capability that can be delivered via a hybrid blockchain allows for speed and flexibility, which is something increasingly necessary in a globalized digital business landscape, but it does so at the cost of introducing centralized control. Despite these benefits associated with hybrid blockchains, this subset of blockchain is not a monolithic field but rather is divided into different applications.

Data Immutability

Most discussions around private and hybrid blockchains focus on restrictions to processes in the data layer (e.g., who can provide the data in the input component or benefit from the PETs component) or the network layer (e.g., who can engage in the transaction validation process or record validation process). Such discussions usually ignore the layer hierarchy, which becomes clear only when approaching a DLT as interacting layers within a system.

The protocol layer, as the basis of all the code, can be altered to change any process in the network or data layer. An example of the power invested in the protocol layer is a hard fork, which is a change made to the protocol so that transactions made before the fork date are no longer reconcilable with the new network processes, or in which transaction data are removed or rolled back. The latter case occurred under the decentralized autonomous organization (DAO) hack, where a portion of the Ethereum community agreed to erase the hack transaction, while the remainder believed that doing so would violate the ethos of a tamper-resistance decentralization, leading to splitting Ethereum into Ethereum and Ethereum Classic. The ability to alter any other layer makes the protocol layer the most powerful of the three layers that comprise a DLT system.

The network layer cannot affect the protocol layer beyond what is allowed by the dictates of the code determined in the protocol layer, but it can impose restrictions on the data layer. For example, transaction processing can be designed to censor or reverse elements of submitted data. The data layer cannot impose limitations on the protocol or network layer, unless allowed by PETs. This ordering determines the hierarchy between the three layers in a DLT, as shown in Fig. 6.2 adapted from Rauchs et al. (2018).

Fig. 6.2. The Layer Hierarchy of a Distributed Ledger Technology (DLT) System. Note: This figure shows that the three layers of a DLT system have different amounts of power. The data layer cannot affect the protocol or network layer beyond what may be allowed in the code. A change in the protocol layer can override pre-existing systems or data in the network or data layers. Source: Adapted from Rauchs et al. (2018).

As the protocol layer can override both the data and network layers, any data stored or processed by a hybrid or private blockchain in which the protocol layer is permissioned can be changed if the entities want it to be. Whether that change involves deletion or rejection depends on the nature of the protocol.

Data Privacy and Anonymity

Blockchain data are a trade-off between anonymity and privacy. In a public blockchain, all transactions and records are viewable: no privacy is available. However, these data only associate a transaction with a wallet or similar identity number. This number is not connected to a “real-world” (off-chain) identity, meaning that the data are anonymous. In a completely private blockchain, any entity must be given permission to include its data on the blockchain. It thereby creates a link between an entity's real-world identity and the data it generates, instead of merely creating a link between a freely available wallet number and the data associated with that wallet. This situation means that a lower level of anonymity is associated with transactions on a private blockchain. However, because only authorized individuals may view the private blockchain transaction data, more data privacy is available.

The degree of privacy and anonymity an organization or individual in a hybrid blockchain enjoys depends on permissioned settings of the various processes in blockchain. Whether inadvertent or intentional, disclosure or access to proprietary or confidential information by the hybrid blockchain's organizing entities may be a legal requirement. Represented most notably by the implementation of the General Data Protection Regulation in 2018, many other data privacy and reporting regulations exist that can equally and thoroughly forestall wider adoption.

Applications

This section summarizes several applications of private, hybrid, and public blockchains to contrast the costs and benefits for each model. A clear contrasting case of public, private, and hybrid blockchains occurs in the parallel development paths of stablecoins and central bank digital currencies (CBDCs), both of which are designed to be a purely digital means of payment. Stablecoins began from the fully public blockchain of bitcoin, with their hybrid blockchains representing certain processes becoming permissioned or private in comparison to bitcoin. In contrast, CBDCs began from private wholesale real-time gross settlement systems run by the monetary authority, and so the hybrid blockchain represents certain processes becoming public. This analysis also includes payment system projects because these can frequently blur the line of new money issuance and token issuance.

This chapter also examines two kinds of identity applications: (1) “goods” identity as represented by transportation tracking projects and (2) “individual” identity as represented by identity verification projects. Identity projects represent another aspect of hybrid blockchains as they potentially use the tamper-resistant data agglomeration's ability of a decentralized blockchain to affiliate data with a single individual, which can then be broadly or narrowly shared, whether or not desired by an individual.

Stablecoins

Stablecoins are a form of cryptocurrency that maintains a fixed price (a peg) relative to another commodity including currencies or basket of commodities. The most well-known stablecoin is the USD Tether, which maintains a peg of 1 Tether for 1 USD. Other stablecoins include the USD Coin (USDC) and DAI, which also maintains a 1:1 USD peg, and Digix Gold Token (DGX), which has a 1:1 peg with 1 gram of gold.

Stablecoin pegs are usually maintained using one of the two methods. In a reserve-backed system, the issuer maintains a reserve of the corresponding commodity that can be exchanged directly upon the receipt of the pegged coin. In a price stability mechanism, non–reserve-based methods are employed to manipulate the price into the desired peg range. Tether, USDC, and DGX all use a reserve-backed system, wherein users can theoretically exchange the stablecoin at the peg rate, drawing upon the reserves, at preselected institutions. The peg is then maintained through arbitrage at other locations. If users can obtain a better rate somewhere else either into or out of the stablecoin, they will trade at the alternate location until the price gap closes.

The maintenance of the reserve becomes a centralization point, as does the platform on which the reserve is exchanged for the stablecoin. Thus, stablecoins with a reserve-backed model become hybrid blockchains based upon the private governance layer, even if the data and network layers are public. In the case of a reserve-backed stablecoin, protocol governance and alteration can only be done by individuals employed by the project to maintain stability of any issuance, which must be met with the appropriate amount of reserves.

In contrast, DAI, a project on the Ethereum blockchain, uses a price stability mechanism, specifically a dual coin system involving a second coin, Maker (MKR), for governance. As a broad description of the mechanism, users can deposit ether as collateral to withdraw a DAI loan on which they must pay an interest rate. The interest rate changes to encourage individuals to withdraw more DAI, or to redeposit DAI they hold, which changes the relative supply of DAI in the market, and through that changes the price of DAI to maintain the peg. The DAO that governs the project, MakerDAO, sets the interest rate on DAI. The ownership of MKR tokens determines an individual's governance power within the MakerDAO system. This system can function as a completely public (nonhybrid) blockchain, as long as holding MKR tokens is sufficiently decentralized. If the other processes in the protocol layer are also open, then a stablecoin using a price stability mechanism could be a public blockchain, in contrast to the reserve-backed stablecoin, which must always be, at best, a hybrid.

Central Bank Digital Currencies

CBDCs are an old idea given new consideration with the rise of cryptocurrencies. In short, the question is whether the monetary authority should issue a parallel, or a replacement, digital form of its currency. Auer, Cornelli, and Frost (2020) provide a review of current CBDC projects.

Discussions about CBDCs predate blockchains and initially envisioned an entirely closed, centralized system of sovereign digital monetary issuance. As Berentsen and Schar (2018) contend, a completely open, decentralized blockchain implementation ‒ bitcoin, but by a monetary authority, which they term a central bank cryptocurrency (CBCC) – is incompatible with the underlying mission of most monetary authorities. A CBCC system would greatly increase an individual's ability to engage in tax evasion or money laundering due to the portability and pseudo-anonymity of the concept. Instead, Berentsen and Schar maintain that monetary authorities should issue central bank electronic money as their digital currencies, maintaining control over aspects of transaction verification, as well as potentially requiring unique and verifiable identification of users to gain access to the digital currency. In other words, central banks are more likely to implement a CBDC, which is a private or hybrid blockchain, than a CBCC, which is a public blockchain.

The question of user access and identification within a CBDC is an important one. As already discussed, a non–public blockchain does not have data immutability and comprises data anonymity for data privacy. By using a hybrid blockchain, the monetary authority could restrict access to the digital currency to only precleared users, such as individuals with passports or those who can clear background checks (retail access) or to prescreened companies wanting to engage in large transactions (wholesale). Bech and Garratt (2017) discuss the question of whether a CBDC should be retail (individual) or wholesale-only (large companies or large transactions). By using a hybrid blockchain and requiring user identification, a monetary authority can perfectly track all the transactions any individual undertakes, which could be used to document any activity the government associated with the monetary authority deems criminal.

Besides the ethical questions that this perfect monitoring raises, additional concerns exist if the CBDC's blockchain is also closed in its transaction verification component. If the blockchain is closed in these components, the monetary authority could, at the behest of the government, prevent or delete any transactions using CBDCs that are deemed illegal or counter to sovereign law ranging from an attempt to hire an assassin to political dissent depending on the government.

In a private blockchain, all these processes would be closed by default, and perfect monitoring and transaction denial would be de facto elements of the blockchain system. Moving to a hybrid blockchain means that at least a few of the processes must become open access and therefore represents a less restrictive framework relative to the original design. However, either of these design decisions is more restrictive than the current design of monetary issuance, namely cash, which is perfectly anonymous and does not have any transaction intermediaries. The only design that can replicate cash ‒ maintaining transaction anonymity and tamper resistance ‒ is a public blockchain. Although a closed protocol layer may not completely undermine a CBDC, it represents a permanent threat to the network's openness and data layer due to the hierarchy of the layers.

Payment System Projects by Monetary Authorities

Not all projects by monetary authorities in this space involve a redesign of money issuance processes. Some projects focus simply on the settlement or payment system design, triggered by the emergence of blockchain systems. Bank for International Settlements and Committee on Payment and Settlement Systems (2003) provide a detailed analysis of the role of monetary authority in payment systems.

These projects face the same concerns as CBDCs. Current experiments using open blockchains find that the scaling costs inherent within standard proof systems make a completely open design unfeasible (De Nederlandsche Bank 2018). However, as the current electronic wholesale payment systems, mostly designed in the 1980s and 1990s, are closed systems, a new system ‒ even a completely private blockchain ‒ would not introduce new restrictions on users or new monitoring on transactions unlike a hybrid CBDC.

Private Payment System Issuances: Libra

Libra is a well-known project in part because Facebook, a social media giant, is developing it. The Libra protocol layer is permissioned with the protocol layer centralized under the Libra Association. Consequently, Libra is an example of a consortium blockchain, which is a blockchain where the protocol layer is under the control of a consortium of firms that must govern according to legal frameworks and agreements external to the blockchain code. An example of the external, non–blockchain-based consortium governance decisions could be who qualifies for inclusion as a member of the consortium, as well as any rules or costs associated with exiting the consortium.

Under the initial design plan, a basket of currencies was to back the Libra currency. However, unlike the stablecoins, whether the Libra Foundation will explicitly use any mechanism beyond market arbitrage to maintain a price window for Libra is unclear. New versions of the plan consider using a basket of stablecoins instead.

Under the initial design plan, only designated entities could issue the wallets for use on the Libra system. This design associates each user's identity with the user's individual wallets and any transaction data the user accumulated while using Libra. In turn, this design allows Libra to provide regulatory compliance to antimoney laundering and international money transmission laws. Similarly, only entities granted permission into the Libra Association would be allowed to engage in the network layer. However, the current Libra design states that it intends for such engagements between association members to be competitive. Overall, the Libra blockchain will be, at best, a hybrid blockchain and not an open blockchain. However, whether the Libra blockchain will actually be a private blockchain or whether components will remain open once the system is launched is unclear.

Transportation Tracking

Transportation markets require coordination among the suppliers, transportation company, and the destination. Some goods may have multiple suppliers ‒ whether the good is a combination of different parts that get sent for assembly by a single supplier, or a good that is assembled by a series of suppliers ‒ each of which takes turns between being a supplier and a destination. The administrative logistics of transportation have resulted in several consortium blockchain projects such as the IBM e-BL project and the Waltonchain project. In both cases, members of the consortium can see elements of the data layer associated with the goods in which they are involved. Relative to the current approach where networks of logistic companies track goods, a hybrid blockchain could represent either a continuation of the pre-existing system or a more open version depending on network membership costs.

In contrast to the concerns with CBDCs, the de-anonymization inherent in these hybrid blockchain configurations represents an improvement over the current system. In the current system, suppliers are not supposed to be anonymous, and any destination should, in theory, have a perfect history of the supply path of any good. In reality, the length and complicated nature of supply chains make this situation nearly impossible for some goods, allowing record falsification or truncation. By allowing a perfect history, though still subject to concerns about data falsification, a hybrid blockchain allows the transportation logistic industry to adhere more closely to its original intention.

Identity Verification Projects by Public/Private Partnerships

A final application of hybrid blockchains is to identity verification projects. Identity verification is important for both governments for voting or taxpayer identification and private enterprises for employment clearance and customer accounts. Blockchain projects in this space attempt to give a single user a verified identity that can be shared with entities as the user chooses or is required, without requiring multiple pieces of documents or individual accounts with each enterprise.

As always, an individual government, private entity, or a consortium controls the protocol layer within these blockchain projects. Distinctions exist in the data layer and the network layer. If only the user or organization with permissioned access can input data into its identity component, the data layer must be closed. If any organization can input data but those data must be verified before being incorporated into the associated identity, then the data input component is open, but the network layer is closed. Although both approaches are examples of a hybrid blockchain, they present different points of models of affiliating data for association with a particular identity. In one model, care must be taken to only provide access to those who “should” be able to affiliate data with an identity, while in the other, the duty shifts to the data validators to only incorporate input data that are approved.

Whether an entity wants the data affiliated with its account may be an insufficient heuristic. In the case of a government identity project, an individual may not want a criminal history affiliated with his or her identity, but the project's design may make it mandatory. A particularly relevant question in this example is who is responsible for ensuring the external data's accuracy. Does this task fall to the blockchain project as the data agglomerator to ensure that all recorded data are correct (i.e., the individual committed the crime) or to the reporter (i.e., the burden is on the government to not falsely associate a criminal history with an individual)?

Key Considerations When Evaluating a Non–Public Blockchain

Without focusing on technical details, any institution or group of organizations seeking to implement a hybrid blockchain should take into account a few core considerations. Every blockchain is different, but the considerations below should form the basis for a robust conversation.

  • Which processes will be public, permissioned, and private? Why? If no need exists for any public processes, then the rationale for using a blockchain is unclear.
  • For processes identified as permissioned or private, which types of entities will participate in those blockchain processes and how do they gain that privilege? Depending on the industry, some organizations may be unable to share large amounts of information on a continuous basis and to comply with industry-specific regulations. Healthcare is an obvious example regarding patient privacy, but industries like insurance, real estate, tax, and other even accounting firms might not want to share too much data.
  • How can membership in processes be revoked? Who can choose to revoke membership, and how completely can the existence of the member be erased? For example, will all data associated with that member be permanently erased or will such data simply be rendered nonvisible?
  • Which entity or entities will provide the necessary resources to develop, test, implement, and maintain the hybrid blockchain? This question reveals the control of the protocol layer, the dominant layer in the hierarchy, and the key determinant for the preservation of the open processes. For example, if the five largest members of a network primarily fund a hybrid blockchain, then these members should have a dominant voice determining how to manage the network. Although seemingly sound in theory, such a concentrated model may be unsustainable and could ultimately lead to a splintering of the original members if the network ultimately grows to 1,000 members. Depending on how membership is granted or removed may not allow members to leave and create an alternative venture, while also preventing them from updating the current procedure.
  • How will this hybrid blockchain be governed and managed from an investor protection perspective? By default, a non–public blockchain model involves enterprises to manage the centralized aspect. This final issue includes questions about the source of profit expected from the hybrid blockchain. Governance and governance issues might not be of specific considerations that are normally discussed in the context of blockchain and technical implementation, but they are important for the sustained success of different blockchain initiatives, especially as some aspects of the blockchain become centralized as is the case for a hybrid blockchain.

Summary and Conclusions

In a hybrid blockchain, at least one layer has a permissioned component and at least one layer has a permissionless component. In a private blockchain, all or nearly all processes are permissioned or private. Various applications of hybrid blockchains are available, each of which could set different processes as permissioned/permissionless. What most hybrid blockchains have in common is a private or permissioned protocol layer, with a mix of permissionless and permissioned processes in the remaining layers. Although the specifics of the hybrid blockchain vary among implementations, these components tend to be similar. Of particular interest to implementing hybrid blockchains are the considerations and potential concerns connected to the governance of these blockchains and the development of applications such as CBDCs. Besides the technical and operational concerns linked to this area, considerations also involve consumer privacy. Regardless of how this subset of the blockchain ecosystem ultimately develops, considerations linked to these areas are likely to be of utmost importance to industry experts and technical consultants.
