Chapter 7

Consensus Mechanisms and Related Issues

Deniz Appelbaum

Keywords: Consensus mechanisms; blockchain; proof of work (PoW); hashing; proof of stake (PoS); mining; cryptography

Introduction

Consensus mechanisms are fundamental to public decentralized blockchain ledgers such as bitcoin. Bitcoin's underlying technology ‒ blockchain ‒ is a cryptographically secured methodology where transactions generated by anonymous participants are continuously and publicly being recorded (de Vries 2019). Without consensus mechanisms, the key features of the bitcoin blockchain ‒ tamper resistance, double-spending prevention, and provenance ‒ would not exist.

Consensus means arriving at a general agreement or unanimity. Consensus mechanisms in blockchains are features to consolidate the preferences and decisions of users and to manage decision-making of the network (Van Rijmenan and Ryan 2019). Consensus algorithms allow the public (permissionless) blockchain to operate without a third-party authority. In totally private (permissioned) blockchains, where participants are known to one another and granted access by the owner and governance is private, consensus is basically by authority or majority-rule. Private blockchains, where an owner allows outsiders to participate, might require some degree of consensus, depending on the application. A good illustration would be a blockchain hosted or owned by a large retailer such as Walmart where each external vendor is invited to participate in a smart contract to provide transparency to Walmart's food supply chain (Hyperledger 2019).

Consensus mechanisms are also deployed to prevent double spending in the digital currency world. Double spending refers to the case of two consecutive participants where the same token (asset) is sent to different parties within a few seconds (Wahab and Memood 2018). When double spending attempts occur within a normal fiat currency system using a bank, the bank would catch this attempt. However, bitcoins and blockchains do not use banks or other central authorities. Instead, bitcoin uses cryptography to make creating double or false transactions extremely difficult mathematically (Norman 2017).

Some contend that consensus mechanisms to address the Byzantine Generals' Problem (Lamport, Shostak, and Pease 1982). The problem basically is as follows: How can one be sure that different participants in distant locations can reach an agreement as to the best course of action? Imagine a Byzantine era (395–1453 ad) army that has an entire city encircled with its numerous divisions, and it has only one chance to attack (Christofi 2019). The city can only be overtaken by surprise. The generals heading these divisions must agree on a battle plan. With consensus being critical, they must agree on the next move and not deviate from the plan. However, traitors could be within their ranks or the messages between the generals may get mislaid or mistranslated. The traitor could be a lieutenant or the commander giving conflicting commands or thwarting messages. This problem could lead to different actions being taken, resulting in potential disaster for the army (Vaidya 2016). Lamport et al. (1982) suggest that the Byzantine army could withstand up to a third of the generals being traitors and still reach a consensus. Nakamoto (2008) put this Byzantine fault tolerance (BFT) algorithm into practice in 2008 with the Proof of Work (PoW) consensus mechanism.

This chapter provides fundamental information about consensus mechanisms and their essential role in blockchains. Any business contemplating adoption of blockchain, whether in digital currency or smart contract format, should understand consensus mechanisms and their implications for broad scale use. A smart contract is computer code operationalized within blockchain that “automatically moves digital assets according to pre-specified rules” (Buterin 2014a, p. 1).

The chapter has the following organization. It begins by providing a background of consensus mechanisms, followed by a discussion of the dominant mechanism ‒ PoW ‒ and its related issues. The chapter then offers a simple example of PoW complexity to further illustrate the difficulty inherent to the PoW process. Next, it presents a discussion of the second most popular consensus mechanism ‒ Proof of Stake (PoS) ‒ and its related issues, followed by a brief review of other methods. A summary analysis of consensus mechanisms concludes this chapter.

Background of Consensus Mechanisms

What kinds of processes in a public distributed ledger require consensus mechanisms? In a platform where all users and participants are “trustless,” somehow these transactions need a functional, reliable, and secure guarantee that they are genuine. Consensus mechanisms fulfill the task of guaranteeing the validity of blockchain transactions. The type of consensus mechanism required is dependent on its degree of centrality and the level of external investment by its users (Hays 2018; Voshmgir 2019). For example, bitcoin requires users to commit resources as an external commitment to its highly decentralized process (Hays 2018). In direct contrast, private blockchains do not require these external commitments to make network decisions. What follows is a discussion of PoW, its underlying hashing cryptography and related issues, followed by a review of PoS and other approaches and their related issues.

Proof of Work

PoW is the original consensus algorithm in a blockchain network. With PoW, adding new transaction blocks occurs with a process known as “mining.” In mining, miners use their computers to compete against one another to complete transactions on the network and get rewarded (Tar 2018). This process involves scanning for the value that when it is hashed, the hash results in a required number of zero bits (Nakamoto 2008). PoW slows down attackers and guarantees blockchain security because it rewards honesty and punishes false transactions (Norman 2017). PoW also reduces the speed with which transactions are verified and new blocks are certified, with the difficulty and parameters controlled by the network.

PoW provides two financial incentives for users to maintain the network: block rewards and transaction fees. Miners are rewarded a set bitcoin rate for each block created, and this amount halves about every four years or 210,000 transactions (Tar 2018). The last halving occurred in May 2020, taking the bitcoin (BC) rate down to 6.25 from 12.50 BC (Hertig 2020; Godbole 2020).

PoW is fundamental to Nakamoto's (2008) original proposal and its subsequent realization as bitcoins. The core components of PoW are:

  • No trusted third party is necessary and the network is peer-to-peer (P2P).
  • New transactions are time-stamped and hashed onto an ongoing chain of transactions.
  • The hashed record cannot be changed without redoing the prior transactions PoW.
  • PoW is accomplished by a pool of central processing units (CPUs) from the P2P network through computation.
  • The longest chain (block of transactions) includes the latest transaction and requires the most CPU work to create the hash. Therefore, it takes the most times, to date, to compute the hash.
  • The system works as long as the majority of P2P nodes are not colluding to subvert the chain since they could collectively represent the majority of the computing power and could compute the hash faster than any other group or participant.

Hashing Explained

Hash functions singlehandedly impart one of the most important properties to the blockchain ‒ immutability. Immutability means incapable of or insusceptible to change and where reverse engineering would be impossible. In the context of bitcoin, the transactions are taken as an input and run through a hashing algorithm, which gives an output of a fixed length. As Table 7.1 shows, in the case of SHA-256, which bitcoin uses, no matter how big or small the input is, the output always has a fixed length. One word, a picture, and a 400-page document all result in the same hash output length.

Table 7.1. Illustration of Different Input Lengths and Their Fixed Output Hashes.

Hello! 334d016f755cd6dc58c53a86e183882f8ec14f52fb05345887c8a5edd42c87b7
Hello! Welcome to this chapter about consensus mechanisms in blockchain! 2128b736fb8d0f26d17b62ac92966fc061e8cc8c1a929102b7efac860752782b

Note: This table illustrates that two different inputs result in hashes of the same length.

Secure Hashing Algorithms

Secure Hash Algorithms (SHAs) are a family of cryptographic hash functions published by the National Institute of Standards and Technology (Wikipedia 2020). SHA 256 produces a 256-bit hash of 64 hexadecimal digits. Bitcoin uses SHA-256 in two major ways:

  • Mining: In bitcoin, miners solve complex computational puzzles to find a block that then gets appended to the bitcoin blockchain.
  • Creation of addresses: The SHA-256 hash function is used to hash the bitcoin public key to generate the public address. Hashing the key adds an extra layer of protection to the person's identity. Plus, a hashed address is simply shorter in length than a bitcoin public key, which helps better in storage.

A cryptographic hash, sometimes called digest, is a kind of signature for a text or a data file. Try hashing a phrase with only changing whether the first letter is capitalized or not by clicking on one of the following hash calculators:

  • https://www.conversion-tool.com/sha256/
  • https://www.xorbin.com/tools/sha256-hash-calculator

For example, Table 7.2 shows the difference that occurs when changing just the beginning letter of a phrase from upper case to lower case.

Table 7.2. Difference in Hashes When Changing Only the Case of the First Letter.

Hello! 334d016f755cd6dc58c53a86e183882f8ec14f52fb05345887c8a5edd42c87b7
hello! Ce06092fb948d9ffac7d1a376e404b26b7575bcc11ee05a4615fef4fec3a308b

Note: This table illustrates how a small change of letter case results in an entirely different hash.

To summarize, PoW in bitcoin blockchains involves giving all of the nodes (computers) of the network this complex hashing problem. The nodes that choose to solve this problem are miners. Mining requires high-capacity hardware and considerable electrical power, as the mining is a repeated guess-and-check process in an attempt to find the right solution. Solving the puzzle does not take special skills or knowledge, just time, equipment, and power, democratizing the process. However, with the increasing availability of large quantum computers, cryptographic hashes are more susceptible to hacking and attacks, thereby challenging the security that cryptography provides (Bernstein and Lange 2017).

Creating a block includes not only the information of that block such as the input address, sender's address, amount, output address, and time stamp but also a portion of the hash from the previous block, the Merkle root of that block, and the nonce. A Merkle root is the hash of all the hashes of all the transactions that are part of a block in a blockchain network. A nonce is the answer to the puzzle, and it produces the hash with the required hexa-decimal string. A nonce means a “number used once” (Rouse 2019). For example, in bitcoin, a nonce currently must produce a hash that starts with 18 zeroes. By using the nonce, one can iteratively guess at the input of the transaction by trying different nonce values until it produces the required hash (Norman 2017). This component of blockchain is considered to be work, which is the unpleasant task of going through all of the nonce's number combinations given the other fixed information, until finding the required hash. Furthermore, the network rewards the miner who finds the lowest value nonce. According to Norman (2017), 2256 possible hash outputs exist. To date, no instance exists where two different inputs have produced the same hash output. The input and hashing process is actually more complex than what is described earlier as the transaction input includes the Merkle root hash. A Merkle root hash occurs when all of the transactions on that block get paired up and hashed together iteratively as a Merkle tree (Norman 2017), resulting in a unique Merkle root hash.

Bitcoin Blockchain and Proof of Work Example Case

In this case, a jewelry manufacturer (Global Bling) is creating a bitcoin blockchain to keep track of purchases of raw diamonds from one supplier (Vantage Mines). Vantage Mines charges varying prices based on diamond grades and current market conditions. Global Bling wants to create an immutable record of its diamond purchases from Vantage, meaning that the transaction records cannot be altered. Global Bling processes each diamond as a separate purchase and only purchases 1 carat diamonds of G color and SI1 clarity (Naturally Colored 2020 ).

The blockchain tracks the date, time, Buyer ID, Seller ID, asset, and transaction amount. The Merkle root hash is not calculated here as each block only contains one transaction. Jackie Bling is the buyer for Global Bling, and Terry Noble is the sales agent for Vantage Mines. Although this chain is private, the transactions are subject to regulatory oversight. Furthermore, Vantage Mines only operates with bitcoin currency. Table 7.3 shows the participant IDs.

Eventually, one randomly discovers that the nonce of “0018” provides a leading 0 as Fig. 7.5 shows:

As Fig. 7.6 shows, the current hash ID of Block #1 is the starting data for Block #2, which is how these two transactions are chained together. This means that if any data in Block #2 are changed, the change that bock's hash, which in turn changes the hash of that block, and so on. For any such change to be accepted, it needs to be revalidated by the miners, who likely would not receive incentives to work on an old block. In addition, the longer the block, the more difficult this revalidation process becomes. What follows is a simple illustration of such a rogue transaction.

Accounting Adjustment for Block #2: On February 19, 2020, Terry suddenly realizes that Transaction #2 should have been 0.65 BC and not 0.55 BC Remember that blockchains are immutable, meaning that transactions cannot be altered. Accounting adjustments happen frequently in business commerce. Can Terry change the transaction? Yes, and this is called Transaction 2X and only the price changes.

As Fig. 7.7 shows, the solution is arrived upon with a nonce of 0013.

Block 2X now has a current hash of 0adfec51, where Block 2 has a current hash of 0d435315. Block 2X cannot join the chain that was started with Transactions #1 and #2. Their hashes are now different. Although they both share Transaction 1, the adjustment shown in Block 2X results in a different current hash that does not match that of Block 2.

Fig. 7.2. Hash Results of the “0000” Nonce. Note: This figure shows the hash resulting from a nonce of 0000.

Fig. 7.3. Hash Results of the “0023” Nonce. Note: This figure shows the resulting hash from a nonce of 0023.

Fig. 7.4. First Block. Note: This figure shows a hypothetical configuration of the first or genesis block in the chain.

Fig. 7.5. Hash Value from the Nonce of “0018.” Note: This figure shows that a nonce of 0018 is the lowest input value that results in a hash of 0000.

Fig. 7.6. Blocks One and Two in the Blockchain. Note: This figure highlights the first and second block and how Block #2 is connected by the hash from Block #1.

Fig. 7.7. Hash Calculation of #2X with the Nonce of “0013.” Note: This figure illustrates the different hash that results from trying to modify the price from Block #2.

Related Issues of Proof of Work Consensus Mechanisms

As previously noted, blockchain networks deploying PoW consensus mechanisms require large quantities of energy and hardware equipment because of the mining process. Currently, many transactions exist with exceedingly long chains, compounded by an expanding mining industry, which result in increasing energy costs to find a block. This high cost of energy and equipment has led to the pooling or centralization of miners and resources. What follows is an expanded conversation of these issues.

Power Requirements

The amount of power that is required to mine bitcoin has become problematic (De Vries 2018). According to Nakamoto (2008, p. 3), PoW involves “scanning for a value that when hashed, such as with SHA-256, the hash begins with a number of zero bits.” Nakamoto acknowledges that mining requires expending large amounts of CPU time and power. The more difficult the hash calculations (e.g., solving for 18 leading zeroes is exponentially difficult), the greater the power demands.

To quantify, these costs or the energy requirements of the bitcoin network are equivalent to that of Denmark on an annual basis. One transaction is equal to the power consumption of an average US household for 24 days. The number of US households that could be powered by bitcoin to date is 7,127,396 (Digiconomist 2020).

These electrical requirements directly affect the cost to mine for bitcoins. The probability of randomly finding the solution to create the block and receive the reward of bitcoins is directly proportional to the miner's investment in power and equipment. Increasingly, more individuals are joining mining pools or concerns to partially compensate for these up-front costs. In mining pools, miners generally absorb their own costs but share in the findings or profits depending on each miner's power contribution. The more power that the mining hardware or equipment consumes, the higher is the hash rate (Beigel 2020). A hash rate refers to the miner's performance, which is the number of guesses a computer can make per second. The higher the hash rate, the higher is the potential profit from mining. Most mining has naturally centralized in counties such as China where electricity is comparatively cheap (De Vries 2018).

Hardware Demand

Early mining occurred in 2009 using CPUs. By the end of bitcoin's first year, miners began using graphic processing units (GPUs) because of their ability to handle repetitive work. One GPU equals roughly 30 CPUs in power (Beigel 2020). In 2011, miners began shifting to field programmable gate arrays, which are 30–100 times faster than GPUs; in 2013, they used application-specific integrated circuits (ASICs) (de Vries 2019). ASIC chips are dedicated to only one function ‒ mining. Nevertheless, being a sole miner is almost impossible and economically infeasible when vast mining pools undertake most mining (Tuwiner 2020).

Centralization of Mining and Mining Pools

The older or longer the blockchain, the harder the mining process becomes. Today, a transaction in bitcoins takes about 10 minutes to mine. Presently, six mining pools control about 75% of the mining power and 81% of that mining power originates in China (Godbole 2019). Software is sophisticated and mining concerns are located close to dams and/or in countries where power is cheap (Alethio 2018). Five mining pools share about 65% of the hash rate: F2Pool, Poolin, BTC.com, AntPool, and Unknown (https://www.blockchain.com/charts/pools). Theoretically, if these big mining concerns were to collude, they could feasibly launch a 51% attack and threaten immutability of the blockchain! A 51% attack on a blockchain refers to a miner or a group of miners trying to control more than 50% of a network's mining power, computing power, or hash rate. This fundamental risk of mining centralization that is inherent to PoW motivates interested parties to seek and develop other methodologies. This chapter covers these other methods in future sections.

Additional Concerns with Proof of Work

Several general points of vulnerability are because of the irreversibility of PoW consensus mechanisms ‒ race attack, Finney attack, vector 76 attack, alternative history attack, majority attack, denial of service attack, Sybil attack, and selfish mining. All of these terms are defined below. These are broad variations of double spending ‒ that is, the result of successfully spending digital currency more than once. Bitcoin users should protect themselves from double spending fraud by waiting for confirmations when receiving payments on the blockchain. Possessing bitcoins is not enforced by business rules and regulatory policy, but by cryptography techniques. Because bitcoin transactions are final, merchants do not need to gather extra customer information for verification of billing address and name. Bitcoin owners are anonymous except for their wallet addresses and county of origin. These challenges result from the features of public blockchains that are mainly designed to take advantage of the transaction immutability that PoW offers.

Race Attack

A race attack occurs when two transactions are created using the same funds at the exact same time, with the intention of spending the coins twice. The race attack is a specific type of double spending attempt. It requires the recipient to accept unconfirmed transactions as payment. A successful race attack is one where the payment recipient's node receives a spend transaction yet the next block that is mined has a different transaction that spends the same coin. Thus, the payment recipient's transaction does not confirm it, and the recipient never receives the funds (Bonadonna 2013).

Finney Attack

A variant race attack, called a Finney attack after Hal Finney, requires a miner's participation. Instead of sending both payment requests to pay say Bob and Alice with the same coins to the network, Eve issues only Alice's payment request to the network, while an accomplice tries to mine a block that includes the payment to Bob instead of Alice. The rogue miner is likely to succeed resulting in rejecting the payment to Alice (Karame, Androulaki, and Capkun 2012).

Vector 76 Attack

A Vector 76 attack, also called a one-confirmation attack, is a combination of a race attack and a Finney attack such that a transaction with even one confirmation can still be undone. Undertaking the same protective action as for the race attack (i.e., no incoming connections waiting for an explicit outgoing connection to a well-connected node) reduces the risk of this attack occurring (Sompolinsky and Zohar 2016).

Alternative History Attack

An alternative history attack can work even if a merchant waits for some confirmations but requires a relatively high-hash rate and the risk of substantial expense in wasted electricity to the attacking miner. The attacker submits to a merchant/network a transaction that pays the merchant, while privately mining an alternative blockchain fork in which a fraudulent double-spending transaction is included instead (Deirmentzoglou 2018). In theory, such an attack can undermine the double-spending protection provided by the bitcoin blockchain.

Majority Attack

A majority attack is also called a 51% attack or greater than 50% attack. If the attacker controls more than half of the network hash rate, the previously mentioned alternative history attack has a 100% probability of succeeding (Deirmentzoglou 2018).

Denial of Service Attack

A denial of service (DoS) attack occurs when so much data floods a node that it becomes too busy to process normal bitcoin and blockchain transactions. Some bitcoin features can deter this situation from happening. For example, too many blockchain nodes may be available for a DoS to effectively launch a flooding attack (Mirkin et al. 2019).

Sybil Attack

If an attacker attempts to fill the network with clients who the attacker controls, thereby creating a Sybil attack, a participant would then be likely to connect only to attacker nodes. Although bitcoin does not generally count the number of nodes, isolating a suspect node from the honest network can be helpful in the preventing the execution of other attacks (Alachkar and Gaastra 2018).

Selfish Mining Attack

A selfish mining attack, also known as a block withholding attack, is an attempt to discredit the network integrity (Eyal and Sirer 2014). Selfish mining attacks occur when an individual in a mining pool attempts to withhold a successfully validated block from being broadcast to the rest of the mining pool network (Golden 2020).

Because of the nature of PoW, all of these attacks on the network could be expensive to undertake. The following websites show the daily updated costs to attack blockchains with a 51% attack.

  • To conduct a basic 51% majority attack of bitcoin: https://goBitcoin.io/tools/cost-51-attack/.
  • To generate a 51% attack on other blockchains: https://www.crypto51.app/.

Proof of Stake

PoS is a P2P cryptocurrency consensus mechanism that King and Nadal (2012) proposed in response to the extreme energy demands and transaction costs posed by Nakamoto's (2008) PoW design. Generally speaking, PoS means a form of proof of ownership or “buy-in” of the currency (Voshmgir 2019). That is, the participant has a substantial commitment or investment from external sources in the digital currency. Recall the earlier discussion where the more anonymous and trustless the users, the more external anchor or commitment is required. PoS exemplifies this condition. Ethereum, the second largest exchange, is planning to switch from PoW to PoS in 2020 or 2021 (Won 2020).

In PoS, the creator of a new block is not a miner but is a validator, selected according to the percentage of coins that this person owns and how long these coins have been staked as collateral (Kim 2019). For example, if the validator owns 5% of the available Ethereum coins, this person has a 5% chance of being selected as a block's validator. The minimum stake to become a validator in Ethereum is 32 ether. If this person is selected, then the validator verifies and validates the new block of transactions. The validation process is simply taking the transactions that show up in the pool at that time, combining them in a block, and publishing it (Kim 2019). Validation could be considered a costless process in that the consensus mechanism is the trust that the validators are so invested in the chain that they work in its favor. The validator receives transaction fees but no block reward. To discourage malicious behavior, all staked coins (the collateral) belonging to the validator are lost if that person tries to verify false transactions (Wang et al. 2019). After a validator submits the block for approval, some time may pass before that person is selected again (Voshmgir 2019).

Since PoS does not require nearly as much power as PoW, the energy savings are substantial. With PoW, only one miner/computer can win so all the others experience sunk energy costs. Although PoS still requires other nodes in the network to approve the block, these computers are not running at maximum capacity as in PoW, and their energy costs are not lost. Ultimately, the true test of PoS at a major scale occurs when Ethereum implements it as Ethereum 2.0 (Voshmgir 2019).

Related Issues of Proof of Stake Consensus Mechanisms

Although PoS reduces the energy required to complete a block, its consensus protocol leaves it open to various attacks and is similar to PoW in this regard. PoS assumes and trusts that validators observe the PoS protocol as doing so is in their best interest, but this assumption is not always the case as the following attack schemes illustrate.

Nothing-at-Stake Attack

In PoS, the potential loss of economic value secures the network. During a block validation, the validator ideally does not incur many realized costs. With nothing-at-stake, a validator incurs no cost to validate transactions on several forks if more than one fork were to occur (Martinez 2018). A validator would be financially self-interested to collect transaction fees on whichever fork the network approves. This scenario also leaves the network vulnerable to double spending attacks (Wang et al. 2019). Ethereum is taking the nothing-at-stake theory seriously by penalizing instigators by seizing some or all of their stake (Voshmgir 2019).

Long-range Attack

A long-range attack is possible where a bad actor goes to the first block and forks the blockchain (Buterin 2014b). Because PoS is essentially a costless process, an attacker can easily populate the new branch with blocks that differ from the main chain. Once this created chain becomes longer than the current main chain, it dominates the network. Several variations of long-range attacks are possible including simple, posterior corruption, and stake bleeding (Deirmentzoglou 2018).

  • With a simple attack, the attacker produces blocks in advance and alters their time stamps to overtake the main chain.
  • With posterior corruption, former validators have no stake in the current chain and their private key might be stolen and used for corrupt purposes to successfully outpace the main chain.
  • In a stake bleeding attack, a bad actor stalls the main chain by skipping a turn to validate, thereby backing up the transactions to a later block. Meanwhile, the attacker adds more manufactured blocks to his/her false chain in a race to overtake the now-stalled main chain.
Precomputing (Grinding) Attack

A precomputing or grinding attack exploits the lack of randomness in the slot leader election process, where the slot leader can influence the frequency of being elected to validate (Vasin 2014). Randomness should be coded or enforced into this election process, eliminating the potential for corruption (Deimentzoglou, Papakyriakopoulos, and Patsakis 2019).

51% Attack

A 51% attack may pose a threat to any consensus mechanism (Deimentzoglou et al. 2019). In PoS mechanisms, one validator or a colluding group of validators can collectively own more than 34% of that chain's stake. Ostensibly a majority attack could challenge the approval of blocks.

Sybil Attack

A sybil attack usually refers to peer networks where members have equal rights. Blockchains should be able to mitigate these attacks if consensus algorithms are being used and enforced (Deimentzoglou et al. 2019). In PoS, a bad actor should be countered by the consensus protocol based on the stake or investment into the network by the participants.

Bribery or Short-range Attack

In a bribery or short-range attack, the attacker bribes the validator(s) with an amount equal to or greater than the block fee to work on the attacker's behalf. This amount would obviously need to be greater than the collateral that the validator has at stake. The validator could lose his/her entire holdings by creating a fake block, in addition to incurring reputational damage, so the bribe would need to be substantial (Deimentzoglou et al. 2019).

Liveness/Denial of Service Attack

A liveness attack is a form of DoS attack unique to PoS mechanisms. In this attack, some or many validators collude and purposefully stop approving and publishing blocks. The chain comes to a halt because the validators are not “live.” To mitigate this issue, the network should require that validators remain “live” on the chain or face financial punishment (Zamfir 2015).

In summary, although PoS does not pose the same energy and equipment requirements as PoW, some criticize the protocol as being naïve (Buterin 2014b). This naiveté exposes it to a broad range of attacks that emerge because of the trust that is native to PoS.

Other Consensus Mechanisms

As robust and secure as PoW and PoS may seem, both are vulnerable in practice to many attack schemes. PoW is energy inefficient subjecting it to centralization and environmental concerns. PoS appears to be naïve and is unproven at any major scale. These issues motivate additional investigation and research for other protocols, which are discussed next.

Delegated Proof of Stake

In a Delegated PoS, users can stake their coins to vote for a certain number of delegates. The weight of their vote depends on their stake. For example, if A stakes 10 coins for a delegate and B stakes 1 coin for a delegate, A's vote has 10 times more weight than B's vote. The delegates receiving the highest number of votes get to produce blocks and are rewarded for creating them (Blockgenic 2018).

Proof of Work/Proof of Stake Hybrid

A hybrid PoW/PoS consensus mechanism uses elements of both PoW and PoS models when determining transaction validation rights (Hays 2018; Wang et al. 2019). In doing so, these mechanisms aim to mitigate the respective weaknesses of each (Zano 2019). A hybrid consensus mechanism begins by having PoW miners create new blocks containing transactions to be added to the blockchain. Once these blocks have been created, PoS miners must vote on whether to confirm them.

Programmatic Proof of Work

Programmatic Proof of Work (ProgPoW) is a blockchain protocol consensus algorithm designed to reduce the mining efficiency advantage of specialized hardware like ASIC miners over less-advanced machines like a standard CPU, meaning average individual crypto participants could mine coins. Ever since the use of the first bitcoin mining ASIC machines, new iterations on the original PoW algorithm have been made with the intent of becoming ASIC-resistant. The goal of ASIC-resistance is to avoid the centralization of PoW mining power that would enable a few top participants to more easily manipulated a protocol (Wan and Long 2019).

Proof of Elapsed Time

Proof of Elapsed Time (PoET) is a consensus mechanism that aims to randomly and fairly decide who gets to produce a block based on their waiting time (Chen et al. 2017). To decide who gets to produce a block, the process assigns a random wait time to each node. The node whose wait time finishes first gets to produce the next block.

Proof of Storage

Proof of storage is a consensus protocol used primarily to verify the integrity of a remote file (Golden 2020). This task is done by sending an encoded copy of the data to a server and then executing a challenge-response protocol to check the data's integrity (Mattila 2016).

Proof of Retrievability

Proof of Retrievability (PoR) is a compact proof by a file system (prover) to a client (verifier) that a target file is intact, in the sense that the client can fully recover it (Bowers, Juels, and Oprea 2009). As PoRs incur lower communication complexity than transmitting the file itself, they are an attractive building block for high-assurance remote storage systems. PoR can be useful as a consensus algorithm for cloud computing systems (Miller, Juels, Shi, Parno, and Katz 2014).

Proof of Activity

Proof of Activity (PoA) is another hybrid of PoW and PoS that attempts to combine the best features of both mechanisms. In PoA, the mining process starts as a standard PoW process with various miners trying to outpace each other with higher computing power to find a new block. When a new block is found (mined), the system switches to PoS, with the newly found block containing only a header and the miner's reward address. Once all validators sign the newly found block, it gains the status of a complete block, gets identified and added to the blockchain network, and transactions start getting recorded on it (Frankenfeld 2019).

Proof of Burn

Proof of Burn (PoB) is an alternative consensus algorithm that tries to address the high energy consumption issue of a PoW system. It operates on the principle of allowing miners to “burn” virtual currency tokens. They are then granted the right to write blocks in proportion to the coins burnt. Iain Stewart, the inventor of the PoB algorithm, describes burnt coins as mining rigs (Kenton 2020). In this analogy, a miner burns his/her coins to buy a virtual mining rig that gives the power to mine blocks. The more coins the miner burns, the bigger is the virtual mining “rig” (Karantias, Kiayias, and Zindros 2019).

Proof of Capacity

Proof of Capacity (PoC) is a consensus mechanism that uses a process called plotting (Wahab and Mehmood 2018). With PoC solutions are pre-stored in digital storage like hard disks (Mattila 2016). This process is called plotting. After a storage has been plotted, meaning it has been filled with solutions, it can take part in the block creation process. Whoever has the fastest solution to the puzzle of a (new) block gets to create the new block. The greater the storage capacity, the more solutions can be stored and the higher are the odds of creating a block (Wahab and Mehmood 2018).

Byzantine-Fault Tolerance Method, Practical Byzantine Fault Tolerant, and Delegated Byzantine Fault Tolerant

The Byzantine-Fault Tolerance method is a solution of the Byzantine Generals' Problem, where the blockchain is designed to run successfully despite the errors or malicious actions of a few and precedes PoW (de Castro and Liskov 2003). PBFT is designed to run practically in asynchronous online environments, such as found in private blockchains (de Castro 2000; de Castro and Liskov 2003). Because PBFT works better in private chains with limited users, DBFT is proposed to allow consensus in public networks (Christofi 2019).

Summary and Conclusions

All consensus mechanisms have the same goal of reaching consensus in a largely decentralized network. Despite having a common goal, they vary substantially in their approach to reaching consensus. Although the perfect consensus mechanism does not currently exist, understanding how such mechanisms have evolved and adapted is worthwhile. To date, the most secure consensus mechanism is still PoW, the original one used by bitcoin. However, PoW relies on miners resulting in their centralization in countries where electricity is cheap. Whether a business would want its transactions validated by a changing pool of miners located in remote locations is debatable.

Currently, PoW appears to be unchallenged in the immutability and security that it provides the bitcoin network and Ethereum (Van Rijmenam and Ryan 2018). It resolves the Byzantine Generals' Problem of authenticity verification and mitigates double spending. However, these features come at a great cost in power, equipment, speed, scalability, and mining concerns. Although researchers are trying to develop other consensus mechanisms that are more scalable for business, nothing as secure as PoW has materialized. PoS has yet to be adopted at a large scale and many other mechanisms are proposed but not supported with additional research and practical testing (Voshmgir 2019). For now, PoW appears to be the only consensus mechanism that provides the features that a broad scale distributed network requires, despite its poor scalability.
