Chapter 8

Token Economies

Alim Khamisa

Keywords: Token economy; Web 3.0; decentralized applications; cryptoeconomics; token engineering; token systems

Introduction

Blockchain networks enable trustless data transactions to take place between an ecosystem of individuals, businesses, and stakeholders in an adversarial environment. Trustless systems do not require the transacting parties to know one another or to rely on a trusted third party (any of which could be arbitrarily malicious actors) to facilitate the transaction. The data transactions can represent any form of value – monetary currency, physical assets like precious metals or real estate, intangible assets like a unit of energy or a loyalty point, or they can represent access to a specific utility including the right to consume a resource or the right to vote. The possibilities are vast. Cryptographic tokens, more commonly called crypto tokens, which are native to the respective blockchains on which they reside, are fundamental to the value transfer mechanism. Crypto tokens are analogous to data packets traversing a network in that bits of value can be transmitted the same way bits of information move over the internet (Walden 2020a). However, a critical distinction exists. For example, data shared over the internet is sent to the recipient as a copy; on a blockchain network, transfer of a digital asset means the sender is no longer in possession of it. Blockchain-based digital assets are designed to be unique, liquid, secure, instantly transferrable, and digitally scarce (ConsenSys 2020).

The concept of a crypto token, often referred to as a cryptocurrency or crypto asset, and henceforth simply as a token, is highly flexible and can represent a wide range of programmable assets or access rights managed by a smart contract and underlying blockchain. Tokens are tradable and transferable among the various participants on the blockchain, and as such, blockchain networks provide the ideal infrastructure for building token economies. Tokens are in fact a breakthrough in the design of decentralized networks. They provide entirely new ways to incentivize network participants to support the network and encourage the frictionless movement of value. Succinctly put by Outlier Ventures, “from capital to computing power, and data to people and their assets, tokens allow us to coordinate and optimize large networks of resources in a decentralized manner and at scale” (Dhaliwal and Gurguc 2018, p. 11). Furthermore, by enabling the development of new open networks, tokens may help to reverse the centralization of the internet, thereby keeping it more accessible and fair. This is ushering in entirely new socioeconomic systems that disintermediate rent-seeking business models and eliminate deep-rooted economic inefficiencies, as is made evident by the fact that token economies strive to be peer-to-peer (P2P) network co-ops. Sharing economy companies employing a multisided platform strategy, and often viewed as a public utility (e.g., Uber, Airbnb, and LendingClub) could also be organized as decentralized nonprofits to benefit citizens.

The world saw a Cambrian explosion of tokens through the cryptocurrency movement that began with the introduction of Bitcoin in 2008 and accelerated with the launch of Ethereum in 2015. This movement followed the open source software movement that began in the early 1980s at MIT with Richard Stallman's GNU project, and was most visibly led by Linux starting in the early 1990s; the open information movement most visibly led by Wikipedia in the early 2000s and intensified with Aaron Swartz's Guerilla Open Access Manifesto in 2008; and preceded the open data movement, which gained momentum with the rise of open APIs and open data platforms like CKAN. Open source blockchain networks and the emergence of popular token standards have democratized the development process for the creation of tokens. Over 7,000 different crypto tokens are currently in existence (CoinMarketCap 2020). Some have experienced significant traction while numerous others took a more precarious path to market with lackluster adoption, many of which have since become defunct. Token economy design entails a rigorous engineering approach with a key focus on incentive mechanism design. Sustainable token economies must incentivize individual actions toward a collective set of goals, which if done correctly, can lead to a virtuous cycle of growth propelled by network effects.

This chapter aims to serve as an entry point for the study of blockchain-based token economies in the context of decentralized networks and Web 3.0, also called Web3. It provides an overview of Web 3.0, token fundamentals, token economy design, and the critical considerations that anyone endeavoring to create a thriving token economy should contemplate.

Web 3.0

The technology stack (infrastructure components) of the internet is currently being reconstructed. To understand why requires examining a brief history of the World Wide Web, more commonly known as the web. Web 1.0, referred to as the “read-only web” by Sir Tim Berners-Lee, inventor of the web, was characterized by simple static websites (Berners-Lee 1996).The power of the web to harness collective intelligence through hyperlinking, cataloging information, and making it searchable drove the success of companies in this era (O'Reilly 2007). Web 2.0, or the current “read-write” web, is characterized as the participative web, driven by interactive user-created content, social networking, and e-commerce (Vickery, Wunsch-Vincent and OECD 2007).

Evolution of the Web: From Web 2.0 to Web 3.0

Decades into the mass adoption of the internet, the data architectures are still based on the client-server model where data are centrally stored and managed (Voshmgir 2019). This architecture has resulted in a highly centralized web. The web's centralized nature makes it vulnerable to security threats, malicious data gathering by intermediaries, privacy intrusion, and adds cost for end users (Shaikh 2019). Web 2.0 enabled rich and seamless interactions on a global scale, but always with a middleman: a platform acting as a trusted intermediary that dictates the rules of these interactions and transactions while controlling all of the user data. While Web 2.0 further democratized participation in the web, creating new opportunities that arose from the ubiquity of mobile connectivity, the economic engine is still largely privatized and monopolized (Zago 2018). Berners-Lee (2018, para. 1) aptly describes this status quo as follows: “[F]or all the good we've achieved, the web has evolved into an engine of inequity and division; swayed by powerful forces who use it for their own agendas.”

Internet-based companies today are stockpiling user data – identities, addresses, searches, likes, messages, ad clicks, and online shopping information – on centralized servers, attracting cyber attackers, raising data privacy concerns, and exacerbating social inequality by serving their own economic interests over that of the general public. Globally, data privacy and transparency concerns are intensifying – as evidenced by the Global Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) – clearing a path for a more decentralized, secure, and transparent web where users regain complete control of their data. Assuming Web 1.0 revolutionized information and Web 2.0 did the same for interactions, Web 3.0 has the potential to revolutionize data privacy, security, value exchange, and more fundamentally, how data are coordinated, distributed, and automated. Open (public) blockchain networks are a foundational layer of the Web 3.0 technology stack. These networks revolutionize where trust is placed – in the code, not in companies or people – by converting energy-intensive computation into economically valuable trust (Berg, Davidson, and Potts 2017).

Fig. 8.1 depicts the evolution of the web from Web 1.0 (read-only web) to Web 2.0 (read-write web) to Web 3.0 (read-write-execute web). Web 3.0 leapfrogs the centralized model of Web 2.0 where trusted third parties provide security and take custody of valuable data. Web 3.0 is a more user-centric web where public blockchain networks eliminate the need for trusted third parties enabling users to assume self-sovereignty over their data and digital identity.

Fig. 8.1. Evolution of the Web. Note: This figure depicts the evolution of the web from Web 1.0 (read-only web) to Web 2.0 (read-write web) to Web 3.0 or Web3 (read-write-execute web). Web 3.0 dApps communicate with a blockchain network through a blockchain client (crypto wallet).

The Web3 Foundation (2020, p. 1) formally defines Web3.0 as “... a decentralized and fair internet where users control their own data, identity and destiny.” It outlines three key accompanying tenets:

  • Users own their own data, not corporations,
  • Global digital transactions are secure, and
  • Online exchange of information and value are decentralized.

Web 3.0 enables user-controlled privacy through self-sovereign identity and full control of one's data. This has enormous implications around how data are shared and monetized, with users being able to participate directly in the economics flowing from the use of their data. Basic Attention Token (BAT), for example, works with the Brave browser to allow users to monetize their attention for viewing ads in exchange for a portion of the payout that would normally be taken entirely by the publisher (i.e., Google). Web 3.0 platforms like BAT and others are likely to transform information networks and economic organizations as the flow of information and economic value converge. Traditional organizations will be converted into distributed markets based on tokens (cryptonetworks) where tokens define whatever is of value within the organization and the market system is used as a distributed coordination mechanism for managing and growing that resource (Systems Innovation 2019).

Stateful Web and the Web 3.0 Stack

Web 2.0 was never built to facilitate the secure exchange of value in a P2P way. This is primarily due to the fact that it lacks “state” or unique data concerning session information and status about each communicating entity in a web interaction. The Internet Protocol (IP) and the Hypertext Transfer Protocol (HTTP), foundational to today's internet, are stateless protocols. As a result, today's internet requires rent-seeking gatekeepers with proprietary rails to intermediate the trillions of dollars of financial transactions and valuable data that propagate across their networks each day. These fragile systems require massive cybersecurity investments to thwart attackers and maintain system integrity. Large internet companies like Google, Facebook, Amazon, Apple, Alibaba, and Tencent all hold state. Thus, these giants alone accrue the value generated by their billions of users. Web 3.0 rewires the backend of the internet by introducing a universal state layer based on battle-hardened cryptographic protocols. For the first time, this unique state layer gives users a way to hold state (economic value) in a digitally native way and transfer it to any participant, enabling truly P2P transactions without intermediaries. With this value settlement layer now in place, a protocol-level metamorphosis has been set into motion; the world is moving from the internet of information to the internet of value.

The technology stack of Web 3.0 is nascent with many building blocks still under development. It is giving rise to decentralized applications (dApps): open source applications that run autonomously on a decentralized P2P network. In stark contrast to traditional apps where the backend code runs on centralized servers, dApps run on decentralized blockchain networks and typically feature a native token. Similar to more traditional apps, a dApp's frontend code and user interface can be written in any programming language. However, unlike traditional apps, some dApps have their frontend code hosted on a decentralized storage network like the InterPlanetary File System (IPFS) or Swarm. IPFS is a P2P hypermedia protocol created as a distributed system for storing and accessing files, websites, applications, and data. It supports a more resilient internet, substantially increasing the difficulty for those attempting to censor content, and can actually speed up the web by sourcing content from nodes in the network in closer proximity to the node making the request (InterPlanetary File System 2019). With some of the key components of the Web 3.0 stack elucidated, Fig. 8.2 presents a highly simplistic visual depiction.

Fig. 8.2. Web 3.0 Stack. Note: This figure shows a highly simplified view of the Web 3.0 technology stack. For simplicity, many key layers and substacks have been abstracted away.

Web 3.0 is still in the early stages of adoption and thus being used primarily by tech-savvy individuals armed with the knowledge and patience to make it work. As the technology develops further, the decentralized web will become accessible to everyone. From a user experience perspective, the ultimate goal is to be able to use dApps without needing to know what lies “under the hood.” Product development teams are working to abstract away the technical complexity and eliminate any unnecessary cognitive load on end users. The transition from Web 2.0 to Web 3.0 will be gradual but the results will be profound – a new more transparent web, collectively owned and trusted to remain neutral to all parties. At the core of this new web are token economies driven by new open source business models that promote shared economics for all parties involved.

Token Fundamentals

As the Blockchain Research Institute describes, tokens today have different features and purposes, but all share several characteristics: they are valuable, representative, digital, discrete, and authentic. Value is partly derived from token demand and the token's issuance policy, which typically ensures scarcity. Tokens are representative in the sense that they stand for the holder's claim to an asset, resource, or right; digital as they are issued on a blockchain and stored in a crypto wallet; discrete in that they can be counted and verified, and are distinguishable among other tokens; and authentic in that authenticity can be verified on the token's respective blockchain ledger (Tapscott 2020). Public blockchains are auditable, indelible, and provide a full longitudinal history of asset creation (and destruction if functionality available) and transaction history.

An array of token types and use cases has emerged in the wake of bitcoin, the first blockchain native cryptographic token. As outlined in the seminal whitepaper, bitcoin was created to enable a trustless system of P2P electronic transactions (Nakamoto 2008). More widely known as a cryptocurrency, it is effectively digital money for the internet. Money has essentially three well-defined functions: it serves as a medium of exchange (MoE), store of value (SoV), and unit of account (Burniske and Tatar 2017). Bitcoin's value is derived from its utility as money, which is rooted in its costly production process and the security of its blockchain. Cryptocurrencies like bitcoin are a core component of the incentive scheme of blockchain infrastructure, rewarded to transaction validators (miners) who may decide to hold on to it as a SoV (like gold), use it as a MoE to acquire goods and services or other cryptocurrencies or tokens, or use it as collateral to securitize debt.

Similar to the Bitcoin blockchain, Ethereum also has its own native cryptocurrency called Ether (ETH). Ethereum and other programmable blockchains enable the creation of new application layer tokens and token economies native to the dApps for which they were created. Here an important distinction can be made between cryptocurrencies, known colloquially as “coins” and tokens. Cryptocurrencies like bitcoin, Ether, and Litecoin have their own blockchains. Tokens, in contrast, are created on top of other programmable blockchains via smart contracts. The Ethereum blockchain has thousands of tokens currently operating on top of its network.

Token Taxonomy

All token types described in this chapter are encompassed under the general term crypto assets, which are digital assets using cryptographic techniques to regulate the generation of units of the asset and to verify their transfer between parties via a blockchain without a central party (Ernst &Young 2018). This taxonomy classifies crypto assets into three major groups: SoV and MoE tokens, utility tokens, and security tokens (Fig. 8.3).

Fig. 8.3. Taxonomy of Crypto Assets. Note: This figure provides a taxonomy of crypto assets. As the domain continues to evolve, new crypto assets may emerge, hence the need for a dynamic classification framework. Some crypto assets may be characterized as hybrid tokens and span across multiple groups. For example, a tokenized precious metal may be considered both a commodity and SoV asset. Crypto collectibles may be both an SoV asset and can also have utility in some cases. Security tokens are beyond the scope of this chapter but are covered elsewhere in this book. Security tokens may include other financial assets such as derivatives not shown in this diagram.

SoV and MoE Tokens

SoV and MoE tokens include cryptocurrencies, stablecoins, and crypto collectibles. Cryptocurrencies and stablecoins are typically used for the purposes of payments; stablecoins emerged out of the need to solve for cryptocurrency volatility (FINMA 2019). Stablecoins aim to achieve stable value relative to fiat currencies by linking the price to one or more underlying assets. The simplest approach is the depository receipt model whereby the stablecoin is a direct claim on a single fiat currency (G7 Working Group on Stablecoins 2019). An example is USD Coin (USDC), which is backed by fully reserved assets and redeemable on a one-to-one basis for US dollars. QCAD, a Canadian dollar-backed stablecoin, operates the same way.

A second design model is the cryptocurrency-backed stablecoin. The most prominent example is Dai, a decentralized stablecoin soft pegged to the US dollar. It is generated, backed, and kept stable algorithmically through smart contract “vaults” that contain the collateral and are inherently noncustodial (MakerDAO 2019). Other stablecoin models also exist, which include linking a stablecoin's value to a basket of reference assets, such as fiat currencies, cryptocurrencies, commodities, and securities, in an indirect way, much like an exchange-traded fund (ETF). Facebook's proposed Libra stablecoins are a prime example, as each currency-specific stablecoin (pending regulatory approval) will be backed by a reserve of highly liquid assets such as cash, cash equivalents, and short-term government securities (Libra Association 2020). Although stablecoin adoption has risen dramatically over the years making global payments faster, cheaper, and more inclusive, only fully decentralized stablecoins void of a central authority are truly aligned with the ethos of Web 3.0.

Crypto collectibles comprise the third token type within the SoV and MoE group. They are nonfungible (i.e., unique and noninterchangeable) blockchain-native crypto assets. Examples include blockchain-based games CryptoKitties and Decentraland where players can create, collect, and trade unique in-game assets such as virtual cats, land, and avatars; crypto art; and crypto stamps (Binance Academy 2020). Crypto collectibles may be viewed as hybrid assets as they can be used as a SoV. Additionally, some have utility, particularly in gaming, as they can serve various functional purposes within their respective dApps as required for game-play or in the generation of new crypto collectibles.

Utility Tokens

Utility tokens provide holders with access to a digital product or service and derive their value from this underlying right. Although they can be traded between token holders, utility tokens are not primarily used as an MoE (Leopold and Vollmann 2019). They are typically issued through a token sale such as a smart contract-based initial coin offering (ICO), which is a mechanism to raise external funding through the emission of tokens in exchange for cryptocurrencies such as ETH. Utility tokens carry a promise that the token can be redeemed for the ICO project's products or services once they are developed although investors in utility tokens do not hold enforceable claims in many jurisdictions (Momtaz 2020). These tokens are typically developed for use within a dApp that resides on top of an existing decentralized blockchain network like Ethereum. The relation between the network and utility token is synergistic in that the network provides security for the token while the token provides the network activity required to strengthen the network's own token economy (MakerDAO 2020).

Several types of utility tokens exist, and new ones are likely to emerge as new use cases are identified. Four types are briefly outlined – governance, discount, work, and burn and mint tokens.

  • Governance tokens: Governance tokens aim to decentralize the governance of a blockchain network and empower the community to participate in a democratic process concerning the evolution or upgrade of the network. Governance tokens confer holders the power to influence decisions concerning the core protocol, product and roadmap, hiring, token treasury management, and changes to governance parameters (Smith + Crown 2019). They are central to blockchain-based voting systems. An example is the MakerDAO ecosystem, where a decentralized community of MKR token holders governs the maker protocol, which consists of the smart contracts that power the Dai stablecoin.
  • Discount tokens: Discount tokens entitle holders to a perpetual discount on services offered through the network or dApp but are structured in a way such that the discount is mathematically equivalent to a revenue or fee royalty, with the caveat that the benefit is only received if the token holder uses the services. In one approach, the discount tokens are not invalidated when used but remain in possession of their holders. The discount that each token confers to its holder is designed to grow in line with the overall adoption and utilization of the network-based service (Felix 2018). Several variations of this model exist revolving around holding/staking tokens for membership access and using (destroying) the tokens to obtain discounts.
  • Work tokens: In the work token model, a service provider can stake the native token of the network or dApp to earn the right to perform work for the network. According to Samani (2018) of Multicoin Capital, “the probability that the service provider is awarded the next job is proportional to the number of tokens staked as a fraction of the total tokens staked by all service providers.” An example comes from Augur, a decentralized P2P protocol that allows users to create their own prediction markets. “Reporters” can stake reputation tokens (REP) in order to report or weigh in on the outcome of events, with REP gained if reported correctly or lost otherwise.
  • Burn-and-mint tokens: The burn-and-mint equilibrium (BME) model utilizes a two-token system: proprietary payment tokens and tradeable tokens. The exchange rate of the two tokens are fixed and typically denominated in a fiat currency. To use the service users must burn (decommission) the “value-seeking” token in order to receive the “payment” token (Adams 2019). Upon burning value-seeking tokens, payment tokens are immediately minted and can be used to access the network's services. Growth in usage of the network causes the value-seeking tokens to become more valuable requiring less of the token per unit of service rendered and vice versa in the case of network decline. This dynamic mechanism drives the network to an equilibrium state. Factom, a decentralized data integrity protocol, pioneered the BME model and Scriptarnica, a decentralized platform for reading, writing, publishing, selling and buying e-books, is another platform that has also implemented this model.

Token Standards

Tokens represent a set of rules encoded in a special type of smart contract called a token contract, which can often be issued with just a few lines of code running on a blockchain network (Voshmgir 2019). They are accessible with a compatible crypto (software) wallet that interfaces with the blockchain and manages the two uniquely related cryptographic keys (public–private key pair) associated with the wallet's blockchain address. Only the person who possesses the wallet's private key can access and transfer the tokens to another blockchain address. In this way, ownership of the private key is equivalent to ownership (i.e., control) of the assets (Antonopoulos and Wood 2018).

Ethereum has the largest and most active blockchain community in the world and has therefore been a popular choice for launching new token projects. The vast majority of dApps currently in existence have been built on this network. The most common technical standard used for creating Ethereum-based tokens is the ERC-20 token standard. It defines a standard interface for fungible tokens (identical value and interchangeable) comprised of a set of rules and requirements that a token must fulfill to be compliant and function within the Ethereum network. Having a clear standard allows token architects to be able to more accurately predict how a new token is likely to function within the larger Ethereum ecosystem. Table 8.1 summarizes the specification as a list of functions defined within the ERC-20 token standard (Vogelsteller and Buterin 2015). This specification forms the minimal interface. However, many projects have extended implementations to support additional features including burning tokens, minting new tokens (i.e., the ability to add to the supply at a predictable rate or based on a trigger), whitelisting (i.e., the ability to restrict actions such as token transfers to specific blockchain addresses), and crowdfunding (i.e., the ability to offer tokens for sale through, for example, a market sale, auction, or reverse auction) (Antonopoulos and Wood 2018).

Table 8.1. ERC-20 Token Standard.

Function Description
Name Returns the name of the token (e.g., “XYZToken”)
Symbol Returns the symbol of the token (e.g., “XYZ”)
Decimals Returns the number of decimals the token uses (i.e., its divisibility)
totalSupply Returns the total supply of tokens created
balanceOf Returns the number of tokens a given address has in its account
Transfer Allows a specified number of tokens to be transferred from the total supply to a user address
transferFrom Allows a user to transfer a specified number of tokens to another user
Approve Checks a transaction against the total supply of tokens
Allowance Checks the balance of the user's account and cancels the transaction if the number of tokens is insufficient

Note: Table 8.1 summarizes the specification as a list of functions defined within the ERC-20 token standard. The standard is extensible; these functions merely define the minimal interface.

A common technical standard used for creating unique Ethereum-based nonfungible tokens (NFTs) is the ERC-721 token standard. It provides basic functionality to track and transfer NFTs (Entriken, Shirley, Evans, and Sachs 2018). The ERC-721 standard further extends the possibilities of fungible ERC-20 tokens with a higher degree of functionality, particularly around token creation and ownership. Crypto collectibles are typically created using ERC-721 NFTs.

A challenge that may hinder widespread adoption of dApps and the tokens that power them concerns blockchain interoperability. Blockchain networks, each with their own unique smart contracts, are fragmented from a standards perspective. Tokens generated through blockchain-specific smart contracts can only operate within their native blockchain ecosystems. Simply put, Ethereum-based tokens can only be traded directly for other Ethereum-based tokens. Furthermore, transaction activity on Ethereum cannot directly be used as an input to trigger the execution of a smart contract on another blockchain. Projects like Cosmos and Polkadot are tackling the interoperability challenge by enabling networks of blockchains to operate together seamlessly. Mass adoption of tokens is more likely in a world of interconnected blockchains.

Token Economy Design

Having discussed token fundamentals, the focus now shifts toward the concept of the token economy and its disruptive potential in driving new innovative business models. At the center lies the token model, which describes what the token does, its core purpose, value proposition, distribution mechanism, and associated functionality. This collective information informs the type of token needed and provides insight into the potential incentive mechanism that can be employed to drive user behaviors and ultimately a sustainable token economy. This section revolves around the general utility token model. Utility tokens represent crypto assets that are intrinsic to the blockchain and inherently consumptive in nature; they are designed to be used or consumed in some way. Utility tokens have shown much promise in unlocking new ways to allocate, coordinate, and govern network resources at scale.

Designing a token economy can be a complex undertaking requiring a multidisciplinary approach. Establishing economic objectives, stakeholder mapping, token engineering, and creating an effective governance mechanism are some of the key activities that must be carried out. A solid grounding in systems theory can inform a first principles approach. Meadows (2008, p. 11) defines a system as “... an interconnected set of elements that is coherently organized in a way that it achieves something.” A system can produce its own pattern of behavior over time. It may be acted upon by external forces, but its response to those forces is characteristic of itself and seldom simple in the real world (Meadows 2008). Open blockchain networks and similar cryptoeconomic dApps are complex socioeconomic systems. Voshmgir and Zargham (2019) assert that cryptoeconomic systems are defined by (1) individual autonomous actors, (2) economic policies embedded in software, and (3) emergent properties arising from interactions of those actors according to the rules defined by the software. A token economy built on a decentralized network is in essence a complex token system where individual actions that advance a collective goal are incentivized through the token. The incentive mechanism driving the interactions (i.e., token transactions) among actors (i.e., humans or autonomous agents) is an integral cryptoeconomic component of the token system.

Cryptoeconomics

Token systems are anchored by cryptoeconomics, which is the study of economic interaction in adversarial environments requiring a deep understanding of incentives, applied cryptography, and P2P networks. Although it considers economic theory, cryptoeconomics is not a subfield of economics; it does not involve traditional macro- and microeconomic theory. It is an emerging field of economic coordination games in cryptographically secured P2P networks (Voshmgir and Zargham 2019) powered by a token. All public blockchain networks are products of cryptoeconomics.

The innovation behind Bitcoin's protocol is that, using economic incentives and cryptographic tools, it compels many actors to reliably reach consensus about the state of the blockchain. Bitcoin relies on cryptographic tools such as public–private key cryptography to give holders control of their bitcoin, and hash functions that enable miners to create, validate, and link blocks of transactions using a proof-of-work (PoW) consensus mechanism. The economic incentive is the block reward, which is a specific amount of bitcoin cryptocurrency, that miners who contribute their computing power and electricity in support of the network receive for successfully validating a block of transactions. Malicious actors who attempt to attack the Bitcoin network to censor or reverse confirmed transactions are deterred by the disproportionately large hardware and operational costs of doing so. In this way, cryptoeconomics provides a security guarantee about the state of the Bitcoin blockchain. More generally, a cryptoeconomic system's security guarantee depends on the strength of its game-theoretic assumptions about how actors react to economic incentives (Stark 2017).

dApps built on top of public blockchains that make use of a native token are also products of cryptoeconomics. dApps assume the security guarantees of the blockchain network on which they are built. However, if they employ a native dApp-specific token, the economic incentives driving their respective token economies are likely to differ from that of the underlying blockchain network. Augur, for example, is built on the Ethereum blockchain network but employs its own REP token as a core element of its economic system of incentives to reward users reporting the “truth.” This incentive mechanism is what makes a decentralized prediction market possible.

Designing cryptoeconomic incentives draws on an area of mathematics, economics, and game theory called mechanism design. Mechanism design theory seeks to study the mechanisms in which a desirable social or economic outcome can be achieved given the constraints of individuals' self-interest and incomplete information. Leonid Hurwicz, Eric S. Maskin, and Roger B. Myerson, who collectively won the 2007 Nobel Prize in Economics, are major contributors to mechanism design theory. Mechanism design builds on game theory where strategic interactions (in a “game”) between rational decision-makers (“players”) are observed and the best strategies for each player and likely outcomes are sought. Mechanism design, however, is often referred to as reverse game theory because it starts with defining the desired outcome and works backward to design a game that, if players pursue their own self-interests, incentivizes them toward that target outcome. Cryptoeconomics focuses on designing token systems in much the same way. However, the mechanisms used to create economic incentives are built using cryptography and open source software, and the systems are typically designed to be distributed and/or decentralized (Stark 2017).

Token Engineering

While cryptoeconomics strongly focuses on cryptographic tools and mechanism design, token engineering threads these theoretical concepts into a practical discipline focused on creating and deploying a token economy. Trent McConaghy, a co-founder of Ocean Protocol who coined the term, defines token engineering as “the theory, practice and tools to analyze, design and verify tokenized ecosystems” (McConaghy, 2018). He derives this definition from the engineering discipline that is grounded in rigorous analysis, design, and verification of systems along with the tools that reconcile theory with practice.

Defining the overarching goals of the token system is a critical step in token engineering. The goals can be distilled into objectives and constraints. Objectives are the things that can be maximized or minimized; a token system needs to optimize for the desired objective function or outcome. Constraints are the things that must be met and are requirements in the design of the system. A token utility canvas can be a useful framework to aggregate much of the information needed to create a blueprint of the token model. Establishing the goals of the token system requires understanding the individual incentives for each actor or group of similar actors participating in the token economy. Stakeholder mapping can be a useful exercise to identify the actors involved, how they relate to one another, and the anticipated value exchange patterns between them. The cryptoeconomic incentive mechanisms can then be engineered such that only those behaviors that address the needs of as many stakeholders as possible while simultaneously contributing to the overarching goals of the token system as a whole are encouraged while destructive behaviors are disincentivized.

A token system that is designed correctly aligns incentives across two key layers of the token economy. The result is token-network fit, a term coined by Dhaliwal and Gurguc (2018), and the team at Outlier Ventures. According to Dhaliwal and Gurguc (2018, p. 52), “Token-Network Fit is analogous to product-market fit. Finding the right token model for the network means creating the correct mechanisms that align incentives across the market and ledger layer such that everyone acts in the best interest of the network. It is useful to view the token as the interface between the ledger and the market layer.” The market layer is where the token economy participants obtain or consume digital resources and exchange value via the token. The ledger layer or blockchain network layer is where the transactions are actually settled. Using Augur as an example once again, REP token holders can perform work by staking their tokens to report on the outcome of events and by doing so they can earn a percentage of the fees generated on the platform, if reported correctly. If reported incorrectly, however, REP tokens are lost. Passive token holders that do not use their REP to stake on disputes and forks are also penalized. In this way, the token carries with it both a responsibility and an eligibility for reward. These incentives and disincentives driving market layer activities contribute to an implicit token economy goal of distributing value to create a more efficient market. The ledger layer is the Ethereum blockchain network on which the transactions associated with each of these activities are settled.

A general goal of all token systems is to create a coordinated outcome that satisfies system-level (i.e., global) goals. In reality, they can produce a mix of unpredictable (stochastic) and predictable (deterministic) outcomes (Dhaliwal and Gurguc 2018). Externalities can cause actors to prefer actions other than those a model assumes (Zargham 2018). Moreover, player rationality is a game-theoretic assumption that cannot be taken for granted. Countless experiments in the field of behavioral economics suggest that human actors in particular, are not rational utility maximizers. System dynamics models can help in exploring possible futures by asking “what if” questions (Meadows 2008). Agent-based models (ABMs), more specifically, can help in modeling the parts of a token system governed by human behavior. Local interactions between autonomous and heterogeneous human agents (individuals or groups) can be simulated to observe which macroscale effects emerge (Ramirez 2020).

Stock-and-flow diagrams are commonly used in system dynamics modeling. In token systems, stocks and flows refer to distinct quantities related to the supply of a token. The stock is the existing supply of tokens that includes all tokens produced in the past minus all tokens that have been consumed or destroyed, while the flow is the extra production of tokens in the next time period (Ammous 2018). A stock-and-flow diagram can show how stocks and flows are interconnected – a stock changes over time through the actions of a flow and feedback loop that interlinks the two. Token systems often have a particular type of feedback loop called a balancing feedback loop. This type of feedback loop is equilibrating or goal-seeking and is a source of both stability and resistance to change (Meadows 2008).

The evolution of the Bitcoin network's hash rate, which is the computational power that miners contribute to secure the network in exchange for block rewards and transaction fees, can be easily modeled using a stock-and-flow diagram. The stock is represented by the network hash rate at a given point in time. The flow is the additional network hash rate added in each two-week interval that follows a mining difficulty adjustment that is triggered automatically by the Bitcoin protocol every 2,016 blocks. The Bitcoin network is at equilibrium when blocks are solved every 10 minutes. Thus, the feedback loop is goal-seeking in that it adjusts the difficulty level of mining a block up or down so that the network continues to solve blocks at the target rate. If the price of bitcoin increases substantially in any intervening period, it may cause additional hash rate to come online due to the influx of new profit-seeking miners. As a result, the block time could descend to sub-10 minutes. If the average block time during the last intervening period was less than 10 minutes, the difficulty level would increase reflexively to bring the system back into equilibrium, and vice versa if the average block time was greater than 10 minutes (stemming from a net loss of network hash rate). A net decrease in network hash rate (i.e., net outflow of the stock) could stem from the profit of mining becoming negative as a consequence of a price crash, a dramatic fall in the block reward (Lasi and Saul 2020) or some other exogenous factor – all are possible triggers of miner capitulation.

The goal of system dynamics modeling is to demonstrate how a complex system behaves as a whole given varying assumptions about agent behaviors, but not necessarily to model reality perfectly. It can be a powerful tool to model the architecture of a token system visually in terms of stocks, flows, feedback loops, and controls. This tool can provide deep insight into the effectiveness of the underlying cryptoeconomics. Simulation software can further assist in approximating the behavior of token systems. Monte Carlo simulations, for example, can uncover the robustness of a system's design by introducing stochastics into parts of the system, such as behaviors of certain agents. A statistical analysis of many runs with the same system parameters can uncover various macroscale effects and shed light on the system's overall stability. Furthermore, A/B testing can be conducted to compare how the system behaves given various sets of different assumptions. Parameter sweeps can be performed to run a series of simulations in which a single control variable or initial condition is modified slightly to see how it affects the overall behavior of the system (Ramirez 2020). The team at BlockScience, led by Michael Zargham, has created an open source toolkit called cadCAD (complex adaptive dynamics Computer-Aided Design), which is a Python-based modeling framework that assists in the design, testing, and validation of complex systems through simulation. A variety of different simulations can be run in cadCAD to help answer the “what if” questions that arise in designing complex token systems, including Monte Carlo methods, A/B testing, and parameter sweeping. Because simulations are never perfect, the system must be evolvable toward the intent of the community participating in and maintaining the token economy (McConaghy 2018). Once a token system is implemented in the wild, effort should focus on revisiting, validating, and fine-tuning the model with real-world data using appropriate governance mechanisms that promote change through a democratic process.

Decentralized network governance is one of the most challenging areas in the design of token systems. Tokens can be used as part of a direct voting mechanism on a blockchain protocol or dApp with on-chain governance to make decisions concerning protocol upgrades, treasury management, ecosystem grants, and an array of other issues. Community participation and control can help to minimize platform risk where the rules of a platform could change against the will of its users (Walden 2020b). Decentralized governance requires an engaged community with sufficiently decentralized ownership (token holders) to ensure it can work. A progressive approach to decentralized governance can work well in lockstep with the various phases of protocol or dApp development and adoption. Governance may start out centralized during early stages of the product, while the development team seeks product/token-network fit. Once the product is more mature and more widely adopted, governance can be gradually passed onto the community in phases until a full handover makes sense. The caveat here is that the community should be capable of maintaining the protocol or dApp and that the governance model properly incentivizes ongoing operations and a sustainable token economy. Melon Protocol, an Ethereum-based protocol for decentralized on-chain asset management, successfully used this approach. The team completed v1.0 of the protocol in February 2019 after three years of development, at which point the company behind the protocol was dissolved and governance was handed over to a decentralized governance system – The Melon Council, a Decentralized Autonomous Organization (DAO).

Summary and Conclusions

This chapter introduced the cryptographic token as a blockchain-native asset that facilitates value transfer, coordination, and optimization of network resources in a decentralized manner and at scale. Although SoV/MoE tokens, utility tokens, and security tokens make up the current universe of crypto assets, the token taxonomy continues to evolve. Tokens are fundamental to Web 3.0, a new fairer and more transparent web built on top of decentralized P2P networks. At its core, Web 3.0 disintermediates economic transactions. It is giving birth to dApps and token economies that unlock a new breed of open source business models committed to the principles of data sovereignty and shared economics.

Designing a token economy entails a multidisciplinary approach, one that is suitable for dealing with complex systems. Complex token systems are anchored by cryptoeconomics, which is an emerging field of economic coordination games in cryptographically secured P2P networks. Mechanism design is a central component of cryptoeconomics that seeks to incentivize actors to collectively achieve the overarching system level goals in a way that also serves their own individual interests. Token engineering extends cryptoeconomic theory into a practical discipline focused on creating and deploying a token system. It involves system dynamics modeling to understand how a complex system might behave. Simulations can be run to test the system's robustness, uncover macroscale effects, and obtain a deeper understanding of agent behavior given a set of assumptions. Token economy design also includes the design of effective governance mechanisms to ensure the community can participate in decision-making so as to limit platform risk. A progressive approach to decentralized on-chain governance can work well provided the community is engaged and ownership is sufficiently decentralized. Tokens and therefore voting power would ideally not be concentrated in the hands of a few.

Thriving token economies achieve economic alignment among network participants and steer them toward a common goal – growth of the network and appreciation of the token's value. A growing user base, engaged developer community, and strong network effects can propel the goal continuously higher. Network effects reward participants relative to their stage of adoption and the value they contribute. By giving partial ownership of the network to early adopters, projects can solve the initial “chicken-and-egg” problem – early investors can also become early users and in this way bootstrap the network on the path to growth. Furthermore, when a new user/investor uses a utility token, this increases the network's value for all other token holders, which starts to blur the line between users and investors. The design space for utility tokens is wide open and has only been narrowly explored to date. The open source foundation of decentralized blockchain networks and associated cryptographic tokens unlocks a massive opportunity for Web 3.0 innovation, unencumbered by socioeconomic constructs of the past, and disruptive to legacy business models of the Web 2.0 era.

(2)Characterize Web 3.0 and identify the attributes that differentiates it from Web 2.0.

(3)Define a utility token and indicate how it differs from a SoV/MoE token.

(4)Explain the difference between fungible and nonfungible tokens and identify the appropriate Ethereum token standards for each.

(5)Explain why mechanism design is a critical component of cryptoeconomic systems.

(6)Discuss how system dynamics modeling is useful to token engineering.
