Chapter 9

Proposed Modifications to Spur Consumer Adoption of Blockchain

Katherine McKechnie, Alexandra M. Dunn and Sayan Sarkar

Keywords: Blockchain; hash codes; smart contracts; cryptographic signatures; verified identity; business; government; consumer adoption; decentralized data; data security

Introduction

Blockchain can only function in society when mass consumer adoption occurs. The blockchain system relies on the individual entering data and creating or editing the blocks to create more blocks and to validate the information. This network makes transactions and accessing data both easier and safer, but it can only do so if the consumer trusts using the network instead of having third-party involvement (Alm et al. 2019). The current centralized system of data storage alleviates the need for trust in the counterpart of transactions because a third party does the work of checking records and verifying if the transaction is legally acceptable and if the counterpart is reliable. However, blockchain speeds up this process and eliminates the need for a third party by decentralizing information (Park and Park 2017). Information becomes accessible to the individual with the correct hash or digital fingerprint, saving time and money. This advancement in technology is impossible without the consumer's support. Adopting blockchain needs to occur across government, business, and individual consumers to hold enough records to validate blocks.

The government's intended use for blockchain covers topics of security and healthcare, as well as financial transactions and voting processes using the Voatz application. Since information is spread through many devices, hacking becomes much more difficult. Each type of data transaction has a specific programming script to allow for different authorizations with every type of transaction. These scripts make the hacking process more difficult because the program is not the same for every transaction. Thus, a hacker would need to have multiple ways to hack just one chain (Park and Park 2017).

Blockchain has many other benefits and applications. For example, using blockchain in healthcare is likely to revolutionize the medical field by allowing more than one medical office to access and add to medical records instantaneously. Doctors can store patient files and link them to other blocks on the same patient's chain thus allowing for complete medical records from any location (Agbo, Mahmoud, and Eklund 2019). Blockchain could also change the way laws and monetary policies are conceived. The software and structure of blockchain can dictate how policies are created and enforced, could lead to digital currency, and decentralize the control of the monetary supply (Jun 2018). Blockchain is likely to improve the current systems by making them more efficient and reliable.

Blockchain can change the way business is conducted because of the peer-to-peer (P2P) network. It can also make transactions more efficient and trusted. Furthermore, transactions can be stored in a different way allowing for records to be linked chronologically and without tampering (Wang, Chen, and Xu 2016). Companies, whether on a large or small business platform, are likely to be more transparent about their proceedings and allow stakeholders to have more insight into their investments. Businesses can also lower the costs of acquiring information as a result of not requiring a third party to validate the quality of transactions (Milani, Bañuelos, and Dumas 2016). Business transactions are likely to be more secure because of the irreversibility of the data blocks as they are entered. The blocks, which hold transaction details, cannot be altered and can create better tracking of events and ownership information. Every block is built from data that are in the block proceeding it so editing a block would damage the entire line of blocks. Thus, a block is not edited but another block is simply added to the line showing the edit in the data. Businesses are likely to run more efficiently and with less costs because of the decentralized network (Tapscott and Tapscott 2017).

The consumer experience may also change as a result of the fading need for third party intermediaries. A network being run by peers requires the individual to participate. This situation means that individuals would have to allow their data to be made into blocks and establish an identity on the block chain. Beyond security of information and ease of access, other incentives are in place to attract consumers (Alm et al. 2019). Blockchain can be modified to have networks that include blocks that can be edited by everyone involved in the data or just a few authorized parties. These blocks protect personal data from getting into the wrong hands and allow for trust in the verification process because of the limits on editors (Zyskind and Nathan 2015). In summary, blockchain is safer and more efficient than continuing the use of third-party intermediaries to move money and data availability into the future.

Government Applications

Applying blockchain to the US government is a task that requires the blockchain system to have a diverse set of functions. Blockchain replaces the need for third party intermediaries by providing data accessibility. That is, blockchain can create more secure data from and between other countries, as well as decentralize records in multiple areas including healthcare, security, and the economy (Carter and Ubacht 2018).

Functions in Government

Data involving personal records (e.g., financial history, voting, and unclassified government documents) as well as transportation and city plans can become transparent to citizens with the correct hash codes. A hash code is a line of code that allows a user to access the data inside a block on the chain. To obtain the correct hash codes, the creator of the block needs to give permission to the requesting party. Alternatively, the creator can restrict permission (Alketbi, Nasir, and Talib 2018). Data are decentralized by blockchain so records such as property values and other financial documents that usually require a third party to release the data, such as a bank or government representative, can be retrieved with the correct hash code.

Eliminating a trusted third party requires confidence in the blockchain software, which is a key to blockchain becoming widely used (Jun 2018). Trust in the software also allows for more reliance on blockchain because of the data security that it provides. Blockchain must prove that it offers greater security and efficiency for users to trust that they can rely on it for storing and accessing their data in the future. Once users gain trust in the blockchain system, they are likely to be more trustful of organizations using blockchain. As a result of applying blockchain, the trust in government systems is likely to increase because of the increased difficulty to commit fraud or corruption (Batubara, Ubacht, and Jenssen 2018). Blockchain removes most, if not all, of the human error by applying a consensus mechanism, which is a device designed to achieve the necessary agreement on a single data value or a single state of the network among distributed processes. As a result of using software to hold records, some laws are likely to change to account for the switch.

Smart contracts are codes that are built into the software to act as law in the network. These contracts change the way the ledger is created and monitored. Although smart contract design currently has flaws, including errors in code, it helps ensure that the law cannot be violated because it is directly built into the software and is not open to human interpretation. The code can be run through test transactions to find and fix the flaws in the code. However, once the code meets an acceptable level of accuracy, the contract is allowed and if not, it is rejected. Contracts that do not use blockchain have ambiguities because people interpret them in different ways. However, with a smart contract, the terms of the contract are absolute with little, if any, room for interpretation. Such a contract allows the government to have some control over how blockchain is used and ensures that the intended uses follow the current set of values and laws. For instance, blockchain can be programmed to record asset sales but only the assets that the government deems legal and for sale (Jun 2018).

Data and information security are a growing issue during today's technological age. Data being stolen or hacked as well as changed by an individual event can cause major problems for the data user. Blockchain's use of consensus algorithms and Proof of Work (PoW) strategy creates a ledger that is distributable but protected so that any one event cannot change the entire set of data. Secure government documents cannot be changed and replaced without creating a trail of blocks showing the edits and additions. The documents can also be decentralized, which increases the difficulty for hackers to obtain complete sets of data. Instead of hacking into one server with access to all government information, a hacker would need to hack into each individual block to obtain the data in their entirety. The documents are complete because all of the data are strung together on the same chain and each block on the chain must be linked to another. Although all the blocks are linked on the same chain, each block has a different hash code so accessing one block does not mean the user has access to every block on the chain.

Citizens can use blockchain's permission abilities by using public-private keys to view released government documents, while still allowing for the central government to hold editing permission. State and national governments can also employ this feature in voting processes to make the voting records more reliable and unambiguous. For example, the Voatz application is a blockchain-based application that allows for secure voting. It can record votes with security that eliminates the opportunity for tampering. Although Voatz could change voting procedures, it would need to be implemented and adopted correctly to avoid user identities being set up inaccurately and result in a lack of consumer trust and understanding (Zhang, Young, and Verhulst 2018).

Governments can also use the permission feature to share information between countries without tampering (Alketbi et al. 2018). To work well, governments need to find a common way to track and record transfers of data over country lines. Blockchain's distributive ledger allows for the transfers to be completed and shared without making a duplicate of the data and sending it to the recipient. This system limits the ways to hack into the data and reduces the number of copies of sensitive data available. Blockchain creates a more secure way to share data without the risk of the data being transferred into too many hands (Berryhill, Bourgery, and Hanson 2018).

Governments should also be able to create public blockchains to distribute information in cities or entire markets. Blockchain can be used to create smart cities that allow people in any city to log into the public blocks and access information about transportation services, emergency planning, and city rules and regulations. Blockchain's distributive ledger system connects everyone with the correct hash codes to each other, essentially creating a large P2P network. Hash codes are shared based on permission given by the data users. This network can then be used to spread information and create new markets. Public keys allow users to access messages and products from a specific vendor, whereas private keys only allow access to select individuals. For example, when purchasing products, the recipient must have the correct private keys to access his or her personal transaction, thus giving markets a new way to sell (Alketbi et al. 2018).

Why Blockchain Is an Improvement

The United States has a centralized system of data that can only be accessed by certain parties. For example, only bankers can access particular financial records. This system can create long and costly processes and has room for errors including incomplete and fraudulent data. To access data now, the person wanting the data faces potential fees for the third party's time and services as well as access fees. This process can also consume valuable time because of the waiting period for accessing and the need for interpreting the data from a third party. Blockchain offers a system that improves efficiency and lowers costs by removing fees that pay a person to obtain the information needed. This information can be available to the individual and thus eliminate the time and money associated with a third party.

Blockchain also avoids the need to have the user duplicate information to send to a recipient. Information is safer because it has fewer opportunities to be leaked or hacked. Blockchain requires a separate block to be built to make the changes, so the information is both secure and more transparent because a mandatory record of the change exists. By decentralizing the data, the information is accessible from different servers and requires hash access codes to see each block of information. In a centralized system, the data are on one server so that most or all of the data can be accessed from many different links all leading to the same centralized data. Although different links are available, they are tied to the same information and can be edited without a record of the changes. This process can affect the information's accuracy and security. A decentralized system allows for the data to be secure, transparent, and accurate because of the required record of edits (Berryhill et al. 2018).

Data being accessible and trusted from multiple sources reduce the need for excess costs to obtain the information. Also, as technology use increases, so has the number of electronic transactions. This increase slows down the number of transactions that can be completed because of the time commitment needed to process and verify each transaction and block. With the efficiency that blockchain provides, a decrease in the time taken to complete a transaction is essential to ensuring real time accessibility to data.

Blockchain provides a high level of security that is valued as people use more technology in their daily lives. As the use of technology has increased, so has the ransomware rate. Ransomware is the act of a hacker locking the user out of accessing data until a demand is satisfied. Although hackers have used cryptocurrencies before as a form of ransomware payment (e.g., it has been used to lock users out of accessing their data until a demand is met), this situation does not mean that blockchain is or will be used to hurt government functioning in the future. Like other technology, blockchain can be used for good and for the right reasons. Recently, the demand is an amount of cryptocurrency that can be used to dictate the PoS in a block (Paquet-Clouston, Haslhofer, and Dupont 2019). However, blockchain does not allow one user to have enough cryptocurrency to be able to overpower the PoS in a block that is not his or her own. Outside of document storage, city, state, and national governments can use blockchain to reduce pollution, crime, and utility use. As technology moves into monitoring a city's demographics, blockchain can offer security that can protect against cyber-attacks and other crises (Kim and Huh 2018). Effectively using blockchain is likely to lead to more trust in city regulations and reports because of smart contracts. The contracts do not permit false reporting of finances or transactions by officials (Collomb and Sok 2016). The consensus mechanism avoids corruption because the data must have the same properties but be individualized (Francisconi 2017).

Business Applications

Both governments and private businesses can effectively use blockchain. Similar to government uses, blockchain has a diverse set of business functions and can replace the need for third party intermediaries. Blockchain for businesses is likely to bring new markets and novel ways of sharing data. Business practices may change because of the increased ease of connecting buyers and sellers.

Positive Disruptions in Business Practices

The applications for business are parallel to those of the government. In private business, blockchain works to secure transactions on smaller business sales like homes, cars, and other payments. The data can be decentralized in a similar way to the government (Wolfond 2017). Because the buyer and seller can access the data, blockchain removes the need for third parties, such as banks, agents, or other regulators, that would usually act as an intermediary. Removing these intermediaries creates a P2P network. Users can easily transfer tangible or intangible assets because of the asset's shared record between the two or more parties involved. A separate copy of the data is unavailable to each party because each shares the codes to a block and can access the same record. This characteristic reduces the costs associated with obtaining documents such as the fees charged by service businesses to retrieve documents, and the payment to read, interpret, and present the data to a client.

Users can retrieve the requested data in real time as the data are updated, providing a new level of speed and accuracy when completing various tasks (Francisconi 2017). In smaller businesses, blockchain technology can provide an easier option for reconciling sales data because a record of purchases is automatically available in both the buyer's shared block and the business' data blocks. The sales are recorded not only in a block shared with the customer detailing the transaction, but also in a block for the business to collect data about sales (Brandon 2016).

Accounting systems are either a single-entry method showing cash flows and balances or a double entry method using a ledger and account charts showing individual account balances. These data are then posted into a general ledger so the information can be shared across the business and in some cases publicly accessible. With modern technology, much of these data are automatically collected and stored in a database for the stakeholder to access when needed. Using blockchain changes how people can view these data. Instead of seeing just what was exchanged in the transaction, the user can also see the cryptographic signature that corresponds to the transaction. This feature gives the stakeholder a more accurate and transparent view of how the business is working and doing financially. The advancement into blockchain also allows for outside stakeholders or auditors to access a company's data easier and more securely (Brandon 2016).

These changes in business can only be done with the cooperation from the majority of businesses. Businesses benefit from using blockchain because of the savings in security of data, overhead costs, and the possibilities to reach new markets. Currently, the cost of securing data with firewalls and protection software could be higher than the cost of implementing blockchain technology. For example, Walmart and Maersk use blockchain to track products on their supply chain, which they estimate can add up to anywhere between a 5% and 20% reduction in processing and administrative costs. Although blockchain speeds up their supply chain, it also reduces the chance of products like groceries spoiling, thus saving the company money (Rogers 2019).

The network requires all users to verify records and third parties to input current records so that the blockchains can build their base of blocks. As each company and user uses blockchain for their data, the level of simplicity as well as security and trust in the network is likely to increase. The more the chain grows, the more trust a user can put in the network. Blockchain's data security comes from the verification process. To complete this process, more data need to be put into the block. Thus, the more information in the chain, the more secure the blocks become (Wolfond 2017).

Verification and sharing of data can also become easier as more companies use blockchain. Blocks can be built off of existing blocks minimizing the number of newly created blockchains. As blockchain becomes standardized across all businesses and more identities are created within it, the acceptance rate should rise. Blockchain thrives off users, so the more use of the network, the easier it is to use and the more secure the network becomes. By linking each data point to an identity already established on the blockchain system, the block is more secure than an identity that is not verified in the system. The unverified identity leaves a gap in the data, which cannot be secured because no PoW is available.

Think about when companies adopted online banking and paperless payments. At first, consumers were skeptical about the network security and whether they should use it. Over time, users learned about the platforms, tried the platforms, and realized their benefits. Eventually, these platforms became more widely accepted, trusted, and used to the point that online banking and scheduling online payments were institutionalized. Consumers also saw that, once learned, online banking and paperless payments are actually easier to use than their old ways of doing things. The same process is likely to hold true for the introduction of blockchain. That is, as companies adopt blockchain, consumers will learn how to use and accept it, which in turn is likely to lead to a larger network.

When businesses use blockchain to follow purchases, blockchain records the customers’ information into their own block (Wolfond 2017). Blockchain also provides a more complete look at the history of property. Property ownership history is valuable information in the real estate industry. The record of data makes identifying ownership easier with data that are never deleted or corrupted but added to in real time (Tunstall, Caplan, Prescott, and Sandler 2018). Creating a new block with a cryptographic stamp showing the time and creator of the block enables linking the background and people to places and times. The blocks provide a chronological link of ownership, which can be followed given the user has the correct hash codes for each node. The ledgers can also be public and shared to the extent that the users have received permission to access the data. Thus, any updates to the blockchain become available to everyone as the changes are made. This example illustrates permission-less blocks because each user does not need individualized permission to access the data within these chains or blocks. Permission-less blocks differ from permissioned blocks because permissioned blocks can only be accessed when owners of the block provide another party with the password. The availability of these data through permission-less blocks can make real-time sales and transfers of ownership easier because no lag time exists between the contract and transfer of assets (Sullivan and Burger 2017).

Business-to-Business Transactions Made Secure and Simple

Blockchain's shared document model reduces further disputes about ownership because each party does not have its own copy of the transaction, but rather the same one block of data that each party can access (Brandon 2016). With the smart contract feature, blockchain monitors transactions across companies and their branches (Milani et al. 2016). These functions make business-to-business (B2B) and business-to-consumer (B2C) transactions more secure. The business owner creates the first blocks in the chain, known as the chainanchor, and can give permission to edit and view as the owner sees fit. The business owner and consumer then verify the blocks. Once verified, the block becomes part of the customer blockchain and the business sales data blockchain. This process can be simplified by placing smart contracts on the blockchains and can be used to collect various forms of data including sales. This process makes data easier to access and more accurate because businesses avoid going through a third party and the distributive ledger model ensures data are the same for all parties involved.

Other than smart contracts, Enigma is another important add-on to the blockchain technology. Blockchain only stores, protects, and organizes data. For example, the data collected are organized and broken into separate nodes, so that the data cannot be hacked in their entirety. As an extension of blockchain, these data can be put into specific computation nodes. Enigma then allows for computing the data blockchain collects. Therefore, adding Enigma enables calculating and manipulating data (Shrier, Wu, and Pentland 2016). Enigma can then be used to inform business decisions and help businesses quickly understand and analyze the data they collect and store in blockchains.

Transactions are also more secure because of the shared data on ownership rights. Any form of property that has ownership rights connected to it can be recorded and authenticated, so ownership is not called into question as often as it is today. The ownership is recorded on a block that can then be accessed by anyone with correct hash codes who is looking for these specific data. These data then link to other blocks when ownership is transferred without deleting the old records of previous owners. This process makes the data more secure from corruption and hacking (Wolfond 2017).

Specific keys and hash codes protect data and allow for selective usage of the data, such that only the people responsible for the data can access and edit the blocks. Each block also requires PoW, which increases the difficulty of hackers to edit the blocks. In addition, hacking into one block does not give a hacker access to other linked blocks. For example, if a hacker wants to change the history of a credit card, the hacker would not only need to hack into one block to change the specific transaction but also need to hack into every other block containing data about the same purchase (Sullivan and Burger 2017). This example illustrates the benefits of the blockchain operating system's compartmentalization. Accessing one part of the data does not give access to all the data. Blockchain's use of hash codes and breaking data into separate nodes does not allow for one broken code to give any access to other nodes (Shrier et al. 2016). These procedures are different than what most systems currently have ‒ namely, firewalls. Once a hacker gets past those firewalls, little, if anything, protects against a hacker continuing to find and edit data.

Consumer Applications

Not only can government and businesses benefit from blockchain but also every day consumers can benefit. Similar to how government and business data are better protected and more secure, consumer data are also more secure. More specifically, blockchain from a consumer standpoint holds individual identities in a new, more secure way. Consumers are likely to have a larger role in their markets as a P2P economy emerges because of implementing blockchain.

Effect on Individuals

Blockchain's purpose is to make data more secure and available for people to access. In the hands of the individual consumer, blockchain poses a threat to service businesses that retrieve and store documents. Currently, consumers place trust in individuals who have credentials and licenses, proper identification, and proof with paperwork to handle important and secure documents. With blockchain, consumers must trust the system of blockchain to work correctly, not a person. This change is a substantial shift in thinking and requires consumer education.

According to Lin and Liao (2017), each block has four parts: (1) hash of the current block, (2) hash of the previous block, (3) time stamp, and (4) main data. Blockchain's distributed ledger system protects data from hacks, corruption, and misinformation. The PoW requires a piece of data called a nonce to be set through a generated algorithm and the block's creator must figure out the nonce to obtain the PoW, which is the verification of a block being accurate with regard to being linked to an identity in blockchain. This system is time-consuming and involves high energy consumption, but it can be simple as long as the nonce meets all requirements. The nonce protects the data from easily being falsified and corrupted because it is difficult to guess or identify. The nonce, data, and hash codes make up what is called the account state.

The requirements for someone to obtain a verified block are to find a value that is less than a difficulty target that has been preset. The other system in place to make data more secure is Proof of Stake (PoS), which is the amount of data belonging to each user in a block. This system is derived from the amount of bitcoin that the user holds. The percentage of bitcoin owned is the percentage of blocks that can be accessed. This amount protects from attacks because the attacker would need to acquire a massive amount of bitcoin to hack into the data. A majority attack requires that 51% of the computing power be in one hacker's hand, which would allow the hacker to compute nonce values and thus permit access to data that can then be modified or disrupt the verification process. However, the more users blockchain acquires substantially reduces the probability that one person could obtain 51% of the computing power as every user divides the amount of computing power that each transaction has.

A business including its ownership rights of contracts or intangible assets such as patents would also be more secure. If ownership comes into question, the user with the proper codes and time stamps can produce them to prove rightful ownership. Each user can create his or her personal identity in blockchain, which would be specific to that individual. Achieving proof of identity eliminates the ability to modify the identity and lessens the possibility of hacking. The ability to create and own one's own identity is called self-sovereign identity, meaning that the identity is created and owned, but the user identity is validated through PoW. This feature differs from the well-known username and password that consumers currently employ in their accounts. Hackers can often easily gain access to consumer accounts by guessing the current password. With blockchain, the application of OneName, allows for an identity to become decentralized and linked to various chains. OneName encodes the identity and allows the identity to be protected by more than one password and, similar to the nonce, an algorithm holding value similar to the encoding of a block. The identity can only be specific to one person or user, so spoofing the identity to hack into the data is nearly impossible (Karame and Androulaki 2016).

Blockchain stores two types of data categorized as on-chain data or off-chain data. On-chain data are data directly stored in the nodes of blockchain. These data are visible immediately and verified by blockchain to be true. In disputes, these data would be most reliable, but limitations exist on the amount of data that can be stored in on-chain data. By contrast, off-chain data have no storage limits, but the data are stored in links to other data not included in blockchain. This characteristic means that the data are not immediately visible and, in the case of a dispute, would not be trusted as much as on-chain data. Off-chain data could be used in the medical care field because the medial test results would be linked to an outside source (Deloitte 2016).

From a customer standpoint, blockchain introduces a new way to conduct business through a P2P economy, which means that more people can buy and sell data and/or products directly to each other without having to go through intermediaries such as retailers. Users can now own data because the data would be in blocks, and the hash codes can be sold as access to the data (Lin and Laio 2017). Blockchain also uses smart contracts to link tangible assets to blocks of data that can then be sold. A smart contract is a self-executing contract with the terms of the agreement between buyer and seller being directly written into lines of code. Thus, a smart contract allows individuals to sell assets to others in a P2P economy. The smart contract is built into the blockchain that conducts the sale. Smart contracts also help prevent tampering with sales and financial corruption because data are stored in different blocks that are securely linked together. Storing data from the sale in an established regulation that cannot be influenced by outside resources prevents tampering with sales and corruption of finances.

Smart contracts can also be scaled up for use in larger businesses. When a customer makes a purchase, the contract is handled within blockchain diminishing the need for an intermediary between the producer and customer (Belle 2017). The chains that allow assets to be transferred are called sidechains. The sidechain goes between two blocks allowing for business transactions such as transfers of asset data to be conducted (Karame and Androulaki 2016). In private, permissioned blockchains payment can be transferred from user to user. Permissioned blockchains are blocks that can only be accessed if given permission by the block's owners. In permission-less chains, the parties can access the data without a password. These transactions are easier to conduct because the payment does not need to go through a third party such as a bank. The transaction still needs to be regulated by the federal government, but it can be conducted in a non-traditional banking way. This shift can make markets more P2P based.

Using smart contracts means the transactions can be monitored and validated in many ways such as requiring multiple signatures of witnesses or meeting certain requirements before completing the contract. Contracts can also be monitored to reflect outside data, called oracles that may affect the transaction such as world events and fluctuation in prices. Furthermore, delivery of products purchased by the customer can be more easily tracked because as products are shipped and cataloged into the locations along the production chain, the information can be updated in the blockchain (Kakavand, De Sevres, and Chilton 2017).

Other records such as health records can be more accessible. Uploading patient records to the blockchain system allows patients to gather and see their records from any doctor they visit anywhere that uses blockchain. This system in blockchain, called MedRec, allows patients to view their entire medical history and any amendments to it. MedRec has the added benefit of enabling patients to see when medications and care are signed and put into effect (Pilkington 2017). The change to blockchain needs to be across many platforms to be effective and could be a market trend. However, to be successful and demonstrate its full use, the masses need to adopt blockchain. Convenience and lower costs are likely to aid blockchain's expansion (Lindman, Tuunainen, and Rossi 2017).

Summary and Conclusions

Security and accessibility of data are growing issues in the modern age of technology. Blockchain has the potential to influence the needs of both the global economy and individuals for security and reliability. It offers a system that allows for safe storage of and easy access to data that are no longer only accessible to intermediaries. Blockchain functions similarly at the government, business, and individual level. Each level requires mass participation and has benefits that cascade to the other levels. Blockchain's effects can be seen in reduced costs of data, new markets, and protection of assets. As consumer adoption grows, so will blockchain's benefits.

Part III
The Frontier of Blockchain Technology

Chapter 10

Blockchain: Speed, Efficiency, Decreased Costs, and Technical Challenges

Amanda Wilkie and Sean Stein Smith

Abstract

This chapter explores blockchain's five key elements ‒ distribution, encryption, immutability, tokenization, and decentralization. It also examines blockchain's potential to revolutionize today's businesses by looking at the efficiency and transparency blockchain brings to business processes. In addition, the chapter discusses the added benefits of traceability and potentially decreasing long-term costs before reviewing some of the known technical challenges blockchain faces today especially pertaining to commercial and enterprise adoption. Limited block size and low-transaction rates potentially inhibit blockchain's ability to scale to meet the needs of current and future enterprises. The lack of blockchain standards, along with creating multiple blockchains, complicates interoperability between the various blockchain platforms. The chapter concludes by offering potential solutions to blockchain's current technical challenges and how enterprises might adapt blockchain in the future.

Keywords: Blockchain; interoperability; technical challenges; scale; transparency; traceability; efficiency gains

Introduction

The development of blockchain is arguably one of the most disruptive technologies of the modern era. The continued acceleration of implementation and integration of blockchain technology across economic sectors reinforce this view. Beginning with the publication of the original bitcoin blockchain whitepaper at the end of 2008 (Nakamoto 2008) and its subsequent dissemination at the beginning of 2009, the bitcoin blockchain has continued to spur innovation, developments, and applications that expand far beyond the financial services sector. As documented within the different chapters of this book, the scope and reach of blockchain technology are difficult to overstate. Yet, a reasonable assertion is a wide swath of economic sectors, which are experiencing the ripple effects of blockchain technology.

This chapter discusses some opportunities and challenges related to blockchain technology, specific to certain industries as well as higher and more broadly applicable levels. It also outlines five key characteristics of blockchain technology and crypto assets and provides a basic understanding of what is happening regarding industry specific applications and developments.

Five Elements of Blockchain

Blockchain has evolved greatly since its introduction through bitcoin in the late 2000s. According to Casey and Vigna (2018), blockchain is a distributed, append-only ledger of provably signed, sequentially linked, and cryptographically secured transactions that are replicated across a network of computer nodes, with ongoing updates determined by a software-driven consensus. Furlonger and Uzureau (2019) identify the five core elements of blockchain and note that these components are existing technologies and techniques simply combined into the novel design of blockchain. In other words, the concept of blockchain does not so much represent an entirely new idea or way of conducting business, but rather it is an amalgamation of technologies and trends that currently exist.

Every blockchain entering the marketplace must be able to meet the requirements to qualify as a blockchain offering: (1) distribution, (2) encryption, (3) immutability, (4) tokenization, and (5) decentralization. Of particular note is the fact that while every blockchain is based on a distributed ledger technology platform, not every distributed leger operates as a blockchain. Organizations have used DTLs for several decades. In fact, many database management systems, operated either internally at an organization or remotely via cloud access protocols, are based in some part on DTLs as outlined below:

  • Distribution: Participants need not be geographically located together. Instead, they must simply be connected to the same network. Each participant receives a copy of the blockchain ledger. Any participant may review the ledger, but participants can only change the ledger under specified conditions. This distribution of information and data between network members is a core strength of the blockchain platform since it enables every record of information to be shared and distributed among network members on a global basis.
  • Encryption: Using public and private keys to secure data provides participants’ control over their identity and other information while allowing them to share only what is needed or wanted in the transaction data. Although encryption lies at the center of any blockchain platform, a pertinent point to factor into any conversation related to blockchain and cryptoasset technologies is how the specific process by which information can be added operates.
  • Immutability: Verified and validated transactions cannot be altered or corrupted as a result of being cryptographically signed, time-stamped, and sequentially linked to the previous transaction on the ledger. Some debate exists around whether the term immutability is more appropriate or if tamper resistant is perhaps more accurate. In either case, the integrity of data, after being encoded on blockchain, is of paramount importance to network members. As enterprises seek to modify blockchains for commercial use, they must be careful to avoid inadvertently undermining this characteristic.
  • Tokenization: The secure exchange of value in blockchain transactions in the form of tokens is what often incentivizes participants to maintain the blockchain network. Tokens may function as both a digital representation of a physical asset and a reward mechanism to incentivize network participation. They may also enable the creation and exchange of new forms of value tokenizing assets, whether off-chain or on-chain, and represent an emerging field of importance for the blockchain space. In short, the tokenization process enables asset holders to extract cash flow and liquidity from assets that might otherwise be unable to fulfill that role.
  • Decentralization: In the case of blockchain, decentralization means more than decentralized storage of data by storing the ledger of transactions on multiple computers or nodes. Decentralization removes the need for a central authoritative entity by distributing the rules of the network, as well as its data, using a software-driven consensus model to protect against fraud and bad transactions. Decentralizing access to the approval and verification of information lies at the core of any blockchain or cryptoasset ecosystem. In other words, the idea and ideology causing the bitcoin blockchain and bitcoin at large to become more mainstream is the very factor that can generate some of the limitations discussed in this chapter.

Understanding these key elements of blockchain is crucial to identifying use cases for and applications of true blockchain solutions as few blockchain projects to date have employed all five elements. According to Furlonger and Uzureau (2019), applications using all five elements are blockchain-complete solutions. In fact, these authors find that traditional data architecture could have done as well as, if not better than, blockchain in 85% of the projects they researched. Mass media coverage of blockchain implementation aside, including the publication of blockchain lists by organizations such as Forbes, obscures the fact that major blockchain implementation remains a future goal rather than current reality.

Nonetheless, all five elements of blockchain are not required to realize some benefit from the technology. According to Furlonger and Uzureau (2019), half of the estimated $3.1 trillion in new business value expected by 2030 will be recognized by 2025 with applications designed for operational improvements using one or all three of the first three elements of blockchain ‒ distribution, encryption, and immutability. The authors refer to these elements as blockchain-inspired solutions, which are often closed, private, or permissioned blockchain networks. They cannot support exchanging value with anonymous participants without the elements of tokenization and decentralization.

Although these key components of blockchain should be a part of any blockchain implementation, they need not be present in the same way. For example, a permissionless, permissioned, or consortium blockchain can operate differently from each other. Although permissionless blockchains represent the initial implementation of blockchain technology, the continued investment in blockchain technology by commercial enterprises has led to a more fragmented marketplace. In other words, organizations recognize the value of blockchain technology but continually seek to make it customized and more practical for specific organizational use cases.

The Promise of Blockchain

Despite continuous conversation both in academe and industry connected to the technology, blockchain is neither distinct nor unique from other technology tools and services. The promise of blockchain depends on the individuals tasked with implementation, specific processes used to implement and monitor implementation, and how blockchain interoperates with existing technology platforms. Education, training, and the implementation of appropriate internal controls around the blockchain and associated information are of the highest importance. No technology solution, blockchain or otherwise, can either address or solve underlying business problems. That said, several fundamental benefits and promises are associated with blockchain that seem to be prevalent regardless of the specific blockchain in question.

Efficiency

Blockchain-inspired solutions offer considerable benefits even without the elements of tokenization and decentralization. Organizations are leveraging these solutions as a way of modernizing outdated systems and automating manual processes to improve record-keeping and transparency, especially in those systems and processes crossing enterprise boundaries (Furlonger and Uzureau 2019). A use case that has led this facet of the blockchain conversation, highlighted by the efforts at organizations like Walmart and IBM, is the efficiencies that can be derived from a supply chain oriented blockchain. Tracing and comparing information that is collected from an array of different systems, when compared to the potential of storing all pertinent information on one common platform, seem cumbersome, costly, and inefficient. Different economic sectors including financial services, insurance, healthcare, retail, and logistics represent additional areas in which blockchain seems well positioned to deliver efficiencies to all network participants. Innovators of blockchain technology seemingly designed it to bring many of the data processing and analysis efficiencies currently contained within individual organizations to a network of organizations.

Transparency

Competition has always driven industries to search for faster, cheaper, and more efficient methods not only to provide goods and services to customers but also to attract new customers. Early adopters of technological innovations, which remove friction from business processes and communication, extend the innovation's competitive advantage in their market. However, as such innovations become mainstream, they eventually become table stakes to compete in today's global markets. As an example, consider the adoption of the internet during the 1990s, which brought the ecommerce revolution leveling some frictions in global trade with faster avenues to communicate with, market to, and ultimately sell to customers in a larger geographical area than previously. Similarly, the internet's predecessor ‒ the telephone ‒ allowed for real-time communication over longer distances than possible before its invention. However, some frictions remain, and new frictions can result from technological innovations. Conflicting cross-border regulation and data security concerns are examples of continued friction in global commerce in the post-internet age. These market frictions include anything that impedes the exchange of assets or adds costs or delays to the sales and delivery processes, such as regulations, bureaucracy, fraud, and intermediaries (Gupta 2018).

Although these frictions affect different industries in various ways, they fall into three primary categories: (1) information frictions, (2) interaction frictions, and (3) innovation frictions.

  • Information frictions: Information frictions delay product delivery and decision-making with incorrect or inconsistent information, while an abundance of data is available but inaccessible (Gupta 2018). Consider the global shipping industry with more than 5,000 container ships circling the globe. Some ships have the capacity to transport up to 20,000 containers of goods at a time. At that volume, incomplete, incorrect, or missing documentation can hold up goods in the shipping process resulting in additional costs and lost revenue. Yet, much of the record-keeping in that industry is paper based (Furlonger and Uzureau 2019). In addition, companies today with digitized processes battle information friction related to privacy and cybercrime risks, which did not exist before the internet and ecommerce (Gupta 2018). This situation indicates that even a globally sophisticated industry, such as global shipping and logistics, can be improved by integrating blockchain technology into existing business practices.
  • Interaction frictions: Interaction frictions occur in business transactions where the cost of doing business is too high or the degree of separation between the producer and customer is vast. The number of intermediaries required in the process amplifies this type of friction. Friction is often a part of doing business, but that does not mean that it must remain, especially in the light of advanced technologies such as blockchain.
  • Innovation frictions: Innovation frictions include internal bureaucracy, legacy systems, and industry regulations that prohibit a company's ability to react to market changes in a timely manner. In essence, innovation frictions most commonly take the form of obstacles and reluctance to embrace new technologies or methods of doing business. Although all industries encounter innovation frictions, the financial services market illustrates these frictions well. Firms in this sector must all comply with know your customer, anti-money laundering, and other rules. Compliance is challenging as these regulations differ across jurisdictions (Accenture and DTCC 2019). Invisible innovation frictions also exist that threaten industry incumbents with new business models made possible by innovative technologies (Gupta 2018). Compliance and consumer protections may ultimately improve the industry at large, but the impact on delaying the introduction of new processes cannot be ignored.

To address market frictions in the global shipping industry, Mearsk and IBM announced their joint-venture called TradeLens, a blockchain-inspired shipping solution designed to improve efficiency in the shipping industry through information sharing and transparency. During a 12-month trial before the platform's announcement in January 2018, 94 participating organizations captured more than 154 million shipping events, such as vessel arrival times, customs releases, and bills of landing. By some participant estimates, improved transparency and information sharing have the potential to reduce the number of steps in answering basic operational questions by 90% and the involvement in answering those questions from five people to one person. In addition, one demonstration during that same 12-month trial avoided thousands of dollars in cost by reducing transit time of packaging materials to a production line in the United States by 40% (IBM 2018). Following this initial success, the TradeLens network expanded, and as of 2020 includes more than 175 unique organizations publishing more than 2,000,000 events to its blockchain ecosystem per day.

Traceability

The traceability of information via a blockchain platform is not necessarily only connected to a blockchain platform, but it is a portion of the functionality that distinguishes blockchain from alternative data management systems. As cited in numerous academic and practitioner texts, an organization's ability to trace, document, and otherwise monitor the information transferred between different network members can definitively be a business case of blockchain. Especially in the aftermath of COVID-19, which has societal, economic, and political implications, the ability of a data management system to trace, report, and document the information reported out of the system represents an added value. Tracing also has direct implications for the attestation and assurance of the information reported to external markets by organizations. The potential of a complete and continuous audit continues to increase.

COVID-19 is just one example of how the global business landscape can benefit from the ability to trace goods and services from origin to financial consumer purchase location. In reality, however, the benefits of increased traceability extend far beyond modifying existing audit and assurance services. Matters that might seem as critically important such as cracking down on illegal replicas of higher end goods would clearly benefit from this increased transparency. However, other examples and applications illustrate the interconnectedness of blockchain, supply chains, and the global economy. Conflict minerals, which are minerals mined in an area of armed conflict and traded illicitly to finance the fighting such as in Africa, may not be making headlines the way they once had. Nonetheless, the ability to continuously and transparently trace the origin of minerals and other goods could improve both the markets and the lives of millions of individuals.

Decreased Costs

Costs related to the processing of information occupy considerable time for every top-level executive. Blockchain seems to offer a potential solution to the issues the many organizations and top-level executives face. However, an area of concern involves the costs required to implement, develop, and fully operationalize a blockchain system and platform. As with any technology implementation, organizations face the trade-off of incurring costs and inconveniences today to reduce costs and complexity in the future. As blockchain implementation accelerates, organizations can realize cost savings and other benefits more quickly.

Here is a partial list of such savings and benefits.

  • Reduce manual processes: The manual checking, reviewing, and confirming of data represent tasks and processes that are time consuming but fail to deliver much in the way of tangible business value to either clients or the organization. For instance, organizations allocate time, effort, and budget within the audit process to confirming previously completed work. As digitization and automation continue to disrupt every economic sector, the current status quo is unsustainable. Auditors must understand both the technical and implementation issues involving blockchain.
  • Increase automation: Another area of potential cost savings involves the insurance industry, which by its nature is a multifaceted and multistakeholder ecosystem. Under current technology systems and platforms, more than half a dozen different organizations may need to review and process an insurance claim before it is approved or denied. The blockchain application of a smart contract, which is code embedded onto an underlying blockchain platform that is executed by an external event, has the potential to streamline this process. For example, once a police report is filed as a result of an accident and those data are entered into the current system, that current system could then initiate a series of transactions and events automatically. Although manual review and approval are still needed during the process, the time and cost of processing data can be reduced because of increasing automation.
  • Permit peer-to-peer (P2P) transactions: Fees and other costs incurred as a result of accepting payment facilitated by existing third-party transactions can be substantial. In fact, estimates of these costs are often in excess of $136 billion in the United States alone in 2018. The initial intent of blockchain was to disrupt third-party financial institutions and allow P2P transacting of value between individuals and institutions. Even if an organization is not using bitcoin or some other kind of cryptoasset, the seamless and integrated nature of how data are processed and handled as a part of a blockchain network can deliver substantial cost savings. In a globalized business environment, the business anecdote relating time to money is growing more relevant.

Technical Challenges

Blockchain, like any other technology tool or platform, has several technical components and factors that need to be resolved to operate effectively. Although not solely a technical issue or concern, the ability of blockchain to transition from a fringe topic to more of a mainstream application is at least partially dependent on resolving outstanding technical issues. Implementing any enterprise level tool or application is bound to need to contend with an array of technical, scaling, and other interoperability issues. Blockchain is no different. To that end, some specific items seem to be recurring issues forestalling wider adoption of blockchain.

Speed and Scalability

Two key challenges to blockchain-complete solutions are the speed and scalability of blockchain networks. Moreover, the size of the blockchain ledger and transaction processing rate limitations affect both speed and scalability (Koteska, Karafiloski, and Mishev 2017). Specifically, speed and scalability preclude the element of decentralization in these solutions. For instance, bitcoin, which employs the proof-of-work (PoW) consensus protocol to support the decentralized governance of the network, has a limited block size of 1 megabyte (MB) with the ability of mining a single block about every 10 minutes. This network cannot handle a high frequency of transactions because it is restricted to a rate of seven transactions per second (TPS). For comparison, the VISA credit card processing network, which consistently processes 2,000 TPS with capacity to accommodate upwards of 10,000 TPS during peak times (Swan 2015).

One solution to combat low-transaction rates is to increase block size. However, increasing the block size of the bitcoin blockchain would require more storage space and result in slower propagation throughout the network. According to the website, that provides data and insights on the bitcoin blockchain (Blockchain.com 2020), the blockchain increased nearly 30% from 198,101 MB at year end 2018 to 256,141 MB at year end 2019.

Limited block size and low-transaction throughput are a trade-off for consensus protocols supporting a decentralized governance model such a PoW (Zheng, Xie, Dai, Chan, and Want 2018). This trade-off makes decentralized blockchain-complete solutions currently inadequate for industries such as financial services requiring high-volume transaction rates. This issue among others linked to scaling and enterprise adoption has led to the development of permissioned, private, or other iterations of blockchain technology. No matter what solution is pursued, the processing speed of the blockchain must be commercially viable. Thus, if an organization cannot process data at an appropriate speed to be competitive with existing systems, the pace of blockchain adoption slows.

Another obstacle to wider blockchain adoption is scaling a blockchain. As blockchain implementation grows, the system must be able to grow at a sustainable rate to meet higher rates of demand. Simply scaling or expanding a blockchain's scope is not as simple as increasing the amount of hardware or the capacity of software allocated to the task at hand. To be compatible with the demands and expectations of enterprises, any blockchain must be able to scale and meet an organization's transaction demands.

Lack of Standardization

Another substantial obstacle to wider adoption and utilization of blockchain technology is unrelated to the technology's technical or operational aspects but to the fragmentation that has developed in this space. As large commercial enterprises build and implement permissioned blockchains, the risk of developing so called “walled gardens” exists. Looking back to the early days of the internet, the earliest networks and applications running on the internet consisted of either closed corporate networks or networks that while available outside of the organization required special access permissioned. This fragmentation threatened to stifle the innovative potential until private sector entities began to develop portals, websites, and other online applications accessible to the mass market.

Blockchain faces a similar dilemma with permissionless blockchains fading from the forefront outside of cryptocurrencies such as bitcoin, and permissioned blockchains organized and managed by a single or small group of organizations moving to the forefront. Although a single organization or network of organizations may be preferable this situation, it can make the development of sector and economic standards more difficult. For example, if a regulator is attempting to develop disclosure and reporting standards related to blockchain for a specific industry, this task is likely if a consensus already exists within the industry. To illustrate, imagine the following situation. The largest 20 organizations in the accounting field, perhaps the Big 4 and other large firms, pool resources to conduct research and develop a template for blockchain for the accounting profession. With this semi-consensus forming in the private sector, conversations with regulators such as the Public Company Accounting Oversight Board would likely be more productive than if these organizations individually presented 20 different blockchain standards.

Interoperability

How do blockchains interoperate and function alongside existing technology systems? This point of consideration, while seemingly overtly technical in nature, is likely to have a substantial impact on the pace of implementation across different economic sectors. No matter what specific iteration or version is analyzed, blockchains are a recording platform that documents and stores previous transactions. In other words, a blockchain by itself cannot interact with, export, or import information onto the blockchain; other applications are needed to operationalize the proposed benefits of blockchain implementation.

Besides public blockchains, such as bitcoin, and private blockchains, such as the blockchain-inspired solutions described earlier, many individual organizations are joining forces with others on blockchain projects. These blockchain consortia center around mutual interests, like industry, geographic location, technology, or common business processes (Furlonger and Uzureau 2019).

As a result, numerous industries have deployed blockchain solutions or such deployments are happening. As one consortium designs and implements solutions and standards based on its priorities, the ability to share data with other blockchain-based systems is not usually a priority. Essentially, the consortium focuses on building a solution to prove its use cases above the long-term initiative of building solutions that will work with complementing blockchain platforms (Hewett, Pawczuk, Nielsen, and Sin 2020). This short-term approach is creating siloed data within these various blockchain ecosystems. Although a place exists for siloed or compartmentalized information for any blockchain system to actually achieve the benefits promised, network members must be able to freely interchange data among themselves.

Wide-spread blockchain adoption requires a way to breakdown these silos. This concept is known as blockchain interoperability. According to Hewett et al. (2020), interoperability is the capacity to exchange and use information as well as to transfer assets between two or more blockchain systems while maintaining the uniqueness of the asset consistent. Thus, two types of blockchain interoperability are the exchange of digital assets, for example, making bitcoin spendable in Ethereum applications, and arbitrary data exchange, such as records of events, among blockchain solutions. The latter example is similar to using an application programming interface (API), which calls to exchange data or trigger events in traditional non-blockchain applications.

This increasing need for interoperability and wider spread blockchain adoption also seems to reinforce the business case for developing consortium blockchains. A consortium arrangement generates several benefits for the organizations involved that not only encourage wider utilization but also make doing so less risky. Specifically, organizations involved in a consortium model can spread the cost, complexity, and liability associated with the development and implementation of a blockchain platform. This approach might seem like an obvious point but is worth noting considering the cost that any large technology project entails.

As a top concern for organizations exploring blockchain, interoperability can be separated into three layers: (1) business model, (2) platform, and (3) infrastructure. While business model considerations tackle challenges such as system governance, data standardization and ownership of data, platform considerations focus on whether the blockchain systems are technically compatible. The infrastructure layer considers components enabling the blockchain platform such as compute, storage, network, and virtualization (Hewett et al. 2020).

At the time of this writing, three approaches are being employed to tackle the challenge of cross-chain interoperability. Cross-authentication is the one approach consisting of three individual technical methods to address interoperability. The simplest of the three, notary schemes leverage a trusted party, or notary, consensus algorithm to come to a conditional agreement and issue a signature used to finalize a transaction on a blockchain. However, this approach centralizes trust in the blockchain environment, which negates the decentralization requirement of blockchain-complete solutions. Relays, the second method of cross-authentication interoperability approaches, allow a secure message to pass between two blockchain platforms. For relays to work, both blockchain platforms must share certain characteristics making relays extremely difficult to employ. Hash-locking is the third cross-authentication method that requires setting up the same event trigger in both blockchain platforms wishing to share transaction data. Several companies have developed cross-authentication interoperability solutions with relays being most popular among startups and hash-locking most popular among enterprise solutions (Hewett, et al. 2020).

The second cross-chain interoperability approach consists of leveraging API gateways. APIs have been used in traditional applications for quite some time to govern access to the application's data and to provide developers tools to interact with the application. An AIP gateway simply organizes multiple APIs organizing requests for the underlying architecture. Their longstanding use in application development make API gateways easier to create and implement than other interoperability approaches. Like notary schemes, API gateways centralize the trust to the operator of the APIs.

The third approach to cross-chain interoperability employs an agent, known as an oracle, to transfer external data to a blockchain. Oracles use smart contracts to add information about real-world events such as temperatures, prices, or other information, onto a blockchain. Once on-chain, that information can be used for business process automation. Like API gateways, oracles are easy to implement and have a proven success rate in non-blockchain environments. On the other hand, oracles do not create true blockchain-to-blockchain interoperability. They simply incorporate non-blockchain systems making a blockchain interoperable to those non-blockchain systems.

Regulatory Ambiguity

Another issue involving the potential opportunities and challenges associated with blockchain technology is the uncertain regulatory landscape. Leaving aside the specifics of regulatory differentiation that continue to exist, the bigger picture perspective around regulation and regulatory issues present both an opportunity and challenge for blockchain implementation.

Regulatory ambiguity and uncertainty from a tax, accounting, financial, and operational perspective creates an opportunity for organizations seeking to move quickly toward wider adoption. Since few consistently enforced and applicable rules and regulations connected to blockchain implementation are available, this situation creates an opportunity for experimentation and potentially new methods of integrating blockchain with existing technologies. A regulatory sandbox, an allowance by regulators permitting organizations to implement new technologies without having to be in compliance with the full scope of existing regulations, is a pertinent example of how this mindset can manifest. Like any new technology, regulation and regulatory opinion have lagged private sector implementation. Such a gap provides first mover organizations with an opportunity to set standards and play a proactive role in further development.

Conversely, regulatory ambiguity and uncertainty can also create hurdles and obstacles toward wider implementation for budgetary and financial planning considerations. Organizational leaders, regardless of personal viewpoints of blockchain technology, are aware of the budgetary requirements and obligations already in place. Blockchain technology requires both up-front (capital) and ongoing (operational) expenditures. Without consistent, understandable, and enforceable regulation policies, or even the promise of consistent guidelines on the horizon, implementing blockchain projects and initiatives could stall. Without clear guardrails and a general understanding of what will be expected of organizations now and going forward, a risk exists that implementation is likely to continue at rates lower than might otherwise be expected.

Regulations are a fundamental part of any industry, any business, or any new technology initiative and play an important role in the business decision-making process. Removing the hype, excitement, or doubt that may accompany the technology itself, blockchain is an emerging technology in a still-evolving regulatory environment. Clearly regulation, or lack thereof, is unlikely to solve or cause all of the problems in the blockchain arena, but it is an important factor that organizations need to assess and understand.

Summary and Conclusions

In its short tenure, blockchain has demonstrated its potential to transform the way businesses operate. This revolutionary technology can streamline outdated and inefficient business processes and eliminate the friction organizations face operating in today's rapidly changing global economy. Blockchain's ability to trace, report, and document information and events in a more transparent manner is an important competitive advantage over legacy systems. In the long run, each of these benefits leads to cost saving that could eventually offset the investment in blockchain.

As with any innovative technology, blockchain has many challenges to overcome. Currently, blockchain can neither compete with the speed of traditional systems nor scale to meet transactional demands of most industries. Yet, blockchain's biggest challenge is not technical in nature. The lack of standards in the blockchain space continues to lead the technology down a path of siloed solutions resulting in multiple blockchains where sharing and exchanging data between platforms are not simple or straightforward. Although these are considerable obstacles to adopting blockchain, they are all issues that pervious innovations, such as the internet, also had to conquer. Organizations around the world are investing in blockchain and applying creative tactics to tackle these issues. As implementors overcome these concerns over time, such matters will eventually become part of blockchain's history as the technology becomes embedded in daily business operations.

Discussion Questions

(1)Describe the business use cases related to blockchain traceability and transparency.

(2)Discuss how blockchain implementation may decrease costs among network partners.

(3)Describe how interoperability issues can complicate blockchain implementation.

(4)Explain how a lack of blockchain standards impedes wider adoption of blockchain technology and platforms.
