Chapter 11

The Importance of Interoperability, Decentralization, and Choice

Kirk Phillips

Keywords: Blockchain; interoperability; internet of blockchains; decentralization; cross-chain compatibility; token bridge; atomic swaps; payment channels; oracles; sidechains

Introduction

After the introduction of the bitcoin blockchain, hundreds of other blockchains including private and consortium chains followed, but they were largely independent ecosystems. Private and consortium blockchains are operated by an administrator and require permission to use, whereas bitcoin and other public blockchains are permissionless, and anyone can freely participate. The full value proposition of blockchains can be realized when they become interoperable, which means value can be transferred among chains and the features of one can be borrowed by another.

Bitcoin solved the double-spend problem, a situation where a user can spend the same money twice, with a perfectly balanced ecosystem by rewarding volunteers to secure the network via mining. The network is slow with around seven transactions per second (TPS), but it is the most secure network in human history and the world's most powerful supercomputer. Shortly thereafter, Ethereum developers staring working on the namesake chain to create a programmable blockchain opening up the world of decentralized apps (dApps) and decentralized finance (DeFi). It is a more flexible adaptable blockchain that differs from but is inspired by the bitcoin blockchain. Ethereum is known as the original smart contracts blockchain. Now dozens of “Ethereums” are available competing for supremacy.

Security and scalability are typically inversely related so decentralized public blockchains suffer from the scalability challenge to compete with high throughput networks that can power the global financial system. The blockchain race is not all about 50,000 TPS networks outperforming VISA but a plethora of innovation for multiple use cases. Some blockchains differentiate based on their consensus model such as touting proof of stake (PoS) as more efficient than bitcoin's energy hogging proof of work (PoW). Users stake coins like bonding to secure a network in the PoS model, whereas miners use specialized computers to secure a network in the PoS model. As of March 2020, Coinmarketcap.com lists more than 5,000 crypto assets and related blockchains. Some blockchains are slight variations of their bitcoin cousin because of the open source model, while others like IOTA, which stands for Internet of Things Application, uses neither blocks, blockchains nor transaction fees. Perhaps a majority of “blockchains projects” are more interested in profiting from the tech hype rather than innovating. In the long run, many winners are likely to emerge offering something unique and valuable.

Interoperability can be defined in several ways. For example, O'Neal (2019, par. 1) defines interoperability as “the ability to share information across different blockchain networks, without restrictions.” Muzzy and Anderson (2020, par. 1) view interoperability as “the ability for blockchains to exchange data between platforms – including off-chain data and transactions – without the aid of third parties.” For the purpose of this chapter, however, interoperability generally means whether one system can work with another. Although interoperability can show up in the blockchain space in different ways, the main context is one blockchain interacting with another. Blockchain interoperability is also referred to as the internet of blockchains. Interoperability is simply cross functionality. Tokens, wallets, dApps, DeFi, and more must evolve into interoperability so the true blockchain and crypto-value proposition can emerge (Down 2019a).

The importance of blockchain interoperability is best understood by looking at the development of the early internet, centralization versus decentralization, and the power of choice. The true internet of blockchains requires interoperability among several domains in the form of on-ramps, off-ramps, bridges, tunnels, and other creative connectors including interoperability blockchains and protocols, programming languages, sidechains, cross-chains, token bridges, wrapped tokens, wallet standards, oracles, atomic swaps, and payment channels among others.

The purpose of this chapter is to examine the development of blockchain interoperability and how it relates to the development of the early internet. It also examines the many different ways of achieving blockchain interoperability and why it is such a critical value proposition for the success of the blockchain ecosystem.

The chapter has the following organization. The next section draws a close parallel to the development of the early internet and how blockchain could follow a similar path unless blockchain interoperability and decentralization have a chance to mature and gain traction. The following section provides a discussion of why the surge of interoperability development is gaining momentum and why blockchain may be able to deliver what the pioneers of the early internet attempted to achieve. Next, a bitcoin primer and economics refresher set the stage for what blockchain solves related to the current financial system. Finally, the chapter explains various interoperability solutions including interoperability blockchains, cross-chain compatibility, sidechains, token bridges, oracles, wallet standards, atomic swaps, and other solutions.

The State of Blockchains and Decentralization

Competition drives blockchain projects to outperform one another on metrics including funding, users, token price, network speed and security. The initial result is a bunch of great projects operating as separate ecosystem silos. The ability to use different systems and still work together is how the internet, cloud-based models, and application programming interfaces (APIs) enable commerce to work. Blockchains need to connect and become one like the mycelium of mushrooms and our brain's neural network.

Interoperability breeds decentralization. The decentralized world adds security, immutability, privacy, provenance, programmable money, self-sovereign identity, and so on. For example, Bitcoin's consensus model makes altering its blockchain infeasible providing a highly secure network and transaction immutability. As a result, the provenance of documents and digital artwork can be cryptographically proven as unaltered and original. The programmability of the Ethereum blockchain has led to major developments of decentralized finance applications, which offer the ability to create programmable money and synthetic assets. Finally, zero-knowledge proofs, a mathematical way to prove data without revealing it, allow individuals to control their own identity rather than having third parties control it. For example, Tradle's app gives users the ability to verify their identity with financial institutions among other use cases. Only blockchain and crypto assets can deliver those high value proposition attributes, but they must be frictionlessly tethered to one another to reach the pinnacle of interoperability.

Decentralization benefits and aligns the incentives of all global stakeholders such as citizens, countries, and companies made possible by blockchain. Sticking with the centralized model and all of its underpinnings is easy if the average person cannot understand or does not care about how blockchain levels the playing field to sustain mankind. Decentralization needs all the help it can get, and interoperability is the critical path.

Early Internet Lessons

The internet started as a government-funded academic research project that continued for about 20 years until the private sector became more interested in commercialization. Given that infrastructure was expensive, universities had an incentive to share mainframe computers and open source the internet development. Eventually all major universities were connected into what was known as the National Science Foundation Network (NSFNET), creating more demand especially from private entities who wanted to commercialize it. The internet was so strained from limited capacity that NSFNET banned commercial activity and private entities simply created private networks as a work around.

The World Wide Web Consortium started in the mid-1990s to focus on standards to maintain the core ideology of interoperability. Tim Berners-Lee was an evangelist for universal protocols and the free flow of information, which he believed was more valuable when information is widely available and accessible. The race of interoperability versus commercialization had begun, and the appetite for making profits as soon as possible at the expense of getting the protocol right eventually won.

According to Muzzy and Anderson (2020, par. 12)

Though interoperability was a core aspiration of Berners-Lee and other early Internet architects, all that mattered to the end-consumers (and thus to the companies seeking to profit from them) was that the Internet scaled to everyday utility as quickly as possible. In this way, the incentives that pushed the Internet to deprioritize interoperability and focus on the everyday usability of the technology are no different than today.

Third parties, also known as private enterprises, simply filled the interoperability gap as information gatekeepers who create the illusion of limited supply and therefore control the price. A handful of entities “balkanized” the internet by wrestling the promise of a decentralized internet away from the public good at a time when regulation was essentially non-existent. Consumers have foregone control of their information and privacy becoming the product of the Facebooks and Googles of the world. Free services are free because the consumer is the product. Thus, data are unsecure, and consumers lack control of their identities or money.

Second Chance

The fact that blockchain arrived just a few decades later with a second chance to get the internet right is a miracle (Oakley 2018). The importance of interoperability and the pursuit of Web3, also called Web 3.0, can be summed up in one sentence ‒ if developers do not get this task done correctly, they probably won't get another chance. Time is of the essence and the interoperability versus commercialization race is on again. Blockchain neutrality is hanging in the balance but interoperability has a chance to connect and decentralize all the work in the blockchain space over the past decade.

According to Down (2019a, par. 6), “Decentralizing the internet with blockchain technology is appealing because it could lead to a more secure and fair internet than the one we know today. There would be no central points to hack and no way for a few powerful actors to take control of the information,” and going further, “If a blockchain service wants a wider user base, it must sacrifice the unique properties of blockchains by delivering the services via a centralized platform.” Decentralization is not just about mass adoption. Instead, it is about achieving a decentralized internet.

Bitcoin Background Economics and Limitations

Bitcoin is known for its transaction immutability proposition resulting from the security of the PoW consensus model. Its fixed and predictable monetary supply provides an excellent store of value and medium of exchange, but it provides a poor unit of account. These are the three properties of money. Some people contend that bitcoin is not a good medium of exchange depending on their context and point of view.

For example, people in the payment card industry like VISA and MasterCard have a filter for judging a network based on high throughput or TPS. Since VISA processes 1700 TPS, on average, with an approximately 25,000 TPS or higher capacity, it would likely view bitcoin as slow and clunky at seven TPS (Visa 2020; Blockchain.com 2020). However, rewriting or reversing transactions on the bitcoin blockchain is economically infeasible. Miners would actually waste resources that they could use to earn block rewards. More simply, bitcoin is economically designed to incentivize participants to play by the rules. By doing so, they get rewarded and if participants do not play by the rules, they waste their own money and resources. Once a bitcoin transaction is sent, it cannot be reversed provided a sufficient number of confirmations because no one party has the power to do so.

For example, consider credit card chargebacks, those pesky expensive transaction disputes from fraud or customers who want to game the system. Credit card information is stolen, and unauthorized charges cost businesses and consumers billions in fraud. A user's credit card information is insecure in centralized databases, and transactions are reversible to compensate for an antiquated system. Bitcoin may be slow but it is highly secure, and a fast TPS network does not mean that it is a robust network. Passing judgment on what constitutes a great medium of exchange may be in the eyes of the beholder. Nonetheless, a lack of speed or high throughput in the bitcoin network does not discount its excellent medium of exchange value proposition.

Even though bitcoin has an outstanding medium of exchange and store of value, the network feature set is fairly limited. No native bitcoin smart contract capabilities and related programming languages exist. A small amount of information such as a hash can be included in a bitcoin transaction proving a document or set of documents has not been altered. This capability, the aforementioned immutability attribute, is invaluable unto itself but bitcoin is not expressive like Ethereum.

De Facto Interoperability

Third-party crypto exchanges account for about 95 percent of crypto trading at the beginning of 2020 and are de facto interoperability mechanisms. If someone has bitcoin (BTC) and wants ether (ETH), that person sends BTC to an exchange platform, sells BTC and buys ETH, and then sends the ETH back to his or her wallet. Third-party exchanges solve the disparate blockchain problem with a centralized marketplace for cryptocurrency trading. They are bootstrapping the blockchain ecosystem while interoperability evolves (Huillet 2019).

The existence of third-party exchanges, which are akin to financial institutions, is ironic considering bitcoin was born out of the cypherpunks, people who believe in privacy-enhancing technology. Bitcoin is a censorship resistant, open, neutral, peer-to-peer (P2P), decentralized universal global financial network independent of banks and counter parties. Ironically, bitcoin, the native currency of Bitcoin the network, is taken out its decentralized home and moved to a centralized third-party exchange for trading most of the time. This situation personifies the independent unconnected nature of blockchains in its first decade.

Interoperability Blockchains (Interopchains)

The emergence of blockchains whose main purpose is connecting new and existing blockchains is one of the most broad and comprehensive solutions for interoperability. For example, if bitcoin's main purpose is security and Ethereum's is programmability, then the main purpose of new blockchains like Cosmos, Polkadot, Wanchain, and others is interoperability. In many ways, interoperability is part of the DNA of these networks so newly created blockchains are automatically connected to blockchains within Cosmos or Ardor for example. Let's use the universe as a metaphor for blockchain interoperability. Solar systems are the first tier of celestial bodies followed by galaxies, local groups, clusters, super clusters, and the all-encompassing universe. The universe is the utopian internet of blockchains, and interoperability blockchains are like galaxies or clusters and the rest of the “independent” blockchains are like solar systems within galaxies. Blockchain connectedness will expand over time while progressing through galaxy mode on the way to a fully accessible universe.

Cosmos

Cosmos created a hub and zone interoperability network using a standard protocol ‒ the Inter-Blockchain Communication (IBC) protocol ‒ to allow blockchains to transfer tokens and data. Cosmos achieves modularity by building a blockchain engine designed to handle the consensus and networking layers while relegating the application or transaction processing layer to developers of new blockchain projects. Otherwise, developers have to create a new blockchain from scratch with all three layers. Consensus is the method where network nodes agree on the blockchain state at any given time, while networking handles the propagation of transactions to nodes in the network. Cosmos bundles these together with an application blockchain interface (ABCI) allowing developers to program in any language. Application development becomes programming language agnostic removing a huge barrier to development friction.

Zones are either new or existing blockchains; hubs are the blockchains connecting the zones. Cosmos is the first hub in the Cosmos network. Hubs are Cosmos' definition of interopchains.

Cosmos is a decentralized network of independent parallel blockchains, each powered by BFT…The vision of Cosmos is to make it easy for developers to build blockchains and break the barriers between blockchains by allowing them to transact with each other. The end goal is to create an Internet of Blockchains, a network of blockchains able to communicate with each other in a decentralized way. (Cosmos 2020, par. 1, 16)

Additionally, both public and permissionless (private and consortium) blockchains can be built on and connected to the Cosmos network.

Polkadot

Polkadot is a different approach to the interopchain model. It uses parachains and a relay chain for interoperability as explained below.

Polkadot is built to connect private and consortium chains, public and permissionless networks, oracles, and future technologies that are yet to be created. Polkadot facilitates an internet where independent blockchains can exchange information and transactions in a trustless way via the Polkadot relay chain. (Polkadot 2020, par. 2)

A parachain is a specialized blockchain focusing on unique application features and transaction processing. Although parachains are similar to zones in Cosmos, parachains are child-chains of the relay chain, the parent chain. The relay chain provides the security mechanism via global consensus for all the child parachains and finalizes all blocks of the parachains into one global state.

Cosmos blockchain zones are independent sovereign blockchains connected via the Cosmos hub or other future hubs and IBC protocol. The hub is not a global state like the relay chain in Polkadot. Therefore, the main difference between the two approaches is blockchain sovereignty and whether a blockchain can function independently of the hub or relay chain, respectively.

One approach is not necessarily better than the other but a game of trade-offs. The task is to choose which trade-off best suits a particular blockchain vision. Parachains are not independent, but they get the benefit of shared security without each parachain having its own set of validators. Cosmos zones are independent sovereign blockchains that have their own built-in security, regardless of whether it was built with the ABCI, but each zone needs its own set of validators. According to Agrawal (2019), Cosmos prioritizes sovereignty. As a result, each Hub and Zone is responsible for its own security. Unlike Polkadot, Cosmos does not follow the shared security model; instead every hub and zone needs its own validator. Cosmos' modularity allows creating a completely private blockchain and still be able to connect it with hubs to send and receive tokens from other public/private blockchains.

Cross-chains

Cross-chains or cross-chain technology is another way to describe interoperability blockchains or more simply “interopchains.” However, cross-chain technology could refer to a platform bridging only two blockchains, which is narrower than blockchain technology with capabilities and ambitions to link an unlimited number or blockchains. Every interopchain is a cross-chain but not every cross-chain is an interopchain (Down 2019b).

Chain-split Refresher

The DAO Hack and the subsequent Ethereum hard fork are two of the most famous and interrelated events in crypto and blockchain history. In spring 2016, the DAO, short for decentralized autonomous organization, was a smart contract-based crowdfunding platform allowing DAO token holders to vote on projects self-funded by the DAO. The DAO set an initial coin offering (ICO) record at the time for about $150 million, but a bug in the smart contract allowed a hacker to drain $50 million. A great debate ensued to rewrite history and roll back the blockchain or to not re-write history. Then on July 20, 2016, a hard fork, which is a backward incompatible upgrade, was deployed to roll back Ethereum as if the hack never happened, resulting in a chain-split into an Ethereum (ETH) chain and an Ethereum Classic (ETC) chain. This action resulted in two chains and two tokens even since forever connected by the blockchain just before the split. Even though these chains share a common trunk, they are ironically incompatible with one another.

Now fast forward to another hard fork in January 2020 called Agharta, which this time is on the Ethereum Classic blockchain. ETC Labs founder, James Wo said

This update is a signal that we want to be compatible with Ethereum. We believe in the success of public blockchains, because they are built on the strength of the community. (Cant 2019, par. 6)

The Agharta hard fork creates backward compatibility between the networks, which allows Ethereum Classic especially to benefit from the massive development on the Ethereum blockchain. In January 2020, ETH had over 2,700 dApps, decentralized versions of the thousands of apps in everyday use, or 76 times the number of ETC's 36 dApps. Agharta included Ethereum's Constantinople and Petersburg protocol upgrades completing the initiative for ETH and ETC cross-chain compatibility (Messari 2020).

Sidechains

Sidechains run in parallel but are independent of native blockchains like bitcoin. The main purpose of sidechains is to provide features beyond those provided by the native chain. The sidechain can be developed more easily and quickly than the native chain could implement the same changes. Decentralized governance of public blockchains typically takes a long time and bitcoin, for example, makes changes much more conservatively than other chains. In some cases, the likelihood of a feature upgrade is quite low on a native chain, and the only way a feature may come to life is getting rolled out on a sidechain. A sidechain does not have a native token but rather creates a two-way peg or a 1:1 peg between bitcoin (tokens) and the “pegged bitcoin” on the sidechain. Sidechains are not exclusive to bitcoin and could be developed in theory for any blockchain. Feature improvements can continue on a sidechain independent of the governance process of a native chain. The native chain has less risk from unforeseen bugs resulting from protocol upgrades. Therefore, features are bifurcated between chains and allow for more flexibility.

According to Back et al. (2014, p. 1), who first proposed sidechains

By reusing Bitcoin's currency, these systems can more easily interoperate with each other and with Bitcoin, avoiding the liquidity shortages and market fluctuations associated with new currencies. Since sidechains are separate systems, technical and economic innovation is not hindered.

The Liquid Sidechain

Bitcoin has two shortcomings in the eyes of institutional investors, exchanges, traders, and fund managers. Bitcoin is a slow network, and transactions are transparent, which is not conducive for higher frequency trading. Bitcoin's block confirmation times are 10 minutes, on average, which is slow in the blockchain universe but ultra-fast in traditional banking. The bitcoin blockchain is a transparent publicly accessible ledger, which is an otherwise great attribute but not good for confidential business transactions. Bitcoin also has probabilistic settlement finality, so a transaction is not final after one block confirmation but rather approaches zero chance of reversal after six blocks confirmation or about one hour. Traders and portfolio managers need to act fast on bitcoin and other crypto price movements, but trading opportunities disappear in 10 minutes or less.

The Liquid sidechain was developed by Blockstack to solve those shortcomings. Liquid sidechain trades have two-minute settlement finality versus 60 minutes (six bitcoin confirmations) with the bitcoin network. Transactions are confidential and cannot be viewed by competitors, which avoids front-running, for example, in the trading world. A Blockstack user would swap BTC for Liquid Bitcoin (L-BTC), the proxy token, on the Liquid sidechain. ABC Fund could send L-BTC to XYZ Exchange and execute trades within two minutes and swap back to BTC to close out of a bitcoin position (Blockstream 2020). According to Samson Mow, Blockstream's Chief Strategy Officer

With Liquid in place, we believe Bitcoin will be in a stronger position to attract institutional trading firms and brokerages, as well as address global liquidity and pricing data challenges faced by these players interested in bitcoin as an asset class. That will be a major milestone for Bitcoin, bringing many new users and applications to the industry. (Parker 2017, Par. 8)

RSK Sidechain

RSK is a smart contracts platform for the bitcoin network also known as a bitcoin sidechain. RSK states, "The term two-way peg (also 1:1 peg) refers to a system that attempts to make two tokens that live in two separate blockchains economically equivalent” (Lerner 2020, par. 2).

RSK introduces smart contracts, which is self-executing code used for various functions on blockchains, for bitcoin opening the door for the explosive innovation seen on the Ethereum smart contract blockchain. Smart contracts allow developers to create dApps so once bitcoin is moved to RSK, dApps can be used that were otherwise unavailable on the bitcoin blockchain. For example, a user sends 5.532 BTC from his bitcoin wallet to an RSK bridge wallet. The exchange turns 5.532 BTC into 5.532 rBTC, wrapped bitcoin, facilitated by a smart contract, which “locks” the bitcoin on the bitcoin blockchain and “mints” or creates 5.532 rBTC on the RSK sidechain. The total bitcoin supply decreases by 5.532 BTC substituted by the newly minted 5.532 rBTC thus maintaining parity of the total BTC supply at any one time. The minting of wrapped tokens such as rBTC does not affect the total supply of native tokens on the Bitcoin Blockchain.

Token Bridge

Sidechains increase the features and usability of native blockchains. By contrast, a token bridge connects two blockchains via dApps created with smart contracts. The bridge is a decentralized connection between the two blockchains as if they were one with no reliance on third parties. As Lerner (2020, par. 2) notes, “A token bridge can connect two arbitrary blockchains, where neither is a sidechain of the other.”

The native token of each respective blockchain needs a token standard to facilitate the “bridge swap” so a token is useable when going from one chain to the next. The token standard wraps BTC into a new token as if it were ETH (ether the Ethereum token). This process is similar to creating rBTC from BTC as mentioned above.

The RSK-ETH Bridge

RSK is creating a token bridge for BTC to ETH and vice versa using the HawkClient smart contract system. RSK uses the ERC20 token standard, which is used in conjunction with Ethereum's ERC777 standard to move BTC and ETH back and forth between both chains. The concept of moving wrapped tokens from one chain to the next is the same whether using a side chain token bridge or a decentralized exchange (Lerner 2020).

According to Adrian Eidelman, a RSK strategist at IOV Labs

Interoperability has been a cornerstone of the RSK vision from the start … We believe being able to offer Bitcoin's benefits to Ethereum users and to connect these respective developer communities is a crucial step for the blockchain ecosystem as a whole. (Baker 2020, par. 4)

The combined market cap for both BTC and ETH is about 70 percent of the total cryptocurrency market cap as of spring 2020, a percentage remaining fairly consistent for several years. Therefore, the interoperability created by the RSK-ETH bridge is substantial and blazes a path for other blockchains to follow.

Blockchain and cryptocurrencies provide the gift of choice in the context of money and value transfer. Before bitcoin, people and organizations basically lived in a one-choice world of central banks. Now they have many choices. The same holds true for interoperability solutions. Multiple smart contract blockchains are available and many choices for bitcoin to Ethereum bridges should follow.

Oracles

Smart contract blockchains do not have a mechanism to get information from the outside world. Information originating on a blockchain is on-chain, and all other information is considered off-chain. For example, a series of transactions conducted by two parties without using a blockchain are considered off-chain transactions. Smart contracts need off-chain, real-world information, to execute different business functions. For example, smart contract crop insurance needs weather facts to determine payouts and DeFi needs accurate crypto price feeds to determine collateralization ratios. The full potential of smart contracts cannot be realized without a pipeline of off-chain data (Levi and Lipton 2018). Oracles provide reliable data to smart contracts and solve the off-chain data problem. Additionally, smart contracts may need data to flow in both directions.

Oracles are a key interoperability solution for combining on-chain and off-chain data in a useable way. Otherwise, blockchains in general are isolated from both each other and the outside world. Smart contracts are only as good as the information they use, and decentralized blockchains need decentralized oracles. Centralized oracles will not work with decentralized blockchains because one centralized component or connection undermines the decentralized value proposition.

Tellor

Tellor is smart contract oracle designed to support DeFi on Ethereum using a staked PoW consensus model.

Smart contracts on Ethereum have no direct access to off-chain information. This has created a reliance on third-party providers of off-chain data points. Our system gets rid of those centralized points of failure by using a network of miners to fetch data for your smart contracts. (Tellor 2020, p. 1)

Tellor miners have an economic incentive to secure the network and provide the most accurate data, which can be challenged by participants. If a miner loses the challenge, that miner can lose staked assets as a penalty.

Chainlink

Chainlink is another oracle solution connecting smart contracts with legacy systems using any API, blockchain, and external data source. Chainlink is blockchain agnostic and eliminates the centralized oracle single point of failure problem. Chainlinks are the nodes in the Chainlink network that simultaneously evaluate the same data, thereby “decentralizing it” and making it provable before sending it to smart contracts.

The Chainlink network provides reliable tamper-proof inputs and outputs for complex smart contracts on any blockchain… Smart contracts require secure middleware to connect them to real-world data. This external data will trigger the contract, creating the need for its high reliability. (Chainlink 2020a, par. 1, 2)

Even if someone solved the general blockchain interoperability issue, the internet of blockchains would provide fairly limited and mostly on-chain use cases. Oracles are the “data valves” for blockchains making them interoperable with legacy systems via their specialized role. The Chainlink Blog describes the importance of specialization as follows:

This idea of chain specialization being more favorable than chain maximalism follows the same principles of the current Internet protocol stack. The Internet is not one monolithic do-it-all protocol; instead it's a layer of protocols that all specialize in specific functions. Protocol stacks bring optimization through layer specialization and hedge risk by decreasing the attack surface of each layer. (Chainlink 2020b, par. 5)

Wallet Standards

A wallet is the primary storage platform for crypto assets. Although many types of wallets are available, noncustodial wallets allow users to control the private keys and therefore assets. Wallets are an end point in the blockchain and cryptocurrency ecosystem. Token holders typically have multiple wallets, which do not provide any global view of tokens in all the various wallets resulting a fragmented user experience. Exchanges are another ecosystem endpoint used to buy and sell crypto assets, further scattering the transactional landscape for businesses and individuals alike. For example, if Bob sent ETH to Alice, she may not know who sent the ETH, its purpose or whether she even received it unless Bob tells her those things. Bob has to complete the transaction using clunky crypto addresses, strings of characters like this ETH address 0x89205A3A3b2A69De6Dbf7f01ED13B2108B2c43e7, creating more friction for the average user. An endpoint interoperability solution would improve the user experience gap.

Foundation for Interwallet Operability (FIO)

The FIO Foundation created the FIO Protocol and FIO chain as an endpoint usability layer integrated by endpoint platforms. Users can obtain both a FIO address and FIO domain turning clunky addresses into human readable addresses much like email. A business would register a FIO domain and allow its customers to potentially register a FIO address under that domain. For example, Token Exchange registers the domain “tokenexhange” where Bob is a customer. Bob creates a FIO address, bob@tokenexchange. Bob could also create a universal FIO address not bound to a particulate domain. Bob and Alice can now easily transact from any wallet to any wallet, know when they received the funds, and know the intended purpose of the funds. Bob could even transfer crypto assets from one wallet to another and keep track of his internal transfers, which is another common challenge in crypto (FIO 2020a).

The FIO Chain is not a sidechain or an “interopchain” and it does not provide cross-chain compatibility. It standardizes the end user's experience but requires a dedicated single use blockchain to deliver these additional features. According to FIO (FIO 2020b)

The FIO Protocol is a decentralized service layer that bridges the gap between crypto endpoints such as wallets, exchanges, crypto payment processors, and any other application in which crypto assets are held and/or transferred. The FIO Protocol is not a wallet. Rather, it integrates into existing products as a usability layer that creates an improved, homogeneous user experience for all blockchain tokens and coins by providing a layer of data and confirmations about transactions on other blockchains. The FIO Protocol does not compete with, integrate with nor interfere with any other blockchain. And it does not send transactions to or from other blockchains. Technically speaking, other blockchains are not aware of the FIO Protocol's existence.

Wallet providers and exchanges are already implementing the FIO Protocol. Taylor Monahan, CEO of MyCrypto says

We're always trying to figure out how to make crypto more accessible to everyone. It's hard to imagine our parents sending and receiving crypto with what exists right now, and FIO could be the next big step in UX that we need. (FIO 2018, par. 17)

Other Innovations in Interoperability

The expressive programmable nature of Ethereum cascaded into massive dApp application development. dApps are smart contracts that provide innovative solutions and allow users to interact with dApps using ETH, Ethereum's native token. BTC holders cannot otherwise use BTC for Ethereum dApps. Therefore, a user would have to sell BTC, potentially with a centralized third-party exchange, and buy ETH creating some level of usability friction. BTC Relay connects Ethereum smart contracts with Bitcoin to solve this problem. This cross-payment interoperability feature is valuable considering the market cap of BTC and ETH is approximately 70 percent of the total cryptocurrency market. “BTC Relay is a building block that allows Ethereum contracts to securely verify Bitcoin transactions without any intermediaries: in short, users can pay with Bitcoin to use Ethereum DAPPs” (BTC Relay 2020, p. 1). BTC Relay links the chains by allowing crypto from one chain to make payments on another chain. Substantial tax benefits are also available from having payment versatility choosing what wallet to pay from and what coin to use (Consensys 2016).

Atomic Swaps and Lightning

One of the first examples of blockchain interoperability was the invention of an atomic swap, a P2P token swap from two different blockchains like bitcoin and litecoin. Alice and Bob can make the exchange without knowing or trusting each other using a hashed time-locked contract. An atomic swap is basically a cross-chain swap that can be done using a payment channel via the lightning network as an example. It uses cryptography to link Alice and Bob's transactions so either both transfer the coins to each other successfully or the transactions do not complete (Lielacher 2018).

A lightning network is a series of off-chain payment channels where two people can conduct a very fast low-cost transaction or series of transactions, which are later settled on-chain. Payment channels also use hashed time-locked contracts, which offer flexibility to cap the total amount transacted or a certain time frame to conduct transactions.

Like atomic swaps, the lightning network utilizes hash time-locked contracts. Where atomic swaps effectively link blockchains, the lightning network links payment channels. This way, if both Alice and Bob have a payment channel open with Carol, they can transact through Carol, without needing to trust Carol. (Van Wirdum 2017, par. 13)

Cross-chain atomic swaps are limited between two blockchains and respective tokens sharing the same cryptographic hash functions. Nonetheless, payment channels and the lightning network create a layer two protocol extending the usability of an existing chain while simultaneously creating an interoperability link between two blockchains sharing the same “cryptographic hash” DNA.

Summary and Conclusions

In general, interoperability makes a set of otherwise incompatible systems work together expanding the network effect and overall value proposition for various user groups. Blockchain development is entering its second decade while multiple projects still focus on outperforming their smart contract or high transaction throughput competitors to gain traction in the marketplace. A tendency exists for interoperability to be an afterthought. The development of the internet offers valuable lessons on how the original vision and ethos of neutrality, interoperability, and accessibility got circumvented by the desire for commercialization and profits. Interoperability takes time to develop organically into Tim Berners-Lee's vision for universal protocols and the free flow of information, yet profit seekers do not possess the patience necessary and short-circuit the vision by focusing on scaling to mass adoption as fast as possible. The internet grew slowly from its government and academic beginnings and demand skyrocketed once everyone saw the potential. This tipping point of demand was the beginning of interoperability losing out to commercialization. Perhaps, blockchain's biggest gift to humankind is a second chance to get the internet right.

Although thousands of blockchains are available, none were inherently designed to incorporate interoperability throughout most of the first decade since the beginning of bitcoin in 2009. Fortunately, a massive wave of development is working on the internet of blockchains. Blockchain technology lends itself to a high degree of expressiveness and composability, so developers are proving the technical challenge is not the limitation of decentralized interoperability. Rather, the quest by entrepreneurs to become artificial information gatekeepers singularly focused on maintaining control and extracting maximum profit is the enemy of the decentralized web (Web3), the internet of blockchains, interoperability and self-sovereign identity, money and communications. Remember, Facebook and Google apps are free because you are the product. People hand over their privacy as compensation for free services, which is a continuation of the byproduct of internet development getting derailed in the early days. If people finally care enough to demand and expect better privacy and security, then the true internet of blockchains has a chance.

Blockchain has too much momentum to lose the race toward interoperability. If anything, blockchain and crypto provide a choice in the context of money, which is something previously unavailable. The fiat central bank model was a one-choice world. Even if information gatekeepers fill interoperability gaps, a fully decentralized web will eventually emerge where people can choose to be in control of their data, identity, and assets. The choice among interopchains provides an example. Additionally, cross-chain compatibility, sidechains, token bridges, oracles, wallet protocols, lightning networks, smart contract layers, token standards, and much more are collectively forming the decentralized internet of blockchains. Users should determine how they want to be in control and choose wisely.

Chapter 12

Convergence with Artificial Intelligence and Other Related Concepts

Lian Duan

Keywords: Artificial intelligence; big data; blockchain; data analytics; finance; healthcare

Introduction

As a driver, have you experienced an intersection with a long line of cars on one road and few cars on the other and thought that this situation could be improved by adjusting the timing of the traffic signals? As a student, have you experienced a course with learning materials that were too hard or too easy and hoped that the instructor would provide the appropriate learning materials to maximize your learning output? For these real-life problems that need personalized solutions, artificial intelligence (AI), an area of computer science that emphasizes the creation of intelligent machines that work and react like humans, can potentially help. AI consists of various information techniques that enable computers to perform intelligent tasks.

These AI techniques can be categorized into classical AI or statistical AI. Classical AI starts with a given set of constraints and rules and tries to reach a conclusion through deductive inference based on constraints and rules. By contrast, statistical AI, also called machine learning, data mining, or data science, is a set of techniques that starts with a given set of data and tries to identify a pattern through inductive inference based on the data. Since both inductive and deductive thought are important components of human intelligence, the ultimate AI should be a synthesis of classical and statistical AI. However, in term of the convergence between blockchain and AI, statistical AI is much more relevant than classical AI because both statistical AI and blockchain deal with data. Therefore, the rest of this chapter uses the general term AI to refer to statistical AI.

To understand how blockchain converges with AI requires understanding the bridging element ‒ data. Data, or pieces of information, represent the abstraction of any tangible events or intangible rules. Scientific research, business, governance, and many other activities use data to monitor whether activities are on the right track or seek hidden patterns for useful applications.

Before the invention of digital storage and computing devices in the 1940s, people created various means to store, share, and process data manually. In 1941, Konrad Zuse built the first fully automatic digital computer ‒ the Z3 ‒ to solve computational problems such as firing a torpedo at a moving warship and simulating rocket trajectories (Zuse 2010). Since late 1950s, the US military started to develop a radar system, called the Semi-Automatic Ground Environment (SAGE), with networking functions to process data from multiradar sites to produce a unified airspace information in a wide area (Schaffel 1991). Since the 1960s, with the supporting technology of computing, storage, and networking database systems (Codd 1970), a cousin of blockchain emerged with wide commercial use.

A database can be considered as a general ledger in accounting – a complete record of everything. However, unlike a general ledger, a database must be able to handle frequent updates from many different users. For example, consider online shopping. After a customer selects needed items and makes a payment, someone inserts the related transaction record into the database. The shipping department is informed to process the related shipping and update the shipping status periodically in the database. Without a centralized database to save the up-to-date information and disseminate it to related users, the collaboration among different users could be substantially delayed. Due to the centralized nature of a database, a centralized database works well within any given organization. However, it starts to fall apart for any applications involving two or more peer organizations as each organization wants to control the centralized database because each distrusts the others. Although a third-party oversight can solve this issue, it adds additional costs.

Yet, meaningful and profitable applications involving two or more peer organizations are common. For example, small and medium-size companies create a substantial portion of local jobs and usually deal with local banks, which have enough historical information to assess their creditworthiness. Without the shared information across banks, these companies are unable to get desired financial services provided by other banks. Before selling any food in a supermarket, it comes through growers, processors, wholesalers, and distributors. Without the information sharing all the way from growers to supermarkets, any food recall or mislabeling leads to unnecessary food waste. All these applications call for a database technique to share and update data across multipeer organizations through a secured, authenticated, verifiable, and immutable mechanism without centralized administration.

As discussed in previous chapters, blockchain is a database platform that enables the collaboration across multipeer organizations and network members. This chapter provides a discussion of the convergence between AI and blockchain for potential useful AI applications across multipeer organizations. The remainder of the chapter has the following organization. The next section introduces basic AI techniques to show how blockchain converges with AI. The following section presents the existing AI applications with a traditional database and its extension with blockchain. The final section offers a summary and conclusions including future opportunities.

Basic AI Techniques

Although existing survey papers for AI techniques often focus on its software component of analyzing data (Tsai, Lai, Chao, and Vaslakos 2015; Hariri, Fredericks, and Bowers 2019), the advance in hardware on collecting and processing data in a more robust system infrastructure setting is also an important component.

System Infrastructure

The system infrastructure for processing data has three components: (1) capture, (2) storage, and (3) computing.

Data Capture

The most straightforward data resource in organizations is the data collected in their database to ensure their daily operation. However, with the new technology development, many other meaningful ways of capturing data are available. For example, the World Wide Web (WWW) has abundant useful information including reviews, tweets, news, and other social media information. These important data sources are useful to understand customer preferences, potential competing products, and breaking events. Since most content on the WWW is created for others to read, organizations need to exert effort to create their own specialized web crawlers (Westlake, Bouchard, and Frank 2017) to monitor relevant websites and convert newly posted information into a special format for computers to analyze. Besides web crawlers, other data capturing techniques include sensors (Gravina, Alinia, Ghasemzadeh, and Fortino 2017) for chemical, light, temperature, sound, and other events; video surveillance (Mabrouk and Zagrouba 2018) for objects like human, animals, and vehicles; and global positioning system (GPS) data (Herring et al. 2016) for moving trajectory. No AI applications use all the possible data capture techniques to collect data because various types of data require different capture techniques and some types of data might be irrelevant to a specific AI application. Yet, identifying and adapting useful and relevant data capture techniques for each AI application are important because different data might reflect the same object or event from another perspectives. For example, information from company financial statement is useful for long-term stock price trend forecasting, while information reflecting sentiment of the general public from social media is more useful for understanding short-term fluctuations (Derakhshan and Beigy 2019).

Data Storage

The most common data storage technique is a traditional centralized transaction database. Yet, it has many limitations such as limited storage capacity, single node failure, quality balance between data update and data query, and collaboration across organizations. Some database techniques are available to solve certain limitations of centralized transaction database. Different database systems need to be adopted and used together depending on the need of specific AI applications. For example, Cassandra is a distributed version of traditional transaction database (Wahid and Kashyap 2019). Instead of saving all the data in one computer server, it spreads data over a computer cluster to increase the storage capacity and robustness to solve single node failure issue. However, Cassandra cannot guarantee data consistency. Therefore, it is ideal for data that can tolerate certain errors, such as reviews, logs, and news, but inappropriate for transaction and trading data that need to be accurate. A data warehouse is designed to save historical data in a summarized cube in a low granularity, which can speed up the data aggregation in higher granularity for further data analysis but lose all the details in the transaction level (Visscher et al. 2017). MongoDB is created to speed up data query by saving tightly connected entities into one file, instead of saving them in different tables to ensure higher data quality (Jose and Abraham 2017). Blockchain is designed for the collaboration across different organizations without third-party oversight but sacrifices the query and update performance.

Data Computing

When the amount of data is beyond the capacity of one computer to process, either a supercomputer or a computer cluster is needed. Although supercomputers have a long history for many critical applications, such a weather forecasting, nuclear simulation, and spacecraft aerodynamics, they are too expensive to be used in a general business setting. More commonly used solutions for companies include computer clusters with Hadoop (Guo, Rao, Cheng, and Zhou 2016) or Spark (Zaharia et al. 2016), or graphics processing unit (GPU) related techniques like Nvidia CUDA (Dyakonova, Khoperskov, and Khrapov 2016). Hadoop is designed to handle expected hardware failure and rebalance workload. The core operation inside Hadoop is MapReduce that generates key-value pairs and then summarizes values with the same key. Any typical AI technique requires many rounds of MapReduce operations and involves input/output (I/O) operations in their hard drives. To speed up Hadoop and reduce its I/O cost, the sibling system Spark can save intermediate key-value pair results in memory instead of on a hard drive to save operation time. Some AI techniques require a huge amount of data, which cannot be saved in one computer but can be handled by Hadoop or a Spark system.

Data Analytics

With system infrastructure to capture, store, and compute data, data analytic methods play an important role for AI applications to gain business insights and make intelligent decisions. One widely accepted taxonomy of data analytic methods categories them into three types ‒ (1) descriptive analytics, (2) predictive analytics, and (3) prescriptive analytics ‒ based on how and when these methods are used. Descriptive analytic methods focus on summarizing patterns from collected historical data. Although descriptive analytics only generate historical patterns, these patterns can be used by predictive analytics to forecast what is likely to happen in the future based on a critical assumption that historical patterns repeat themselves in the future. With the forecasted results by predictive analytics, prescriptive analytics leverages these values to do the optimal planning to meet the future need.

Descriptive Analytics

Classical statistical measures, such as the mean, standard deviation, skewness, and kurtosis, are the most widely used descriptive analytics. However, these classical methods usually treat the entire data set as a homogeneous group and overlook patterns in a subpopulation. Therefore, more sophisticated methods, including association rules and clustering, are developed to search these hidden subpopulation patterns.

Association Rules

These methods search for associated events since events are not isolated and help in choosing correct interventions to get a desired outcome if these meaningful connections can be identified. For example, doctors diagnose a patient's condition according to association patterns found in past data on diseases and symptoms. Technical analysis in finance searches for connections between signals generated from past data and future stock price movement. In the early twentieth century, statisticians extensively studied and proposed many classical methods for measuring associations, such as the Pearson correlation coefficient (Pearson 1895), chi-square (Elderton 1902) and regression analysis (Neter, Kutner, Nachtsheim, and Wasserman 1996). These classical methods work well on thousands of manually cleaned records with tens of preselected variables and have advanced the knowledge boundaries in many disciplines. However, the era of big data with trillions of records, millions of variables raises serious challenges to the effectiveness and efficiency of these classical methods. Hence, their performance becomes an even more serious problem when searching for higher order correlations that consider confounding and interaction factors together with statistical randomness, bias, errors, and the like.

Between two events and , association rules search for the gap between and , where is the probability of in the entire population and is the probability of when occurs. Many ways are available to quantify the gap between and . For example, added value (Kannan and Bhaskaran 2009) measures their difference by , and lift (Brin, Motwani, Ullman, and Tsur 1997) measures their ratio by .

Although all the above methods provide straightforward ways to calculate correlations, a major issue is that the estimated probability from the data set might differ from the latent truth due to statistical randomness. Since any method that fails to consider statistical randomness is likely to suffer from imprecise estimation and generate many false patterns especially in big data applications, researchers offer another type of method based on null hypothesis tests, including chi-square (Elderton 1902) and the likelihood ratio (Neyman and Pearson 1992). The calculated p-value with the null hypothesis test provides the probability of getting the current sample data set from independent pairs and can be used to tell correlated pairs from uncorrelated pairs. However, these p-values cannot be interpreted as correlation degrees because they are affected not only by correlation degrees but also by the occurrence of pairs. Since effective decision-making relies on more reliable estimations of latent true correlation degrees, these p-values might be misleading in some cases.

Clustering

Different from association rules searching for interesting patterns from all possible patterns, clustering assigns each record to groups in which records have similarities. A cluster can be a group of patients with similar symptoms or products with similar functions, and clustering is used to strike a balance between one-size-fit-all (efficiency) and personalized treatment (effectiveness). After assigning all the heterogeneous records into different groups, it helps to achieve a better balance for a relatively effective solution with a comparatively low cost. For example, Iorio, Frasso, D'Ambrosio, and Siciliano (2018) use a clustering approach for portfolio selection to avoid the unnecessary calculation by selecting similar securities in the same group.

The three types of clustering methods are: (1) centroid-based, (2) density-based, and (3) grid-based.

(1)The centroid-based clustering generates a central vector and assigns objects to their nearest cluster center. The typical method is K-means (MacQueen 1967). As centroid-based clustering assigns objects to their nearest cluster center, each cluster has a spherical shape, but it might not be true for many applications in land use, tumor shape, and traffic trajectories. Although no spherical shape clusters exist in some applications, some arbitrary shapes of regions with similar density records occur.

(2)Density-based methods are proposed to solve this issue. The first density-based method is DBSCAN (Ester, Kriegel, Sander, and Xu 1996) for all the clusters with a similar density. However, in some cases, different cluster might have different density and other methods like OPTICS (Ankerst, Breunig, Kriegel, and Sander 1999) and LDBSCAN (Duan, Xu, Guo, Lee, and Yan 2007) are proposed to solve this problem. Both centroid-based and density-based methods are assigning each record to its cluster, which is computationally expensive.

(3)Grid-based methods try to divide the entire feature space into grids and merge objects in the same grid altogether into a cluster instead of handling it one by one. Typical methods in this category include STING (Wang, Yang, and Muntz 1997), OptiGrid (Hinneburg and Keim 1999), and DGB (Wu and Wilamowski 2016). All the above methods are nonoverlapping clustering where each record is assigned to a cluster. However, in some cases, overlapping clustering is more reasonable. Take students in a college for example. Two students might be assigned to the same group because they have the same major but can also be assigned to two different groups because of their different athletics interests.

Predictive Analytics

Although descriptive analytics summarize past patterns, predictive analytics use past patterns to predict what is going to happen in the future assuming that previous patterns repeat in a similar way in the future. The five types of predictive analytics methods are: (1) regression, (2) decision tree, (3) Bayesian statistics, (4) neural network, and (5) support vector machine. A typical predictive analytics method starts with a data set with historical data. Among all the attributes in the data set, one attribute is identified as the target attribute, which takes a while to collect its data, and the remaining attributes are identified as normal attributes, which have their value instantly. Then a predictive analytics method tries to summarize the relation between the target attribute and normal attributes. With this relation and the value of normal attributes for the current data, the target attribute of the current record can be forecasted.

(1)Linear regression: The first method in regression is the linear regression model (Neter et al. 1996), which builds a linear relation between a target attribute and normal attributes for any given data set. A drawback of linear regression is that it is only for numeric target attributes, and cases exist where the target attribute is binary. For example, whether the current transaction is fraudulent or not, or whether this customer is likely to subscribe the service or not. To solve this issue, logistic regression (Hosmer, Lemeshow, and Sturdivant 2013) uses a logistic function to model a binary output. Besides the binary issue, linear regression might hold a wrong assumption of a linear relation in some situations. To handle the potential of a nonlinear relation, some propose nonlinear models, such as LOESS (Cleveland and Devlin 1988) and LOWESS (Howarth and McArthur 1997).

(2)Decision tree: A decision tree is a type of methods using a utility function to judge the degree of purity that has been improved for a given branch division (Safavian and Landgrebe 1991). By searching all the possible branch divisions, decision tree methods select the branch division that most improves the degree of purity for the current division and continues the branch division iteratively. The branch selected in the early stage might trap the entire decision tree into a local optimal that is much worse than the global optimal. Random forest randomly selects a subset of attributes for decision tree construction and uses ensembled decision trees to alleviate low performance local optimal issue (Liaw and Wiener 2002).

(3)Bayesian statistics: Bayesian statistics use the Bayes' theorem to understand the relation between normal attributes and the target attribute. Naïve Bayesian, which is the most straightforward method in this category, assumes each attribute is independent from each other for inference (Rish 2001). When the assumption of independency is correct, the performance of Naïve Bayesian is high. However, assuming each attribute is independent from each other might be incorrect in many situations. If the attribute dependency exists, Bayesian network is the technique to integrate attribute dependency to improve prediction performance (Friedman, Geiger, and Goldszmidt 1997).

(4)Neural network: A neural network is a method used to construct a network with input nodes, layers of hidden nodes, and output nodes (Hecht-Nielsen 1992). It starts with some random number in each edge connecting node from input layer through hidden layers to output layer. Based on how far the calculated output value is from the actual output value, the edge weights are adjusted accordingly. Although a neural network was proposed in the 1960s, it has attracted great attention in the last decade due to some major advances in hardware capacity, abundant graphical and voice data collected, and advances in algorithms, which are related to the buzz word “deep learning.”

Two important methods are a convolutional neural network (Lawrence, Giles, Tsoi, and Back 1997) and a recurrent neural network (Mikolov, Karafiát, Burget, Černocký, and Khudanpur 2010). A convolutional neural network has a critical application in image recognition. Usually, one image could contain many objects. It relies human effort to mark the region related to each object in one picture, which is not scalable to a big data set and hurts the performance. To solve this problem, a convolutional neural network uses a moving filter to segment an image into many small images. When two different images contain the same object, a convolutional neural network can automatically map the right segments in different images to the same object when having enough data. Such a moving filter segment mechanism no longer needs manual marking.

A recurrent neural network is designed to model time or sequence dependent behavior, such as language, stock prices, and weather. Different from other neural networks that model each record independently from other records, a recurrent neural network feeds back the output at time or sequence t to the input of the same network layer at time or sequence t+1. Such a loop feedback makes the sequence of prediction more consistent.

(1)Support vector machine: Support vector machine is the method used to find a linear hyperplane to separate two classes (Suvkens and Vandewalle 1999). Because it is restricted to a linear hyperplane, a support vector machine is less likely to be overfitting. However, finding a linear separable hyperplane might be impossible for some complicated problems. To solve this issue, two possible extensions are available. One approach uses some nonlinear kernel function to map the original data into a higher dimensional space where the data can be linearly separated (Shimodaira, Noma, Nakai, and Sagayama 2002). Another approach adopts a hinge loss function to tolerate some errors over the margin (Xu, Cao, Hu, and Principe 2017).

Prescriptive Analytics

Although predictive analytics is used to predict what is likely to happen in the future, prescriptive analytics use the prediction to search for the optimal plan to meet the future need. This type of work is traditionally in the area of operations research, which is considered as a subfield of applied mathematics. Sometimes, the terms management science or decision science are used interchangeably with operations research. It is related to any real-world objective related to either maximizing a positive objective (e.g., profit, performance, or yield) or minimizing negative objective (loss, risk, or cost). Management science has wide applications in financial engineering, manufacturing, supply chain, transportation, and public sector work.

Techniques in this area have two major types: (1) convex programming (Grant, Boyd, and Ye 2006) and (2) heuristic search (Bonet and Geffner 2001). Convex programming is the type of problem in which the global optimal value can be found in theory. However, many convex programming problems are computationally expensive, and the global optimal might be unavailable given current computing power within a reasonable timeframe. This branch in convex programming includes linear programming (Chvatal and Chvatal 1983), second-order cone programming (Alizadeh and Goldfarb 2003), semidefinite programming (Vandenberghe and Boyd 1996), and geometric programming (Boyd, Kim, Vandenberghe, and Hassibi 2007).

Another more widely used technique is heuristic search, which is used to find a suboptimal solution for problems that cannot get the global optimal value in theory or the computational cost of getting the global optimal value is too high. Some methods in heuristic search include simulated annealing (Van and Aarts 1987), genetic algorithm (Weile and Michielssen 1997), and tabu search (Glover and Laguna 1998).

Driven by the technology in predictive analytics, prescriptive analytics (operations research) becomes more tightly connected with predictive analytics. For example, take classic portfolio optimization. The return and variance of securities are estimated using their historical average. However, during an uptrend market, if a given security experiences a substantial price drop but such a price drop is not large enough to reverse the uptrend, predictive analytics predicts this security has a higher return than its average in an intermediate term. If the portfolio has turnover in an intermediate term, its performance can be improved by connecting predictive analytics and prescriptive analytics.

AI Applications with Database and Extension with Blockchain

Essentially, the current wave of AI applications is data driven, which requires the fundamental support from database techniques. Among all different areas that can be greatly affected by AI, finance and healthcare are two major sectors leading the change because these two industry sectors generate large amount of structural data and have advantages in developing AI-driven applications. This section provides a discussion of AI in finance, healthcare, and other domains as well as its extension with blockchain techniques.

AI in Finance

AI technology is used to reduce human intervention, which can improve service efficiency and reduce costs. Its applications in finance can be categorized into: (1) wealth management, (2) risk control, and (3) others.

(1)Wealth management: Services related to wealth management include portfolio management, financial product recommendation, and personalized marketing. In portfolio management, price prediction plays a critical role in understanding market trends and identifying investment opportunities (Ding, Zhang, Liu, and Duan 2015; Heaton, Polson, and Witte 2017). Jiang, Xu, and Liang (2017) propose a reinforcement-learning framework to identify turnover opportunity and use a portfolio-weight memory strategy to restrain from oversized adjustments.

(2)Risk control: Besides portfolio recommendation, Xue, Zhu, Liu, and Yin (2018) work on the financial social network group recommendation for investors to identify groups with the same risk preference. Risk control has applications in risk assessment and fraud detection. Khandani, Kim, and Lo (2010) apply predictive analytics methods to forecast credit card holder delinquencies and defaults by combining customer transaction and credit bureau data. Rushin, Stancil, Sun, Adams, and Beling (2017) study the performance of predictive analytics methods, including logistic regression, gradient-boosted trees, and deep learning, for credit card fraud detection. Olson, Delen, and Meng (2012) compare decision tree, neural network, and support vector machine to predict bankruptcy.

(3)Others: Other useful applications of AI in finance include user identity authentication through face recognition (Feng, Zhou, Dan, Zhou, and Li 2017) as well as speech recognition and natural language processing to enable smart question and answer interaction (Yih, Chang, He, and Gao 2015).

AI in Healthcare

Recent AI advances have many applications in healthcare, which may trigger a discussion on whether AI doctors can eventually replace physicians. Although completely replacing physicians in the foreseeable future is highly speculative, current AI techniques occupy a place to assist physicians in making better decisions and may even replace manual decisions in certain areas like radiology (Hosny, Parmar, Quackenbush, Schwartz, and Aerts 2018).

Initially, AI applications in healthcare focused on the structured electronic medical records. However, not all the medical records can be saved as structured records such as image and clinical notes. Now, more applications attempt to integrate these unstructured images and language as useful data sources for meaningful healthcare applications.

The most widely used methods in healthcare are still predictive analytics from disease diagnosis and treatment selection to outcome prediction. Chen et al. (2020) collect additional user lifestyle information together with their medical historical data to improve the performance of skin condition diagnosis solely based on images. Delen, Walker, and Kadam (2005) compare the performance of decision tree, neural network, and logistic regression for predicting breast cancers. Love et al. (2013) propose a stroke treatment model by using a Bayesian belief network constructed through existing clinical practice guidelines, meta-analyses, and clinical trials.

AI in Other Domains and Extension with Blockchain

AI can also affect other areas beyond finance and healthcare. For example, Pardo et al. (2018) propose a system to deliver personalized learning materials based on students' instant learning progress and their historical data. Ramasubbareddy, Srinivas, Govinda, and Manivannan (2020) construct a system to predict the crime activities in a geographical location at a point of time to help police stations to distribute their manpower. Majumdar, Naraseeyappa, and Ankalaki (2017) use different data analytics methods with existing crop, soil, and climatic data to optimize the agriculture production and make it more resilient to climatic change.

Although AI applications are possible in almost every aspect of human life, an important issue not previously discussed is how data quality affects a meaningful AI application (Liu, Li, Li, and Wu 2016). According to a popular phrase “garbage in, garbage out,” data quality is critically important. Imagine a system that records customer gender inappropriately. The system may recommend lipsticks to more male then female customers. If a medical monitoring system gets a patient's heart rate input as his or her body temperature input, the monitoring system is likely to generate many false alarms.

The current wave of data analytics is driven by a large amount of data for a more statistically reliable estimation. It also requires high quality data to improve accuracy. Because of data quality issues, blockchain techniques can help in both ways. First, blockchain techniques can provide data that are previously unavailable. For instance, consider a supply chain system between Walmart and Proctor & Gamble Company (P&G). Determining how much shampoo to manufacture depends on how much has been sold. For P&G, it can only get the sales data when Walmart starts to replenish its inventory. By that time, P&G has already over or under produced the amount of shampoo. Although P&G can use predictive analytics from other related data sources to forecast the amount of sales, it can never be as accurate as the actual sale. With blockchain techniques involving Walmart and P&G, P&G can get the instant sale data, which are unavailable to it and can greatly help the firm determine the exact number of products to manufacture to meet the market needs.

Now consider a food supply chain system consisting of growers, processors, wholesalers, and distributors powered by blockchains. It involves more parties than the previous supply chain system between Walmart and P&G. This blockchain greatly helps all parties reduce their unnecessary loss when a mismatch exists between their manufacturing and the market needs, and ensures the quality of data from one peer to another. Such quality of data is critically important in finance and healthcare because having incorrect data may lead to lost sales for a business or a loss of life in healthcare.

Summary and Conclusions

This chapter has discussed the relation between AI techniques and blockchain. Blockchain's impact on AI has two dimensions: (1) it offers important data that might be previously unavailable and (2) if offers high-quality data to improve performance. However, like other technical advances, blockchain is only part of the overall solution. It should be integrated with data collection, data transfer, data analysis, domain knowledge, and the potential impact to society. Consider the recommender system in Amazon or any other online retailer. In 2000, Amazon did not collect or analyze customer browse data because these data are not the final transaction sale. Gradually, Amazon realized the value of browse data by improving its website accessibility and easing its customers' task of finding a needed product. Until recently, Amazon used browse data to identify substitute products. For example, customers might compare the profiles of Sony and Samsung televisions on its website, but few are likely to buy both television sets. Therefore, Amazon can use transaction data to identify related products such as a TV and wall mount but cannot provide the valuable insights between substitute products. The recommendation of substitute products can be achieved only by using customer browse data. Therefore, the more important issue is to step out of the narrow focus of each technique and start with a meaningful application. Doing so enables selecting the most desirable technique to achieve the goal and to realize its real social impact.

Discussion Questions

(1)Identify the two branches of AI research and the branch more relevant to blockchain.

(2)Identify techniques that serve as the foundation for the current mainstream AI applications.

(3)Specify three data analytical methods and how they relate to each other.

(4)Discuss how blockchain can be integrated with AI applications.
