Chapter 13

Risk Management and Transference Issues in Blockchain Technologies

Joseph Brunsman

Keywords: Blockchain; risk management; insurance; cryptocurrency; bitcoin; risk transference; indemnification

Introduction

As blockchain and cryptocurrencies continue their ascent, businesses from nearly every industry are investigating how these technologies can provide a competitive edge and increase security. Seemingly, any business that does not adopt these technologies is likely to be left behind in the marketplace. However, inevitability of adoption and increased security does not mean that businesses will be invulnerable to the costs associated with data breaches, the theft of cryptocurrencies, and other associated losses. As such, a business should understand how the insurance market may or may not cover its losses. Indemnification may often hinge on the inclusion, exclusion, or definition of a single word or phrase buried deep within an insurance policy.

Granted, insurance coverage would not be a concern if blockchain and cryptocurrency technology were invulnerable to malfeasance and impervious to intrusions by malicious actions. However, such a belief is a myth. Although arguably more secure than centralized databases in many circumstances and applications, blockchains and cryptocurrencies are like any other technology or invention in the digital age ‒ imperfect.

The most prominent example of blockchain vulnerability occurred with the cryptocurrency Ethereum. The DAO, a type of venture capital fund directed by investors to run on the Ethereum network, was created in April 2016 as a means of decentralized crowdfunding for Ethereum related projects. In practice, this decentralization meant that a user could send ether – the cryptocurrency used on Ethereum – to the DAO for proportional voting rights on what projects would be funded. By June 2016, a malicious third party had discovered a recursive call bug in the DAO contract and had used that vulnerability to siphon approximately $50 million in ether cryptocurrency. Of note, this exploitable bug was not a flaw in Ethereum per se, but nonetheless would result in many Ethereum developers potentially losing large amounts of their investment via the DAO (Kiffer, Levin, and Mislove 2017).

The Ethereum community struggled with how to best resolve this issue. One faction wanted to remain with the classic Ethereum, whereas the other wanted to “fork” the blockchain (Kiffer et al. 2017). Notably, there are two types of forking. In a hard fork, the blockchain is split to include both a new blockchain and an old blockchain, which exist simultaneously. In a soft fork, only the newly created blockchain is considered valid and all users must adhere to the new standards (Lin and Liao 2017). Effectively, this hard fork would erase the transactions made by the attacker and become its own network, though keeping the name Ethereum. The remaining faction declined to erase the transactions made by the attacker and named its network Ethereum Classic (Kiffer et al. 2017).Despite other Ethereum forks occurring since that time, a recent audit of Ethereum 2.0, at the Ethereum Foundation's request, revealed that numerous issues and potential vulnerabilities remain unresolved (Least Authority TFA GmbH 2020).

Although the DAO/Ethereum fiasco was a perfect example of the now well-known 51% attack method, whereby a malicious group of miners controls more than half of network's hash rate, researchers from the University of Memphis postulate other possible attack vectors. Specifically, these vectors could betray vulnerabilities in blockchain technology or its implementation. Such methods include key attacks, identity attacks, manipulation attacks, service attacks, malware attacks, application attacks, reputation attacks, with perhaps the most daunting of all being quantum attacks (Dasgupta, Gupta, and Shrein 2019).

Quantum computing could quickly make or break blockchain technology overnight. As recently published in the prestigious magazine Nature, before 2030, quantum computing could quickly calculate the one-way encryption on which many blockchains are based. In practice, a break in one-way encryption could enable anyone with a quantum computer to impersonate any user, gain access to any assets, and render the technology obsolete unless updated (Fedorov, Kiktenko, and Lvovsky 2018).

The threat of quantum computing breaking the traditional security backbone of blockchains is real enough that at least one organization, The QRL (Quantum Resistant Ledger) Foundation, is working on the problem of post-quantum ledgers and cryptography (The QRL Foundation 2020).

As demonstrated, adopting blockchains and cryptocurrencies involves risk. Prudent businesses that may want to adopt these technologies should attempt to mitigate and transfer the potential for risk to a reasonable degree. Although various risk transference mechanisms exist, the most common and misunderstood is insurance.

The most accessible method of demonstrating insurance coverage is by using an example. Consider a large accounting firm that is using cryptocurrency for payment transactions and blockchain technology for storing the personally identifiable information (PII) of their clients. The Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) notifies the firm's managing partner that researchers have discovered what appears to be the bank's entire client list online for sale, including social security numbers, dates of birth, names, addresses, and bank account numbers. Following an immediate internal analysis, the researcher discovered that someone transferred 40% of the firm's cryptocurrency reserves, totaling $1 million at current exchange rates, the prior evening to unknown accounts. The breach appears to have originated when a staff member entered his username and login credentials into a fraudulent pop-up screen on his computer.

With the personal information of 90,000 clients now in jeopardy, the firm is facing a high probability of the minimum following costs:

  • Breach notification and credit monitoring costs for 90,000 individuals.
  • Internal computer forensics and remediation costs.
  • Possible class action lawsuits.
  • Possible regulatory claims.
  • Paying for a public relations and crisis management consultant.
  • Long-term reputational losses resulting in client departure.
  • Business interruption losses.
  • Loss of cryptocurrency funds.
  • Other costs that may arise as the situation unfolds.

While the managing partner is facing a daunting series of bills to be paid and client phone calls to answer, he is concerned with two large expenses: (1) experiencing the costs of navigating the breach from investigation to client notification and potential legal action, which could cost millions and (2) recouping the $1 million in cryptocurrency. The ultimate question is whether his firm's existing insurance policies can cover these costs.

Considering that blockchain is such a new technology, only truly debuting in 2009, little case law exists on which to base actionable guidance. The remainder of this chapter notes actual cases or administrative decisions where possible. Also covered are common policies likely to be held by the firm in this scenario, though the specific wording of any particular business's real world policy varies by insurer and circumstance.

Commercial Crime Insurance Policies

A natural place to begin searching for insurance coverage following an alleged crime would be a crime policy. Crime policies are multifaceted and can cover the following general areas: fidelity, forgery or alteration, on premises or in transit theft, funds transfer fraud, and computer crime. Of the previous coverages listed, funds transfer fraud and computer crime appear to be the most promising regarding their ability to potentially afford coverage for the loss. Funds transfer fraud means that the insurance company, “will pay the insured for the insured's direct loss of money and securities contained in the insured's transfer account directly caused by funds transfer fraud” (Travelers Form CRI-3001 Ed. 01-09, p. 4). Assuming that the firm had the cryptocurrency in a “transfer account” and could meet the lengthy definition of “funds transfer fraud,” the ultimate issue is whether its cryptocurrency could first be classified as a money or security. This classification choice currently remains ambiguous.

Within the policy, “money means a medium of exchange in current use and authorized or adopted by a domestic or foreign government, including currency, coins, bank notes, bullion, travelers' checks, registered checks, and money orders held for sale to the public” (Travelers Form CRI-3001 Ed. 01-09, p. 12). “Securities means written negotiable and non-negotiable instruments or contracts representing money or property including:

(1)tokens, tickets, revenue, and other stamps, whether represented by actual stamps or unused value in a meter, in current use; and

(2)evidences of debt issued in connection with any credit, debit, or charge card, which cards are not issued by the Insured, but excludes money” (Travelers Form CRI-3001 Ed. 01-09, p. 13).

Although cryptocurrency is not specifically mentioned within the previous definitions, could the firm make a reasonable argument to the insurer that its cryptocurrency should be considered money or a security? Unfortunately for the firm, the answer is complicated, but likely not in its favor.

The legal meaning of “money” within the United States is defined by the Uniform Commercial Code (UCC). Specifically, money means

…a medium of exchange currently authorized or adopted by a domestic or foreign government. The term includes a monetary unit of account established by an intergovernmental organization or by agreement between two or more countries. (Uniform Commercial Code 2019, p.§ 1-201. General Definitions)

Placing this definition in harmony with other portions of the UCC, one can argue that money only includes physical mediums of currency such as printed paper or coins. By extension, even if a particular cryptocurrency is backed by a government or used as a medium of exchange between governments, at the present moment the UCC as it is currently written would preclude any purely digital currency as being considered “money” (Schroeder 2016).

As for securities, their legal definition varies by jurisdiction. Within the US, the general test on whether an instrument may be considered a “security” lies in the “Howey test” from the 1946 case of SEC v. W. J. Howey Co. In short, the test generally states that for an instrument to be classified as a security, it must be an investment of money in a common enterprise where an expectation of profits generated by the third party exists (SEC v. W. J. Howey Co. 1946).

Using the Howey test, and other considerations, the SEC's Strategic Hub for Innovation and Financial Technology (FinHub) published a framework for analyzing whether a cryptocurrency is considered a security. Unfortunately, the framework is neither binding nor considered legal advice. Further, the notion that a cryptocurrency is a security can change depending on various circumstances (US Securities and Exchange Commission 2019).

To add clarification, SEC Chairman Jay Clayton stated the following in an interview, “Cryptocurrencies: These are replacements for sovereign currencies, replace the dollar, the euro, and the yen with bitcoin. That type of currency is not a security” (Rooney 2018).

Whether the firm could successfully argue that its cryptocurrency is considered a security depends on several factors. Should the firm attempt to litigate the matter – an expensive proposition by itself – it likely faces an uphill and prolonged legal battle. Further, the firm is unlikely recover its cryptocurrency as either money or as a security. Perhaps other coverage could be found in the computer fraud section of its policy.

In the firm's crime insurance policy, computer fraud means, “The use of any computer to fraudulently cause a transfer of money, securities, or other property from inside the premises or financial institution premises:

(1)to a person (other than a messenger) outside the premises or financial institution

(2)a. premises; or

(3)to a place outside the premises or financial institution premises” (Travelers Form CRI-3001 Ed. 01-09, p. 7).

Unfortunately for the firm, no consideration is given within the definition of computer fraud for the data breach related to any experienced expenses. At issue here is whether the cryptocurrency could be considered “other property.” Within the policy at hand, “other property” is defined as, “any tangible property other than money and securities that has intrinsic value” (Travelers Form CRI-3001 Ed. 01-09, p. 12). Although the firm may be able to argue that its cryptocurrency had, “intrinsic value,” the ability to argue that it was “tangible property” is debatable but unlikely.

In the recent case of Ox Labs, Inc. v. Bitpay, Inc. (2020a), the court wrestled with the idea of whether Ox Labs' bitcoin could be considered tangible property. Notably, this court preempted Ox Labs' argument by stating that the firm was “not aware of any authority addressing whether Bitcoin is tangible or intangible property…” (Ox Labs, Inc. v. Bitpay, Inc. 2020a). Bitpay argued that the cryptocurrency should be considered an intangible property due to its purely digital nature. Though the case venue was a U.S. District Court in California, Bitpay cited the footnote in a case from a U.S. District Court in Pennsylvania that stated, “Bitcoin is the most prominent example of cryptocurrency, an electronic form of currency with no tangible format” (Ox Labs, Inc. v. Bitpay, Inc. 2020c).

Ox Labs countered by arguing, in part, that bitcoins are not an idea that exists purely in the owner's thoughts, but rather rely on “a shared public ledger… which records all confirmed transactions.” Ox Labs continued with an argument of analogy as an earlier ruling in the California Court of Appeal held that a check for money was considered tangible property (Ox Labs, Inc. v. Bitpay, Inc. 2020b). Explaining the analogy, Bitcoin could be considered much like a check in that it is a manifestation that could be exchanged for money; a “quasi-tangible property” (Ox Labs, Inc. v. Bitpay, Inc. 2020a).

Ultimately, the court sided with Ox Labs. At least in this situation, the court considered bitcoin a quasi-tangible property (Ox Labs, Inc. v. Bitpay, Inc. 2020a). However, this relatively recent decision occurs in a novel area of the law with a specific fact pattern. Knowing whether this decision is likely to hold in higher courts or how courts from other jurisdictions may view this decision is extremely difficult.

Of additional concern in commonly worded commercial crime policies is whether the theft and transfer of the cryptocurrency occurred directly or indirectly. Specifically, the following case involving Bitpay, Inc. illustrates how this issue might play out in practice. Although this issue may seem pedantic at face value, consider the allegation in the case of Bitpay, Inc. v. Massachusetts Bay Insurance Company (MBIC). Bitpay – this time on the receiving end of a bitcoin loss – alleged that it had fallen victim to a fraudulent email scheme. Bitpay stated that its chief financial officer (CFO) received an email from a third party asking for a comment on a bitcoin-related document. Through a series of events, the CFO of Bitpay relinquished his credentials on a website controlled by the hacker – similar to the accounting firm in the presented hypothetical scenario. The hacker was then able to send fake authorizations to Bitpay resulting in a loss of $1,850,000 worth of bitcoin (Bitpay, Inc. v. Massachusetts Bay Ins. Co. 2016).

Of particular note in this case, Bitpay's crime policy contained the following language:

Computer Fraud

We will pay for loss of or damage to “money,” “securities,” and “other property” resulting directly from the use of any computer to fraudulently cause a transfer of that property from inside the “premises” or “banking premises”:

  • To a person (other than a “messenger”) outside those “premises”; or
  • To a place outside those “premises” (Bitpay, Inc. v. Massachusetts Bay Ins. Co. 2016).

Further, Bitpay's crime policy was amended to ostensibly avoid the cryptocurrency as money issue discussed previously. In part, the policy amendment read: “The following is added to the definition of Money in Section F, Definitions, of the Conditions and Limitations Section: Money means: (c) or other funds, Bitcoins; or books of account and other records, recorded in writing or in electronic form” (Bitpay, Inc. v. Massachusetts Bay Ins. Co. 2016).

When Bitpay tendered a claim to its crime policy insurer, MBIC denied coverage for the claim. Subsequently, Bitpay brought a claim against MBIC for refusing to pay the claim and for bad faith in doing so (Bitpay, Inc. v. Massachusetts Bay Ins. Co. 2016).

In response, MBIC noted that due to the phishing scheme, “[t]he facts ... do not support a direct loss since there was not a hacking or unauthorized entry into [insured's] computer system fraudulently causing a transfer of Money” (Bitpay, Inc. v. Massachusetts Bay Ins. Co. 2016, Exhibit B). In other words, MBIC argued that the crime policy did not cover a business email compromise due a phishing scheme. If Bitpay had been directly breached, for instance by malware imbedded in its computer system, MBIC would more likely have covered the loss. Ultimately, the parties settled so knowing how the case would have ended if a judge or jury was required to render a verdict based on the merits is speculation.

If the policy examples had been present in the accounting firm scenario above, the firm probably would have either accepted a declination of coverage regarding the reimbursement of lost cryptocurrency assets or litigated the matter and hoped for a favorable outcome. Regardless, businesses should not assume that coverage for cryptocurrency losses would be afforded with a face-value approach to insurance policy interpretation. As such, legal counsel should assist businesses when negotiating insurance terms and policy language.

Commercial General Liability Policies

Given that bitcoin may be considered a “quasi-tangible property” under some circumstances and in some courts, the next logical place to investigate coverage for blockchain and cryptocurrency related losses would be a commercial general liability (CGL) insurance policy. Although the policy forms vary greatly across the market in terms of coverage specifics, they can generally be broken into three parts (Jerry and Douglas 2012).

(1)Coverage area A is meant to cover property damage and bodily injury. The firm in the hypothetical scenario may attempt to argue that the business sustained property damage and therefore could seek some coverage under this element.

(2)Coverage area B is meant to cover personal and advertising injury. Likewise, the firm may argue that some injury may arise as a result of the “publication” of the client information stolen from its blockchain, and thus coverage may apply.

(3)Coverage area C is meant to cover the medical payments associated with bodily injury. This coverage element is unlikely to provide any possibility of recovery following the hypothetical situation and is not discussed.

Regarding Coverage A, a standard policy may include the following definition of property damage:

Property damage means:

  • Physical injury to tangible property including all resulting loss of use of that property, including all resulting loss of use of that property. All such loss of use shall be deemed to occur at the time of the physical injury that is caused it; or
  • Loss of use of tangible property that is not physically injured. All such loss of use shall be deemed to occur at the time of the “occurrence” that caused (Hartford Form HG 00 02 06 05 (2005), p. 20).

Unfortunately, the definition also includes the following, which appears to eliminate any notion of coverage for blockchain related losses:

As used in this definition, computerized or electronically stored data, programs, or software are not tangible property. Electronic data means information, facts, or programs:

  • Stored as or on;
  • Created or used on; or
  • Transmitted to or from;

computer software, including systems and applications software, hard or floppy disks, CD-ROMS, tapes, drives, cells, data processing devices, or any other media which are used electronically controlled equipment(Hartford Form HG 00 02 06 05 (2005), p. 20).

Further, this sample policy also contains an explicit exclusion to all electronic data, stating,

Damages arising out of the loss of, loss of use of, damage to, corruption of, inability to access, or inability to manipulate electronic data. As used in this exclusion, electronic data mean information, facts, or programs stored as or on, created or used on, or transmitted to or from computer software, including systems and applications software, hard or floppy disks, CDROMS, tapes, drives, cells, data processing devices, or any other media which are used with electronically controlled equipment. (Hartford Form HG 00 02 06 05 (2005), p. 5)

Although the term blockchain is not explicitly stated in these exclusions, the insurer seems to be attempting to block coverage in section A of its policy for all digitally related losses. Nonetheless, the firm may be able to argue that its cryptocurrency should be considered a loss of use of “quasi-tangible property” as defined previously in the case of Ox Labs v. Bitpay (Ox Labs, Inc. v. Bitpay, Inc. 2020a). It could also point to a recent declaration by the Internal Revenue Service (IRS) in Notice 2014–21 that “For federal tax purposes, virtual currency is treated as property.” (US Internal Revenue Service 2014, p. 2). However, the insurer could likewise contend that courts also find that “Virtual currencies can be regulated by [the Commodity Futures Trading Commission] CFTC as a commodity” (Commodity Futures Trading Comm'n v. McDonnell 2018, p. 226) and thus are not covered under the policy.

Attempting to deconflict these positions under the auspices of Coverage A language could prove costly for the firm in the hypothetical scenario. Now, the firm in this hypothetical example would need to look toward any Coverage B language, which may indemnify the firm for its blockchain. In other words, could some element of coverage for its breach be found as a result of “personal and advertising injury”?

Guidance may be found in the recent case of Travelers Indemnity Company of America v. Portal Healthcare Solutions. In this case, the United States Court of Appeals for the fourth Circuit provided coverage for a class action data breach claim against Portal. More specifically, the court considered an online exposure of the medical records in the care of Portal an “electronic publication” (Travelers Indem. Co. of Am. v. Portal Healthcare Sols., L.L.C. 2016).

At face value, this ruling could provide for some modicum of coverage under a CGL for breach related expenses, but caution should be taken. This case centered around the specific facts and circumstances as they related to exacting policy language. Not every CGL policy provides such beneficial policy language or could every business point to such a case as a persuasive argument due to the structure of the US court system.

In a sample CGL policy from a different insurer, Coverage B includes the following:

We will pay those sums that the Insured becomes legally obligated to pay as damages because of “personal and advertising injury” to which this insurance applies. We will have the right and duty to defend the Insured against any “suit” seeking those damages. However, we will have no duty to defend the Insured against any “suit” seeking damages for “personal and advertising injury” to which this insurance does not apply. We may, at our discretion, investigate any offense and settle any claim or “suit” that may result. (ABA Insurance Services Form CG 00 01 Ed. 04/13, p. 7)

Could the firm argue that the costs associated with the breach, such as credit monitoring, breach notification, and the like, are damages the insured is legally obligated to pay as a result of “personal or advertising injury”? Unfortunately, this argument is highly unlikely due to the fact that further within the policy an exclusion is stated that appears to explicitly disallow coverage for data breach related expenses:

This insurance does not apply to:

Access or Disclosure of Confidential or Personal Information

“Personal and advertising injury” arising out of any access to or disclosure of any person's or organization's confidential or personal information, including patents, trade secrets, processing methods, customer lists, financial information, credit card information, health information or any other type of nonpublic information.

This exclusion applies even if damages are claimed for notification costs, credit monitoring expenses, forensic expenses, public relations expenses or any other loss, cost or expense incurred by you or others arising out of any access to or disclosure of any person's or organization's confidential or personal information. (ABA Insurance Services Form CG 21 06 Ed. 05/14, p. 1)

Finally, every business should be aware that insurance companies providing CGL policies now have various standard endorsements available to them to exclude, or include, coverage for data breach costs. The Insurance Services Office (ISO), the de facto policy language standards creator for the insurance industry, has made and continues to make data breach exclusion endorsements, which insurers can use as a basis for their own policy language.

Cyber Insurance Policies

The final policy for the firm in the hypothetical to seek coverage for both breach notification costs and cryptocurrency losses is within a dedicated cyber insurance policy. Although many other traditional policies now offer some type of coverage that could be thought of as a cyber coverage, these policies are generally done via endorsement and are typically narrow in coverage and limit availability.

Cyber insurance policies generally cover an insured's liability to third parties as well as the costs incurred by the insured when a cyber event occurs. The costs incurred by the insured party could range from breach notification costs to data restoration and business interruption reimbursement costs. Compared to more traditional insurance policies, cyber insurance policies vary widely in their coverage features and policy language. Indeed, the term, “cyber insurance” is not a legal term, but merely a term that is generally meant to describe the type of policy that deals with digital losses. Even for the firm in the scenario, the nuances of policy language and features could point to everything from likely coverage to probable declination.

At issue for any entity seeking coverage for blockchain-related losses under a cyber insurance policy is the notion of “custody and control.” Consider the following definition of a data breach found in one cyber insurance policy: “Data breach means the acquisition, access, or disclosure of personally identifiable information or confidential corporate information by a person or entity, or in a manner, that is unauthorized by the insured organization” (Hiscox form CYBCL-CYB P0001S CW (10/19), p. 13).

Further investigation of policy language reveals the following:

…personally identifiable information means the following, in any form, that is in your care, custody, or control, or in the care, custody, or control of any third party for whom you are legally liable: 1. non-public personal information as defined in any foreign, federal, state, or local statute, rule, or regulation…. (Hiscox form CYBCL-CYB P0001S CW (10/19), p. 15)

The specimen policy in question does not define “care, custody, or control.” This ambiguity is not an anomaly found in a single cyber insurance policy. Consider the following clauses found in another cyber insurance policy:

Data Breach means the theft, loss, or Unauthorized Disclosure of Personally Identifiable Information or Third Party Information that is in the care, custody or control of the Insured Organization or a third party for whose theft, loss or Unauthorized Disclosure of Personally Identifiable Information or Third Party Information the Insured Organization is liable. (Beazley Form F00653 112017 ed., p. 6)

One of the core features of blockchain technology is its decentralized architecture. Under the auspices of a blockchain, no one entity can necessarily control information as was done with centralized databases. For the hypothetical firm in question, this situation could prove a large hurdle to coverage.

No cases appear to provide guidance on how a court should directly interpret the control and custody problem as it relates to blockchain. At face value, an insurer could easily argue that the nature of blockchain relinquishes some element of control and custody. Therefore, when the insured engaged with blockchain technology, it knowingly relinquished some factor of control and custody and thus should be denied coverage.

If a business can overcome the custody and control limitations in its policy, other considerations must still be made, and these are likely be contractual. For instance, one business may somehow maintain custody and control of a blockchain, though others have access to its information. The parties would first need to find some method of apportionment for the responsibility of paying for particular losses as a result of usage.

When contemplating coverage for the cryptocurrency loss, consider the following excerpts from two different cyber insurance policies. The first policy contains the following policy language:

Social Engineering means the intentional misleading or deception of an employee or executive by a person falsely purporting to be your client, vendor, employee, or executive through pretexting, phishing, spear phishing, whaling, a business email compromise, or any other confidence trick communicated by email, text, instant message, telephone, or other electronic means, which results in your transfer, payment, or delivery of money or securities.

Money means:

1. currency, including Bitcoin or any other digital currency, cryptocurrency, or electronic currency, coins, and bank notes in current use anywhere in the world and having a face value (Hiscox Form CYBCL-CYB P0001S CW (10/19), pp. 14–17).

With this policy language, the firm in the scenario would probably recover the loss of its cryptocurrency.

The second policy contains no analogous coverage for social engineering as shown above. Simply, it contains coverage for “eCrime.” Within the policy “eCrime” coverage is meant:

To indemnify the Insured Organization for any direct financial loss sustained resulting from:

  • Fraudulent instruction;
  • Funds transfer fraud; or
  • Telephone fraud; that the insured first discovers during the Policy Period (Beazley Form F00653 112017 ed., pp. 2–3).

In this scenario, the firm believes its funds were transferred fraudulently. Hence, the second coverage option might provide coverage. However, further investigation of the policy reveals the following:

Funds Transfer Fraud means the loss of Money or Securities contained in a Transfer Account at a Financial Institution resulting from fraudulent written, electronic, telegraphic, cable, teletype or telephone instructions by a third party issued to a Financial Institution directing such institution to transfer, pay or deliver Money or Securities from any account maintained by the Insured Organization at such institution, without the Insured Organization's knowledge or consent. (Beazley Form F00653 112017 ed., pp. 8–9)

Perhaps, the hypothetical firm could argue that its cryptocurrency was “money” held in a “transfer account” at a “financial institution” (Beazley Form F00653 112017 Ed.).

Further within the definitions section of the policy, “Money means a medium of exchange in current use authorized or adopted by a domestic or foreign government as a part of its currency.” “Financial Institution means a bank, credit union, saving and loan association, trust company or other licensed financial service, securities broker-dealer, mutual fund, or liquid assets fund or similar investment company where the Insured Organization maintains a bank account” (Beazley Form F00653 112017 ed., pp. 7–11).

Further exclusions and clauses within the policy reinforce the outcome, but they are inconsequential to this discussion and scenario. No coverage is likely afforded to the firm under this second policy scenario because its cryptocurrency is not defined as money under the policy. Attempting to argue that its cryptocurrency should be considered money through litigation could find the firm facing the same definitional barrier of “money” defined by the UCC as previously discussed in the section on crime policies.

Even if the firm in the scenario was fortunate enough to have obtained the first policy, which appears to allow for the recovery of the cryptocurrency, a further question remains. What is the value of the cryptocurrency and how is that value calculated? Given the potentially wild swings in the value of cryptocurrencies, the loss may have been valued at $1 million at the time of loss, but replacing the “number” of cryptocurrency coins could result in a value either much more or less than the loss experienced by the firm.

Within traditional property insurance policies, the amount the insured receives in the event of a loss of its property is generally valued in one of two ways. The first is known as replacement cost value (RCV). Under an RCV agreement, the insured is usually indemnified for the cost to create an equivalent replacement for the lost property at current market rates. Under the second method, actual cash value (ACV), the insured is generally indemnified for replacement cost less depreciation (Jerry and Douglas 2012). For example, if the insured bought a car at $50,000 but its equivalent replacement was only $20,000, the insured would receive $20,000 under the ACV.

Such traditional reimbursement calculations prove insufficient with fluctuating cryptocurrency values. As a whole, the insurance market does not appear to have yet developed a suitable standard that would appease all parties involved. Even for the policy that includes “cryptocurrency” within the definition of money, no guidance exists on how to value that cryptocurrency at the time of loss. Perhaps the only clue to how the insurer would argue the value of the loss is found in an insuring clause dealing with cyber extortion (ransomware) costs, which is tangential to the hypothetical firm's situation detailed prior.

If the ransom demanded consists of Bitcoin or any other digital, crypto, or electronic currency, cyber extortion costs will also include reasonable and necessary costs incurred by you with our prior written consent to obtain such currency. In that event, we will use the United States dollar equivalent determined by the rate of exchange published by the exchange in which you obtain the Bitcoin or other crypto or electronic currency on the date you obtain it in order to determine the value of the ransom paid. (Hiscox Form CYBCL-CYB P0001S CW (10/19), p. 12)

If the insurer contends that the reimbursement for each cryptocurrency coin will be valued as of its purchase date, this approach could potentially leave the firm with a sizable loss. If this situation were the case, the firm could probably litigate the matter, but no analogous or precedential case appears to point to a probable outcome. In other words, whether the firm recovers some, any, or all of cryptocurrency as valued at the time of its loss is likely to be a coin toss.

For businesses concerned about this ambiguity in the potential for coverage in their cyber insurance policy for blockchain and cryptocurrency related losses, there is hope. Nearly every facet of an insurance policy is negotiable for the right price. However, any business wanting to customize its insurance policy language should seek the guidance of competent legal counsel.

Hope for the Future and Other Solutions

Although the above discussions about the ambiguity of insurance coverage for blockchain and cryptocurrency losses may sound bleak, all hope is not lost. The insurance industry is well-aware of the impact of blockchain and cryptocurrencies and the near inevitably of its mass adoption in nearly every industry. The industry is slowly and cautiously offering additional specific coverages or policies that could overcome many insurance obstacles relating to blockchains and cryptocurrencies.

In a 2019 blog post, Philip Martin, Coinbase's vice president of security, detailed that his company had procured an insurance policy with a $225 million limit. The firm's policy allegedly reimburses individual customers for losses that would occur in their hot wallets (Martin 2019).

Cryptocurrency affiliated companies such as Coinbase may offer insurance to both general businesses and individuals for their cryptocurrencies (Coinbase 2020). Although this situation does not address the issue presented with cost of a blockchain breach, it does point toward a step in the right direction.

Failure to obtain insurance from third parties does not mean that businesses needing to insure against blockchain-related losses are without options. Absent proper or timely advancements made by insurance companies to address the insurability of blockchain and cryptocurrency related losses, other solutions are available. Businesses involved in blockchain could require all entities with access to maintain funds held in escrow – where a third party holds and disburses money on behalf of the transacting parties according to a set of predetermined terms – to cover the losses associated with any claims or losses. In insurance parlance, this situation is known as “self-insurance.” Although beyond the scope of this chapter, drawbacks exist for self-insurance ranging from troublesome to catastrophic. Depending on a company's unique risks, those drawbacks could be minor when compared to having no insurance.

Alternatively, the businesses could engage in captive or micro-captive insurance arrangements. Here, blockchain affiliated businesses would create their own licensed insurance company to provide coverage for the group. This approach allows the greatest flexibility in terms of setting premiums to be paid and coverage features. For smaller businesses, this approach could be fiscally and administratively untenable, but for larger businesses it may provide the flexibility needed.

Finally, businesses could take a hybrid approach to blockchain and cryptocurrency implementation. Under this method, a business would use blockchain technology for information that would not require client notification, would not likely result in the loss of trade secrets, and would not reasonably result in an increased risk of litigation if compromised. Whether this approach is a tenable solution ultimately depends on the specifics needs and information held by the business.

Summary and Conclusions

Businesses should understand that planning for the potential losses and damages that may arise from using blockchain and cryptocurrencies require particular diligence. Traditional claim types experienced by a business have historically been insurable absent unique circumstances. Blockchain and cryptocurrencies present unique insurability challenges that are likely to persist as these technologies become more mainstream and novel loss circumstances are encountered. Whether any one blockchain and cryptocurrency insurance coverage case could be precedential hinges not only on the exact insurance policy language presented but also on the fact pattern of the case, such as whether the blockchain was private or a consortium and whether the cryptocurrency was bitcoin or ether.

Ultimately, these warnings should not be interpreted to dissuade a business from adoption, but merely to caution it to be particularly cognizant of risk management in this arena. Using outside legal counsel familiar with these technologies to provide the greatest likelihood of coverage under novel or legacy insurance policies is likely to be essential. As the courts work through the multitude of issues found with interpreting legacy coverage clauses as they relate to blockchain and cryptocurrencies, businesses should also remain ready to request specific changes to coverage language at their policy renewal as dictated by unique needs. The insurance market will eventually adapt, but so too must businesses in how they manage and insure their risks.

Discussion Questions

(1)Discuss how cryptocurrencies are classified by the various government entities.

(2)Explain whether a standard commercial crime policy affords coverage to a business for blockchain breaches and cryptocurrency losses.

(3)Explain whether a standard commercial general liability policy affords coverage to a business for blockchain breaches and cryptocurrency losses.

(4)Explain whether a standard cyber insurance policy affords coverage to a business for blockchain breaches and cryptocurrency losses.

(5)Identify the alternative insurance mechanisms available for businesses.

(6)Discuss the various attack vectors and vulnerabilities that may be present in blockchains.

Chapter 14

Legal and Regulatory Issues in the Temporary Regime

J. Scott Colesanti

Keywords: Securities and exchange commission; cryptocurrency; alt-currency; blockchain; investment contract; virtual currency

Introduction

In the view of regulators, blockchain is defined only in the context and presence of cryptocurrency. Indeed, the National Conference of State Legislatures (NCSL) has declared that all digital currency transactions are recorded in a blockchain (Morton 2018). More importantly, the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) lists initial coin offerings (ICOs) as “fundraising events” tied to “a blockchain technology or cryptographically secured ledger” (SEC Complaint, Kik Interactive 2019, p. 8). Concomitantly, a decentralized autonomous organization is “a ‘virtual’ organization embodied in computer code and executed on a distributed ledger or blockchain” (DAO Report 2017, pp. 2‒3). With blockchain and alt-currencies being repeatedly uttered in the same breath, the strong hand of the SEC reaches blockchain seemingly without question. In turn, the omnipresent discipline by the $2 billion agency poses the most formidable legal challenge to the technology enabling digital capital formation and services.

To be sure, justification exists for the present undefined draconian approach. The launch of cryptocurrency was occasioned by occurrences of theft, excessive speculation, and outright fraud. According to Popper (2015), a 2013 academic study concluded that 45% of the bitcoin exchanges had gone under, resulting in several taking the money of their customers with them. In February 2014, Mt. Gox, the first cryptocurrency exchange, filed for bankruptcy after 850,000 bitcoins went missing (Allman 2014). The resulting legal proceedings continue in multiple nations until this day.

Further, the persistent cybersecurity threat has caused widespread alarm. In March 2019, $195 million worth of cryptocurrency was lost when the owner of a cryptocurrency trading platform died in sole possession of its digital key. The debacle foisted the trading platform into court protection, prompting calls for national legislation by the Canadian Securities Administrators. According to Owram (2019), crypto-assets amounting to almost $1 billion were stolen in 2018 from platforms around the world.

Separately, the sheer volatility of cryptocurrency has consistently warranted attention and inevitable comparisons to the Dutch tulip bubble craze or tulip mania of 1600s. In 2013 alone, bitcoin rose from $13 each to over $1,100 each. By 2018, bitcoin traded at over $18,000 per coin; a year later, that market value had plummeted to less than $5,000. Regardless of or perhaps because of these demonstrable swings, the investment potential of alt-currency had far eclipsed any notion of crypto as a means of currency or barter. By mid-2019, a widely held view was that less than 2% of all bitcoins were being used for their originally intended purpose of facilitating trade without fiat currency (Kharif 2019).

Nonetheless, in the past decade, American federal agencies have resisted the call to define cryptocurrency with certainty – even while politicians evidenced strong but polemical views on the degree of necessary government intervention. The Treasury Department has never branded any cryptocurrency as legal tender. The Financial Crimes Enforcement Network (FinCEN), an enforcement arm of the Treasury Department, has twice issued guidance reminding that parties “mining” bitcoins for others or exchanging bitcoins for cash must comply with the registration requirements of the money laundering regulations promulgated under the Bank Secrecy Act (Department of the Treasury 2013, 2019). To date, FinCEN has stopped short of subjecting cryptocurrency transactions exceeding a monetary threshold in value to reporting requirements.

Meanwhile, the Internal Revenue Service (IRS) has issued guidance advising that profits on crypto-related investments should be reported as gains on investments. The guidance initially spoke generally of such treatment under the tax laws (IRS Notice 2014), while an update explained the application of the same provisions to convertible securities and similar instruments (IRS Notice 2019). Such guidance is not as strong as an IRS regulation or Congressional statute because they are not legally binding or permanent.

Overall, the peer-to-peer system imagined by Satoshi Nakomoto could hardly be said to have welcomed regulation (Nakamoto 2010). Indeed, the fundamentals of peer-to-peer payment systems decried government intervention. Yet, collectively, the popularity of cryptocurrency, its lack of finite definition, its volatile pricing, and potential for fraud collectively call for government oversight. Against such backdrop, the world's foremost business regulator would find remaining dormant impossible. Accordingly, the purpose of this chapter is three-fold: (1) to explore the birth of the regulation of blockchain by the SEC, (2) to discuss the legal means by which digital assetization comes within the securities laws, and (3) to offer an outlook for the future. The chapter has the following organization. The first section discusses the application of the securities laws followed by sections addressing SEC pronouncements, state/other remedies, and concluding observations.

Application of the Securities Laws

As primary enforcer of the most expertize system of securities statutes, the SEC owns nearly 100 years of experience in enforcing a mosaic approach born of the Great Depression of 1929. Foremost among these laws are the Securities Act of 1933 (“the 1933 Act”) and the Securities Exchange Act of 1934 (“the 1934 Act”; collectively, “the Acts”), both of which bestow jurisdiction among federal courts to hear cases imposing discipline far exceeding traditional European and state notions of business regulation.

The key definition in this protocol is “security,” which the Supreme Court clarified in the Tcherepnin case as having the same meaning under both the Acts (Tcherepnin v. Knight 1967). Counterintuitively, the existence of a security far surpasses shares traded on a stock exchange, or even deals carefully crafted to exclude either the coverage of the securities laws or the moniker of “stock.” Rather, owing to the New Deal spirit of expanding investor protections, the presence of a security for purposes of the American securities laws owes to a test created by the Supreme Court in the landmark Howey case (SEC v. W. J. Howey Co. 1946). That test seeks to identify passive investors, while – again owing to the Tcherepnin case – discerning the “economic realities of the transaction.” Table 14.1 shows the four elements of the judicially-created Howey test.

Table 14.1. Summary of the Four Howey Test Elements.

Mandatory Element Overview Lead Authorities
(1) Investment of money Need not be cash, but must be a “tangible consideration” (including Bitcoin). Teamsters v. Daniel (1979); SEC v. Shavers (2014)
(2) in a common enterprise Promoter and investor interests must coincide. SEC v. Glenn Turner Enterprises (1973)
(3) with the expectation of profits Investor must be lured by specter of financial gain. United Housing Foundation v. Forman (Sup. Ct. 1975)
(4) derived from the essential managerial/predominant efforts of others. Investor efforts must be ministerial or inconsequential. SEC v. Life Partners (1996)

Note: This table lists the parts of a conjunctive test fashioned by the Supreme Court in SEC v. W. J. Howey Co. (1946). The test determines whether an agreement in substance equates to an “investment contract” under the federal securities laws.

In the past 40 years, case law has expanded to apply the securities laws to business models such as franchises (SEC v. Aqua-Sonic Products Corp. 1981) and unsecured promissory notes (SEC v. Thompson 2013). Moreover, the intent of the parties to define or exclude exempted transactions is irrelevant, as demonstrated by Great Rivers Coop. v. Farmlands Indus (1999) and United States v. Leonard (2008), respectively.

Thus, the SEC has chilled quixotic offers of profitable investment by labeling “promoter” and “investor” to expand its reach in widely disparate areas. Examples include condominium subletting agreements (Bamert v. Pulte Home Corp. 2011), animal breeding farms (Sheets v. Dziabis 1990), “death bonds” (SEC v. Life Partners 1996), and internet-gaming coins (SEC v. SG Ltd. 2001). Thus, the fact that the SEC would take on the challenge of protecting American “investors” in alt-currencies is unsurprising.

The robust case law centering on the elastic Howey test enables such agency paternalism. That dynamic standard rarely encounters restraint. It also affords use by multiple enforcers including the Department of Justice (DOJ) and serves as a portal to express statutory remedies. The most commonly sought remedy is registration with the SEC, a costly solution that nonetheless provides all potential investors with issuer information. Additionally, common remedial measures invoked by satisfaction the judge-made Howey test are 1933 Act Section 12(a) (1) – providing “rescission” (i.e., reimbursement) for investors sold unregistered securities (Section 12(a) (1), Securities Act of 1933) – and 1934 Act Section 10(b) and effectuating SEC Rule 10b-5 (Section 10(b), Securities Exchange Act of 1934). The latter of these measures provides the broadest means of labeling and capturing fraud and intentional misstatements and indirectly enables punitive damages. Since 2013, both of these statutory weapons enable punishing allegedly wrongful investment activity phrased in digital asset terms.

Forced Fit to Cryptocurrency and Blockchain

Since 2013, application by the SEC of the securities laws has primarily targeted three types of defendants:

(1)Ponzi schemers soliciting funds for investments in either business models using digital technologies or cryptocurrencies (SEC Investor Alert 2013),

(2)Companies seeking to match buyer and seller and thus acting as unregistered “exchanges”, a term closely guarded by the SEC (SEC Order 2018), or

(3)Third parties touting number 1 and/or 2 above while not disclosing related remuneration. (SEC Press Release 2018; Mott 2020).

Of greatest interest to business people, lawyers, and students is the stretching of existing SEC approaches to reach deals reliant upon blockchain. The SEC has not often failed in this bold reach. Table 14.2 below describes noteworthy cases in recent years against issuers, a self-described “exchange”, or third parties.

Table 14.2. Example of SEC Cases Against Crypto-defendants.

SEC Defendant Overview Result
(1) Shavers (SEC v. Shavers 2014) Alleged Ponzi scheme operator sued for offering unregistered shares in a company designed to trade cryptocurrencies. Bitcoin found by a federal court to equate to money for purposes of threshold securities law analysis; defendant ordered to pay more than $40 million.
(2) Coburn (SEC Order 2018) Operator of trading platform charged with running an unregistered “exchange.” Defendant ceased operations and paid disgorgement, interest, and fine exceeding $380,000.
(3) Munchee (SEC v. Munchee Inc. 2017) “App” offering digital coins in return for restaurant reviews alleged to have issued unregistered securities. Defendant consented to a halt of its offering on its second day and returned to investors all proceeds.
(4) Zaslavskiy (United States v. Zaslavskiy 2018) Real estate developer charged by the DOJ with securities fraud in connection with two unregistered ICOs; defendant marketed “The First Ever Cryptocurrency Backed by Real Estate.” Guilty verdict obtained; defendant pleaded guilty in June 2019 and was sentenced to 18 months imprisonment.
(5) BlockOne (SEC Press Release 2019) Company sold $900 million worth of unregistered digital tokens. $24 million civil fine paid.
(6) Kik Interactive (SEC Complaint, Kik Interactive Inc., 2019) Messenger app sued for allegedly selling $100 million worth of unregistered securities in the form of digital tokens. Settled in October 2020 for $5 million.
(7) DJ Khaled (SEC v. DJ Khaled, 2018); Floyd Mayweather(SEC v. Floyd Mayweather Jr. 2018); Steven Seagal (SEC v. Steven Seagal, 2020). Celebrities charged with violating securities law provision prohibiting touting securities without disclosing remuneration. Defendants paid disgorgement and fines exceeding $900,000.

Note: This table lists examples of government applications of the securities laws to cryptocurrency/blockchain defendants since 2013. All examples except #6 represent final determinations.

SEC Disciplinary Cases

A closer review of SEC cases in the subject field reveals a progression from cryptocurrency as the means of investment to largely constituting the security itself. Although the view that cryptocurrency itself equates to a “security” has only been espoused in scholarly commentary (Yang 2014), the SEC enforcement program has come alarmingly close to embracing a majority of alt-currency deals as within agency reach.

In the seminal Shavers case, the SEC brought charges against a Ponzi schemer who used online “posts” to promise a 7% weekly return on investment in his trading company. The defendant instead used the proceeds largely for personal purposes. The federal court, employing the Howey test, readily concluded that element 1 thereof was met by the exchange of bitcoin, declaring that bitcoin “can be exchanged for conventional currencies” (SEC v. Shavers 2014, p. 3).

Subsequently, the SEC enjoyed a string of uninterrupted victories clawing back monies for investors or swelling government coffers with fines. Indeed, the Howey test elements of “money” and “profits” (i.e., elements 1 and 3) pose nearly no obstacle to application. Investors in startups willingly trade consideration and consistently show a desire for profit. Thus, the challenge for the SEC lies in the “common enterprise” and “efforts of others” requirements (i.e., elements 2 and 4, respectively). Two examples of detailed SEC charges explain the theory by which crypto-deals come within – and perhaps even expand – American securities law.

First, in the Telegram Group case (SEC v. Telegram Group, Inc. 2019), the SEC set forth its position that, beyond essential managerial efforts by promoters (i.e., element 4), the absence of any required investor efforts to create profits sufficed. Thus, in alleging that “the principal means by which investors would reasonably expect to profit is through their resale of [tokens]” (SEC v.Telegram Group, Inc. 2019, p. 25), the SEC obviated the need to allege or prove that the promoter issuer actively encourage a third-party market. The case resulted in the successful halting of an offering by a foreign-based mobile messenger application determined to be tied to the “world's most adopted cryptocurrency wallet” (SEC v.Telegram Group, Inc. 2019, p. 26).

Second, in the Ackerman case, the SEC halted an offering by a physician who had secured $33 million in an advertised effort to “pool money to invest in cryptocurrencies” (SEC v.Ackerman 2020, p. 2). The SEC alleged that the physician diverted millions of dollars of such contributions for personal use. In alleging the presence of a security, the SEC complaint alleges that the defendant falsely claimed that his controlled entities “successfully traded various cryptocurrencies through various crypto-exchanges using proprietary algorithmically driven software for other pooled investment groups” (SEC v.Ackerman 2020, p. 7).

The SEC continues to seek damages. The significance of SEC v. Ackerman (2020), as in many SEC cases, is the presumed presence of a security when crypto-profits are promised. Indeed, no Howey test analysis is undertaken. Of course, the elemental challenges of the Howey test are expressly satisfied where the promoter expressly promises the existence of a third-party trading market for offered coins and/or expresses a desire to wholly own all managerial efforts.

However, scrutiny of a broader selection of crypto-cases thus reveals that to raise the question of a security's presence is largely to answer it in the affirmative. Moreover, a further advantage to SEC involvement in regulating a novel field is the attendant and inevitable civil class action that ensues. Such actions by supplemental enforcers of the securities laws are described below.

Class Action Litigation

Class actions seeking return of investments in blockchain and alt-currency abound, even though the grounds for such broad SEC interpretation of relevant definitions and anti-fraud prohibitions are vulnerable. First, in determining the presence of a security, the crypto-purchase arrangement is subject to greatly varying models. Paperwork is nearly non-existent, eliminating comfortable comparisons to a statutory “investment contract.” As such, digital asset arrangements do not readily satisfy even the generous definitions afforded by either the 1933 Act or the 1934 Act.

Second, some issuers may attempt in good faith to create “utility tokens” of minimal use beyond a finite ecosystem. Just as a credit card offers reward “points” for frequently using a line of credit, some coin offerings may legitimately seek to benefit purchasers choosing a particular application or model.

Nonetheless, the precedent being created by the SEC fuels one of the many advantages of using federal securities law: overlapping precedents. The SEC and private plaintiffs routinely use holdings from parallel private and governmental case decisions to their advantage. Further, the SEC often “weighs in” to urge its interpretation of key securities law claims and elements on private lawsuits. A review of two private cases from New York and California demonstrates the application of the Howey test to ICOs to facilitate class action lawsuits brought by investors in failed companies that had promoted using blockchain in conjunction with a new cryptocurrency.

In Coffey v. Ripple Labs (2018), the plaintiff alleged a “never-ending ICO” that would result in the issuer inevitably controlling 80% of the available digital coins. The complaint alleged that the defendant's admission to seeking investments in coins to fund “its operation and its network” suffices as satisfying the common enterprise element of the Howey test, while the admitted reliance on the defendant's expertize satisfies element 4 (i.e., “efforts of others”). The private suit has survived motions to dismiss and is pending in California federal court.

More pointedly, in Balestra v. ATBCOIN LLC (2019), a class action was brought forth against an issuer and two of its founders for a violation of the 1933 Act by selling unregistered securities through an ICO. ATBCOIN was a technology-based startup, the purpose of which was to facilitate rapid and low-cost digital financial transactions leveraging blockchain technology. In denying the defendants' motion to dismiss, the court found all four of the elements of the Howey test satisfied.

Specifically, between June 12, 2017 and September 15, 2017, ATBCOIN conducted an ICO and promised to launch a resulting ATB blockchain. By the end of the ICO, ATBCOIN raised over $20 million from thousands of investors, but the promised blockchain had not materialized. Within a year, Balestra's coins had dropped in value by more than 85% from the purchase price.

ATBCOIN did not file a registration statement at any point either before, during, or after the ICO. Thus, the plaintiff sued for rescission under Section 12(a) (1) of the 1933 Act. In denying the defendants' motion to dismiss, the court held,

[T]he “touchstone” of an investment contract [is] the presence of an investment in a common venture premised on a reasonable expectation of profits to be derived from the entrepreneurial or managerial efforts of others… ( Balestra v. ATBCOIN LLC 2019, p. 12).

When discussing the Howey test, the court emphasized that the analysis should be based on the economic realities of the underlying transaction. Noting that all potential profits were “entirely reliant” on the success of the blockchain platform, the decision likewise emphasized that the issuer had advertized “serious people from many prosperous countries” were investing in the coins ( Balestra v. ATBCOIN LLC 2019, pp. 16‒17).

Additionally, the argument by the defendants that coin purchasers had complete control over their coins was to no avail, as the court found that the purchasers had no control over whether the new blockchain would function as promised. Thus, in both SEC and private actions, the most likely hurdle to be surmounted by the defense may be Howey's element 4. However, even that hurdle has not proven substantial, and many more actions seem likely to come. Such actions rest primarily upon the SEC's informal but loud public statements.

Timeline of SEC Pronouncements

Despite the absence of SEC Rule or proposal, the SEC has used other means to solidify its embedded stance that digital asset offerings come within the securities laws. The following discussion details four such public rationales for the uninterrupted flow of disciplinary cases.

In July 2017, the SEC issued a strict interpretation of cryptocurrencies as investment contracts and thus securities via a release titled “Report of Investigation Pursuant to Section 21(a) of the Securities Exchange Act of 1934: The DAO.” A Section 21(a) report announces the lack of disciplinary action being taken against a particular investigative target. The 2017 DAO Report reiterated the fundamental principles of the federal securities laws while explaining

…their applicability to the new paradigm – virtual organizations or capital raising entities that use distributed ledger or blockchain technology to facilitate capital raising and/or investment and the related offer and sale of securities (DAO Report 2017, p. 2).

The DAO Report concluded that Slock.it, a German cyberspace corporation, had issued tokens that were later found to be in fact securities. The SEC added much language on the obligations of all issuers to comply with the federal securities laws:

The Commission is aware that virtual organizations and associated individuals and entities increasingly are using distributed ledger technology to offer and sell instruments such as DAO Tokens to raise capital. These offers and sales have been referred to, among other things, as “Initial Coin Offerings” or “Token Sales.” Accordingly, the Commission deems it appropriate and in the public interest to issue this Report in order to stress that the U.S. federal securities law may apply to various activities, including distributed ledger technology, depending on the particular facts and circumstances, without regard to the form of the organization or technology used to effectuate a particular offer or sale (DAO Report 2017, p. 10).

The SEC found that investors in DAO tokens used ether (ETH), a virtual currency used on a decentralized platform that runs smart contracts known as the Ethereum blockchain to make their investments. Each investor tendered ETH in exchange for DAO tokens. Despite the lack of traditional currency to satisfy the “investment of money” prong of Howey, the SEC concluded that the investment in DAO tokens was “the type of contribution of value that can create an investment contract under Howey” (SEC v. Shavers 2014, p. 3).

Legally speaking, the SEC combined discussion of the commonality prong of the Howey test to the DAO tokens in its discussion of the “reasonable expectation of profits” prong of the Howey test. The DAO tokens met the final prong of the Howey test (i.e., that the profits be derived from the managerial efforts of others) because the investors

…relied on the managerial and entrepreneurial efforts of Slock.it and its cofounders, and the DAO's Curators, to manage the DAO and put forth project proposals that could generate profits for the DAO's investors (DAO Report 2017, p. 12).

Months later, the approach was cemented as a legal presumption in a speech by the SEC Chair to investment professionals in December 2017:

A key question for all ICO market participants: “Is the coin or token a security?” As securities law practitioners know well, the answer depends on the facts. For example, a token that represents a participation interest in a book-of-the-month club may not implicate our securities laws, and may well be an efficient way for the club's operators to fund the future acquisition of books and facilitate the distribution of those books to token holders. In contrast, many token offerings appear to have gone beyond this construct and are more analogous to interests in a yet-to-be-built publishing house with the authors, books and distribution networks all to come. It is especially troubling when the promoters of these offerings emphasize the secondary market trading potential of these tokens. Prospective purchasers are being sold on the potential for tokens to increase in value – with the ability to lock in those increases by reselling the tokens on a secondary market – or to otherwise profit from the tokens based on the efforts of others. These are key hallmarks of a security and a securities offering (SEC Public Statement 2017).

The Chair's warning to investment professionals concurrently acknowledged a presumption that related parties would, where appropriate, be subject to the securities laws:

I also caution market participants against promoting or touting the offer and sale of coins without first determining whether the securities laws apply to those actions. Selling securities generally requires a license, and experience shows that excessive touting in thinly traded and volatile markets can be an indicator of “scalping,” “pump and dump” and other manipulations and frauds. Similarly, I also caution those who operate systems and platforms that effect or facilitate transactions in these products that they may be operating unregistered exchanges or broker-dealers that are in violation of the Securities Exchange Act of 1934 (SEC Public Statement 2017).

The ubiquitous nature of digital offerings was bound to stem the tide of polarized regulation. By March 2018, the SEC had begrudgingly accepted the popularity of such market centers while cautioning that investors “should use a platform or entity registered with the SEC, such as a national securities exchange, alternative trading system, or broker-dealer” (SEC Public Statement 2018). As a concurrent American Bar Association article acknowledged, ICOs had become both frequent and advised by lawyers, despite it becoming commonplace to at once decry the ungovernable nature of digital assets and yearn for regulation thereof (Tashea 2018).

Of greater note, the grandstanding approach to regulation inspired outright dissent at the highest level. The SEC is a bipartisan agency headed by five Commissioners drawn from both political parties. Accordingly, in her fall 2019 remarks, Commissioner Hester Pierce decried

…our lack of a workable regulatory framework has hindered innovation and growth. The only guidance out of the SEC is a parade of enforcement actions and a set of staff guidance documents and staff no-action letters (SEC Public Statement 2019).

Other SEC officials and members of Congress have joined Commissioner Peirce in her criticism of the SEC's litigious approach, thus increasing the likelihood that the SEC's luck in applying the broad Howey test may eventually run out.

In the interim, the vast amounts of monies being invested in cryptocurrencies ensure a showdown between entrepreneurs and the SEC. Formal rulemaking would aid both regulator and regulated. Perhaps such answer lies more with expanding upon the nonaction that the SEC has taken to date, a no action letter from April 2019 (SEC No Action Letter Re. TurnKey Jet Inc. 2019). Table 14.3 shows an SEC No Action Letter issued to a coin issuer.

Table 14.3. SEC No Action Letter Issued to a Coin Issuer (“TurnKey Letter”).

Securities Act of 1933
Section 2(a)(1)
April 3, 2019
Response of the Division of Corporation Finance
Re: TurnKey Jet, Inc.
Incoming letter dated April 2, 2019
Based on the facts presented, the Division will not recommend enforcement action to the SEC if, in reliance on your opinion as counsel that the Tokens are not securities, TKJ offers and sells the Tokens without registration under the Securities Act and the Exchange Act. Capitalized terms have the same meanings as defined in your letter.
In reaching this position, we particularly note that:
  • TKJ will not use any funds from Token sales to develop the TKJ Platform, Network, or App, and each of these will be fully developed and operational at the time any Tokens are sold;
  • The Tokens will be immediately usable for their intended functionality (purchasing air charter services) at the time they are sold;
  • TKJ will restrict transfers of Tokens to TKJ Wallets only and not to wallets external to the Platform;
  • TKJ will sell Tokens at a price of one USD per Token throughout the life of the Program, and each Token will represent a TKJ obligation to supply air charter services at a value of one USD per Token;
  • If TKJ offers to repurchase Tokens, it will only do so at a discount to the face value of the Tokens (one USD per Token) that the holder seeks to resell to TKJ, unless a court within the United States orders TKJ to liquidate the Tokens; and
  • The Token is marketed in a manner that emphasizes the functionality of the Token, and not the potential for the increase in the market value of the Token.

This position is based on the representations made to the Division in your letter. Any different facts or conditions might require the Division to reach a different conclusion. Further, this response expresses the Division's position on enforcement action only and does not express any legal conclusion on the question presented.
Sincerely,
Jonathan A. Ingram
Chief Legal Advisor, FinHub
Division of Corporation Finance

Note: This table displays the SEC's guidance to a company issuing tokens. A No Action Letter generally explains that the government shall not take disciplinary action if the company adheres to its business plan as revealed to the SEC. No Action Letters are not binding on third parties.

The advantage of the TurnKey Letter is the SEC's demonstrated willingness to allow certain coin offerings to proceed without SEC registration. Nonetheless, the pronouncement's disadvantage is its implied restriction on initial capital formation, a factor present in nearly all token/coin offerings.

Other Pending Solutions

When state approaches are too varied, model “codes” can often harmonize the legal field. For example, all 50 states have adopted the Uniform Commercial Code in largely common variations. Closer to the topic at hand, the Uniform Securities Act of 1954 succeeded in inspiring and/or conforming State “Blue Sky statutes” throughout the country.

Likewise, a budding movement exists to consistently adopt a proposed “Virtual Currency Businesses Act” among State legislatures (Uniform Regulation of Virtual Currency Businesses Act 2020). As this chapter is finalized, that movement has garnered only a modicum of interest.

Such formal legislation among the states ranges from measures inviting virtual businesses through tax advantages (e.g., New Jersey) to those memorializing salutary federal developments (e.g., Wisconsin), to those demanding registration (e.g., New York). Perhaps more telling are the standards evolving from state disciplinary actions against promoters seeking to maximize investor interest in technologies through misstatements and/or fraud. In a 2014 disciplinary complaint, the Missouri Securities Commission expressly faulted the defendants (“Virtual Miners”) for not disclosing, among others, that virtual currencies are not backed by a central bank/are not insured, and no way is available to reverse a virtual currency transaction (Virtual Mining Corporation 2014).

Concurrently, the umbrella organization for the states has publicized a cautious tone. The North American Securities Administrators Association (NASAA), an entity that predates the federalization of securities laws and serves as the voice of state securities regulators, routinely lists crypto-fraud among its top 10 investor concerns. Although the organization has no rulemaking or enforcement apparatus, its warnings can be both pointed and colorful:

Virtual reality may exist only in science fiction, but consumers now are able to purchase goods and services with virtual money such as Bitcoin, PP Coin and other digital currencies. Unlike traditional coinage, these alternatives typically are not backed by tangible assets, are not issued by a governmental authority and are subject to little or no regulation. The value of Bitcoins and other digital currencies is highly volatile and the concept behind the currency is difficult to understand even for sophisticated financial experts given the complicated mathematical algorithms that determine when new blocks of coins will be released. This environment has provided fertile ground for scam artists to capitalize on the increasing popularity and acceptance of digital currencies. Investors should be aware that investments that incorporate abstract money systems present very real risks, including the possibility of virtual reality leaving an investor virtually broke (NASAA 2014).

Such characterization, while undoubtedly part of the debate over the appropriate degree attending ideal regulation, does not answer the question. Accordingly, the harsh solution of application of the federal securities laws appears poised to continue, with noteworthy fines and resultant headlines. In the long term, the greatest chance for peaceful coexistence between the regulators and the entrepreneurs advancing blockchain is perhaps concrete SEC rulemaking. The SEC's ability to fashion formal guidance exceeds even its storied litigation talents. Further, after 10 years, ample precedent for meaningful compromise has been set by case decisions, No Action Letters, state initiatives, and industry comment.

Summary and Conclusions

Cryptocurrency and blockchain experienced a challenging start, with early players incurring liabilities including charges ranging from ill-preparedness to fraud (Buterin 2012; Zetter 2012; Henning 2013; Leger 2014; Clark-Wendel 2014; Raghavan 2014; United States v. Ross William Ulbricht 2014). Adding to the regulatory uncertainty were issues of agency indifference and overreach (Greene 2014; Commodities Futures Trading Commission v. McDonnell 2018). Moreover, investor introductions to the technology warned of a world fraught with peril (Diekmann 2014, FINRA Bulletin 2014).

Polar positions on regulation materialized (Maney 2014; Robbins 2014). Meanwhile, commentators openly noted the lack of legal consistency/clarity (Yang 2014; Yui and Hyuga 2014; Tashea 2018). Against this challenging backdrop, the SEC publicly emerged as the primary regulator of alt-currency and blockchain (Testimony of SEC Chairman Jay Clayton 2018; Hearing on Fiscal Year 2019 2019). Although the states have also unpredictably taken occasional harsh stances (Weinberger 2019), a federal agency that has neither lobbied Congress for statutory change nor issued its own rules is largely setting the agenda. The attentive student thus plumbs SEC pronouncements and disciplinary and similarly centered private claims for guidance while cognizant of the inevitable, more cemented regulation that lies ahead.

Discussion Questions

(1)Explain how the SEC came to be the primary regulator of cryptocurrency and blockchain.

(2)Explain the legal authorities supporting the application of American securities law to cryptocurrency and blockchain.

(3)Identify the criticisms of the SEC's rapid and expansive reach.

(4)Discuss noteworthy state initiatives to bring cryptocurrency transactions and blockchain technology within traditional means of regulation.

(5)Discuss the most immediate and expected federal regulatory change serving to best protect investors while concomitantly aiding capital formation.
