Chapter 15

Regulatory Ambiguity and Its Impact on Blockchain

Shehan Chandrasekera

Keywords: Blockchain; virtual currencies; bitcoin; Internal Revenue Service; Notice 2014-21; capital gains taxes; cost basis

Introduction

Virtual currencies (VCs) such as bitcoin have gained popularity since their introduction in 2009. According to the Internal Revenue Service (IRS), more than 5,000 cryptocurrencies are available and the number continues to increase. Between 2009 and 2019, people have gained access to substantial wealth by engaging in various activities such as trading and mining in the cryptocurrency space. Regulatory agencies like the IRS, Commodities Futures and Trading Commission (CFTC), Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC), Financial Crimes Enforcement Network (FinCen), and Financial Industry Regulatory Authority have tried to regulate various aspects of the crypto sphere. In general, lack of a unified vision and coordination among these regulators have contributed to the general regulatory ambiguity. For example, the IRS treats cryptocurrencies as property. The CFTC treats some cryptocurrencies as commodities. The SEC believes many crypto tokens are securities. Attempts to regulate the environment have partially and/or entirely failed by applying decades old rules and regulations to a cutting-edge technology like blockchain. This chapter primarily focuses on the efforts taken by the IRS and how those efforts have generally led to confusion among taxpayers and blockchain participants.

Tax Implications of Virtual Currency

Unlike US dollars, which only work as a medium of exchange, VCs have multiple use cases. VCs are often used as speculative investment asset. They can be mined to earn a passive course of income. Finally, they can also work as a medium of exchange. Each use case would yield slightly different tax implications.

General Treatment

The IRS first came out with VC guidance in 2014 by issuing Notice 2014-21. According to this notice, the IRS treats VC as property for federal income tax purposes. Therefore, general tax principles applicable to property transactions apply to VC transactions. Contrary to popular belief, the IRS neither treats VCs as foreign currency nor subject to laws related to foreign currency. The taxation of VCs can be easily understood by categorizing it into different users of VC and use cases. Understanding the application of current tax guidance is important before investigating more complicated transactions and ambiguous rules.

Investors

Investors are individuals who buy and sell crypto assets for speculative purposes. Gains and losses arising from these transactions are capital gains/losses, just like stock transactions. Thus, net short-term gains on VC trading transactions are taxed as ordinary income and net short-term losses offset ordinary income up to the $3,000 limit on capital losses. Net long-term gains are taxed at the preferential long-term capital gains tax rates, and long-term losses can be offset against ordinary income, again, subject to the $3,000 limitation. Table 15.1 illustrates the calculation of capital gains and losses.

Table 15.1. Calculating Capital Gains and Losses.

Example 1: On January 1, 2018, someone bought one bitcoin (BTC) for $5,000 and later sold it for $8,000 on July 25, 2018. The gain of $3,000 ($8,000‒$5,000) is short-term and is taxed at the taxpayer's ordinary income tax rate.

Example 2: Assume the same facts as Example 1 except that the person sold the BTC for $10,000 on February 15, 2019. In this case, the gain of $5,000 ($10,000‒$5,000) is long-term and is taxed at preferential rates.

One cryptocurrency can be converted/exchanged into another cryptocurrency or a token, which is a taxable event according to Notice 2014-21. When one VC is converted into another type of VC or a token, gains/losses must be recognized in US dollars. As a result, the trader could owe a tax liability but have no real currency to pay it with.

Example 3: On October 1, 2018, Bob bought one BTC for $5,000, which is the original cost basis. On October 20, 2018, the market price of one BTC increased to $10,000, which is a 200% gain on initial investment. On October 20, 2018, ether (ETH) decreased in price, so Bob saw a buying opportunity. He bought 20 units of ETH using the one BTC previously purchased. In this situation, one ETH = $200.

Calculation

Step 1: Calculate the value of new property received

Value of 20 ETH bought = $4,000 or (20) ($200)

Step 2: Calculate the number of original tokens spent to get the new token

BTC spent to buy 20 ETH = 0.4 or ($4,000/$10,000)

Step 3: Calculate the gain/loss

Proceeds of the BTC sold = $4,000 or (0.4) ($10,000)

Cost basis of the BTC sold = $2,000 (0.4) ($5,000)

Gain = $2,000 ($4,000 − $2,000)

BTC remaining at hand = 0.6 or (1BTC − 0.4BTC)

Cost basis of the BTC at hand = $3,000 or (0.6) ($5,000)

Cost basis of 20 ETH at hand = $4,000

Note: This table shows how capital gains and losses arising from virtual currency transactions are calculated.

Gains/losses are recorded on the IRS Form 8949 (Sales and Other Dispositions of Capital Assets) as transactions not reported on Form 1099-B. Since current cryptocurrency exchanges do not provide taxpayers with 1099-B forms summarizing all their crypto transactions, taxpayers are responsible for tracking the basis and sales price for each transaction. In addition, since the IRS treats VCs as property, wash sale rules are inapplicable to investors.

Rules related to the tax lot identification (ID) method are another important subject to discuss when talking about investors. According to the 45 frequently asked questions (FAQs) the IRS issued on October 9, 2019 (Internal Revenue Service 2019a), taxpayers can choose the specific ID method as long as they can support the cost basis of those units they are deemed to be selling. Specific ID method among other methods such as first in, first out (FIFO) and last in, last out (LIFO) dictates which exact units are being sold for gain and loss calculation purposes.

To successfully identify a specific unit, information must include the:

  • acquisition date and time of each unit,
  • basis and the fair market value (FMV) of each unit when acquired,
  • date and time each unit was sold, exchanged, or otherwise disposed of, and
  • FMV of each unit when sold, exchanged, or disposed of, and the amount of money or the value of property received for each unit.

If the taxpayer cannot specifically identify the units as described above, the IRS deems crypto assets sold or exchanged to be disposed under the FIFO basis. Taxpayers are also required to maintain records that are sufficient to establish the positions taken on tax returns. Therefore, they should have records documenting receipts, sales, exchanges, or other dispositions of VC and the VC's FMV.

Miners

Mining is the process of adding transaction records to bitcoin's public ledger. Bitcoin mining is intentionally designed to be resource-intensive and difficult so that the number of blocks found on each day by miners remain steady. Individual blocks must contain a Proof of Work (PoW) to be considered valid. Mining operations use considerable energy and powerful computers to mine these coins. Mining is somewhat unique from other cryptocurrency-related transactions because mining is the process by which cryptocurrencies like bitcoin first come into circulation.

Miners must include in gross income the FMV of the tokens mined as of the date of receipt. For taxpayers who engage in mining as a trade or business as outlined by the IRS, the net income generated is subject to self-employment tax. Miners can deduct mining-related costs such as equipment, utilities, costs of noise insulation and electronic devices, allocable rent, and repairs on Schedule C. If someone is mining as a hobby, the income should be included on the taxpayer's tax returns, and the taxpayer is prohibited from deducting any expenses.

Although not clearly written in the guidance provided by the IRS, a reasonable assumption is that tokens mined are “inventory” in the case of a taxpayer who runs a mining operation that rises to the level of trade or business. In this instance, selling those tokens would generate ordinary income as opposed to capital gains or losses. Treating mined tokens as inventory is more aligned with the tax basis of accounting and should not be confused with the generally accepted accounting principles (GAAP) basis reporting. The tax basis of accounting is a less rigorous way of keeping books and records compared to GAAP, as it only focuses on cash receipts and outflows versus the full GAAP reporting structure. Since the IRS treats VCs as property and the mined coins in the hands of the hobbyist miner represents a capital asset, if taxpayers are mining as a hobby and when those tokens are subsequently sold, that would generate capital gains or losses.

Payer/Payee

Payees can use VCs as a method of payment. VCs paid by an employer to an employee or contractor should be included on Form W-2 and Form 1099-MISC, respectively. The amount to be reported on these forms is the annual aggregated FMVs of the VCs at the date of disbursements. Since the FMV of VCs relative to the US dollar is highly volatile, payers should keep accurate and complete records to support the FMV reported and deducted as an expense in the books.

Payees should include in gross income the FMV of VC received at the date of the receipt. Payees must report income even if they do not receive a Form 1099-MISC or Form W-2 from the payer. This situation may be a common given that many payers are unaware of VC reporting requirements.

Like Kind Exchange

Before the Tax Cuts and Jobs Act (TCJA), certain exchanges of property could be made without triggering a taxable event. According to IRS Notice 2014-21, VCs are classified as a property for tax purposes. By relying on this broad definition and §1031 of the IRS code allowing tax deferred property exchanges, some practitioners recommended like kind exchange treatment for cryptocurrencies. Many sophisticated, high-volume cryptocurrency investors, colloquially known as whales, took advantage of this aggressive strategy and deferred cryptocurrency gains to future years.

However, TCJA closed any possibility of this deferral by changing §1031, so that it is limited to real property. As a result, conversion of one cryptocurrency to another may result in taxable gains. In such cases, taxpayers may not have US dollars available to pay the tax bill.

Charitable Contributions of Virtual Currencies

VCs can be contributed to qualified charitable organizations and are eligible for charitable donation deduction. Since the IRS defines VCs as property, donations of VCs are subject to non-cash property donation rules. The amount to be deducted on Schedule A depends on how long the taxpayer has kept the asset. If the person donates a VC held for more than 12 months, the taxpayer gets a deduction equivalent to the FMV at the time of donation. If the person donates a VC held for less than 12 months, that person receives a deduction equivalent to the lesser of FMV at the date of donation or cost basis. In general, the taxpayer can deduct donations less than $500 on the tax return Form 8283. If the deduction exceeds $5,000, the donor must obtain a qualified appraisal from a qualified appraiser.

Airdrops and Forks

According to Revenue Rule 2019-24 (IRS 2019b, p. 2), “a hard fork is unique to distributed ledger technology and occurs when a cryptocurrency on a distributed ledger undergoes a protocol change resulting in a permanent diversion from the legacy or existing distributed ledger.” After a hard fork, the crypto holder ends up with a new token (forked coin) in addition to the original coin held. According to this revenue ruling, forked coins are taxable as ordinary income at the time the taxpayer receives them. The IRS calls this a “hard fork followed by an airdrop.” For example, taxpayer A holds 100 units of Crypto R, a cryptocurrency. On Date 2, the distributed ledger for Crypto R experiences a hard fork, resulting in the creation of Crypto S. On that date, 25 units of Crypto S are airdropped to A's distributed ledger address, and B has the ability to dispose of Crypto S immediately following the airdrop. Taxpayer A now holds 100 units of Crypto R and 25 units of Crypto S. The airdrop of Crypto S is recorded on the distributed ledger on Date 2 at Time 1 and, at that date and time, the FMV of A's 25 units of Crypto S is $50. Taxpayer B receives the Crypto S solely because B owns Crypto R at the time of the hard fork. After the airdrop, transactions involving Crypto S are recorded on the new distributed ledger and transactions involving Crypto R continue to be recorded on the legacy distributed ledger. In this instance, taxpayer A would recognize $1,250 of ordinary income.

Schedule 1: “Virtual Currency” Question

The latest regulatory development around the crypto tax compliance is the introduction of an informational question on IRS Form 1040, Schedule 1. The draft 2019 Schedule 1 Form released in December 2019 first introduced this informational question. This question asks, “At any time during 2019, did you receive, sell, send, exchange, or otherwise acquire any financial interest in any virtual currency?” This broad question can be called the “VC question.” By including this type of question, VC tax compliance once a niche subject is headed mainstream. As a result, both taxpayers and tax practitioners must know how to properly address this question going forward.

If somebody even remotely deals with VCs in some capacity, that person is likely to check “yes” on the question on Schedule 1. This question will also capture both taxable and non-taxable transactions involving VCs. For example, even if a taxpayer purchased cryptocurrencies during 2019 and held them on his or her wallet, the taxpayer has to check “yes” on this question because he acquired a “financial interest” in VC. Furthermore, the VC question is similar to the foreign financial bank account question on Schedule B that asks

At any time during 2019, did you have a financial interest in or signature authority over a financial account (such as a bank account, securities account, or brokerage account) located in a foreign country?

According to Michael Desmond, the IRS chief counsel, the IRS has seen much success with Schedule B question and hopes to see the same results by adding the VC question on Schedule 1.

In summary, this section has provided some of the general guidance issued by the IRS to regulate VC transactions. This guidance provides a general framework for taxpayers. However, the guidelines largely fail when addressing sophisticated transactions and dealing with intricacies in the blockchain technology.

Regulatory Ambiguities

This section outlines some regulatory ambiguities and inconsistencies that continue to exist within the regulatory framework.

2019 Virtual Currency Guidance May Not Be Binding

According to the US Government Accountability Office (GAO) (2020), the 2019 FAQs issued by the IRS are not binding and could be subject to change. The GAO is an independent, nonpartisan agency that works for Congress. On February 12, 2020, the GAO published “Virtual Currencies: Additional Information Reporting and Clarified Guidance Could Improve Tax Compliance (GAO-20-188)” report after analyzing the IRS's efforts in the crypto tax compliance space. The GAO reviewed IRS forms and interviewed various stakeholders such as IRS officials, FinCen, other federal agencies, tax practitioners, and crypto exchanges to produce this report.

According to the IRS, its authoritative interpretation of tax law should be published through Internal Revenue Bulletins (IRBs). For example, on April 14, 2014, the Notice 2014-21 was featured on IRB 2014-16. On October 9, 2019, the IRS published FAQs on its website further explaining the original cryptocurrency guidance ‒ the IRS Notice 2014-21. Since an IRB did not feature the 2019 FAQs, the GAO maintains that the 2019 FAQs may not be binding on the IRS. Also, the IRS has changed 2019 crypto tax guidance several times without alerts or public disclosure. For example, the IRS added two extra questions and answers to the original 43 FAQs during December 2019 without announcing anywhere. More recently, the IRS abruptly removed gaming tokens such as Robux and V-bucks from the explanation of “What is virtual currency?”

Furthermore, the IRS did not add any disclaimer on the page indicating that the FAQs are non-authoritative guidance and subject to change. Changing information without alerting taxpayers is also a violation of the first article in IRS's Taxpayer Bill of Rights ‒ “The Right to Be Informed.” According to the GAO (U.S. Government Accountability Office 2020, p. 21), “If taxpayers make decisions based on guidance that is non-authoritative, including FAQs, those taxpayers' confidence in IRS and the tax system could be undermined if the content is later updated and IRS challenges taxpayers' positions.” Thus, issuing guidance that does not comply with the IRS's own guidelines and making changes without notifying taxpayers have caused confusion among stakeholders in the crypto space.

Are Frequently Asked Questions Applied Retroactively or as of the Date of Issuance?

Both taxpayers and practitioners have asked whether FAQs issued on October 9, 2019 are applicable retroactively or only going forward. The IRS has not provided any direct answer to this question. According to Michael Desmond, the IRS chief counsel, the new guidance merely elaborated on the original Notice 2014-21 (CoinTracker 2020). He views these new rules as being active since 2014. This interpretation presents some challenges to taxpayers who decided not to recognize any income for forks based on a “lack of guidance” premise before the issuance of Revenue Rule 2019-24 on October 9, 2019. For example, during August 2017, the bitcoin network faced a hard fork and everyone holding bitcoins received an equivalent amount of bitcoin cash. The receipt of bitcoin cash would have been ordinary income to the taxpayer per guidance issued on October 9, 2019. However, when the fork happened, taxpayers did not have any guidance on how to report the value of bitcoin cash on the tax returns. IRS officials have failed to comment on whether those taxpayers should amend their tax returns.

Hard Forks and Airdrops

Proposed taxation on forks and airdrops do not align with the industry practices. First, the IRS has apparently misunderstood these terms. Although the IRS views an airdrop as event that is followed by a hard fork, this is not the case. An airdrop is a distribution of a cryptocurrency token or coin, usually for free, to numerous wallet addresses for marketing purposes. In practice, an airdrop and a hard fork are two mutually exclusive events and are hence unrelated. Therefore, the examples provided in Revenue Rule. 2019-24 could be misleading.

Furthermore, examples mentioned on the revenue ruling assume that the value of the new coin received after a hard fork is easily attainable. Again, this situation is not the case in practice. Once a blockchain goes through a hard fork, the resulting new coin minted may not have an immediate value in the market. One could argue that at the time of receiving these new assets, the FMV is zero because no liquid market exists for these newly minted coins at the time of receipt. The revenue ruling does not instruct taxpayers how to deal with these practical matters.

Interpreting Third-party Information Reporting Standards

Currently, no uniform information reporting requirements are available for US-based cryptocurrency exchanges. Because existing laws are ambiguous, stakeholders interpret laws in different ways. Exchanges that believe they are third-party payment settlement networks issue Form 1099-Ks to users who have more than 200 transactions and $20,000 gross proceeds in a tax year. Some exchanges issue Form 1099-Bs believing they are barter exchanges. Other exchanges issue Form 1099-MISC while a few do not report anything to the IRS or taxpayers. Table 15.2 shows how nine major US cryptocurrency exchanges are handling third-party information reporting.

Table 15.2. How Nine Major US Cryptocurrency Exchanges Deal with Third-party Information Reporting.

Number of Exchanges Findings
2 Issue Form 1099-Ks for some taxpayers
1 Issue Form 1099-Bs
1 Issue Form 1099s (Does not specify the exact form)
3 Website states nothing will be reported
2 No information on third-party information reporting on the website

Note: This table reports the results of a GAO survey on how nine major US cryptocurrency exchanges are handling third-party information reporting.

According to IRS officials, VC exchanges may be subject to the 1099-K reporting requirement if they fall into the legal category of “third party settlement organizations.” Exchanges are subject to the 1099-B requirement only if they are brokers or barter exchanges. The IRS does not have an official position on whether VC exchanges are required to report customers' trading activity on Form 1099-B. Ambiguity may also exist regarding when, if at all, Form 1099-MISC (U.S. Government Accountability Office 2020) requires reporting on VC sales.

Foreign Reporting Guidance Is Unclear from the Internal Revenue Service and Financial Crimes Enforcement Network

The IRS and FinCen have not issued any direct guidance on whether VCs held in offshore locations are subject to the Foreign Account Tax Compliance Act (FATCA) and Report of Foreign Bank and Financial Accounts (FBAR). As the GAO reports, IRS officials have not issued guidance about VC and FATCA because the instructions for Form 8938 clearly explain how taxpayers are to interpret FATCA requirements. However, those instructions do not mention anything about VCs or provide directions needed to determine whether VC holdings must be reported. For example, the instructions state that a financial account is any depository or custodial account maintained by a foreign financial institution, but do not explain under what circumstances, if any, an account that holds VC could be considered a depository or custodial account.

Generally, taxpayers must also report foreign non-account assets held for investment as opposed to held for use in a trade or business, such as foreign stock and securities, foreign financial instruments, contracts with non-US persons, and interests in foreign entities. According to the IRS, VCs held in offshore locations may be reportable non-account assets depending on facts and circumstance of each case. Not having a clearly defined rule is extremely frustrating for taxpayers. Unsophisticated taxpayers may neither know nor have the resources to apply “facts and circumstances” legal test to determine whether the holdings are reportable.

Concerning foreign reporting, Foreign Bank Account Report (FBAR) is another type of requirement taxpayer must follow. Generally, a taxpayer must file FinCen Form 114 if he or she has more than $10,000 in any foreign financial accounts during the tax year. According to FinCen officials, FBAR reporting is not required for VCs because the FBAR regulations do not define a VC held in offshore accounts as a type of a reportable account. Although FinCEN has provided responses to direct questions regarding this matter, it has not made that information readily available for the public by posting on their website (U.S. Government Accountability Office 2020).

Staking Reward Taxation

Proof of Stake (PoS) is a relatively new concept that has steadily been gaining popularity in the crypto community as a better alternative to a Proof of Work (PoW) system on which the most popular cryptocurrency, namely bitcoin, operates. Technically speaking, PoS provides those with a stake of network tokens the right to earn rewards for validating blocks. In simple terms, staking is similar to having an interest-bearing bank savings account. Dash, Neo, OKcash, and Tezos are some cryptocurrencies someone can stake. How staking works is simple. Someone can leave these coins in his or her wallet and/or an exchange that supports staking and receive periodic payouts based on the amount of funds that are staked. Clearly, staking rewards are taxable. However, the exact tax treatment for staking rewards is unclear (Sutherland 2019). This area is one where no regulator has issued guidance. To the general public, staking rewards resemble interest income because the process is similar to depositing funds into a bank account and receiving interest based on an annual interest rate. The higher the deposit, the more interest income is earned. Applying this logic, staking rewards look similar to interest income, which is generally reported on IRS Form Schedule B Part I.

Understanding how the Internal Revenue Code (IRC) defines “interest income” is important to determine if staking rewards are actually interest income for tax purposes. According to 26 CFR §1.61-7 (Internal Revenue Service 1966),

Interest income includes interest on savings or other bank deposits; interest on coupon bonds; interest on an open account, a promissory note, a mortgage, or a corporate bond or debenture; the interest portion of a condemnation award; usurious interest (unless by State law it is automatically converted to a payment on the principal); interest on legacies; interest on life insurance proceeds held under an agreement to pay interest thereon; and interest on refunds of Federal taxes.

Clearly this definition of “interest income” does not have anything that even remotely resembles income derived from staking cryptocurrencies.

In addition, per Deputy v. Du Pont, 308 US 488 (U.S. Supreme Court 1940, p. 1), “Interest in its usual import is the amount which one has contracted to pay for the use of borrowed money. In the business world, interest in indebtedness means compensation for the use or forbearance of money.” Now, the key here is that the interest is derived from having money as principal. Are the coins staked treated as “money” for tax purposes? Not really. According to Notice 2014-21 (Internal Revenue Service 2014), cryptocurrencies are treated as property. Therefore, one view is that staking rewards are not interest income for tax purposes although they may share many characteristics of interest income in the real world.

According to 26 CFR § 1.61-8 (Internal Revenue Service 2004), “gross income includes rentals received or accrued for the occupancy of real estate or the use of personal property.” Personal property is any property that is not real property like land and building. According to Notice 2014-21 (Internal Revenue Service 2014), VCs are treated as property, and all general rules applicable to property apply to VCs. By viewing cryptocurrencies being staked as “property,” someone could contend that the holder is renting a property and receiving rental income. Income received from renting an asset or property is clearly not interest income. If this is the case, staking rewards could constitute rental income and may also be subject to passive/non-passive income categories depending on one's level of participation in the staking ecosystem. Taxpayers typically report rental income on Schedule E of Form 1040.

Thus far, all IRS communications related to cryptocurrency taxation have been “general guidance” including Notice 2014-21, 45 FAQs, and Rev. Rul. 2019-24, not tax law. The guidance describes how the IRS believes existing tax laws are applied to VC transactions. They are intended to help taxpayers with tax filings and improve compliance. Since these guidelines are not law, someone can argue against certain positions taken by the IRS in a court of law. Again, the taxpayers are left with interpreting general guidance and doing the best they can until the IRS issues more solid guidance.

Schedule 1: Virtual Currency Question

The IRS included the VC question on 2019 Schedule 1 to get more visibility into US cryptocurrency holders. This question asks, “At any time during 2019, did you receive, sell, send, exchange, or otherwise acquire any financial interest in any virtual currency?” This question is broad. Unfortunately, the IRS has not explained what transactions to include in each category (i.e., receive, sell, send, exchange, and financial interest). In the absence of any bright line rules, a category like “financial interest” could be interpreted in different ways. One could argue that if a taxpayer owns an interest in a pass-through entity where a VC mining operation is conducted, that taxpayer would have an indirect “financial interest” in VCs and be required to check “yes” for the question. On the other hand, one could argue that the affiliation of VCs through a passthrough entity is too remote to establish a “financial interest” for the purposes of this question.

Furthermore, some taxpayers are concerned with answering this question and getting unwanted attention from the IRS. Several situations exist where taxpayers would check “yes” for the VC question and not report anything on the tax return because no reportable transactions took place in the current year. This situation would occur if a taxpayer transferred funds between accounts owned, purchased VCs, received a gift, or sent a gift. For instance, if a taxpayer received a considerable gift in VCs, that person would have to check “yes” on the VC question. However, this transaction would not be reported on any forms. Some taxpayers wonder if this situation would raise a red flag and receive unwanted attention from the IRS.

Taxation Related to Capital Formation Is Nonexistent

Blockchain technology introduced new ways of raising capital for startups. It started with initial coin offerings (ICOs) and later developed into security token offerings (STOs) and initial exchange offerings (IEOs). These token offerings have been subject to much scrutiny from the SEC. The SEC believes that majority of the token offerings are security offerings and should be registered with the SEC or applied for an exemption.

The IRS has not addressed taxation of these offerings. The existing “property” tax rules do not generate any sensible outcomes in many scenarios related to capital formation. For example, if an entity raises 10,000 bitcoins (BTCs) through an ICO, it has to recognize income equivalent to FMV of those BTCs at the time of the receipt. Assuming the entity is a corporation, this initial capital injection would also be taxed at the corporate level. This approach is not sensible because if an entity were to raise $10,000 from investors, those funds would not be treated as income and have no tax impact. Another ambiguous situation occurs when a startup releases a new VC to the market with some value attached to it. Since the startup created this token, would the token have a zero basis? Or is the token's basis the research and development cost spent until the date of release? Although the IRS does not answer these questions, stakeholders are expected to find solutions.

Why Crypto Tax Compliance Is so Low?

An eventful year for cryptocurrency taxation was 2019. After five years from the issuance of the original crypto guidance in 2014 (IRS Notice 2014-21), the IRS instituted several initiatives to police crypto tax compliance.

  • August 2019: The IRS sent out tax notices (Letter 6173, Letter 6174, and Letter 6174-A) to 10,000 taxpayers with cryptocurrency transactions.
  • October 9, 2019: The IRS issued 43 Q & As elaborating on the originally issued Notice 2014-21. It also issued Revenue Ruling 2019-24 addressing forks and airdrops.
  • October 10, 2019: The IRS released a draft 2019 Schedule 1, which asks taxpayers, “At any time during 2019, did you receive, sell, exchange, otherwise hold any financial interest in any virtual currency?”

The above initiatives are in place because of extremely poor compliance rates. According to Michael Desomnd, the IRS chief counsel, the IRS receives about 150 million tax returns annually. Various sources report that between 7% and 11% of adults in the United States have some sort of economic affiliation with VCs. This means that the IRS should receive roughly 12 million tax returns with some sort of cryptocurrency transactions. However, the amount of returns received with such transactions is far lower. As a matter of fact, because of this high degree of non-compliance, the IRS's immediate goal is not to achieve perfect compliance or develop more detailed guidance, but to move taxpayers from reporting absolutely nothing to report something on tax returns. Poor compliance is primarily because of three reasons: (1) poor to no information reporting, (2) reconciliation burden, and (3) crypto holders' ideology coupled with a lack of education.

Poor to No Information Reporting

Third-party information reporting directly enhances taxpayer compliance. For example, under the current information reporting regime, a copy of Form 1099-B (Proceeds From Broker and Barter Exchange Transactions) prepared by a brokerage service goes to the IRS and the taxpayer. If the taxpayer does not report what is reported on Form 1099-B, the agency generates an automatic CP2000 notice to rectify the omission. This so-called matching mechanism also works as a great deterrence and encourages taxpayers to report accurate amounts.

Interestingly, under the current interpretation of the law, cryptocurrency exchanges are not required to issue Form 1099-Bs to their users. This situation is because most of the exchanges are not registered as brokerages under the US laws and dealing with “stocks and securities.” Currently, they treat themselves as third-party payments settlement organizations. As a result, they are only required to produce Form 1099-Ks if the user exceeds $20,000 in transaction amount and has more than 200 transactions in a calendar year. Taxpayers who meet these criteria are far fewer than the actual number of crypto holders in the United States. Those who do not receive a Form 1099-K believe that they do not have any tax reporting obligation.

Reconciliation Burden

Being compliant is also not easy for those who receive Form 1099-Ks. This form only reports the gross proceeds and does not provide any meaningful numbers to the taxpayers to prepare their tax returns. The burden of tracking the cost basis of crypto assets, determining the holding period (short-term vs. long-term), identifying the proper disposition method (e.g., FIFO, last in, first out (LIFO), and highest in, first out), and valuing crypto to crypto trades fall with the taxpayer. An unsophisticated taxpayer is likely to ignore reporting these transactions merely because of the administrative burden and compliance cost. Even for the seasoned tax practitioners, because of the technological nature of crypto transactions, calculating gains and losses for tax purposes manually is virtually impossible in many cases.

One may think that the potential solution is to mandate crypto exchanges to issue Form 1099-Bs like traditional brokerages. However, this solution is an impossible task in the crypto world. Typically, a crypto exchange only has access to cost basis information for the transactions occurring in its exchange. For example, if a taxpayer transfers coins from another exchange and/or an offline wallet, the reporting exchange lacks any data on the US dollar cost basis of those transferred coins. Furthermore, some foreign exchanges do not even collect taxpayer information or keep good transaction data useful for US tax purposes. These exchanges do not participate in any type of tax reporting.

Fortunately, this problem has a solution. With third-party data aggregator tools like CoinTracker.io, taxpayers can link multiple exchanges and wallets to a CoinTracker.io account. The software reconciles all the transactions and generates a taxpayer friendly capital gain/loss report to be included in the tax return. Since the traditional matching mechanism is not functional in the crypto space, such software is essential to calculate cryptocurrency gains and losses for taxpayers, tax practitioners, and the IRS.

Ideology

Besides poor information reporting and reconciliation burden, liberal ideologies of crypto users lead to much intentional non-compliance. Cryptocurrencies run on blockchain technology, which is based on the premise of decentralization. In a decentralized world, no central authorities exist such as banks, tax collectors, and governments. Therefore, strong crypto enthusiasts are against paying taxes on cryptocurrency trading gains. Furthermore, technologies such as blockchain and cryptocurrencies are often incorrectly associated with 100% anonymity. By relying on this premise, many strong crypto users believe that the IRS cannot find them.

Summary and Conclusions

The VC space has grown dramatically since the inception of bitcoin in 2009. The current IRS guidance lacks specificity to address intricacies of this emerging world. The IRS treats all cryptocurrencies as “property” based on IRS Notice 2014-21. Although this classification is helpful, it is too generic and subject to interpretation. As a result, taxpayers, cryptocurrency exchanges, practitioners, and other stakeholders are expected to presume reasonable rules applicable to cryptocurrency related economic events.

Discussion Questions

(1)Discuss whether the treatment for cryptocurrencies is consistent among various US regulators.

(2)Explain how cryptocurrencies are taxed in the United States.

(3)Discuss how staking rewards should be taxed.

(4)Indicate how the IRS is trying to increase cryptocurrency tax compliance.

Part IV
Blockchain Applications in Business

Chapter 16

Considerations for Blockchain Adoption and Integration

Michael Nizich and Michael Campisi

Keywords: Blockchain; system development life cycle; blockchain implementation; blockchain cost of ownership; blockchain life cycle; blockchain maintenance; implementation costs; implementation risks; life cycle approach

Introduction

Previous chapters included discussions of the functionality of blockchain technology and its benefits to an organization under several different circumstances in concept. They also discussed how this desirability is based on specific attributes and characteristics that make the technology highly beneficial in some cases. These attributes include the fact that the technology is decentralized, synchronized, traceable, immutable, secure, scalable, collaborative, auditable, and programmable.

In broader terms, the data can be stored outside of the organization's internal network; it can easily accept new nodes and changes to the data can be traced back to the original authors. In addition, once the data are written, they cannot be changed and are highly encrypted for security purposes, the validity of the record must be agreed upon by all parties, and those transactions are each digitally signed. Finally, the entire system is customizable to the methods or processes of how the organization does business for each type of transaction.

Although these attributes make implementing blockchain technology desirable, they are also what make the implementation complex, which necessitates careful considerations and planning during implementation into an organization. An under-planned or rushed implementation of a blockchain solution into an organization can result in unnecessary consulting fees and a damaged or unusable legacy database management system. Even worse, it can cripple an organization by limiting access to its historical data and/or to its new blockchain data because of a faulty and flawed implementation.

This chapter discusses various topics involved with integrating blockchain technology into an organization and the challenges faced when starting the process. It introduces such topics as estimating implementation costs, attracting and retaining qualified people, selecting a blockchain network model, evaluating an organization's capabilities, identifying risks of blockchain implementation, and maintaining the blockchain. In addition, this chapter discusses an organization's total cost of ownership (TCO), decision metrics, and other considerations during the implementation life cycle.

Preparing for Blockchain Implementation

When implementing a new system, management should consider various technical and non-technical factors to ensure the successful implementation of that system and integration with other existing systems. The next section discusses these technical and non-technical challenges that an organization may face during blockchain implementation.

Blockchain Technology Background

Before discussing various considerations for blockchain adoption and implementation, reiterating several points mentioned in previous chapters helps to provide a foundation for discussing the key attributes of a complete blockchain system. A blockchain application is a peer-to-peer (P2P) system for validating, time stamping, and permanently storing transactions and agreements on a shared ledger that is distributed to all participating nodes (Nakamoto 2008).

The initial intent of blockchain was to serve as a technology to drive and support cryptocurrencies based on fundamental principles stemming from cryptographic theory, P2P networking, and game theory. In addition, blockchain is essentially a technology that enables a decentralized exchange of data and is considered a distributed ledger of an evolving and expanding list of timestamped and encrypted transaction records organized in blocks, with each block being linked to a previous block, forming a chain (Christidis and Devetsikiotis 2016).

A blockchain is a distributed database that is not owned, controlled, or managed by a central authority (Barker, Smid, Branstad, and Chokhani 2013). It is also a distributed database that exists on a P2P network (Koteska, Karafiloski, and Mishev 2017) where the copies are held by multiple independent parties, or nodes, and are kept synchronized; where new records are validated and added using consensus; where each record, or block, is strongly linked to the prior one, forming a strong chain of records; thus ensuring that records cannot be altered or removed.

Many new platforms and use cases for blockchain technology have been proposed (Challener, Vachino, Howard II, Pikas, and Anil 2019). This situation requires carefully and systematically considering the different factors that an organization needs to address before adopting and implementing blockchain.

Several features and attributes of blockchain make it attractive for various organizational solutions. However, they need to be discussed and approached with caution during implementation planning since each requires special technological considerations for that component to function properly. Omitting any of these considerations could cause a faulty blockchain implementation, create security vulnerabilities, render the blockchain inoperable and valueless to the company, and ultimately create organizational losses that in some cases may be unrecoverable.

Listed below are some of these features and attributes. Blockchain:

  • is digital and made up of software (coding including algorithms) and data;
  • involves a ledger and a record in the form of a database representing transactions;
  • holds distributed and identical copies of the distributed ledger across a network of computers, also known as nodes;
  • uses a consensus model or a set of rules for how each participant in a blockchain should process transactions and how those transactions should accept or reject the processing done by other participants; and
  • incorporates cryptography deploying public key infrastructure to verify that a message comes from the purported sender and to authenticate the contents of the message (Hoser 2016).

Adopters need to discuss and consider these factors and attributes of blockchain technology during the implementation phase of the blockchain design because each requires different decisions and actions to enable the functionality property in a blockchain system. These factors and attributes are discussed in more detail later when addressing the various activities in each section of the blockchain life cycle.

Identifying the True Purpose for Implementing Blockchain

Any new system implementation usually starts with identifying a need that requires addressing. The same holds true for blockchain implementations. Identifying the real purpose of the decision to implement a blockchain solution is essential. Is the decision based on requirements by industry regulatory agencies? Is it driven by a desire to be competitive in an organization's market space? Or is the decision simply to prepare an organization for a world that is likely to be run on a blockchain system and the organization wants to be an early mover?

Regardless of the reason to move to a blockchain solution, an organization needs to be prepared to implement a solution to meet some specific goal. If the goal is to meet regulatory requirements, it must establish what the requirements are, how others are meeting those requirements now given that blockchain is still a new and emerging technology (American Council for Technology-Industry Advisory Council 2019), and whether the solution be accepted for meeting these requirements. If an organization's goal is to raise its competitive stance within its industry, then it must establish how the blockchain solution is likely to differentiate the organization from its competition and more importantly how it will market the solution to make those differentiations known. Finally, if implementing a blockchain solution is to prepare an organization for the future, it needs to determine which commercial solution is best to become the future market leader.

Regardless of the reason and purpose for an organization's decision to move to a blockchain solution, it needs to accept that changes will occur. During a blockchain implementation, nearly every area of the six-component framework ‒ hardware, software, people, procedures, data, and networks ‒ will change. Is the organization ready to do this?

Identifying the Real Cost of Implementing Blockchain

As with any project implementation, cost is always a factor that governs whether a project gets completed on time, as specified, or at all. The many direct and indirect costs of implementing a blockchain solution can be overwhelming to some organizations that are unprepared to expend the real cost of a blockchain solution. Before discussing these direct and indirect costs associated with implementing blockchain, keep in mind that many blockchain frameworks are open source and free of purchase and download costs. When deciding between private and public blockchains for a project, the costs are often for developers and management personnel to create and maintain a network. In addition, blockchain use involves a cost, which is a drawback of decentralization and the blockchain technology. The users must pay for the transactions and computational power. One reason that users choose centralized solutions is because they are not constantly reminded that an action has a fee (Pedersen, Asger, Risius Marten, and Beck 2019).

An organization should consider several specific costs to assure a successful implementation. Any oversight of these costs could spell trouble for the implementation team as it may need to need further funding, which can cause delays and potentially a lower quality implementation. These costs involve hardware, software, data conversion, and programming costs, adapting internal procedures and processes, and recruiting and retaining quality personnel.

Hardware Costs

As with other technologies once implemented, blockchain needs to keep running at peak efficiency with as little down time as possible. Like other database solutions such as a Microsoft SQL Server, Oracle, or IBM, it needs to be fast, powerful, and include redundancies to keep the servers working at peak performance. Similar to other systems, blockchain needs regular maintenance to the various nodes of the system to assure they are operating properly including full utilization of their processors, memory and network interface cards since each of these components can affect how a blockchain performs and the time involved in validating the transactions that get added to a block for permanent immutable storage.

These costs can be in the form of hardware purchases and upgrades but also firmware updates for the specific hardware in question. These types of specialized maintenance need require costly information technology (IT) professionals who can perform the operations with the least amount of down time and disruption to the business.

Software Costs

Decisions on blockchain software can be daunting and can make or break a blockchain implementation. If an organization chooses a platform with known limitations because of faulty preparation, it may face costly upgrades and complex data conversions from one vendor to another.

When selecting a software platform for a blockchain project, a firm has several choices and selecting a platform is only part of the challenge. The initial cost, TCO, and personnel costs to maintain the blockchain all a play a role in the decision. Table 16.1 lists popular blockchain technology software platforms and frameworks that have emerged as major players in the field.

Data Conversion and Programming Costs

A blockchain solution for an industry usually includes a smart contract that contains the details of a specific transaction between two entities and provides the various attributes and benefits of security and immutability discussed earlier in this chapter. In a private blockchain, these transactions are stored centrally and verified by internally controlled miners who validate each transaction and smart contract. A public blockchain connects to a larger public network of distributed nodes and public miners validate anything added to the blockchain. Several factors are important to consider in each scenario.

First, the developers and personnel who are knowledgeable enough to manage and operate the blockchain system are the biggest costs. Attracting and maintaining talented and skilled personnel to keep a network running is a key to success. Like any system, updates, connection issues, and system crashes need to be addressed by capable individuals who are often difficult to find.

Second, a firm's sensitive and extremely valuable data may be moving from a proven database management system such as a SQL Server or Oracle to an open source, potentially public, fairly new, and in some cases unproven technology. The potential costs for high-end consultants to maintain and repair the system if damaged and even attempt to recover lost or damaged data like a current relational database management system system could be high.

Adapting Internal Procedures and Processes

In all information system implementations, processes or procedures are available to manage the data being entered into and retrieved from the system. These processes can be anything from how a user accesses a system to how it formats certain reports in the system. In the case of blockchain implementation, the user needs to establish what processes are being changed because of the new system and how these changes are going to affect the organization's overall performance in meeting its goals.

As an example, assume that a user is accustomed to accessing data from its Oracle enterprise resource planning (ERP) system to verify individual banking transactions, but now must access a blockchain database to access the same information. How does that affect the performance of the employee and the organization? What happens if the current system does not speak to the blockchain? What are the direct and indirect costs in loss of employee performance if these processes are not addressed?

Attracting and Retaining Qualified People

A blockchain implementation is only going to be as good as the people secured to build, configure, and maintain the system. Blockchain is still a new and emerging technology for non-cryptocurrency operations. As most blockchain frameworks are open source, an organization needs a team of experienced developers to design and launch its network as well as to maintain it once the user begins depending on it for business operations.

Selecting a Blockchain Network Model

Regarding networks within a blockchain application, the discussion changes a bit based on whether the user has chosen an open (public) solution or a closed (private) solution. In a public blockchain solution, the ledger is available to the public and shared or replicated on possibly thousands of distributed nodes that can be updated and accessed. This approach reduces the demand for a single high-performance network in an organization, but it places the data in a public ledger and ultimately at risk of attack attempts.

If an organization selects a closed (private) blockchain solution, then it should consider both the need for a high performance server and network for fast access and processing and series of nodes that can perform proof of work (PoW) operations to secure the blocks in the database. This option can increase control and security of the blockchain but be expensive.

Evaluating Organizational Capabilities

For a blockchain implementation to be successful and meet its organizational goals, the organization must have the necessary technical and organizational abilities to make it happen. An organization must identify key internal and external resources that it needs both during and after implementation. The following section discusses a few of the organizational capabilities that should be considered before committing to a blockchain implementation.

Technical and Organizational Capability

An organization must identify that it has skilled personnel with blockchain experience on staff to guide the implementation. Has the organization secured enough contractors with high-level blockchain experience to manage the blockchain network and to design the smart contracts? Does the organization have access to willing and vetted partners who can mine the data for a public blockchain? If the organization decides on a private blockchain, does it have the resources available to internally mine the data to create a secure, immutable environment offering a trusted network and dataset?

Personnel Qualifications

During implementation, an organization needs access to a team of professionals who are both loyal to the organization and highly skilled specifically in blockchain implementation. Below is a practical example.

An organization decides to make its corporate offerings more attractive to a larger number of potential customers. Therefore, it wants to move its online financial transfer data over to a blockchain solution, so it can tout the high level of security in a marketplace of less secure solutions in an otherwise high risk world. In this situation, the organization needs to decide on a public or private blockchain design, establish an information technology storage and processing solution that is highly dependable, select a blockchain technology platform, and create the coding required to establish the smart contracts that identify how to create the transactions. Next, the organization needs to establish the encryption methods and levels to secure the blockchain. These requirements are usually unachievable by the average IT staff because they require highly skilled staff specifically in blockchain technologies.

This example demonstrates the severity and importance of being prepared to implement the blockchain solution as a faulty or poorly planned execution could cripple an organization by making its data invalid, inaccessible, or available to the public. Making sure the organization has the staff in place to get things right the first time and keep them right once in a maintenance mode is imperative.

Implementation Risks

An organization faces many risks during a blockchain implementation. If it decides to move forward with a blockchain solution, then the benefits should outweigh the risks of the implementation. These risks usually related to the type of blockchain implementation. For example, assume than an organization decides to implement a public blockchain solution to establish a supply chain feature that guarantees an immutable record of when supplies reach a certain part of the supply chain. It also uses blockchain as a marketing tool to attract new customers. In this situation, the risk to the organization is fairly low because it likely has another system that tracks inventory and supply chain management running in parallel to the new system.

However, if an organization decides to move its official financial transaction data to a public blockchain to allow reducing its workforce and giving a new global workforce access to its financial records, then the risks to the organization increase. An organization making this decision is likely to experience risk not only involving customer satisfaction, acceptance, and confidence but also in the technical performance of the blockchain and the overall security of the public blockchain because of acts by cyber criminals.

Total Cost of Ownership

With any new system, an initial cost of implementation occurs usually includes software licenses, hardware and networking purchases, installation services, data conversion, and user training. These items are required to get any new system installed and running properly as well as to have users using the system daily. These initial fees and costs exclude the ongoing fees required to keep the system running over time.

TCO usually refers to the annual costs of operation include hardware, networking, and software maintenance, data issues, adjustments, and upgrades, and enhancements over a five-year period. For example, if a system costs $100,000 to install initially and it costs $20,000 annually, then the five-year TCO is $200,000. Usually an organization incurs annual operating costs of about 20% of the total initial purchase cost. It should have a plan to pay these costs or run the risk of being unable to maintain the system over a designated period.

Because of its complexity, newness, and exploratory nature for some organizations, the initial and ongoing cost of blockchain can be substantial. Many blockchain experts charge $500 an hour and often move between jobs, which makes securing such individuals over the long term difficult. An organization may face a minimum installation cost of $1 million for a basic blockchain system to replace a key operational system and a five-year TCO of between $2 and $3 million to operate, repair, upgrade, and enhance that system during that period.

If the organization selects a public blockchain solution, then fees are associated with the number of transactions, transaction sizes, number of nodes, and consensus protocol being used. These costs add up on top of any of personnel and support contracts needed to assure the blockchain's functionality. By comparison, a company installing a new SQL Server database, converting all of its data from Oracle to SQL Server, and then keeping that SQL Server running for five years needs the initial Microsoft licenses, servers, and consultants to install and convert the data. It also needs to hire a database administrator to manage that database over the next five years.

Decision Metrics

As with any new system, a company decides on obtaining that system because it is experiencing a loss or deficiency in some area of its business it deems unsustainable. Thus, a new technology could solve this problem. These systems could eliminate cumbersome paper-based manual processes or allow remote access to organizational data from outside the office. In either case, company analysts should be able to estimate whether the system is acceptable over a specific time horizon.

Organizations have many ways to measure a project's attractiveness such as accounting-based return on investment. It could use other techniques to make this decision such as the payback period, discounted payback period, net present value, internal rate of return, and modified internal rate of return depending on its level of sophistication. The key point is that the organization wants the expected benefits of the blockchain system to exceed its predicted costs.

Maintaining the Blockchain

So far this chapter has discussed the costs of blockchain implementation, risks of implementation, and system's TCO, and also identified decision metrics. Some of these topics directly related to the blockchain's ongoing maintenance after completing the initial implementation. Assume that a company has invested $1 million on a blockchain solution to replace the financial transaction ledger portion of its ERP system. Now, the company's staff, vendors, and other stakeholders depend on that new form of data for the company's operation. Also assume that the company has not budgeted and prepared for the ongoing maintenance costs to keep the system running and to keep the data in the system accurate, secure, and immutable. This lack of preparation could put the company at great risk and would be unacceptable to its stakeholders. It could also potentially lead to system failure and returning to the original system.

In the case of a blockchain implementation, an organization needs to plan for the new system's maintenance for a period of five years. Such plans should focus on maintaining the hardware, software, and data as well as training new users and consultants, upgrading the system, providing smart contract programming, and ensuring the availability of talented personnel to manage the blockchain when problems arise.

Challenges and Considerations to Blockchain Implementation

Before implementing blockchain, a company's management needs to understand the challenges it may face. Given that blockchain technology is still in its testing phase, its implementation has some issues that must be addressed when trying to establish an efficient, secure, and ultimately organizationally beneficial system. This section discusses several areas that management should address during the implementation process. These areas include identifying the purpose of the blockchain project, the project's technological challenges, its initial cost, and the organization's technical ability to achieve a successful implementation. Other areas involve the personnel requirements of operating a blockchain network, risks of implementation, TCO of running the blockchain solution, decision metrics, and the organization's ability to maintain and enhance the blockchain over time.

Technological Challenges

An organization is likely to face specific technology challenges during blockchain's implementation phase (Koteska et al. 2017). These challenges include performance issues with blockchain technology such as throughput, latency, size and bandwidth, scalability, security, and authentication. Each challenge is discussed below.

System Throughput Challenges

Blockchain solutions can process from 3 to 20 transactions per second (tps) (Xu, Chen, and Kou 2019) with a maximum possible theoretical throughput of seven tps. In comparison, a VISA transaction network can process 2000 tps and can handle up to 47,000 tps (Trillo 2013). When adopting and implementing a blockchain solution, an organization must be prepared for a limit on the tps that the system can maintain.

System Latency Challenges

The latency factor, which refers to the speed that blockchain processes transactions, is an obstacle to its universal acceptance (Rossi, Mueller-Bloch, Thatcher, and Beck 2019). To provide security, the time needed to complete one transaction can be up to 10 minutes. For larger transfer amounts, the cost of a double spend attack can last about an hour. A double-spend attack is a problem unique to digital currencies in which one user can spend the same digital asset more than once. In comparison, a VISA transaction completion process takes seconds at most (Swan 2015; Yli-Huumo, Ko, Choi, Park, and Smolander 2016). When adopting and implementing a blockchain solution, an organization must consider this time factor when deciding on what critical operations for which to use the blockchain solution.

Data Size and System Bandwidth Challenges

Because of the various attributes of blockchain technology including SHA-256 encryption and certain features of immutability, the size of a blockchain database can quickly become quite large. As an example, at one point, the blockchain in the bitcoin network was over 50,000 megabytes, with estimated growth of 214 petabytes each year (Swan 2015; Yli-Huumo et al. 2016). An organization must consider the projected size of the new blockchain solution and plan for its expansion over time.

System Scalability Challenges

In a blockchain solution, one of the technology's most valuable attributes is its security features. To maintain this level, security requires many individual nodes providing PoW on each block. This situation causes a scalability challenge to an organization.

The size of the data on blockchain, transaction processing rate, and latency of data transmission all affect the scalability of the blockchain solution. For example, the time between the transaction submission and confirmation on Bitcoin is around 1 hour and about 3 minutes on Ethereum (Xu et al. 2019). This scalability challenge can cause problems for an organization long after initial implementation.

Data Malleability Challenges

A certain level of data malleability is involved in a transaction that introduces risk to the blockchain security. In some cases, an attacker can modify and rebroadcast a transaction, which can cause problems with the transaction confirmation (Decker and Wattenhofer 2014; Yli-Huumo et al. 2016). The possibility of these attacks should be known to the implementers, so they can mitigate these attacks improving the system's security.

Transaction Authentication Challenges

In a blockchain transaction, each party in the transaction authorizes the transaction to be added to the blockchain. As a result, private keys used for this authentication process can sometimes be compromised. An example of this situation occurred with the Mt. Gox case when someone attacked and stole the storage of customer private keys placing the blockchain security at risk (Bos et al. 2014).

System Security Challenges

One of blockchain's most attractive features is its security. Based on other limitations of blockchain discussed in this chapter, blockchain's enhanced security feature makes it a fair trade-off between latency and scalability issues and security. However, implementers of a blockchain solution should be aware of the challenges and comprises systems using a public versus a private blockchain solution.

One problem with a public distributed ledger is its highly speculative nature with a trade-off between the dimension of the network and decentralization (Atzori 2017). For example, Il-Kwon et al. (2014) show that the bitcoin blockchain has a possibility of a 51% attack, which suggests that one miner can fully control of most of the network. Various accounts of different security breaches have occurred in bitcoin including denial-of-service attacks and account hacking using Trojan horses and viruses. According to Vasek and Moore (2015), scammers cheated 13,000 bitcoin victims out of $11 million between September 2013 and September 2014. In the first half of 2019, Su (2019) reports that hackers committing crypto crimes stole over $4 billion in cryptocurrency, which was up from $1.7 billion dollars in 2018.

Life Cycle Approach to Implementation

When implementing complex systems, managers traditionally use methods to carefully complete various phases of the implementation before starting the next phase. This type of project management ensures that a company prepares properly for the next phase of implementation increasing its probability of success.

Different methodologies are available to manage this process including systems development life cycle (SDLC), Waterfall, Spiral, Agile, and DevOps. This section uses a traditional SDLC model to discuss the factors that an organization should consider during blockchain implementation. The traditional SDLC consists of various phases of system implementation and allows discussing considerations needing to be addressed during the planning, analysis, design, development, testing, implementation, and maintenance phases of the blockchain implementation.

Planning Phase

Planning is the first phase in the systems development process. It identifies whether a need exists for a new system to achieve a business's strategic objectives. In the case of a blockchain implementation, an organization should identify its problem, goal, and why it wants to implement a blockchain solution. An organization should consider the following areas when deciding to implement a blockchain solution.

  • Establish why the organization wants a blockchain solution.
  • Decide how it plans to use the blockchain system.
  • Estimate the system's TCO.
  • Establish how the organization plans to implement the system and over what period.
  • Establish what systems or parts of systems it plans to replace or augment with the blockchain solution.

Systems Analysis and Requirements Phase

The second phase involves a company working on the source of its problem or the need for a change. In a blockchain implementation, management analyzes possible solutions to identify the best fit for the project's ultimate goals. The blockchain planning team should consider the following questions:

  • What software solutions are available? Table 16.1 provides a list of blockchain providers and frameworks.
  • What type of blockchain system does the company plan to implement ‒ public or private?
  • What data does the company plan to store on the blockchain?
  • How is the new blockchain system likely to affect existing systems?
  • What personnel adjustments are needed to install and maintain the system?
  • What consensus method does the company plan to use ‒ Proof of Work, Proof of Stake, Delegated Proof of Stake, Proof of Burn, Practical Byzantine fault-tolerant mechanism, Proof of Identity, Proof of Elapsed Time, or Proof of Importance?
  • What hardware and networking changes does the company need to make to support the new system?

Systems Design Phase

The third phase describes the necessary specifications, features, and operations that are needed to satisfy the functional requirements of the proposed system. For a blockchain implementation, an organization should consider what blockchain platform to use for the solution. Choosing a platform that is more suitable to the project is beneficial because it is likely to affect later needs.

For example, bitcoin is used to transfer cryptocurrency only but Ethereum can be used to transfer both cryptocurrency and organizational data. In contrast, the primary use of Hyperledger is to transfer organizational data. By comparing a platform's scalability and other factors, an organization can select the platform that best suits its needs to meet organizational goals. Converting from a public blockchain platform to a private platform and vice versa is extremely difficult, cumbersome, and costly if the organization makes the wrong decision early in the planning process.

Development Phase

The real work begins during the fourth phase ‒ development. At this point, an organization brings on a programmer, network engineer, and/or database developer to do the major work on the project. In the case of a blockchain project, an organization could navigate the project as follows:

  • Acquire all hardware and software solutions.
  • Install and configure the blockchain solution on the new network.
  • Create the data structure and smart contracts to create the transactions.
  • Establish nodes for PoW and begin validating transactions.
  • Establish procedures for how employees are to interact with the blockchain.

Much of the work identified in the design phase is accomplished in this phase. For a blockchain project, this step can include elements such as key management, address formats, block signatures, and permissions. Some elements can be changed at run-time but not later, so making a wise decision is advisable.

This phase is where an organization implements or creates many of the application programming interfaces (APIs). Items most likely needing an API include generating key pairs and addresses, performing audit related functions, conducting data authentication through digital signatures and hashes, providing data storage and retrieval, and engaging in smart-asset life cycle management – issuance, payment, exchange, escrow and retirement, and smart contracts.

Integration and Testing Phase

The fifth phase involves the integration and system testing of programs and procedures, which are normally carried out by a quality assurance professional to determine if the proposed design meets the initial set of business goals. During a blockchain implementation, an organization would typically use this phase to test each portion of the new blockchain solution to evaluate if the data from internal transactions are being transferred properly to the blockchain, if the system is impeding other critical systems, if transactions are being properly validated, and if encryption has been properly implemented to secure the data in the blockchain.

Implementation Phase

In the sixth phase, the actual installation of the newly developed system occurs. This step puts the project into production by moving the data and components from the old system to the new system usually via a direct cutover. During a blockchain implementation, an organization would use this phase to transition from a testing phase to a fully functioning blockchain solution that is integrated with its normal daily operations and processing of business transactions. The organization begins to rely on the data that are in the new blockchain system to be accurate, timely, secure, and immutable for the company to recognize the benefits and goals that it set out to achieve during the planning phase of the SDLC.

Operation and Maintenance Phase

The seventh and final phase involves maintenance and regular required updates. In this step the IT staff can fine-tune the system to boost performance, add new capabilities or meet additional user requirements. In a blockchain system, this phase may include enhancements of coding and procedures that handle key management, address formats, block signatures, and permissions. It may also include server and network administration and troubleshooting or node management and mining performance during the PoW validation.

Summary and Conclusions

This chapter has discussed various considerations an organization should make while implementing a blockchain solution. Blockchain has many desirable attributes including the technology being decentralized, synchronized, traceable, immutable, secure, scalable, collaborative, auditable, and programmable. However, because every business process does not automatically recognize these attributes, management should carefully consider whether to adopt and implement blockchain.

Organizations face many challenges when implementing blockchain because of the technology's relative newness. In addition, they face such issues and concerns involving throughput, latency, size and bandwidth, scalability, security, and authentication with each playing a role in the success of an organizations implementation. The chapter also discussed such areas as TCO, decision metrics, personnel abilities, and system performance.

Discussion Questions

(1)Identify and discuss the attributes of blockchain technology that add value as a technology-based system but also require the implementation team to make special considerations during implementation.

(2)Discuss the various costs involved with implementing a blockchain solution within an organization.

(3)Discuss the technical and organizational capabilities that an organization should examine before venturing into a blockchain implementation.

(4)Discuss why an organization might decide to implement a blockchain solution.

(5)Explain technological challenges that an organization may face when implementing a blockchain solution.
