Chapter 17

Blockchain Applications in Finance

Steven Cosares, Kristin Kalish, Thomas Maciura and Andrew C. Spieler

Keywords: Blockchain; distributed ledger technology; shareholder voting; foreign exchange; information systems; parametric insurance; dividend payments; insurance

Introduction

Blockchains and their distributed ledger technology (DLT) are often characterized as disruptive, meaning that the approach is so ground-breaking that if an institution does not complement its existing operations to take advantage of the opportunities offered by blockchain, it may not only miss out on newly created lines of business, but may lose some of its existing profitable positions in the marketplace. Blockchains are designed in a way to distribute ownership of data across many parties and counterparties. With relevant data in the hands of more people, participants can engage in peer-to-peer (P2P) transactions with little or no centralized authority or control. Thus, blockchains can pose serious threats to companies that do not take them seriously (Jepkemei and Kipkebut 2019). Since most financial institutions are already well-adapted to using advanced network-based information systems to obtain, maintain, protect, and deliver proprietary information (Baltzan 2020), they are poised to embrace the new opportunities that blockchains facilitate, especially for those markets with no definitive regulator or authority.

This chapter provides examples of how implementing blockchain enables such opportunities. Shareholder voting, for example, is already largely automated, but still has major inefficiencies that blockchain can reduce. Similarly, the foreign exchange (FX) market is fractured with many transactions occurring on different platforms with disparate counterparties. The DLT of blockchains can improve the efficacy of the FX post-trade processes. Similar benefits are available for some insurance products, where events that would justify a payout are easily recognized, and claims can be processed automatically. These examples should motivate thought about additional novel approaches to integrating blockchains with the more traditional information systems solutions companies use to support their operations.

An important consideration that companies make when choosing to become a participant in a blockchain is how much of their valuable proprietary data they would be willing to share in a network that often contains their competitors. Even if specific data regarding, for instance, the identities of a company's customers is encrypted in the public ledger, another party who is storing the blockchain has access to more public data and can derive additional metadata about the company, like the volume and frequency of its transactions. However, without mutual ownership and ubiquitous storage of blockchain data, the benefits of DLT that ensure data availability and data integrity cannot be achieved. Thus, collectives, cooperatives, and coalitions must be formed between businesses and their partners, businesses and their customers, businesses and their regulators, and businesses and their competitors, if they are to embrace the opportunities offered through blockchains. Additionally, some financial institutions may find that, in order to survive, they have to offer a new set of services in networks that are composed of former customers that they lost to some blockchain-enabled alternative.

Opportunities and Limitations of Blockchains

A traditional information systems solution for a financial institution tends to be a large and complex set of applications that maintains proprietary data for the company that owns it. Data and information are treated as critical enterprise resources because of not only the high cost to obtain, maintain, protect, generate, and distribute it to appropriate parties but also the critical business activities supported by the resource that give a company financial health and an edge over its competitors. For these privately owned solutions, the integrity of the data depends on the practices of the company alone.

A blockchain, on the other hand, stores little more than a ledger of verified transactions and some supporting rules (“contract” information) for each. Unlike large-scale information system (IS) solutions that may store large volumes of data from across lines of business to support both the current and anticipated needs of an enterprise, blockchain solutions tend to be more focused, especially since the data in a blockchain are generated, stored, and shared by all or most of the network participants. The distributed ledger is designed to maintain data integrity, especially in an environment where the participants have mutual distrust in one another, which explains why applications involving cryptocurrencies, like bitcoin, are often coupled with blockchain technology (Reiff 2020). The potential for some cryptocurrency to displace a sovereign currency also explains why financial institutions, like banks, need to embrace the opportunities and challenges offered by DLT.

Even though some of the data items in a blockchain are encrypted, thereby protecting the privacy of some information, network participants can still generate metadata about the transactions in it. For example, measuring the total number of bitcoins owned or the total amount traded each day is possible without knowing exactly who owns the currency and how much they own. Since all members storing the chain see the same set of blocks, any profitable opportunity or competitive edge that a party may develop, for example, from effective data mining or clever programming, is derived solely from the party's talent. So, smaller companies and entrepreneurs have a similar ability to profit from a blockchain as larger enterprises.

Because a diverse set of parties, sometimes having competing objectives, often share the data in a blockchain, all parties have an interest in the data's content and veracity. Thus, blockchains are better suited for markets where parties must either compete or cooperate than in markets where a single enterprise requires ownership of the ledger. Thus, blockchain solutions that are owned by a single company might need to be shared with its clients to allow for verifiable transaction data and a sufficiently high level of trust in the data set.

Alternatively, competing enterprises may agree to share a blockchain, with appropriate data-hiding, in order to generate a sufficient number of nodes to assure integrity in the maintenance of the blockchain. However, when a company relinquishes ownership and control of its data, it loses the ability to use its own processes to maintain and secure relevant information and hinders its ability to use the data for a competitive advantage.

By design, a non-trivial amount of time and computational effort is involved to add new blocks to the blockchain. Thus, DLT cannot support financial operations that must be completed or executed quickly or transactions that generate a large amount of data. For example, if someone is interested in using a blockchain for stock price discovery in multiple markets, the transaction data must be available in a matter of milliseconds. On the other hand, a blockchain solution may be better suited to cases where such data can be reasonably maintained for commodities that are not as liquid (i.e., where the number of units available is relatively small and their prices are unlikely to change much over some arbitrary span of time).

Shareholder Voting

One of the few legal rights that shareholders have is to vote their shares at every annual meeting or other important corporate event. Historically, small shareholders have participated less than large shareholders and institutional investors due to the fractured voting process. Aside from the general apathy from small shareholders that may not invest the time to research and/or vote their shares, the process is skewed to benefit large shareholders. Shares in publicly traded companies can be voted in several ways ‒ traditional paper ballot, attending the annual meeting, web-based and telephone voting. Further, differences in share classes can influence the number of votes per individual share. Shareholders can choose to vote on corporate issues, whether they are individual investors or institutional investors or they can vote via proxy, whereby their voting rights are transferred to an intermediary such as a mutual fund, investment advisor, broker-dealer, or activist investor.

Shareholders who hold shares directly with a corporation are considered record owners, while shares that are held by a third-party intermediary are considered to be owned by that party (i.e., held in “street name”) (Nord 2019). Common shares may be structured differently depending on company, industry, or legal area of jurisdiction. The standard principled share structure is one vote per share, but time-phased voting rights reward shareholders with superior voting rights after reaching a predetermined holding period. Time-phased voting primarily exists in Europe, specifically within Italy (BlackRock 2018). Finally, share classes provide some shareholders with more than one vote per share owned. For example, Alphabet, Google's parent company, has A, B, and C classes of shares, which account for representation of one, 10, and zero votes per share, respectively (Alphabet Inc. 2019).

Electronic and Paper Voting

The process of shareholder voting has been largely migrated to electronic methods, with 95% of the 482 billion voted shares processed by Broadridge submitted via web, application, or automated voice response in 2018 (Schifellite 2018). The process of voting electronically creates many efficiencies, most notably in the collection and aggregation phase, which in turn makes tracking easier and reduces cost. Increased reliance on virtual responses can create safety vulnerabilities for hackers to exploit, potentially allowing illegitimate parties to alter voting information or acquire sensitive data. Another key issue hampering electronic voting is the complicated system of share ownership through multiple parties, creating a chain of ownership that can obfuscate the holder of record and the beneficial owner.

As mentioned previously, the majority of shareholder voting takes place electronically. Ballots are collected electronically via the web, an application, or by automated voice response. This form of response collection continues to grow as physically mailed proxies decreased from 25% of all accounts processed in 2017 to 24% in 2018. This reduction generated savings of over $1.3 billion on paper goods and postage for corporate share issuers and mutual funds when compared directly to full voting by mail (Schifellite 2018). The ability to vote digitally also allows broader participation from the shareholder base as not all shareholders can attend or choose to attend annual shareholder meetings. From a process perspective, retail investors who hold shares through a brokerage account receive a message from their brokerage notifying them of the upcoming voting event and often receive another notification via email. Owners have the right to exercise their vote or can delegate that right through proxy to the brokerage or another designated party. The process is similar to paper voting although individuals have to complete the form manually and return it via mail. Paper voting allows individuals who may not have access to technology or lack digital familiarity to still cast their vote.

Depository Trust Company

About 85% of exchange-traded securities are held with the Depository Trust Corporation (DTC), registered under the US Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) as a clearing and securities depository (Securities and Exchange Commission 2007). Shares deposited at the DTC are considered to be in “street name” or belonging to the DTC participant. The DTC operates as a subsidiary of The Depository Trust and Clearing Company (DTCC). The DTC's main function is to hold securities on behalf of participants, as well as facilitating the transfer and pledging of securities as collateral held by the DTC (Depository Trust and Clearing Corporation 2020). For example, when Bank A buys shares of a company from Bank B, the shares are moved from Bank B's DTC account to Bank A's DTC account. The DTC is a member of the US Federal Reserve System, and many exchanges require DTC eligibility for shares to be listed on their exchange. For an issue to be DTC eligible, participants must submit a request for newly issued securities with the DTC and may also submit requests on behalf of previously traded securities that have not yet been deemed eligible (Depository Trust and Clearing Corporation 2020). Participants within the system are typically new issue underwriters such as banks and broker-dealers but may include other financial institutions taking part in the underwriting process.

Share Classes

A single corporate issuer may have billions of shares outstanding, across multiple share classes with separate voting rights. Within the United States, more than 250 constituents of the Russell 3000 had multiple share classes (Council of Institutional Investors 2019). Listed below are some of the more unique equity capital structures:

  • Aflac (AFL). The insurance company has a time-phased voting structure. Shareholders receive one vote per share, until the position is held for four years; at that point they receive 10 votes per share.
  • Ford Motor (F). The automobile manufacturer grants Class A shares one vote per share, while the Class B shares have a special clause indicating that they always control 40% of the vote.
  • Genie Energy (GNE). The energy service company Class A shares receive three votes per share while class B shares have one-tenth of a vote per share.
  • Snap Inc. (SNAP). The social media company offers Class A shares that have no voting rights, while Class B and C shares have one and 10 votes, respectively.
  • Stitch Fix (SFIX). The online retailer grants Class A holders one vote per share, while class B holders receive 10 votes per share. This structure is set to expire in 2027.

Complications

The process of shareholder voting in the United States is sometimes convoluted, redundant, translucent, and scattered. Necessary counterparties within the system include brokerages, banks, custodians, transfer agents, proxy solicitors, proxy service providers, proxy advisory firms, and vote tabulators (Rubin and Tanaves 2010). The issue of voting rights between beneficial and record-holders further complicates the system, as Delaware law states that “the corporation's stock ledger is the only evidence as to who the company's shareholders are and this stock ledger determines who may vote” (Nord 2019, p. 713). This law essentially states that if chain of ownership cannot be properly rectified, third parties may be able to vote on behalf of parties that otherwise were entitled and potentially willing to vote. Furthermore, for companies traded on the New York Stock Exchange (NYSE), NYSE Rule 452 states that brokers may vote shares that have not been voted at least 10 days before the scheduled meeting (Murphy 2009).

All these complications lead to problems of fair and honest representation and call into question the integrity and accuracy of the contests. In fact, one Delaware lawyer believes that a 10% margin of victory should be viewed as an inconclusive result (Kahan and Rock 2008). These systemic inefficiencies in the voting process are burdensome to the entire share ownership system as they potentially infringe on an owner's desire to maintain proper oversight on management, which in some cases can adversely affect shareholder returns. The system can also work against management if proposals are voted down by the slightest of margins or if they cannot achieve a quorum. The migration of voting to digital platforms creates additional concerns around security. Specifically, increased pressure exists to secure exchange points, and maintain and fortify data, though these problems also exist with paper materials.

Blockchain for Voting

DLT has the ability to reduce the operational and data burden placed upon counterparties within the shareholder voting value chain. By removing layers of inefficiencies and streamlining communication, blockchain appears to be a reasonable solution for the convoluted system of share ownership. By nature, blockchain is decentralized, meaning that all parties within the chain must reach a consensus for a block to be processed or mined. Combining this feature with the fact that the system must be permissioned may allow parties to relay information more quickly with trusted partners and most importantly have a clear and distinct line of ownership. If successful, this system is likely to reduce long-run costs for remaining counterparties and help restore more power to shareholders.

Corporate services company Broadridge Financial Solutions began developing a blockchain based proxy system in 2018. The company announced a pilot test revealed the most promising one for future application within exchange-traded and close-end funds (Collins, Kozakis, and Wisdom 2018). The technology leverages smart contracts, which are computer programs stored within blockchains that specify certain conditions (Orcutt 2018). With respect to voting, a smart contract stipulates who can vote, when voting closes, and what parties can access specific information. When votes are submitted onto the blockchain, the individual submits a block that can only be deciphered and viewed by the proper counterparty, vote counter, and voter. Since the block is cryptographically signed, it is highly secure. From a security perspective, since each block is added to the chain, considerable effort would be required for any bad actor to cause widespread harm. For example, if a hacker wants to remove vote 100 from the chain from a total of 150 processed blocks, the hacker would have to gain consensus to undo blocks 150 through 101 in order to invalidate block number 100. To substantially change voting results becomes increasingly difficult as the number of votes and blocks mined increases, a key underlying tenet of blockchain.

Blockchain provides the largest benefit for voting in creating streamlined processes and reducing costs in the long run. DLT has shown theoretically and in limited use cases these two capabilities, and development may drive expansion of useable tools. Although security appears to be at least on par, if not better than the current system of passwords, larger scale adoption would surely degrade the security, or at least increase vulnerabilities. Immutability allows all the participants that need to know see a non-proprietary community-based truth. The problems with implementing DLT, as with some other sectors covered in the book, are cost and uncertainties, as the technology is still relatively new (Nakamoto 2008).

Insurance Applications

Many insurance products are, by design, ideal for storage in and support by a blockchain solution, especially when different companies offer similar products. Simply speaking, when a customer purchases a product, like life insurance, he or she agrees to pay a certain periodic premium. The initial product purchase and its terms are stored as a transaction in the blockchain, as is each periodic payment made by the customer. When a well-defined event occurs, such as a policyholder's death, a trusted third party that has a copy of the blockchain may be tasked with recognizing when such events occur and making sure that the policy's beneficiary receives the predetermined payment after the event occurs. In simple cases, the beneficiary and the insurance company need not take any action for the payment to be processed. The blockchain, which is stored by multiple insurance providers, third parties, and policyholders, would contain all of the mutually trusted information necessary to process claims.

Application in Flight Insurance

A blockchain solution would be most applicable to insurance products with simple contracts. For example, “parametric” insurance products protect a policyholder against the occurrence of an event by paying a predetermined amount, rather than an amount that is based on the actual loss experienced. In 2017, AXA used the Ethereum blockchain to store the transactions associated with a product that pays a flight's cost if it fails to take-off within two hours of its scheduled departure time. When such events occur, they are stored in the public record, so they are easily verified. A simple, automated process is available by which valid policyholders of record were paid (AXA 2017). Unfortunately, even the cleverest of disruptive technologies cannot defy the market's invisible arm. In 2019, AXA discontinued the program because it failed to meet its financial objectives (Hill 2019). However, AXA did not deem the experiment a failure because of what it claims to have learned from the experience. AXA hopes for better outcomes with other parametric insurance products, such as those providing farmers with protection against extreme weather events.

This type of solution might be directly applicable for casinos in localities where sports-wagering is legal. Since the outcomes of every professional match, race, or game are publicized, they can be easily verified. A collection of casinos, regulatory agencies, large bettors, and other interested parties might share a blockchain that stores the verified (prepaid) bets placed on the games, the terms of the wager (e.g., the odds and any point spreads, and the amount due to the winners after each game). A trusted party can be employed to perform the payout process.

Application in Risk-pooling

State regulators sometimes call upon insurance companies to cover geographical areas or industry groups that are particularly vulnerable to large losses if they want to pursue other lines of business in their states. For example, a program called the “wind pool” enables hurricane-prone states such as Florida, Louisiana, Texas, and the Carolinas to offer insurance covering wind and hail damage, despite the frequency of severe storms in that part of the country. Insurance providers participating in the program can share the proceeds and the payouts from such products with each other to mitigate their individual risks. Much of this collective risk can also be ceded over to a company that specializes in reinsurance, which is, in essence an insurance company for insurance companies (PwC 2016).

These companies provide payouts after particularly devastating events. By using blockchain technology, the pooling participants, their reinsurers, and large policy holders store the transactions and the contract data on payouts. Triggering events, which are typically severe and newsworthy, would be relatively easy to recognize. The blockchain solution would assure that appropriate record-keeping is trusted by most of the parties involved. Because of the pooling of the risks, an event's overall severity would be easier to assess because the contracts often cover aggregate losses. Thus, no need exists to require data from individual policy holders.

Blockchains shared by multiple, competing insurance providers may also facilitate additional benefits. For example, data from across policies from multiple providers could be mined in a way that allows interested parties to identify a geographical cluster that houses some unique risk such as a cancer cluster. The collective data may also help identify individuals or groups whose risk metrics have been miscalculated and have been overcharged or undercharged for their premiums. In another example, a moderately-sized storm affecting all the houses in a neighborhood affects all providers doing business there. Given that Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA) reporting requirements would be the same for all providers, a blockchain solution in which information is shared may provide opportunities beyond risk-pooling.

FX Trading

Key institutions including central banks, global money center banks, buy-side and sell-side institutions, and corporations dominate FX transactions. The market is composed of hedgers aiming to reduce borrowing costs or to hedge the currency exposure of a cash flow stream, and speculators who seek to profit from the direction or mispricing of FX rates. Instruments used include FX swaps, spot transactions, currency options, and currency swaps. At any point in time, participants can hold multiple FX positions across currencies, timelines, and instruments, with many trades offsetting one another. This section provides an overview of the existing infrastructure behind FX trading and how blockchain may be applicable for improving the system.

Key Participants

A handful of large multinational organizations influence the FX market on a daily basis. This market has become concentrated primarily due to the benefits of scale and technology. In 2018, for example, the 10 banks with the largest market share represented 74.9% of total bank market share in FX trading, with the 10 largest asset managers accounting for 69.4% market share within their industry. Across institution types including banks, asset managers, leveraged funds, and FX trading platforms, the 10 largest operators had, on average, 74.6% of market share. A considerable overlap exists in each category with the money center banks, such as UBS and JPMorgan appeared in the top five across all listed categories (Euromoney 2018). Due to this concentration, technological innovation has not necessarily been at the forefront or top of the budget list for the entrenched market leaders. As technology developed, some larger institutions started to take notice of DLT, joining multi-bank and cross-industry consortiums. Many of these banks have begun to adopt blockchain strategies leveraging the immutability and visibility of a permissioned-based system, with many of them being built on the Hyperledger blockchain.

Instruments

Below are the four most frequently used FX trades and a brief description of how each one operates.

  • A spot transaction is a trade occurring at the prevailing market price of the currency. For example, if the USD–Yen rate is (¥) 110.57, this represents the most recent spot rate.
  • An FX swap is a two-legged transaction where a party borrows currency and simultaneously lends another currency in the same amount to the counterparty. At expiration, each party returns the borrowed currency at the agreed upon forward rate from contract initiation.
  • A currency option provides the buyer rights to buy or sell a given currency at a specified rate at or before an agreed-upon expiration date.
  • A currency swap is an agreement where counterparties exchange cash flows and principal of two different currencies. Each party pays the interest of the swapped loan amount, and at expiration, the principal is returned to each party at the spot rate or a prior agreed price (Association of Chartered Certified Accountants 2020).

FX Operations

Behind every FX transaction is a trail of paperwork starting from the initial trade order. Many institutions including banks and asset managers have large teams of middle- and back-office personnel to facilitate moving currencies for both their clients and their own account. After a trade has been placed, each party within the transaction sends details of the allocation to the central clearinghouse, which then confirms the trade information with the counterparties' trade instructions. Following the match confirmation, the clearinghouse sends the confirmed details of the trade back to each counterparty, often via SWIFT messages. SWIFT stands for Society for Worldwide Interbank Financial Telecommunication. The information is also shared with each of the counterparties' custodians.

Often the transacting parties have hundreds of FX trades at any given time that must be tracked and settled. To reduce the amount of resources dedicated to tracking and settling trades, institutions use a trade netting system, which aggregates the debits and credits by currency, allowing parties to make one payment instead of hundreds of disparate cash outflows. Contracts are settled physically or on a cash basis. Physical settlement entails the long investor taking delivery of a currency to his or her account, while a cash-settled trade pays the monetary difference between contract and expiration price. Fig. 17.1 shows a high-level overview of the post-trade process.

Fig. 17.1. Overview of the Post-trade Process for Foreign Currency. Note: This figure summarizes the post-trade steps and responsible parties in a foreign currency transaction. Source: Authors' illustration.

Blockchain Applications in FX

Over the last few years, major players in the FX market have started to build projects, largely on the Hyperledger platform, to better manage their positions and post-trade efficiency. The focus is to leverage the permeability and security of permissioned-based systems to track position prices and reduce potential error points. The system's decentralized nature allows verified internal and external parties to receive the necessary information for the completion of the trade cycle.

Hyperledger

Hyperledger (HL) is an open source blockchain project, under the Linux Foundation, with over 230 organizations as members as of 2018 (The Hyperledger White Paper Working Group 2018). The system was created and is maintained in a manner to promote collective advancement of blockchain projects, as opposed to disparate proprietary systems. Hyperledger is governed by a community of participants who contribute to and maintain the network, and elect other participants to drive directives on development and implementation. HL has five DLT frameworks that can be used to build upon, dependent on the projects applications, while some like Hyperledger Fabric can be used across industries. The core operating tenets of HL are modularity, security, interoperability, cryptocurrency agnostic, and application programming interfaces (APIs) (The Hyperledger White Paper Working Group 2018).

  • Modularity includes reusable building blocks, allowing components to be tested, changed, or combined independently of the system. It allows different builders to borrow capabilities from one another to improve their projects.
  • Security can be attained by distributing information away from silos reducing critical vulnerabilities. Reduced touchpoints decrease vulnerability points.
  • Interoperability refers to the exchange of data and information compatibly across varied complex systems.
  • Cryptocurrency agnostic means that projects are built to work with a multitude of tokens, cryptos, and altcoins, which allow users from different ecosystems to participate, further expanding building capacity across existing and new cryptocurrency projects.
  • APIs allow various applications and counterparties to connect quickly with HL's DLT.

HL Fabric is a platform built atop Hyperledger's infrastructure, intended to offer confidentiality, adaptability, and scalability for different businesses and use cases. One of Fabric's key features is its ability to operate as a network of networks, allowing smaller groups to create a separate ledger of transactions (Hyperledger 2020). Having the opportunity to participate in the broader network provides the advantage of visibility into the system, while being able to create separate channels allows participants to conduct unique transactions with specific parties. Furthermore, the transactions in the separate chain are accessible only to those within the new network.

Blockchain in Practice for FX

The first mainstream implementations of Hyperledger for FX post-trade activities occurred in 2018 when Goldman Sachs and Morgan Stanley used CLSNet, a payment netting service built on DLT (CLS 2018). The system was built in tandem with IBM and runs on Hyperledger Fabric. The primary determinant in using HL Fabric as opposed to the standard netting process was to increase standardization and automation, as well as leveraging the ability to create channels. HSBC is also using blockchain to process FX transactions. This technology, called HSBC FX Everywhere, is a shared permission-based ledger with participants from inside the bank. In 2019, the bank announced the settlement of $250 billion across more than three million FX transactions. Although the trades are a minority of the bank's FX business, the results have been positive, with HSBC realizing increased efficiencies and transparency. Notable benefits include trade confirmation and settlement automation by matching and netting, along with increased clarity around trade process flow and balance sheet capabilities (Blostone 2019).

Blockchain in Real Estate

Similar to other applications within financial services, blockchain may be used throughout the real estate value chain. From the retail buyer to commercial real estate enterprises, various intermediaries and inefficiencies exist that create redundancies and additional costs. A real estate transaction has a life cycle that includes multiple points of verification, confirmation, and exchange of cash flows, which can be laddered differently across groups and individual properties. Each transaction or exchange of information creates paperwork for the involved parties, which includes banking counterparties, the buyer and seller, and their brokers. The process can also include interactions with local and federal governments, institutions that are not the most expeditious. At each point, counterparties must be certain that the other participants in the transaction are trustworthy and legitimate. This section examines how blockchain may be implemented to fix these and other related problems in real estate, predominantly through the lens of financial services applications. Many of these applications entail similar use cases to the other sections in this chapter, largely revolving around reducing inefficiencies and counterparties, while improving system visibility for participants.

Blockchain for Listings

The real estate market is one of the most complex and fragmented sectors within the financial services industry. Pricing, for example, is largely performed on an individual appraisal basis, with factors such as location being a major determinant of value. Individual brokerages may have separate appraisals of value on their books, dependent upon either their proprietary designation of value, or that of multiple providers, as no single consolidated marketplace or exchange exists. The Rex MLS Blockchain, built upon the Ethereum blockchain, seeks to fix this problem. Rex's technology allows users to list their properties on the system, with the listing party receiving the Rex cryptocurrency. Users can access listing data for free through the platform, which essentially acts as an open global listing service, reducing listing and transaction fees (Kejriwal and Mahajan 2017).

Digitizing Identities on the Blockchain for Real Estate

The largest scale application for blockchain in real estate likely lies within the digitization of identities and properties. The act of digitizing identities away from the current system of paper-based methods of passports and state-issued identification relies largely on the governments issuing such documents, and the ability to gain the trust of users following large-scale personal data breaches in the preceding few years. The SelfKey Foundation is trying to address this problem through its SelfKey blockchain. Within the system, users receive unique identifying keys: a private key and a public key to help third-party verification. Users first must upload their paper identification materials, which are verified by the applicable issuers and verifiers to confirm the party is legitimate (Selfkey 2017). Once users are verified, they may use their credentials to transact with counterparties. For example, a SelfKey-verified corporate property owner can use his or her public key to apply for loans at multiple banking institutions, with the process of requesting verification only needing to be performed at a single point in time. This procedure can help institutions and individuals reduce the amount of time spent interfacing with banking and governmental counterparties, allowing them to better focus on their core competencies of assessing and selecting real estate.

Blockchain for Dividend Payments

Dividend payments using blockchain typically occur in a native cryptocurrency, meaning holders of a specific crypto receive more of the crypto as a payment. Within the capital markets, an effort exists to examine whether blockchain may apply to the recording and distributing dividends. Although many applications remain conceptual, some early adopters have started implementing blockchain in the market. In a novel transaction, online retailer Overstock.com announced it would be issuing a preferred stock dividend, paying shareholders one share of a digital preferred stock for every 10 shares of common stock (Nelson 2020). The digital preferred shares trade on a distinct trading system based on the tZero ATS blockchain, a subsidiary of Overstock.com. To trade the digitally enhanced securities, an investor must create an account through Dinosaur Financial, the sole active brokerage for tZero ATS (tZero.com 2020). The security's information is represented on the chain as a pseudonymized carbon copy of the securities ownership record, which is expected to be DTC eligible (Securities and Exchange Commission 2020).

In this sense, blockchain is being used as a testing ground to see if the theorized benefits can be shown in practice, with the additional benefit of being able to benchmark performances in real-time. Other use cases being explored include the issue of double taxation upon cross-border dividend payments, specifically in Denmark. Differences in tax rates allow parties domiciled outside of Denmark to be refunded the difference between their countries tax rates and that of Denmark. Parties must provide the Danish tax authority (SKAT) with banking statements and local tax documents to confirm tax payments, creating inefficiencies and opportunities for tax avoidance (Hyvärinen, Risius, and Friis 2017). By implementing a permissioned-based blockchain with the relevant counterparties, the system aims to reduce the necessity for reproducing paperwork and improves the transmission and verification processes currently in use.

Summary and Conclusions

In summary, increasing interest exists in how blockchain can help to create greater transparency, efficiency, and resiliency within financial services. Multiple participants, including those in academia, research, and corporations, are driving the effort. As the systems and processes employed by the financial community, some of which predate the internet (Nord 2019), begin to falter under the strains of regulation and the ever-increasing size and complexity of data and information systems, institutions are likely to explore new technologies to meet their needs. As discussed in this chapter, many segments within financial services have begun to roll out live testing of blockchain solutions in relatively small samples. Thus far the results have been largely encouraging, with many gains being realized through reduction and optimization of processes. For example, sharing data for reinsurance has not only streamlined the process to make payouts but also has the potential to save millions of dollars in record-keeping costs by eliminating the need to key redundant data into multiple data systems. However, some doubt about DLT still remains, most notably around security, and how systems may perform under stress of larger volumes or more complex transactions. Nonetheless, as the number of resources applied to blockchain technologies increases, many of the technological limitations can be overcome. The financial sector is likely to continue to be among the first to expand its operations to embrace the opportunities offered by this disruptive technology.

Chapter 18

Blockchain Applications in Healthcare

Alevtina Dubovitskaya

Keywords: Blockchain; healthcare; blockchain applications; blockchain adoption; patient’s privacy; compliance

Introduction

A person's health-related information evolves over time and is usually stored and processed by multiple entities in various formats, substantial volumes, and for different purposes. A patient might visit multiple medical sites during treatment or follow-up resulting in such information being scattered among numerous clinics, hospitals, medical devices, and laboratories. Thus, various entities are processing a person's healthcare data in anonymized and non-anonymized form. Because of such complexity and the number of participants, tracking every data transaction is virtually impossible. Because a patient often does not even know where these data are processed and for what purposes, the patient's privacy rights become threatened.

Knowing where the data are stored and being able to exchange and interpret the data (data interoperability) for treatment or research purposes can improve personal treatment outcomes (Hsiao, King, Hing, and Simon 2015) and can advance medical research by enabling precision medicine and artificial intelligence (AI)-driven healthcare (Rajkomar et al. 2018). Retrospective medical data are employed for comparative effectiveness research and in public health (National Information Center on Health Services Research and Health Care Technology 2020). Yet, healthcare data are highly sensitive and the patients' needs to authorize any data access or manipulation to ensure the patient's privacy. According to the regulations, a patient's consent is required before data sharing, unless the data are de-identified, such that re-identification of the data subject is impossible (U.S. Department of Health and Human Services 2020). Also, a patient has the right to erase all his/her data or to opt-out from a clinical study at any time.

Toward supporting privacy rights of the patients and a “patient-centric” approach for healthcare data management, the Office of the National Coordinator for Health Information Technology (ONC) recently proposed a rule on interoperability and information blocking, with a strong focus on patients' ability to access their own electronic health record at no cost. Achieving interoperability and privacy simultaneously seems contradictory. How can data availability and exchange be ensured when required, while letting patients control who can access their data and for which purposes? How can proof be efficiently obtained that patients have given their consent?

The intent of ecosystems for health information exchange (HIEs) is to ensure that the patient data from electronic health records can be shared nationwide securely, efficiently, and accurately. However, HIEs have limited adoption and many regional networks are still isolated from each other (HealthIT.gov2020). Furthermore, the current system lacks standard architecture, resulting in the failure to ensure a proper security level and enforced access-control policies over shared patients' data. Moreover, HIEs are generally designed as a single fully trusted entity solely responsible for managing and storing electronic health record (EHR) data from multiple participating hospitals. Although a centralized system may be easier to manage, it suffers from a single point of failure and can become a performance bottleneck for real world deployment. Furthermore, a centralized authority having access to sensitive health information has more security and privacy concerns from the users. Discontinuation of GoogleHealth wallet in 2012 (Anonymous 2020), for example, shows that patients are concerned about their privacy and aware of the potential risks, including misusing their sensitive data. Alternatively, most of the data can be stored and managed in the encrypted form (e.g., using homomorphic encryption), for increased security and privacy. However, homomorphic encryption requires large amounts of memory and extensive computations (Moore, O'Neill, O'Sullivan, Doröz, and Sunar 2014) that can be problematic, or even prohibitive, for a hospital environment. Encrypting the data only partially can improve the efficiency of such methods (Gentry, Halevi, and Smart 2012). However, in medical settings, a need often exists to access and analyze all historical data including images in plain for better healthcare decisions. Therefore, the question about facilitating medical data sharing, while ensuring privacy, security, and auditability, remains open. No single approach exists that can satisfy these requirements simultaneously. Thus, an interdisciplinary approach that allows the entities to collaborate in a distributed but trusted environment is in demand.

The possibility of using emerging blockchain technology for healthcare data management has recently raised major attention in both industry and academia (Azaria, Ekblaw, Vieira, and Lippman 2016; Dubovitskaya, Xu, Ryu, Schumacher, and Wang 2017, 2019b; Dillenberger et al. 2019; Hölbl, Kompara, Kamišalić, and Zlatolas 2018; Vazirani, O'Donoghue, Brindley, and Meinert 2019). Blockchain provides a unique opportunity to tackle some of the major challenges in healthcare data management, such as enabling data sharing and integrating patient-centered care, data provenance allowing verification of the data's authenticity, and optimizing healthcare processes. Yet, regardless of current high interest from both the industrial and academic perspectives, blockchain-based healthcare data management systems are not yet in place (Dubovitskaya, Xu, Ryu, Schumacher, and Wang 2019a).

This chapter first summarizes important domain-specific requirements for compliant healthcare data management, which can be fulfilled by applying blockchain technology in numerous healthcare scenarios. Next, the chapter describes different approaches for healthcare data storage and management using blockchain. A discussion of the current barriers for the adoption of the blockchain technology and potential future directions toward developing blockchain-based healthcare systems concludes the chapter.

Motivation and Advantages of Using Blockchain in Healthcare

This section first examines the requirements for secure and trusted healthcare data management. Then, it discusses use-case scenarios that can benefit from adopting blockchain technology, particularly, how specific properties of the blockchain technology can be used to address the requirements in different use-case scenarios.

Requirements

As for any system managing sensitive data, the following properties are essential: confidentiality, integrity, availability, and privacy of a data subject. Ermakova, Fabian, Kornacka, Thiebes, and Sunyaev (2020) define the aforementioned properties in healthcare settings.

  • Confidentiality implies preventing the disclosure of information to any unauthorized individual or system (Sattarova and Kim 2007). In healthcare, confidentiality means flexibility for the patient to set up and revoke fine-grained access-control rights to the healthcare data that he or she owns, supporting the minimization principle of data-sharing: only share the data that are required to be shared, and revoke the rights when no access to the data is needed. At the same time, the system provides flexibility to share medical data without patients' involvement or explicit consent as defined by law emergency situations.
  • Integrity refers to the trustworthiness of data or resources in general and is usually phrased in terms of preventing improper or unauthorized modification of the data. Integrity includes data integrity (the content of the information) and origin integrity (the data source, often called authentication) (Bishop 2003). In healthcare settings, auditability and non-repudiation of users' actions ensure that medical data can be changed only by authorized users to allow for accuracy and consistency of medical records (Ermakova et al. 2020).
  • Availability refers to the ability to access and use the information or resource desired. Availability is an important aspect of reliability and system design (Bishop 2003). Archiving and recoverability, timely access to the current medical data, as well as long-term storage of healthcare records are important ingredients required to ensure that medical data are available for the patient anytime and to the other users with respect to the patient's will (Ermakova et al. 2020).

In addition, for a healthcare system to comply with domain-specific legislations, each patient needs to provide consent to share his or her data both for specific purposes such as primary care and research studies. Such a requirement can be seen as one aspect of a patient's privacy. This concept is close to confidentiality but with the following difference. Although confidentiality refers to the data, privacy refers to the person and his or her right to decide whether to keep these personal data confidential. Privacy can be defined as a combination of the following rights: the right to decide and control what information to share, who can access the data, and the right to stay anonymous (Schoeman 1984; Walters 2001). The latter is highly relevant when data are shared for research purposes. Data anonymization can be an alternative to consent management.

Elger et al. (2010) discuss the main laws and guidelines that describe how to prepare healthcare data for use in medical research including de-identification and pseudonymization. Automatic de-identification approaches allow faster de-identification and can also be used with large data volumes (Meystre, Friedlin, South, Shen, and Samore 2010). By applying such methods, if proved that the desired anonymity level is achieved, requirements of the Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act of 1996 (HIPAA) in the United States and General Data Protection Regulation in the European Union can be waived, and data aggregation would become easier and faster, while ensuring subject privacy.

In practice, adding data interoperability, traceability of the data is required to support patient's privacy. Traceability of a healthcare data is the ability for the patient to retain the identities of the origin of the healthcare information related to him or her, the entities who accessed the data, and the operations performed on the data, such as access to the data or updates (De Lusignan et al. 2011). Data traceability is particularly important in legal cases, as well as for the patient, in defining and enforcing that person's access-control policy, in allowing meaningful data aggregation for research purposes, and in enabling reproducibility of research (Dubovitskaya 2018).

Applying Blockchain in Different Healthcare Scenarios

Kuo, Kim, and Ohno-Machado (2017) name key benefits of blockchain for biomedical/healthcare applications in comparison with traditional distributed databases: decentralized management, immutable audit trail, data provenance, robustness/availability, and security/privacy. A growing number of existing blockchain technology implementations reveals multiple advantages of using this new technology in different aspects of healthcare. Blockchain can be used in primary care to achieve patient-centric data management while ensuring the patient's privacy and advancing personalized medicine; in connected health and pharmaceutical supply-chain by bringing optimization of various healthcare processes, especially when multiple stakeholders are involved; and in medical research to ensure compliance to accelerate clinical studies (Dubovitskaya 2018).

In the framework of data sharing for primary patient care, this new technology can be used with the following purposes. As Fig. 18.1 shows, because of sensitivity of the healthcare data and their volume, the data themselves are usually encrypted and stored locally (i.e., in the hospitals where the data were produced or exchanged on demand) or on the compliant cloud storage (i.e., temporal buffer for data exchange). Storing a reference pointer to the data location and the hash or digital signature generated over the data on the immutable ledger ensures the healthcare data's traceability and authenticity. A patient also can use the ledger to store his or her consent and enforce the access-control policies: specify who can access what kind of data during what period of time.

Fig. 18.1. Blockchain-based Approach for Data Exchange in the Primary Care Settings. Note: The figure demonstrates a common approach for on- and off-chain data storage in the primary care settings, the data are encrypted and stored off-chain: (a) only locally: in the hospitals where the data were produced and then exchanged on demand; and (b) on the compliant cloud storage (i.e., temporal buffer for data exchange). The system metadata are stored on-chain and consist of the information about the data location and a hash or digital signature over the data and permissions for the data-access, defined by a patient.

The aforementioned approaches can facilitate and speed-up data-sharing process for both patients and caregivers for the diagnosis and treatment, as well as for audit and court cases, if required (Azaria et al. 2016; Dubovitskaya et al. 2017; Mamoshina et al. 2018). Keeping track of the actions performed with the data such as generation of the new information, updates, and data exchange, allows a patient to consolidate the data from multiple sources and keep the full patient's history (Hussein et al. 2018). Enabling patient-controlled data sharing is especially relevant for cancer care when local clinical institutions have limited oncology expertise and resources, and telemedicine is used to search for appropriate service provider, arrange the payment for the service, and provide necessary consultation and diagnosis (Zhang, White, Schmidt, Lenz, and Rosenbloom 2018b; Zhu, Shi, and Lu 2019).

Treatment control by connecting patients, healthcare providers, health insurer/insurances and pharmacies allows service providers to address inefficiencies of the healthcare processes by setting up systems for automatized and trusted claim processing and reimbursements for prescriptions management. The performance of claims processing using blockchain technology can be measured in seconds, whereas the common approach is measured in days, as it often involves sending the required data, including bills and prescriptions, by post (Culver 2016). The possibilities of real-time claims can power a multitude of different improvements, including eliminating human mistakes, cutting costs for claims information processing (Yip 2016), and ensuring unforgeability of the healthcare data required for the processing of the claims (Wang and Song 2018). Li, Nelson, Malin, and Chen (2019) propose a blockchain-based solution for managing prescription history to avoid incompatibility of the prescribed medications. A promising approach to transparent and auditable opioid prescription monitoring is likely to provide incentives for writing fewer prescriptions (Zhang, Schmidt, White, and Lenz 2018a).

As for supply-chain processes in almost any industry, blockchain can be used in the pharmaceutical supply chain (Queiroz, Telles, and Bonilla 2019). Increased trust and transparency, monitoring of the production, possibility to track pharmaceutical goods for the end-user (patient) throughout the supply chain, and detecting and reporting problems are some improvements that blockchain can bring (Mettler, 2016; Schöner, Kourouklis, Sandner, Gonzalez, and Förster 2017; Chien et al. 2020).

Applying blockchain technology in biomedical research (1) allows patients to contribute with their healthcare data while ensuring privacy and security (Mamoshina et al. 2018; Raisaro et al. 2018; Albanese, Calbimonte, Schumacher, and Calvaresi 2020); (2) speeds-up the phase of participants recruitment for clinical trials (Angeletti, Chatzigiannakis, and Vitaletti 2017), (3) makes available real-time EHR data in common data format (Schöner et al. 2017); and creates mechanisms to collect large and integrated heterogeneous data sets of various ownerships and to enable cross domain and international collaboration (Shae and Tsai 2018).

Blockchain-based Healthcare Data Management: Technical Aspect

This section reviews existing design approaches and implementations of blockchain-based systems in healthcare. In particular, it discusses the advantages and potential weaknesses of different realizations of blockchain technology in healthcare systems. This section also presents potential convergence of blockchain and AI in healthcare applications.

Managing Data On- and Off-chain

Because of the sensitivity of both healthcare data and metadata, permissioned blockchain technologies are often employed in designing blockchain-based healthcare systems. However, using private permissionless blockchain technology implementations has also been proposed as an alternative approach in multiple frameworks (i.e., when only anonymized information is stored on the ledger). Cryptocurrency can be used to attract and incentivize the users and can offer monetization of the healthcare data. In general, both approaches ‒ using permissionless and permissioned technology implementations ‒ assume that highly sensitive healthcare data are not stored on the ledger, but are managed off-chain. The same applies to some private information about participants of the consortia or network and business contracts between them.

Off-chain data management means leveraging any approach other than distributed ledgers for data storage and management such as using local database or cloud-based storage. In such situations, the ledger only stores the hash or digital signature, pointers to data sources or locations and immutable log of the actions such as adding new information, accessing the data. Patient consent in a form of the permissions specified by the patients, and some other metadata about healthcare information can also be managed on-chain. Corresponding smart contracts are then required to ensure correct management of different types of on-chain data.

Approaches for distributed peer-to-peer (P2P) data-storage are often combined with the private permissionless networks. A distributed hash table (DHT) is a key-value store where the keys are hashes and widely used to coordinate and maintain metadata about P2P systems. The Inter Planetary File System (IPFS) is a high performance content-addressed block storage model, employing DHT to find and request the content from any node in the network (Benet 2014). Several frameworks (Kulemin, Popov, and Gorbachev 2017; Mamoshina et al. 2018) suggest combining DHT such as Kademlia (Maymounkov and Mazieres 2002) and IPFS as off-chain data storage with Ethereum blockchain for creating marketplaces for healthcare data.

Although sensitive data are often managed off-chain, cases are available when broadcasting all the transactions and making all the on-chain data available to the whole blockchain network are undesirable. In healthcare, one example can be a consortia of healthcare actors including healthcare professionals, insurance companies, and research institutions. If metadata and permissions corresponding to a patient's healthcare data are stored on-chain, separating the data flows may be required. That is, the patient may prefer to share more information with medical doctors, and only be willing to provide a subset of such information for the research purposes.

In permissioned settings, several options are available for setting up the access-control policy and ensuring confidentiality and privacy of the data stored on-chain. For instance, in R3 Corda blockchain implementation (Brown, Carlyle, Grigg, and Hern 2016), access-control policy is defined at the transaction level, meaning that only a specified set of users can access the data from this transaction. A similar concept is implemented in Hyperledger Fabric, via the channels (i.e., private subnets), which are similar to the idea of defining access-control policy on the transaction lever (Androulaki et al. 2018). This allows flexibility regarding access-control to the data stored on the ledger, but makes impossible guaranteeing that all network participants have a copy of the same ledger. Although such approach can be beneficial for certain use-case scenarios, it contradicts the idea of replicating the same ledger among participants.

Private data collection is another approach used to share private information with only authorized organizations in an auditable manner and without creating a channel. In case of private data collections, the private data are sent P2P to only the peer(s) authorized to see them. These data are not on the ledger but are stored in a private local database, which can be accessed by smart contracts, executing on these authorized peers. A hash of that data is written to the ledgers of every peer on the channel and serves as evidence of the transaction.

Periodic publication of the hash of the ledger's current state to the bitcoin blockchain is an approach used by another permissioned blockchain technology platform such as Exonum (Yanovich, Ivashchenko, Ostrovsky, Schvchenko, and Sigorov 2018). The hash is publicly auditable by anyone having access to the Exonum blockchain and therefore ensures non-repudiation in the applications built on top of Exonum. Several frameworks for blockchain-based healthcare data management and analytics are based on Exonum blockchain implementation (Kotsiuba et al. 2018; Mamoshina et al. 2018; Grishin et al. 2018).

Combining Artificial Intelligence and Blockchain for Managing and Monetizing Healthcare Data

Blockchain technology can also be used in combination with machine learning (ML) and AI. Blockchain can be leveraged to ensure the verifiability and transparency while building and employing models and decision-making processes in AI systems (Calvaresi, Mualla, Najjar, Galland, and Schumacher 2019; Weng et al. 2018). In turn, AI tools can be used to detect the presence of attacks or a malicious behavior in the blockchain network, and invoke the appropriate defense mechanisms. AI-based governance can be explored to improve the performance of blockchain-based systems (Dinh and Thai 2018).

Multiple independent groups of researchers have recently proposed marketplaces for genomic data (Kulemin et al. 2017; Grishin et al. 2018; Mamoshina et al. 2018) and combine principals of both AI and blockchain. The main idea of the proposed frameworks is to simplify and incentivize the data acquisition process and data management, provide users with the possibility of taking ownership of their data, and monetize their data based on transparent pricing models. Such an approach allows speeding-up the phase of participant recruitment for clinical trials, creating mechanisms to collect large and integrated heterogeneous data sets of various ownerships, and enabling cross-domain and international collaboration, while preserving privacy of the users. However, monetizing such data poses a threat to the privacy of the users' relatives that reveal their data because of the correlations between the genomic data of individuals within the same family.

Blockchain technology can also be used to track the data that have been released in anonymized form, including the anonymity level of the data. Kiyomoto, Rahman, and Basu (2017) propose a blockchain-based distribution scheme for anonymized datasets. Blockchain can be used for recording all transactions related to anonymized datasets between network participants. One can argue that keeping track of all the transactions can put the anonymization at risk. However, recording all the transactions can be used as an input to compute the risk of being re-identified if more data about the data subject are released and to prevent violating the data subject's privacy (Dumas, Hull, Mendling, and Weber 2019).

An excellent example of a recent advancement in management and analysis of anonymized healthcare data is MiPasa – a blockchain-based multi-party and multi-source verifiable data platform (MiPasa 2020). MiPasa is leveraging permissioned blockchain technology to set up a trusted, integrated, transparent yet privacy-respecting and responsibly governed data sharing network. As Fig. 18.2 shows, the data in different formats, aggregated from heterogeneous sources, are made available through the APIs for data visualization, data analysis, and decision-making using ML and AI, and sharing and broadcasting gathered insights. Distributed permissioned ledger technology is used to implement the versioning of the data feeds and to verify the data immutability by keeping the log of hashes and digital signatures of the updates, such as adding a new dataset, or updating an existing one with the new information. Privacy experts are involved in the data processing to ensure and ascertain that the privacy of the data subjects is not violated.

Fig. 18.2. MiPasa Ecosystem and Its Functionality. Note: This figure demonstrates participants of a MiPasa ecosystem, their roles, and how the platform is being used. The blockchain network is maintained by platform enabling partners to guarantee the system’s integrity. The append only ledger provides the required immutability.Technology provider HACERA employs zero-knowledge proofs (i.e., mathematical methods used to verify claims without sharing or revealing underlying data) to ensure data privacy and anonymized statistical data analysis. The platform allows data providers to publish their data. MiPasa combines data from multiple sources and of different structures. Dataset providers include national bodies and independent organizations such as the Center for Disease Control and healthcare ministries of various countries. MiPasa also supports private and paid-for data in addition to the freely available data. The data undergo pre-processing and preparation to be leveraged by data-analytics tools. Data consumers, researchers, and auditors are represented by the actors from different domains including scientists, regulators, pharmaceutical companies, insurance companies, among others. They have a possibility to explore and use models already developed, or access the data directly for specific research purposes.

Blockchain Adoption

This section discusses some existing barriers of adopting blockchain technology in healthcare. It begins by discussing the limitations of the design and existing implementation of the blockchain technology. Next, the section reviews the potential approaches to address such limitations. Finally, it concludes with recently proposed approaches of employing blockchain technology in the context of the COVID-19 pandemic.

Barriers

Blockchain technology consists of a set of cryptographic techniques and approaches for distributed data management in permissioned and permissionless settings. Thus, existing barriers when managing identities, credentials, life-cycle of the keys, used for encryption/decryption and creation/verification of digital signature, remain highly relevant. In a growing number of frameworks and applications of blockchain in healthcare, various approaches have been proposed, including smart-cards, mobile phones, wallets for keys, and credentials management. Yet, an ideal approach that can guarantee reasonable security, scalability, and ease of use is still to be defined.

Nonetheless, despite recent development and advances of the blockchain technologies, current implementations still have limited capabilities including the number of supported transactions per second as well as the amount and structure of the data that can be stored on blockchain and efficiently retrieved. Overcoming such limitations is a prerequisite for mass adoption of the blockchain in healthcare, as well as in any other area, where a robust system with multiple users managing sensitive data is required. Moreover, blockchain technology cannot guarantee that, at any point in time, every participant/peer in a network has a valid state of the distributed ledger (i.e., a state shared by the majority of the participants). Node's invalid state can be caused by software/hardware faults and attacks. The peer also may still participate in the network albeit having an invalid state. Thus, a user/client must not rely on a single peer for a query about the state. Therefore, a robust approach to dynamically choose which peers to query and how to interpret the inconsistent query replies is required (Dubovitskaya et al. 2019a).

As mentioned previously, healthcare data are often stored in a single location where it was produced, or on a designated server, temporarily creating a potential single point of failure. Another similar threat, relevant mostly for permissioned blockchain technology implementations, is a membership server responsible for the users and blockchain peers management. Although decentralization of the data-storage or permission-management services can eliminate both risks, setting up such distributed and trusted consortia as well as defining and supporting the distributed architectures are not obvious in practice.

Because of the fact that multiple actors normally design, implement, and verify the chaincode/smart-contracts, a bias that can be introduced involving a human-made mistake tends to be limited. Avoiding such mistakes is particularly relevant and desirable in the applications that aim at optimizing the healthcare business-process, such as ones related to claims processing and payments. Given than people still implement the smart-contracts, ensuring the absence of an accidental mistake and malicious behavior that can influence the desired fair outcome is impossible. AI can also be leveraged for automatic generation of smart contracts, but up to now, no such approach has been found.

Healthcare data are required to be available from anywhere at any time, yet compliant with the access-control policies specified by the patient. Thus, providing a possibility for the patients to learn how to define and revoke such policies and what are the potential benefits and consequences of each data-sharing (or revocation) action is important. At the same time, the access-control policies might be expressed differently at various locations and systems and across different types of data. Therefore, defining unified rules for the global reachability of the data is challenging. One issue with permissioned blockchains is that because of its consortium-oriented nature, making it global (i.e., create a single consortium with unified governance) is likely impossible (Dubovitskaya et al. 2019a). Moreover, in the healthcare domain, emergency situations occur regularly, and data might be required urgently. If a patient was unconscious and delivered to a medical institution, and the access-control policy is defined such that no caregiver from the medical institution has a right to access the patient's EHR, then updating the permissions and granting access to the data to a caregiver is impossible. Robust and secure “break-glass” mechanisms for emergency situations are required to address this limitation (Dubovitskaya et al. 2020).

According to the General Data Protection Regulation in Europe, a patient has “the right to be forgotten.” This right cannot be easily compatible with the immutability property of the most of the blockchain technology implementations. However, applying different cryptographic techniques such as asymmetric encryption, threshold encryption, and proxy re-encryption could be used to address such limitations. Another relatively recently proposed approach requiring further study and evaluation is using so-called redactable blockchains, first introduced by Ateniese, Magri, Venturi, and Andrade (2017). A healthcare system designed by Hylock and Zeng (2019) already employed redactable blockchains. For generating the block identifier, redactable blockchains use a specific type of hash functions (“chameleon” hashing) that employ a trapdoor – a secret parameter that allows to find collisions. That is, one can change a block's content or remove blocks without needing to integrate the change in all the consequently added blocks on the ledger. One or multiple users possessing the secret parameter can make this change. Therefore, the policy regulating the access to the trapdoor is critical in such blockchain-based systems. Moreover, after modification is done, the updates have to be broadcasted in the network thus creating an additional network load.

Toward Blockchain-based Healthcare Systems

The Estonian government is employing a keyless signature infrastructure called KSI (Buldas, Kroonmaa, and Laanoja 2013) in multiple healthcare scenarios, including clinical trials, pharmaceutical supply-chain, and data management for primary care. In such an approach, no data are registered into the ledger itself, but hashes of data and history of any data movement are. The hashes with the timestamps are organized in a special tree-like structure, and the resulting hash is then publicly distributed. This procedure ensures data authenticity and integrity of the data stored off-chain, as well as the integrity of the log of all the data processing actions. This approach shares similarity with standard blockchain technologies because it is also based on the hashing and uses tree-like hash structure. However, such an approach lacks some important blockchain characteristics including data replication according to a specific consensus mechanism and smart-contract functionality.

During the global spread of the COVID-19 virus and pandemic, the need to manage healthcare data efficiently and securely as well as to digitize and optimize the healthcare processes becomes even more critical. Blockchain technology has already demonstrated its potential in related areas. The hospitals in China are collaborating with blockchain companies and pharmacies to deliver patients' medication to their doorsteps. By using blockchain, hospitals could ensure timely delivery of medications with accurate tracking (Ting, Carin, Dzau, and Wong 2020). Another example is MiPasa, a blockchain-based multi-party, multi-source verifiable data sharing platform for managing the anonymized data related to COVID-19.

Blockchain-based identity management approaches as well as keyless signature infrastructure are currently under consideration for their use in designing so-called “immunity passports.” From a medical perspective, implementing such immunity passports would generate polemics (Kofler and Baylis, 2020). From a technical point of view, ensuring both unforgeability of such information and privacy of the individuals can be achieved using the blockchain technology.

Summary and Conclusions

This chapter discussed requirements for healthcare data management, focusing mainly on security and privacy aspects, because of the high sensitivity of healthcare data. It also analyzed different approaches, describing how blockchain technology can satisfy these requirements based on existing research and practical implementations in various areas of healthcare.

Different on- and off-chain mechanisms for data management are being exploited to build efficient and secure healthcare systems based on blockchain. Convergence between blockchain and AI in healthcare is apparent in the recent trends. Although blockchain technology has a potential to revolutionize healthcare data management processes, barriers exist involving technical, organizational, and compliance aspects when integrating blockchain technology. The chapter discusses these barriers together with possible ways to overcome them. These measures include increasing awareness and providing appropriate training for patients and healthcare professionals, designing regulations able to clarify disputable situations, and improving the characteristics of the blockchain and underlying technologies. Given the tremendous amount of work directed toward bringing blockchain technology to healthcare in recent years, this technology will eventually be adopted and provide undeniable benefits to various areas in healthcare.

Discussion Questions

(1)Explain under which conditions compliance with the Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act (HIPAA) in the United States and General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) in the European Union with respect to the healthcare data management can be waived.

(2)Discuss the purposes of ecosystems for health information exchange (HIEs) and their limitations.

(3)Identify the major application areas in healthcare where blockchain technology can be employed and the advantages of using blockchain in these areas.

(4)Explain how the immutability property of blockchain can contradict with existing regulations in healthcare and the approaches used to achieve compliance with “the right to be forgotten.”

(5)List the barriers to adopting of blockchain-based systems in healthcare.
