Chapter 19

Blockchain Applications in Real Estate

Joshua Harris and Ehsan Nikbakht

Kewords Blockchain; real estate; mortgage proesses; title insurance; closings; underwriting loans; investment management

Introduction

Properly understanding the potential for blockchain applications within the real estate industry requires grasping the unique and complex nature of real property. Real estate or real property is an alternative investment, which is a separate asset class distinct from traditional assets such as stock and bonds, acquired and managed by its own set of norms, laws, procedures, and standards. Fig. 19.1 shows the steps in a typical real estate transaction. After the first step ‒ negotiations between a buyer and a seller for the price and terms agreement ‒ the process goes through a complicated and time-consuming sequence of events including but not limited to the following: exchanging comments between the attorneys, conducting engineering inspections, signing a contract before a final closing, making escrow deposits, issuing bank appraisal and underwriting loans, ordering title insurance and verifications, satisfying local/state code requirements and variances, receiving loan approvals, obtaining insurance, and executing a closing to transfer the property. The purpose of this chapter is to examine possible applications of blockchain in real estate and discuss the issues and challenges involved in these implementations.

Fig. 19.1. Anatomy of a Real Estate Deal. Note: This figure shows that a typical real estate transaction goes through 12 sequential steps starting with buyer and seller negotiation and ending with a final closing.

Real property or real estate is commonly referred to as a “bundle of rights” associated with or pertaining to a physical piece of land, structure, and improvements (Union Test Prep 2020). Real property includes deeded interests, which are legally referred as “estates,” mortgages encumbering real property, as well as transferences of rights to use and enjoy real property such as leases and easements. All blockchain applications discussed in this chapter relate to one or more of these forms of real property. Thus, any blockchain application developer must understand the legal elements of any property interest for which the developer wants to enhance via a blockchain application. The laws and regulations of the federal government, the 50 states plus the District of Columbia, and each county and city in which the property is located may affect the ownership, transference, and management of these various real property interests. This situation leads to the first challenge any viable blockchain application must meet ‒ identifying the underlying asset that goes through transaction and subsequent processes.

Issues and Challenges

The following section provides a discussion of some issues and challenges in adopting blockchain technology in the real estate industry including the case of the parcel locations, titles and proof of claim, obligation to real property asses, and property records.

The Case of Parcel Location and Data Management

Successfully deploying a blockchain application to an aspect of the real estate industry requires a linkage of the real property interest to be transacted or managed to its physical parcel. In other words, a property should be matched with (linked to) the location of each specific physical asset. For most properties in the United States, the most reliable, consistent property information record resides at the county level, typically in a property tax assessor's office. This situation is due to the fact that nearly all local and state jurisdictions in the United States impose an ad valorem tax at the individual parcel level. An ad valorem taxis a tax whose amount is based on the value of a transaction or property. The process of recording might be fairly simple, yet in many cases still a complex and an apt opportunity for a public blockchain application involving the creation of a unified, nationwide parcel identification network from which additional records, such as ownership and encumbrances, could be added and maintained. To create a single record, a county property assessor typically generates a unique identification code for each parcel or property it taxes. These codes can go by many names such as a parcel identification number or something similar. Mailing addresses, which are used by the US Postage Service, are wholly inadequate for uniquely defining a legally identifiable parcel of real property. These addresses are more of arbitrary designations of the post office and local municipalities such as conformity to location systems used by emergency responders to a 911 call.

The only immutable identification that could have any potential for nationwide standardization of parcel identification is likely a system based on geographic identification with map-based coordinates such as latitudes and longitudes. Latitude and longitude are two-dimensional, but parcel identification can require additional dimensions such as unit number in apartment and condominium projects. Blockchain application developers should strongly consider using latitudes and longitudes as part of a system of parcel identification. The process of taking addresses, property legal descriptions, and local jurisdictional boundaries and geocoding them, which is the process of standardizing the data entries by latitude and longitude, has largely been accomplished by many private vendors and public entities. Of course, a parcel's physical identification is only the first step in creating a unified real property identification system, which could serve as a backbone to further blockchain-enabled applications.

Chain of Title and Proof of Claim of Real Property Assets

The challenge of proving ownership and transferring ownership of real property assets is as old as the concept of private ownership of property. In feudal times, all land was generally deemed owned by the king or kingdom and thus the right to use was by royal decree or some functional equivalency. Unlike other physical goods, the doctrine of possession as proof of ownership is far from sufficient or even practical for real property. To illustrate the point, assume that a person living in a house may be a renter subject to a lease, an owner in fee simple (legal phrase roughly meaning “sole owner”), or an owner subject to any myriad of restrictions, encumbrances, and limitations such as a mortgage pledged to a financial institution. This situation creates a unique challenge, which is generally solved in a practical means that many blockchain enthusiasts can appreciate.

The general solution employed in most local jurisdictions in the United States is proof of ownership and encumbrances via the keeping and inspection of governmentally administered official records. Any deed, note, mortgage, easement, or other document affecting the title of a parcel of real property is generally recorded in the official records of a local jurisdiction, typically the county. The instrument recorded is placed in the official records via an identification system such as book and page and then stamped with the time and date of the official moment of recording. Time is a crucial determinant in the validity or priority of a lien or deed type record. In fact, most laws of title operate on a “first in time, first in line” doctrine. This record, which is publicly viewable to anyone by law, becomes the basis for the “chain of title,” which can be used to prove ownership of interests in real property. A county's official records maintain records that crudely resemble a form of a centralized public blockchain.

For proving or even determining ownership, a person or entity would need to review the entire set of public records to link each transfer document, usually called a “deed,” from owner to owner to establish whether the person or entity claiming ownership has legally defensible ownership. This search process would also reveal any and all deficiencies to “free and clear ownership” such as active mortgages, liens, and easements. Thus, the “title” to the property is not a single record, such as is the case with an automobile, but instead a collection of all the documents proving ownership. An entire industry exists of title abstractors, title insurers, and real estate lawyers who solely specialize in this process for the benefit of those transacting or financing real property assets. Any successful blockchain application for real estate must work within this framework or otherwise encapsulate its records and processes to be fully functional.

As a final note on title and ownership, the physical nature of parcels is neither fixed nor immutable. A parcel of land can be split or subdivided, and ownership interests can be fractionalized or otherwise subdivided, which is an extreme case of a deeded week timeshare. When this situation occurs, a deed containing the new legal descriptions, which is a means of physically identifying the parcel, of the split parcel is filed in the official records. Thus, any system of blockchain-enabled property records must encompass this complexity into any single parcel record. The final element of a real property ownership is the parties owning or having an interest in each parcel.

Parties with Interests or Obligations to Real Property Assets

Blockchain application developers looking to service the real estate industry can do so by facilitating or improving some aspect of an asset's transaction or operation. Several potential applications are discussed below. However, proper identification of the parties that own, use, have related interests, or are bound to provide services to a property could be required for a fully functioning record of a real property asset to be used in future applications. The first set of relevant parties can be called owners, meaning those who own the ultimate equity in the real property asset. They generally prove or receive such ownership via a recorded deed. The second set can be defined as users or more commonly tenants who receive their interest via leases, which are signed privately but are rarely ever recorded in public records. The third set is those with ownership of encumbrances upon real property such as mortgages and liens. These interests are generally recorded in the public records in the same location as the deeds are recorded. However, this situation is not always the case. A lien or encumbrance can be created and thus binding to the real property by action of law; a bankruptcy judgment against an owner of property is one such example. Although a publicly available legal record may exist, it may not be in the same jurisdiction and frequently does not reference the parcel(s), which are now legally encumbered by its existence.

This last point is important as it explains the existence and value of the title insurance industry. Title insurance companies and their lawyers extensively scan all relevant public records by parcel as well as by owners and past owners of the parcel to determine if any such “unrecorded” liens or judgments exist. Protection against an error in this search process is one item “insured” by title insurance in addition to potential fraud or error in a past conveyance or other record of the parcel being insured. Many of the missions of blockchain startups focused on real estate have been aimed at improving the efficiency, cost, and speed of real estate transactions. The difficulty of proof of clear ownership to transfer cannot be understated. Any successful venture must account for these realities. For a blockchain property record to be complete, it must include a proper indexing and record of all current and past owners and holders of liens and encumbrances.

One final set of parties that could be tracked with respect to real estate is the set of entities who are obligated to provide critical service to the property. These parties include local municipalities, state agencies (e.g., water management districts and other special purpose agencies), utility companies, and insurance companies (e.g., fire insurance and personal liability coverage) to name a few. Although a blockchain-enabled property record system could function without tracking these items, the more complete the record the more commercial value any such system can provide. For example, financial institutions lending on mortgages on real property need to know if the property is insured against causalities, whether they are a named insured, and if the local property taxes are paid current on an ongoing basis. Ling and Archer (2017) provide a complete review of the nature of real property. Hypothetically, blockchain applications could be used to improve, simplify, and more efficiently execute these tasks. To make such improvements possible, the property record must contain the relevant information on an up-to-date basis.

Blockchain-powered Real Property Records

As discussed, real property records are complex, fractured, and subject to local nuance and legalities. As such, a commercially viable, unified real property record system could be a blockchain application with high levels of value creation by itself. Private entities, such as CoreLogic and Zillow, are building or have built such databases for commercial purposes (Zillow 2020). The value of the data created and captured has proven to be highly monetizable. For the development of blockchain applications for real estate, such a blockchain-powered real property record system may be required. In fact, imagining a successful system without one would be difficult. Further, the vast majority of the items discussed herein are contained in databases or systems that are open to the public by law. Thus, a blockchain application developer could theoretically connect all of the various data points from their various sources and produce a single blockchain record without the need of obtaining permissions or submissions from all the owners of the data or the real property assets themselves. The remainder of this chapter presumes that such a blockchain-backed property record system exists and is usable for the applications to be discussed. In practice, application developers should keep in mind the reality of data limitations when determining the functional scope and scale of any individual blockchain application for real estate.

Blockchain Applications for the Main Areas of Real Estate Transactions

Improving the means for consummating real estate transactions is a clear opportunity for blockchain applications. The process of transacting real estate can be exceptionally costly and time consuming due to the fractured and complex nature of real property as well as the localized nature of property. Compared to other areas of the economy, such as financial services, much room is available for improvement. The three main areas of real estate transactions open for development and implementation of blockchain applications include the (1) search process, (2) due diligence process, and (3) the closing process, which are all interrelated and discussed below.

As Fig. 19.1 shows, before commencing a real property transaction, a buyer and seller must locate each other and arrive at mutually agreeable terms to consummate the transaction. Historically, licensed real estate agents who serve buyers and sellers of property have managed this process. Real estate agents can charge between 3 and 6 percent of the gross sales price for their services, which are typically delivered personally to each buyer and seller and are quite time consuming. Interestingly, what has empowered the need to hire a real estate agent when selling a property has been the need to have the agent place the property as available for sale in an often-proprietary system generally called a multiple listing service (MLS), which is a database established by cooperating real estate brokers to provide data about properties for sale. Most MLS systems are privately owned by a local board of realtors and thus only member realtors can place a listing in the MLS. This situation gives the realtor great control of the information efficiency of available homes for sale. Furthermore, the rules of most MLS systems require the seller to pay a commission to both the listing agent and any “cooperating” agent who brings a buyer. Although the internet has leveled the information asymmetry somewhat, private MLS systems are still the dominant means of finding buyers for property in most markets nationwide. As such, a blockchain has the potential to enable the system for matching buyers and sellers and to create value and lower costs for facilitating the search process. Via websites like Zillow, buyers can already enjoy this open access but sellers still face relative disadvantages for not listing with a realtor. In fact, most real estate websites receive data feeds from the various realtor-controlled MLS systems.

A functional system that allowed sellers to list their homes for sale, buyers to present their desire to buy, and parameters on which they are searching such as price, size, and location could allow for new, more efficient forms of real estate transactions. Smart contracts and other elements of a blockchain-enabled value chain could further enhance this system. Finally, success in this domain need not mean eliminating or circumventing real estate agents. The complexities of property could always lead to the desire of buyers and sellers to have personal representation and consultation during real estate transactions. Blockchain applications could make these professions more efficient and proficient.

After a buyer and seller have agreed upon a contract for sale, a process known as due diligence occurs where assumptions of the buyer and representations by the seller are confirmed. Once due diligence is complete, the transaction can close and ownership is transferred. Many details must be verified and validated during due diligence. These discussions are generally done with limited technological assistance.

Blockchain could enhance the process in at least two distinct ways. First, a trusted, complete record of past transactions and records could be reviewed more efficiently via a blockchain reducing the time and cost of such reviews. Title insurance companies do much of this work as part of issuing title insurance. In fact, the bulk of the cost of title insurance is generally to pay the cost of a professional's time to actually “check title” before issuing the insurance commitment. In theory, the cost of title insurance could be reduced substantially if the title could be verified via a blockchain instead of the costly, inefficient process discussed previously. Although insurance against fraud and prior errors would still be required (Lulich 2018), the likelihood of error by the title searcher could be reduced. This approach alone could save thousands of dollars per transaction.

The second way blockchain could improve the due diligence process is by maintaining a record of physical due diligence steps and other elements of transaction management for the benefit of the buyer, lender, and closing agent. Physical condition assessments are generally performed, as are termite and pest inspections and other similar consultations, to determine the property's quality at the time of sale. These reports are generally shared between the buyer and vendor of each service but must often be transmitted to the lender for that party's own due diligence. A blockchain application could make this process more efficient, less costly, and improve trust in future transactions for the lender and buyer when they sell the property. Blockchain technology can also enhance and facilitate the security process regardless of functions and activities involved (Milani, Garcia-Banulos, and Dumas 2018).

Overall, a blockchain-based property record could be appended and updated with information procured during due diligence. This updated information has value to future buyers, lenders such as during a refinance transaction, insurance underwriters, and others. At present, no efficient means is available of passing this information in a trusted system from buyer to future buyer or lender. The result is the costly and time-consuming process of redoing aspects of due diligence for each transaction. Although this process is somewhat unavoidable due to the physical nature of real estate, transactions such as mortgage refinancing could see substantially lower due diligence and closing costs if efficient blockchains could retain the information from the past transaction in a trusted manner.

The recording and ownership records of real property are relatively inefficient and substantially antiquated when compared to other financial transactions. In most counties, deeds are still physically delivered by courier, who is an employee of the closing agent, to the official record-keeping office for recording. Official records are generally digitized in most jurisdictions, but they cannot be uniformly searched through or retrieved as all the counties systems are not linked. This situation leads to a potential for a replacement system based on a public blockchain.

A public blockchain that replaced, or at least supplemented, the official records of counties would be a major breakthrough for the real estate industry. The value creation would be immense as it could vastly lower the cost of maintaining such records while improving their accuracy and efficiency for use in future transactions. Human error in the recording office is still a major source of errors in official records leading to claims against title insurance policies. Further, if real property ownership records could be placed onto a public blockchain, the entire process of closing and financing real estate could conceivably be revamped and made more efficient. Implementation is far more challenging due to the fractured nature of the records and the multitude of jurisdictions and laws in place.

Blockchain Applications for Real Estate Finance

Real estate is a unique asset class in part because debt financing is readily available for transactions of all sizes including single-family homes to large multibillion-dollar portfolios. Further, the amount of financing can routinely reach 80 percent above the value or purchase price, especially in residential mortgage financing, thus making the lender the largest stakeholder by dollar volume at the time of the transaction. Further, since mortgage financing is more standardized than deeds and ownership, and generally subject to less fractured regulation, envisioning blockchain applications for real estate finance is easier than other segments. In fact, the residential mortgage industry has relied on the Mortgage Electronic Registration System, Inc. (MERS) to facilitate electronic record keeping and management of mortgage assets by lenders for decades to overcome the inefficiencies of the local mortgage recording and transfer systems. In many ways, MERS acts like a centralized, private blockchain of mortgage data for use by loan servicers and investors/traders of loans in the secondary market. The three main areas for potential development of blockchain applications in real estate finance are mortgage origination, mortgage servicing, and secondary market operations. Blockchain technology is now transcending its classic boundaries such as applications for bitcoin and other assets (Crosby, Nachiappan, Pattanayak, Verma, and Kalyanaraman 2016). Real estate could be a good example of a new domain, relatively unexplored, for this emerging technology.

The most successful blockchain operation is one that would cover all three functional areas seamlessly. The blockchains that would best power mortgage operations may need to be kept private due to the sensitive nature of the data. However, both borrower and lender would benefit from the sharing of these data to future lenders/loan buyers and certain third parties so accessibility by permission should be a core feature. The entire mortgage process could conceivably be replaced or revamped as a blockchain-enabled smart contract where all steps of the loan's life are managed via a blockchain. Although such an application could require substantial changes in law and regulation as well as in consumer perception, it is within possibility. The real estate industry is going through a series of innovative technology disruptions, which create both risks and opportunities in the years ahead for both domestic and global markets (Cbinsights 2019).

Blockchain Applications for Mortgage Originations

The costliest, most time consuming, and complex aspect of financing real estate is the originations process where new loans are created and funded. This process involves analyzing the borrower to make an initial lending decision, examining and verifying the value and details of the property, closing and recording the loan in the local public records, and creating and maintaining the closed data file for secondary trading of the loan. All of these processes are data intensive. In fact, the mere existence of blockchain-enabled property record systems as already discussed could greatly enhance the expediency of approving a loan by keeping so much information in verified form in one location. The merger of the borrower's private data, such as credit and income, along with appraisal and valuation data of the property, could create a mortgage “file” in the blockchain that would hypothetically make the underwriting process far *simpler and more accurate. The result could be lower origination costs, reduced processing time, and lower defaults from errors and fraud. On net, taking these actions could reduce the cost of financing to the borrower in the form of lower interest rates and fees. Further, a blockchain system could also be used to enhance the search process between the lender and borrower, which is a similar issue as discussed regarding the sale of property. Mortgage origination is possibly the segment of the real estate industry currently most open and ready to implement blockchain applications. In financial services, including real estate mortgages, the value-added feature of innovative technological advances such as blockchain could substantially affect the success of all parties involved (Crosby et al. 2016).

Blockchain Applications for Mortgage Servicing

After the loan is closed or originated, it must be serviced. Servicing refers to collecting payments from the borrower, paying taxes and insurance from escrow or maintaining proof of such payments being made each year, and transferring funds to the loan's owner, which can change frequently due to secondary market transactions. The process is relatively simple for a performing loan but is data intense and potentially costlier than needed. An efficient blockchain could reduce the labor and effort in loan servicing. Although the gains from improvement are perhaps minimal in this function, any successful mortgage finance blockchain needs to account for the servicing operations as it links originations to all future tasks and could facilitate low cost refinancing transactions by having complete data files readily accessible. Further, when special situations occur, such as payment default or insurance loss, the blockchain could greatly enhance the efficiency by which the servicer manages these situations. Even simple processes like ordering loan payoffs for sale and refinance transactions could operate more smoothly and less costly if servicing the loan occurred via a private blockchain.

Blockchain Applications for Secondary Market Operations

A factor making residential, and increasingly commercial, loans so low cost on a relative basis to borrowers is the ability to sell, trade, and bundle them into securities post closing. The liquid nature of individual loans makes them relatively more valuable than other real property assets and a deep industry of traders and investors exists to facilitate these markets. Given the use of systems such as MERS, stems that trade mortgages via a blockchain could plausibly be successful. The linkage of a mortgage's “trading file” with its origination and servicing data files would greatly improve trust and transparency between the buyer and seller of the loan and reduce the risk of fraud and error. Further, the blockchain could facilitate the trade via a less costly, more efficient settlement mechanism than currently available. The net result could lower costs for all steps along the mortgage finance value chain all the way back to origination (Pauw 2018). Brueggeman and Fisher (2018) offer a more complete understanding of real estate finance and mortgage operations.

Blockchain Applications to Real Estate Operations

Given the size and scale of real estate operations, meaning the daily leasing, property management, and investment management tasks, blockchain applications could possibly improve various aspects to benefit all parties. On a relative basis, these applications may be easier to implement than the ones in previous sections as they have much fewer legal and regulatory burdens to overcome. Yet, they would require substantial change in current procedures that many owners may not see as inefficient. The three main areas for potential development of blockchain applications in real estate operations are property management and leasing, physical maintenance and monitoring, and investment management and reporting.

Blockchain Applications for Property Management and Leasing

With approximately one-third of all households renting their residence and most commercial real estate being leased by the businesses that use them, property management and leasing are major tasks associated with real estate investing that must be carried out at millions of individual properties nationwide. Blockchain applications could connect and standardize the data across multiple properties and tenants for better management by the property owner. Such clean data could be used for better investment and asset management decisions. Further, leasing of properties faces the same search process considerations described in the earlier section on search process of transactions. Finally, the lease itself could be revamped as a blockchain-enabled smart contract, which is also far easier to conceive than with mortgages due to the less regulated nature of leases and landlord–tenant relationships. In fact, digital signing of leases is becoming commonplace in residential apartment leasing, making the transition to smart contracts relatively feasible today. A blockchain can also monitor payment performance by tenants creating a record that could benefit the tenant in future transactions and assist the landlord in future leasing decisions. Salustri (2018) provides a review of blockchain uses in property management.

Blockchain Applications for Physical Maintenance and Monitoring

Owners of real estate face the challenge of maintaining and monitoring the physical condition of the property they own. This task is compounded in difficulty for remote located owners with large portfolios. Owner/investors often rely on third-party property managers and maintenance companies to do this work on their behalf. Unfortunately, work is not always performed to schedule, resulting in costlier repairs buildup over time. Devices and systems that monitor building status and maintenance logs could conceivably be connected to a blockchain application that would create a record of service on the property and potentially alert the owner to impending issues or overdue maintenance items via smart contract type functionality. Further, this property log could be allowed for inspection by passive investors and future buyers increasing their trust in the owner/manager and enhancing overall returns and values. The type of technological enhancements to building systems needed to generate the data that are being installed and remote management and monitoring has already been greatly enhanced. Thus, blockchain applications may allow these data to be better shared for enhanced valuation creation and cost reductions (Saleem 2018). An example includes the monitoring and sharing of energy use and environmental data with various agencies and stakeholders. Many cities are passing laws and regulations meant to curtail energy use. Thus, building owners are likely to have a greater need to prove they are meeting energy saving mandates. A blockchain application could be the solution.

Blockchain Applications for Investment Management and Reporting

Interest and demand for real estate investments has been increasing for decades. The Jumpstart Our Business Startups Act or JOBS Act of 2012 created pathways for more individual investors of all wealth levels to invest in real estate deals and funds via mechanisms like crowdfunding (Lynn and Pinedo 2012). The rollout of real estate crowdfunding platforms, deals, and funds has been slow but increasing. One challenge has been the investment management and reporting required between the deal sponsors and the passive investors. A lack of trust and infrastructure exists to facilitate these processes. Blockchain applications could possibly be used to administer the investments of a crowdsourced real estate fund by integrating with property management and other systems. A hypothetical system would allow groups of small investors to fund deal via a blockchain-powered smart contract and/or “tokenized” means of ownership. The same blockchain system could then be used for periodic reporting and payment distributions. It could also be used for secondary market transactions of the investment interests by the passive investors. In fact, the lack of liquidity and ability to sell these investments midterm is a major roadblock to achieving scale for the industry (Bodner 2018). These blockchain-enabled secondary markets could be a standalone service for the transactions of other private real estate investments without any other blockchain functionality.

In this regard, the potential for real estate investing to be enhanced via blockchain applications is like other opportunities found in financial markets and investment products. Real estate may be more in need on a relative basis due to the size and complexity of real estate transactions. Stocks and bonds are far more easily traded, especially in small increments. Other than publicly traded real estate investment trusts (REITs), no practical means is available of trading or transacting partial interests in privately held real estate assets.

Summary and Conclusions

Real estate is an immensely complex asset class that touches the everyday lives of nearly every household, business, and investor. Because owning and transacting in the asset class can be slow, costly, and complex, it is ripe for improvement via blockchain applications. The first step to successful blockchain application development for the real estate industry is creating a parcel identification and data management system from which transactional and relational data can be appended. From there, applications can be deployed to improve real estate transactions, the real estate finance and mortgage system, title search and insurance, closings, and real estate operations and management. In some domains, such as real estate finance and investment, new subindustries such as secondary trading of crowdsourced equity investments could be created using blockchain applications as the backbone infrastructure. Succeeding in the practical launch and implementation of commercially viable blockchain applications for the real estate industry may neither be easy nor without major challenges. Yet, it offers potential profitability to those who manage to solve the unique challenges the industry and real estate asset class have experienced in the market.

Discussion Questions

(1)Discuss the concept of proving (verifying) real estate ownership.

(2)Identify a major challenge for using blockchain in real estate.

(3)Explain debt financing for transactions in real estate.

(4)Explain the use of blockchain in mortgage services.

(5)Indicate how blockchain may reduce the challenge of maintaining and monitoring the physical conditions of a real estate property.

Chapter 20

Blockchain Applications in Supply Chain

Kaushik Sengupta

Keywords: Blockchain; supply chain; smart contracts; RFID; TradeLens; food trust

Introduction

Since the invention of the blockchain technology and introduction of bitcoin in 2008 (Nakamoto 2008), researchers and corporations have been looking at adopting the technology in the supply chain space. Adoption of this technology is still new. Although many companies are in the early stages of determining the paths to adopting this technology, studies indicate the potential of adopting blockchain (Moore 2018). Given that the technology provides the potential for major benefits across multiple companies within a supply chain, the future of adopting blockchains in supply chains looks promising (Pawczuk, Massey, and Schatsky 2018).

Adopting blockchain technology in supply chains has the potential to generate substantial benefits for companies in the supply chain.Current supply chains, with their distributed systems of intracompany enterprise planning systems, do not integrate seamlessly across disparate systems. Even where such systems are connected through interfaces, transaction records reside in multiple systems, and no single mechanism ensures that the data at any particular point in the supply chain are accurate. Likewise, no mechanism controls changes to the information related to a product entity from the stage where the product's components are sourced to its assembly stages to the distribution stages. A company in such a supply chain can alter the information related to the product based on its own needs and issues. Other companies in the supply chain that are either upstream or downstream of this specific company can do the same. However, all companies in the supply chain would have to rely on the information provided by the other supply chain partners without a recourse to any assurance that the information is accurate. As a result, many cases of fraud, deceptive practices, and risks exist across many supply chains (Hoffman 2008; Cohn 2016).

Blockchain technology, through its distributed ledger system that is transparent to all partners in a supply chain, would go a long way in mitigating such risks. In such a system, the data reside on a distributed system that is visible to all supply chain partners. More importantly, any changes made by a company to a specific data cannot be done without other partners in the supply chain agreeing to or signing off on the change. Such a process is known as the consensus mechanism used by the blockchain in question. This irrefutable nature of the data in a blockchain through the interconnected blocks largely removes any data tampering and fraud issues. Therefore, the advantages in this area would be substantial. Other than data accuracy, additional benefits would accrue from reducing inventory and lead times thereby resulting in more accurate forecasts making the demand–supply matching problem easier to resolve for many companies. The advantages from adopting the blockchain technology in supply chains are apparent to many companies, and the industry has already started to recognize this potential (Furlonger and Kandaswamy 2018). Some early research studies already highlight other derived benefits such as a better way of tracking sustainability efforts and quality (Saberi, Kouhizadeh, Sarkis, and Shen 2019; Manupati et al. 2020).

Although the initial trends show promise of adopting the technology, many companies have also been cautious of jumping into full-scale implementations (Queiroz and Wamba 2019). Companies currently grapple with several issues when making the decision. Some key issues relate to the return on investment (ROI), what happens to current technologies, trust among supply chain partners, and top management support.

The purpose of this chapter is to provide an overview of the application of blockchain technology in supply chains as well as the expected trends and current issues related to this topic. The chapter is organized as follows. The next section provides a background on how blockchain technology is applied in the supply chain context. Areas of benefits are then highlighted including specific cases where blockchains could have major benefits for the supply chain. Subsequently, the chapter provides a discussion of related issues: (1) the role of existing technologies in a blockchain environment, (2) the role of smart contracts in the blockchain, (3) the adoption path of the technology and how issues related to interorganizational integration and trust are key factors in this adoption, and (4) the importance of top management support. Lastly, the chapter concludes with a summary and closing questions.

Blockchain in the Supply Chain Context

Blockchain originated from the digital currency aspect with the seminal contribution from Nakamoto (2008). However, much of the blockchain technology has little to do with digital currencies like bitcoin and more to do with the underlying data and framework structure. Thus, blockchains are pertinent for supply chains in this context.

Any supply chain from the raw materials stage to the retail stage encompasses a number of companies and exchange of information. A typical supply chain consists of multiple tiers of suppliers, the original equipment manufacturer (OEM), wholesalers and distributors, and retailers. Obviously in some cases, these stages are merged – for example, when a wholesaler becomes the retailer or when the manufacturer takes the role of a retailer for products that are shipped to customers directly from the factory. Transportation, logistics, and shipping companies form the backbone of many of these stages by providing a vital service of physically moving products.

Traditional supply chains have involved such different companies to interact and exchange information across built-in interfaces where such interfaces can extract information from different database systems existing at the various companies. Enterprise resource planning (ERP) systems were developed to be able to integrate information across multiple functions within an organization. Since these ERP systems became the repository of all information, disparate ERP systems needed to be interfaced to exchange information across supply chain partners. This situation resulted in costly and hard to manage interfaces, and establishing business processes across multiple companies in the supply chain to enable collaboration and exchange of information. Given this technology backbone, a transaction record for a product as it moves through the supply chain gets transmitted across multiple ERP systems through various interfaces. Additionally, all companies involved in this chain add to the existing information and modify the record accordingly based on different needs and priorities. This situation has resulted in a traditional supply chain lacking the visibility across stages. Companies typically do not have visibility beyond one or two stages removed from their own position in the chain (Zelbst, Green, Sower, and Bond 2019).

Blockchain is designed to address the above issue. Since the transaction record in a blockchain environment resides in a unified system, problems associated with reconciling data across multiple systems do not arise. Furthermore, a single company cannot make unilateral changes to the data without an agreement from the other companies in the supply chain. Fig. 20.1 depicts how a blockchain-enabled supply chain would work. The framework shows two supply chain stages where a product is shipped from Supply Chain Stage 1 to Supply Chain Stage 2. So, the two stages could be viewed as two separate companies in consecutive stages in a supply chain with product shipping completed by a distribution logistics partner.

Fig. 20.1. A Blockchain-enabled Supply Chain. Note: This figure shows ageneric framework indicating the various components of a blockchain-enabled supply chain. The two stages can be visualized as two connecting stages with Supply Chain Stage 1 shipping orders to Supply Chain Stage 2. Source: The author.

The blockchain in this case works on a peer-to-peer (P2P) network. This network would be the companies within the supply chain and would typically be a private blockchain or a permissioned blockchain where specific companies are invited to be a part of the blockchain based on their roles in the supply chain. In a supply chain context, a permissioned blockchain would be the standard approach as opposed to a public blockchain where any entity could become a member of the blockchain. A permissioned blockchain would restrict data access to only those members on the blockchain. Such access control is required because of the sensitive nature of the transaction including proprietary and contract-related data shared between supply chain partners.

Once an agreement is reached through the P2P network, the block is initialized, and any transactions related data, as shown in Fig. 20.1, are appended to the block. No central owner of the data exists as data on the block are appended and updated once validation and agreement occur among the block's members. Additional blocks could be added to the initial block when new data need to be added to the transaction record. Here too, the same mechanism of agreement and validation is followed. Once the product reaches Supply Chain Stage 2, the data are validated and appended with specific information as noted. This event triggers a smart contract, which automatically updates any contract-related information on inventories, product specifics, and triggers a payment to Supply Chain Stage 1.

The above framework indicates two pillars of a blockchain within the supply chain context (Cole, Stevenson, and Aitken 2019). First, the data portion of the blocks contains all the pertinent information related to the transaction. The peers within the network validate and approve all updates and additions to the existing data. Additional blocks are created and added to existing blocks as the product and the transaction move through the supply chain. Second, the smart contract portion of the block is an automated mechanism built in as part of the blockchain's capability. A smart contract is an automated trigger that executes a transaction based on the terms and conditions within a buyer–supplier contract. As soon as the product receipt information for a transaction order is updated at the buyer's end, the smart contract factors in the changes to the order including the receipt of the product by the buyer and triggers a payment to the supplier.

The cash conversion cycle (CCC) is an issue in supply chains given the lead time of product delivery where an upstream partner is not paid until the product is delivered to the downstream supply chain partner. The CCC is a metric that expresses how much time the company needs to sell its inventory, how much time it takes to collect receivables, and how much time it has to pay its bills without incurring penalties.In many cases, this situation could easily extend to weeks or months. Apart from the long CCC, the disconnected set of processes adds to the delay since the updates in a non-blockchain system have to be executed on multiple, disconnected ERP systems. Smart contracts eliminate this problem. Automatically triggering of payments based on order receipt through smart contracts reduces the CCC drastically.

The advantages of using the blockchain technology in the supply chain context manifests in multiple ways, as follows.

  • No single company owns the data or can change it unilaterally without validation from the P2P network partners.
  • Errors in transaction records, whether they are accidental or deliberate, are eliminated because of this shared and distributed ledger system.
  • CCC is shorter because of the smart contract-enabled payment triggers.
  • Although shipment lead times are unaffected by moving to a blockchain-based system, the blockchain system leads to more accurate information in the supply chain. This improvement, in turn, increases the accuracy of demand forecasts and reduces inventory levels.

Companies have started realizing these benefits, and the next section highlights how they can realize the benefits of implementing the technology. A cross-industry perspective is provided in these discussions to keep the information generic and applicable across multiple industries.

Areas of Benefits and Improvements

Although some companies have started implementing blockchains for their respective supply chains, research and widespread adoption of the technology is still at an early stage. Case study based methodology is a common approach in early stage research. This approach allows researchers to understand the early adoption scenarios and also helps in building theories for broader understanding of the issues. van Hoek (2020) examines blockchain pilots in three early adopter companies. A systematic review of research studies by Wang, Han, and Beynon-Davis (2019) reveals studies where specific cases have been used as a basis for understanding the early adoption issues. This section discusses supply chain issues that multiple companies across various industries are trying to solve through adopting blockchain in their respective supply chains.

The supply chain issues discussed in this section cover the various roles played by different companies within the context of a supply chain. For instance, a manufacturing company captures issues related to the upstream supply chain (i.e., on the sourcing side). Likewise, a retailer has a role in the downstream supply chain (i.e., on the customer side). A logistics provider captures the role of shipping and distribution companies, which form a vital link in the end-end movement of products in any supply chain. However, many of these typical roles span across the entire supply chain in the attempt of using blockchain as an end-end solution to address several known supply chain issues across multiple industries.

Product Safety and Recalls

Blockchain is designed to address product safety and recalls related issues. With the distributed ledger system, where every company in a supply chain is responsible collectively for the shared information and with the traceability of information, safety and recall issues become easier to identify. As long as the specific cause for a product safety or recall issue is identified, the cause can be traced back to the point in the supply chain where this originated. Since the data related to a product and its associated transactions are stored in the blockchain, this tracing can be executed rapidly, thereby reducing the time of response to any safety or recall issues. Moreover, because of the blockchain's irrefutable nature, a single company cannot unilaterally change or tamper with the existing information in the blocks, making the information required to complete the tracing highly accurate.

Food product safety is a critical example in this context. Industry standards in cases of recalling food products once a problem has been identified are usually a two-hour window from the time of first notification of the recall situation to a complete quarantine of the affected product (Goomas and Ludwig 2017). In reality, this recall latency time is much longer. With blockchain-enabled tracing, the time can be reduced to minutes. Walmart has been working with IBM to trace food products in the supply chain. The pilot started in 2016 with more suppliers getting involved in the study since 2018. Manufacturers such as Dole, Driscoll's, McCormick and Company, Nestle, Tyson Foods, and others are currently involved in the project (IBM 2017). In one such instance with mangoes as the product, the tracing was executed in only 2.2 seconds.

Provenance (2017) was an early adopter role in tracing products in the food supply chains. This social enterprise has had successful pilots in tracing tuna sourcing in Southeast Asia and has been working with a large consumer cooperative to trace fresh produce from farm to the supermarket.

The Walmart pilot has evolved to a more widely available industry solution. IBM Food Trust is a permissioned blockchain, and companies in the food supply chain can apply to be members of this private network (IBM 2019). In fact, building on the initial success, Albertsons, the world's second largest retailer, recently announced that the company is joining the IBM Food Trust Blockchain (Coindesk 2019).

In all these cases, the objective is to be able to trace issues in product safety at a much faster pace than what is currently possible. Although the blockchain technology allows this rapid increase in the response time, it does not stop or prevent the safety issue from appearing. However, the intent for all companies is to create an ecosystem where such rapid traceability becomes the norm. Consequently, the rapid tracing and alert system should make supply chain partners more careful about their practices leading to an eventual, possible reduction of product safety issues.

Global Shipping and Cross-border Logistics

Cross-border logistics and international shipping are a disjointed system of many different trade and shipping companies. This system also entails manual processing, paperwork-based system, and varying cross-border laws and customs. Trade documentation and processing take up to 20 percent of the actual physical transportation cost for consumer goods ( The Economist 2018; IBM 2018). Maersk, the world's largest shipping line, reported in 2014 an instance of 30 different companies and over 200 transactions in a shipment from Africa to Europe ( The Economist 2018). With a $4 trillion industry and 80 percent of all consumer goods shipping handled by the ocean shippers, this industry is a fertile area for implementing a digitized blockchain.

The international shipping industry with its associated trade partners creates a complex network of many companies that rely primarily on manual transactions and paper-based processing at many points in this distribution chain. Lack of end-end visibility and inefficiencies leading to higher costs is an obvious outcome from such a disjointed process.

IBM's initiative with Maersk to create TradeLens (Maersk 2019a) created the industry's first seamless and end-end blockchain platform. This permissioned blockchain is open to any company that wants to become a member and participate in digitizing its shipping supply chain. It has several benefits: a distributed and shared system across multiple companies; a digitized transaction record; real-time traceability of shipments; more accurate estimates of shipping lead times and costs; and an eventual reduction of trade intermediaries and agencies. TradeLens has the potential for revolutionizing the global shipping chain as more companies join the network. With the recent addition of CGA CMA and MSC, two of the world's largest shipping companies, about 50 percent of all global shipping is already on this platform (Maersk 2019b).

A blockchain-based distribution and logistics system would also be an advantage for the manufacturers. The typical lack of visibility for manufacturers beyond one or two immediate supply chain tiers would be largely eliminated. With this system, a consumer goods product company could trace the shipment of its products from the suppliers to the ground transportation company to the ocean liner to the customs warehouse to the retailer. As more inefficiencies are discovered, delays and costs can also be traced to specific points in the supply chain, thereby increasing the visibility and identifying areas where times and costs can be reduced.

Inefficiencies at the shipping ports are a major source of delays and costs, and companies are already starting to realize the benefits of blockchain implementation. Several initiatives have been launched in the global shipping industry that is using the blockchain technology. Hyundai Merchant Marine (HMM 2017) reported successful pilot tracing shipping containers from South Korea's Busan port to China's Qingdao port. Marine Insight (2019) reports several initiatives by different companies and consortia to establish blockchain-based platforms. These initiatives include pilot projects using the Ethereum blockchain, establishing the TradeLens platform, launching of the Silsal platform by Abu Dhabi ports and EY's marine insurance blockchain platform. Furthermore, several of the world's top ocean carriers and shipping ports established the Global Shipping Business Network (GSBN), an open platform based on the distributed ledger concept (Marine Insight 2018).

The benefits accrued collectively and individually by companies in the global shipping and logistics industry by adopting a blockchain-based platform are obvious to many such companies, which is a primary reason so many developments have occurred over the last several years. Some of these blockchains could become so prevalent that they evolve into an industry standard. Companies that are not a part of these solutions must then decide if they should become members of these networks to sustain themselves in the evolving logistics chain. Except for the GSBN consortium, all of the other current platforms are permissioned blockchains, so companies must seek out memberships to be a part of these networks.

Although development is needed and would benefit all supply chain partners, two aspects are important to consider. First, the future role of trade agencies and intermediaries is debatable. At present, many of these trade intermediaries exist because of the disjointed structure of a shipping chain and the presence of a myriad of cross-border laws, customs, and processing requirements. With a seamless end-to-end shipping supply chain and a shared, distributed ledger, trade intermediaries may not be needed anymore. Second, recent development shows the emergence of several blockchain platforms such as TradeLens, FoodTrust, CargoX, ShipChain, and many others. These platforms have used either the IBM Hyperledger Fabric blockchain or the Ethereum blockchain. Looking at the various developments and growing consortiums/networks, the global logistics network may end up with several such blockchain-based solutions. Therefore, a manufacturing company would need to be a member on several such networks depending on the sourcing and distribution networks of their products. So, while any number of such blockchains would be superior to the current system of manual transactions across disconnected systems, companies may still have to deal with different blockchain platforms if they need to be a part of several such networks. This situation is not a drawback by any means but differs from realizing a singular, end-end supply chain that many manufacturers crave for ease of product planning and supply.

Current and Emerging Adoption and Implementation Issues

The examples relating to product tracing and recalls as well as to applying blockchain to cross-border logistics highlight where the blockchain technology can be applied, and companies can get the benefits from such a distributed and shared system. Given the early stages in the adoption process of the technology, companies are grappling with several issues to determine the path forward. This section discusses some of these key issues.

Role of Existing Technologies

Although blockchain adoption in the supply chain has potential benefits, uncertainty surrounding specific ROI becomes a key factor for companies. Given the early stage adoption status, some concerns exist as to whether blockchain is overhyped to the same extent as some of the previous technological advancements (Verhoeven, Sinn, and Herden 2018). Therefore, a key success factor with blockchain technology involves whether companies can use their existing technologies with the platform. Two widely used technologies implemented by companies as a response to technological developments in the supply chain are radio-frequency identification (RFID) and enterprise resource planning (ERP) systems.

RFID

Developers of RFID in the late 1990s and early 2000s viewed it as an enhanced system of storing product related information and tracking products as they moved through the supply chain. The primary advantage of RFID over the existing barcode-based technology lies in the ability to scan RFID tags based on the radio-frequency instead of the “sight-based” scanning in barcodes. This technology made scanning with RFID easier resulting in more accurate information. During the early years of RFID adoption, much institutional pressure existed on many companies to adopt the new technology (Lee and Ozer 2007). Many companies also faced customer-initiated directives that they had to follow to maintain the business relationship. Some of these pressures did not leave a positive attitude toward RFID in many companies.

Given this experience, companies may be wary of adopting blockchain as the next hype to be emphasized. Comparing the implementation of RFID to that of blockchain, the latter has a much larger footprint. In RFID, the information is stored mostly on the company's systems and shared with immediate supply chain partners. In blockchain, this information would be stored on a distributed and shared system, owned by all entities in the supply chain. Since the ROI is uncertain, this issue concerns many managers (van Hoek 2019).

However, unlike in the case of RFID, the initiative for implementing blockchain is not coming from the customers (van Hoek 2019). Being able to apply their RFID system to the blockchain platform would be more palatable for companies. The RFID tags already contain various information about the products. So, if this information can be extended to the supply chain on the distributed blockchain system, then companies could leverage the installed RFID technology on the blockchain platform.

ERP Systems

Like RFID, the ability of companies to use their existing ERP system infrastructure on the blockchain platform is a key issue for many companies. ERP systems have a large install base, and companies who have invested in such systems want to bring the blockchain technology to their ERP systems (Harpham 2018).

ERP systems are inherently inward facing. That is, they are built for the enterprise to bring all the data from different functions within the organization to one centralized system. Any information sharing and collaboration needed to execute supply chain processes between two companies are accomplished through application programming interfaces (APIs), which are the programming interface to extract and use data from multiple ERP systems. In many ways, bringing the blockchain to the ERP system would be possible where the ERP system within an organization would still be the backend system for data access. With an overlying blockchain layer, the traceability aspects of information would then be added to the capabilities of the ERP system. Data needed for execution of the interorganization supply chain processes resides on the blockchain layer and the ERP system within the organization would interface with the blockchain to transmit information to and from within the organization to the blockchain. As such, a need exists to develop APIs that would integrate the blockchain with the ERP system. In the end, these APIs would essentially bring the traceability aspects of supply chain specific data to the ERP systems (Banerjee 2018).

Transaction Automation through Smart Contracts

The role of smart contracts (SCs) outlines how SCs provide the automated capabilities of triggering and processing supply chain transactions on a blockchain enabled system. Payments for order transactions based on the terms and conditions in a buyer–supplier contract are executed upon receipt and verification of the order by the buyer. In a traditional supply chain, this event requires processing and verification of transactions over multiple disjointed systems and the involvement of multiple trade intermediaries. In a blockchain system, the information is shared and maintained on a central ledger system. Therefore, any updates to the transaction can be executed in an automated manner. Additionally, the supply chain partners can collectively ratify any validations for changes in order information. Therefore, once the product is delivered to the buyer, automatic triggers based on the conditions in the contract can initiate the payment to the supplier. Such automatic triggers, which form the basis of the SCs, make payments much faster solely due to the distributed and shared ledger system in a blockchain.

As such, the way SCs are designed, no human intervention is necessary to execute the payment after the product has been received. Programmatic codes could make the changes and trigger the payments. However, companies should be aware of potential issues in the proper execution of SCs. According to Greenspan (2016), SCs are just blocks of codes, and an automated trigger assumes that funds are actually available for the transaction. Furthermore, the information contained in a SC may have potential legal issues related to contract law (Smart Contracts Alliance 2016). The sharing of SC related information across multiple supply chain partners in a blockchain smart contract leads to the irrefutability of information in the contract, which could also run into regulatory and compliance issues. Given the nascent stage at which the practical manifestation of SCs are in a blockchain-enabled supply chain, companies must recognize these potential issues.

Trust among Supply Chain Partners

Mutual trust among organizations in a supply chain is critical for any supply chain to function properly. In traditional supply chains, most of a company's information resides in its ERP systems. Data related to supply chain collaboration shared with the company's supply chain partners are limited to demand and supply forecasts and transaction data when a batch or order of products are manufactured/shipped. Additionally, known intermediaries such as financial institutions, trade partners, and government agencies handle transaction-related reconciliation and disputes.

With blockchain, much of these data is shared with the company's supply chain partners. Sharing mutual information automatically creates a notion of trust among the supply chain partners. Trust is the backbone for a blockchain. Because it requires a distributed ledger, a consensus must exist among the supply chain partners regarding the shared data. Once posted on the blockchain, the data cannot be altered without mutual consent among all entities on the blockchain (Chang, Iakovou, and Shi 2020). Therefore, a situation involving mutual disagreement or lack of trust among the supply chain partners could lead to a scenario where the blockchain fails to work.

Top Management Support

Like with any new technology in its early adoption stages, successful implementation of a blockchain-enabled supply chain requires active support from a company's top management (Clohessy and Acton 2019). From the blockchain perspective, this support is even more important because of the requirement of discussions and mutual agreements among management of the participating companies on various items: (1) compliance requirements regarding data sharing, (2) identification of roles in the permissioned environment, (3) smart contract logic for the automated transactions, (4) policies for admitting new members, and (5) agreement with the underlying technology provider for the blockchain platform. Top management would have to determine the company's technology readiness to adopt blockchain and also if the current systems have an affinity toward adopting the new system (Wong, Tan, Lee, Ooi, and Sohal 2020). In a study by van Hoek (2020) on early adopters of blockchain in the supply chain space, managers highlighted this factor as a key determinant of ensuring eventual success of blockchain's rollout.

Summary and Conclusions

The application of blockchain has tremendous potential for supply chains. Traditional supply chains have been notorious for disconnected systems across the companies, lack of visibility, inefficiencies in distribution and logistics, and long payment cycles. Such supply chain networks consist of a large, geographically distributed system where the companies usually do not trust other companies in the network. Additionally, no single company knows the end-end supply chain of its products, and fraud/counterfeiting is a persistent issue that everyone knows about but no one can solve. A seamless system that is shared and distributed across all supply chain partners and where no single company can unilaterally change any of the data provides a unique option for mitigating many of the current problems.

In many ways, the concept of the blockchain from a supply chain perspective is fairly straightforward. As a product is manufactured, assembled, and distributed from one end of the supply chain at the raw material stage to the opposite end of the chain at the retailer, the product moves through multiple companies and locations. As the product moves through the supply chain, transaction data related to the product, usually as part of the order or batch, changes, and new data are appended to the existing data. Sharing all these data on a distributed ledger where none of the companies unilaterally own the ledger creates visibility, traceability, and accountability among the companies. Furthermore, pinpointing sources of problems and issues in the supply chains such as product safety, recalls, counterfeiting, and shipment delays becomes easier. Thus, companies in such an environment cannot hide behind the corporate wall. In many ways, blockchain is designed to ensure accountability for all companies in such a supply chain. Associated outcomes result in more accurate forecasts, lower inventories, faster shipments, and possibly fewer intermediaries.

The promises of a blockchain-enabled supply chain have created a flurry of activities among many companies and consortiums. The potential exists for substantial growth in these networks as more companies become members of the blockchains. However, as with any new technology adoption, companies must be aware of potential issues with the technology and avoid possible pitfalls that may get in the way of realizing the benefits from a successful implementation. However, blockchains have the potential of disrupting current supply chains. Companies must be prepared to take advantage of the benefits that the new technology promises.

Discussion Questions

(1)Describe permissioned blockchains and discuss why they should be the type of blockchain to adopt in the supply chain context.

(2)Explain how a blockchain-enabled supply chain creates advantages for providing better product tracing, reducing counterfeiting, and eliminating shipping trade partners and intermediaries.

(3)Discuss the possible developments in adopting blockchain for the global logistics industry.

(4)Discuss if and how companies can leverage existing technologies when implementing a blockchain platform.

(5)Identify potential issues that companies face with smart contracts in the supply chain.
