Chapter 21

Crypto Accounting Valuation, Reporting, and Disclosure

Sean Stein Smith

Keywords: Crypto assets; blockchain; stablecoins; smart contracts; accounting treatment; financial reporting; disclosure

Introduction

A crypto asset is a general term used to describe a digital asset that uses cryptography, peer-to-peer networking, and a public ledger to regulate the creation of new units, verify transactions, and secure the transactions without the intervention of another party. One type of crypto asset is a cryptocurrency, which is a type of intangible, digital currency used to a store of value and way to transfer that value among users of the currency. Although not all crypto assets are cryptocurrencies, the two terms have the same definition from an accounting perspective.

The origin of crypto assets and cryptocurrencies started during a bull market. The extended bull market beginning with the market bottom in 2009 until early 2020 buoyed asset prices on a global basis. During this period, accounting for various crypto assets on a mark-to-market basis seemed like an appealing idea because of the fact that asset values were increasing. Investors, acting as rational actors from both a reporting and asset return perspective, would seemingly prefer mark-to-market reporting during a bull market rather than during a bear market or even a period of price stagnation. During this bull market, neither the Financial Accounting Standards Board (FASB) nor the International Accounting Standards Board (IASB) addressed the accounting and valuation specifics connected to crypto assets. Only following the dramatic decline in crypto asset prices beginning in 2018, did practitioners examine these issues with increased rigor. This inaction seems to reinforce the FASB's lobbying to relax mark-to-market accounting guidance during both the final crisis of 2007–2008 and the current market downturn.

One item needing further examination is whether crypto assets act as correlated or uncorrelated assets. Some proponents of crypto assets believe that because of their novel technology underpinning, they would inherently behave as uncorrelated assets compared to equities (Hackett 2020). As the market entered a bear market in 2020, crypto asset prices declined alongside the broader equity space. This positive correlation proved painful for some crypto investors and also seemed to undermine the position that crypto assets trade more like gold or other traditional hedges and less like other financial instruments. These events, alongside the absence of guidance, further amplified the complications around valuing, reporting, and disclosing crypto assets.

This chapter attempts to identify and examine methods for crypto asset reporting, disclosure, and valuation that need to be addressed and clarified to accelerate adopting blockchain technology as a technology platform and crypto assets that function as financial instruments. It also raises pertinent questions linked to this area.

Accounting for Crypto Assets

The accounting for crypto assets is an issue that needs to be explained and clarified moving forward both from an operational and information/disclosure perspective. Some disparity exists about how crypto assets are likely to be reported and disclosed going forward, especially as these treatments are connected to jurisdictional issues. Despite the current disparity in accounting treatment and reporting, several fundamental issues need to be a part of this broader conversation. The underlying issue and disparity are directly connected to the lack of authoritative accounting guidance in the United States and elsewhere, and the subsequent publication of various whitepapers outlining potential accounting treatments. The specific accounting treatments and policies in different nations, states, and provinces continue to evolve as the market changes, but understanding the baseline issues is necessary for any more advanced examination. Currently, neither FASB nor IASB has issued any authoritative guidance on how the accounted for, report, or disclose crypto assets in the financial statements. Consequently, any accounting policies currently in place may eventually be irrelevant or erroneous when guidance ultimately emerges.

Intangible Classification

A key issue underlying the accounting and reporting debate related to blockchain and crypto assets concerns crypto asset's place in the wider accounting lexicon. This lack of clarity forms the basis for specific follow-up issues connected to valuation, disclosure, and placement in the financial statements. Although no authoritative guidance exists about how to treat these different crypto assets as of mid-2020, an emerging consensus seems is to treat crypto assets as intangible assets. No single firm or publication can stake claim to this consensus, but the Big 4 accounting firms have been moving in that direction (Stein Smith and Castonguay 2019).

This view seems reasonable given the fact that crypto assets are intangible, but this surface-level analysis only touches on a few issues associated with this emerging consensus. For example, if crypto assets are to be treated as intangible assets, what kind of intangible assets do they represent? Broadly speaking, the two major categories of intangible assets are definite lived and indefinite lived assets. In both instances, a process needs to be in place to potentially reflect and report any changes in value connected to impairment. Although such a treatment seems reasonable for intangible assets such as copyrights, trademarks, and goodwill, it does not appear to work as well for crypto assets because of their price volatility.

Crypto Asset Volatility

Cryptocurrencies tend to be relatively volatile in nature, which seems to reflect both the emerging nature of the asset class and the lack of established and legally codified use. Volatility is not a unique characteristic of crypto assets and has been addressed previously, especially during both bull and bear markets (Alford and Boatsman 1995; Kiger 1974; Song 2017). However, the method of classifying and reporting these assets can impact an organization's financial position. For example, if an organization is holding cryptocurrencies – whether they are stabilized by external assets or decentralized such as bitcoin – how should it report the unrealized gains and losses associated with these holdings? Given the need to recognize the impairment process resulting from a change in the economic landscape or business environment, this process might need to be conducted daily.

Disregarding compliance and paperwork issues, another factor that needs to be considered is that once an asset is impaired, it should not be restored to a level above its previous level of valuation. For example, if a patent, copyright, or other intangible asset suffers an impairment or loss in value, that asset cannot be revalued above the value it had obtained before this impairment as per FASB guidance (Tuovila 2020). This treatment renders the idea of accounting for crypto assets as intangible assets virtually impossible. A review of the price volatility of cryptocurrencies demonstrates just how frequent these markdowns and markups would have to do be. Conversely, treating and accounting for cryptocurrencies as equivalent to investable securities would allow the realized and unrealized gains and losses to be reported on the income statement as they occur. Since the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) and Commodities and Futures Trading Commission (CFTC) indicate that certain crypto assets operate as equity securities and commodity equivalents (Body 2019), categorizing and treating crypto assets as equivalent to equity or commodities seems like a legitimate pathway of analysis based on current guidance and the apparent desire of regulators to not stifle innovation (Weizhan 2018).

Complicating Factors

Another issue is how the reporting of investments, specifically unrealized gains and losses on crypto-asset holdings, appears to remain unaddressed in the crypto-asset marketplace. Put simply, how should the valuation and reporting of different crypto assets, held at different organizations for various purposes, be shown for financial reporting purposes. Treating the accounting for different crypto assets differently seems not only prudent but also something that should occur to reflect market realities. Before examining the specifics of how varying treatment for crypto assets dependent on use might manifest itself in the marketplace, practitioners should be aware of two primary categories of cryptocurrencies: decentralized and permissionless or centralized and permissioned.

As a component of the underlying value proposition, decentralized cryptocurrencies are not connected, tethered, or otherwise stabilized by a central government, central bank, or other external asset. Consequently, increased price volatility is likely to occur. For example, bitcoin, the largest by market capitalization and most well-known cryptocurrency, has experienced considerable volatility. Given that volatility appears to be an embedded component of decentralized cryptocurrencies, how should this volatility be reported and disclosed from a financial reporting perspective by accounting practitioners? The continuation of these price swings even after adopting and implementing blockchains at different enterprises indicates that this volatility, especially downward volatility, is not decreasing as quickly as some proponents and investors might have hoped (Hajric 2019). This situation also undermines the growing consensus toward accounting for all crypto assets as intangible assets. These crypto assets must be able to be marked-to-market – upward and downward to reflect business realities.

Permissioned or increasingly centralized crypto assets might not represent the version of crypto assets that blockchain purists would consider as an ideal future state because a permissioned or centralized blockchain or crypto asset requires a third party, central clearinghouse, or at least approval by some organizations associated with the blockchain to process and approve transactions. Yet, simply ignoring these types of crypto assets is unreasonable. From Libra to Paxos to the potential of crypto assets issued by a government, these developments continue to change the conversation around accounting, reporting, and disclosure for crypto assets. Even with the shift toward centrally managed crypto assets, multiple issues remain connected directly to the reporting, accounting, and disclosure around these financial instruments. These issues manifest themselves via how crypto assets are reported on the financial statements, caused by the ambiguity surrounding accounting, valuation, and disclosure requirements. This situation results from a lack of authoritative guidance from an accounting perspective as well as a regulatory landscape that continues to emerge and shift as new products and services enter the marketplace.

Valuation of Crypto Assets

Separate but related to the issue of accounting for crypto assets is the need to indicate how to value such assets. Unlike equity and debt markets, both of which have exchanges that provide liquidity and methodologies for valuing traded assets, crypto assets remain an emerging area that can complicate the valuation process.

Valuing widely traded and liquid crypto assets such as bitcoin, litecoin, ether, or other major cryptocurrencies is a relatively straight forward process. Prices and market capitalization for these widely traded and held cryptocurrencies are well-known, relatively transparent, and not subject to excessive arbitrage. Since the daily volume is widely available to market participants, assigning appropriate valuations closely mirrors the steps used with equity and debt instruments including those associated with deriving valuation of specific instruments that trade as derivatives or commodities (Barth, Beaver, Hand, and Landsman 2005).

The valuation of debt or equity securities can be summarized as following on one the following relatively popular valuation methodologies. For equity securities, examples of valuation techniques include the discounted cash flow approach, market multiples, and asset-based valuation. Research is available on what effect, if any, accounting adjustments have on accounting for equity investments and equity valuations (Graham Jr. and Lefanowicz 1996). Several methodologies for valuing debt instruments focus on the present value of cash flows including interest and principal repayment. Analysts also use binominal interest rate trees, matrix pricing, forward or spot valuation pricing, or a simpler discounting valuation technique to value financial instruments.

Given that many of these crypto assets appear to be traded and behave like equity securities, a few methodologies seem to make sense for practitioners seeking to correctly value and report on these assets. Some crypto assets may not have an underlying asset or enterprise that can be analyzed, but stablecoins, which are crypto assets underpinned by an external asset such a fiat currency or commodity, are normally supported or otherwise connected to an underlying asset leading to the stablecoin label. Applying a multiple to the crypto-asset valuation, as it either connects to the underlying asset or the potential for this underlying asset to have alternative uses, is perhaps one of the most logical and straight-forward valuation techniques. Despite this, however, crypto assets do not seem to neatly fall into either category of equity or debt instruments. No globally applicable valuation or reporting standards have emerged.

Setting aside stablecoins for a moment, several general trends have appeared as to how to value and report different types of crypto assets. Yet, the sheer number of traded crypto assets is likely to result in the vast majority of these cryptocurrencies not having transparent or liquid data. Assuming this premise is valid, the methodology for valuing thinly traded, newly issued, or otherwise illiquid crypto assets is an issue requiring further examination. Not surprisingly, several approaches have emerged. Market approaches, specifically using quoted prices or comparable crypto assets as the basis for valuation, seem to mirror methods used for valuing equity securities, but might have insufficient levels of comparable market information to make such approaches accurate. Conversely, income approaches seem more appropriate for stablecoins or security tokens versus decentralized cryptocurrencies such as bitcoin since both of the former tend to be connected to a business or the cash flows generated by an organization. Other valuation methods that may work for certain crypto assets are discount rate approaches, similar to debt instruments, or project specific techniques similar to how analysts evaluate project assessments using metrics such as the internal rate of return (Johnson, Button, and Daniel 2019).

Although elaborating the specifics of different valuation methodologies goes beyond the scope of this chapter, the main takeaway is that unethical actors can take advantage of this information asymmetry in such an emerging and nascent marketplace. Thus, simply relying on market capitalization or trading volume can lead to the following scenario. An unethical or otherwise fraudulent actor can create tokens out of thin air numbering in the trillions, and sell them for fractions of a dollar (below $0.01, for example) creating billions of dollars in value that does not actually exist. Therefore, reliance on market capitalization on other established ways of valuing crypto assets might not work as well as they do for other markets.

However, analysts can use several alternative metrics to value crypto assets that might more closely mirror the valuation approaches used for private equity or other illiquid assets. Such methods might entail using an external valuation expert, seeking out market equivalents that are more widely traded, or taking advantage of broader market trends in an attempt to extrapolate a market proxy or price point.

Another issue is whether the businesses using crypto assets are likely to have different valuation and accounting treatments. In other words, does the manner in which crypto assets are being used warrant different accounting treatments? For example, would an organization whose primary business is buying and selling crypto assets account for and report these assets differently than an organization that simply accepts crypto assets as a form of payment? Although an organization serving as a market maker might logically account for these crypto asset holdings on a mark-to-market basis, should different organizations use varying accounting methods? Marking-to-market, as illustrated by the dramatic changes in value at the Silicon Valley Community Foundation, demonstrates the extreme volatility as well as reputational and financial harm that can results if an organization is unprepared to deal with the reporting and disclosure issues that can arise from having substantial crypto-asset holdings (Schleifer 2019).

The accounting treatment and classification of crypto assets has yet to be clarified. Still, the Internal Revenue Service (IRS) released several updates during 2019 focusing on collecting taxes on crypto-asset transactions and gains (Bayadakova 2019). Thus, the IRS appears to be leading the regulatory conversation. Currently, the IRS treats all crypto assets as taxable personal property and every transaction generates a tax liability. Recent FASB updates have sought to increase the amount of investments whose gains and losses (unrealized and realized) are run through the income statement (Financial Accounting Standards Board 2016). A reasonable expectation is that an increasing percentage of financial instruments is likely to be accounted for on a mark-to-market basis as trading securities.

Stablecoin Reporting

A stablecoin is a crypto asset, normally taking the form of a coin or token, that is somehow connected or supported by an underlying asset. This underlying asset can either be a currency unit such as the dollar or Euro, or be a physical commodity such as gold or oil. In any case, the primary potential benefit of such a crypto asset is likely to be reduced as a result of the connection and support of the crypto asset by the underlying existing physical asset.

Viewed through the lens of broader adoption and use by individuals and merchants, stablecoins appear to be the next step in crypto-asset development. Instead, stablecoins seem to represent a halfway point between fiat currencies and decentralized cryptocurrencies. Backed, supported, or otherwise connected to an underlying asset, these stablecoins or asset-backed-coins purport to have lower associated volatility. They also appear to be more closely aligned with the initial goal of cryptocurrencies to serve as the foundation to an alternative financial system (Russo 2018). The components distinguishing stablecoins from other cryptocurrencies also complicate the accounting and disclosure that should occur involving this subset of crypto assets.

Stablecoin Considerations

Some unique considerations related to the accounting and disclosure connected to crypto assets are mentioned below.

  • How should changes in the price or volume of the underlying asset be reported both on the financial statements and in footnotes? For example, if a stablecoin is redeemable or pegged to the price of oil or gold and that price substantially changes, say by plus or minus 10%, what measures and disclosures are in place to ensure communicating this information to the marketplace?
  • Should redemption clauses and other governance-related activities be a part of the disclosures that are reported? Specifically, what are the stablecoin holders entitled to in the case of redemption? This information might be pertinent depending on the institution in question.
  • What, if any, reporting and disclosure should be conducted as related to the reporting of the underlying assets held by a third-party intermediary or other custodian? Even if the organization itself does not hold the underlying assets, reporting some type of information connected to the valuation and other policies used by this third party seems prudent.

Stablecoins represent something of a paradox in the crypto-asset space even as the number of stablecoins continues to increase and new varieties linked or otherwise supported by external assets develop. The underlying goal of stablecoins is the same that bitcoin and other early proponents of cryptocurrencies supported, which is the development of an alternative financial system with currency units not dependent or controlled by a government or other centralized entity. To accomplish the desired change, stablecoins may actually further complicate the accounting and reporting conversation. By introducing another asset, additional considerations are linked to how these assets should be reported and disclosed. Put simply, the stabilizing nature of stablecoins, which are designed to facilitate use by individuals and merchants as fiat alternatives, may complicate the process of functioning as legitimate fiat alternatives or replacements. The inability to use stablecoins as a legitimate fiat alternative and medium of exchange is primarily caused by the additional accounting and reporting complexities that can arise from having to account for both the crypto asset and the underlying asset. How these stablecoins are used vary from coin to coin, but the reporting and disclosure issues persist regardless of the specific utilization. However, any stablecoin is likely to create a two-tiered reporting and disclosure structure as a byproduct of the derivative relation connecting the crypto asset and underlying asset.

Beginning as an offshoot of the wider decentralized cryptocurrency, the stablecoin space continues to attract additional sources of development and investment as more offerings enter the marketplace. The accounting processes for stablecoins also raise additional considerations connected to the underlying asset be it a commodity or fiat currency. These underlying assets change in value over time as a result of market forces, additional use of these crypto assets, and other macroeconomic forces.

Custody

Something that needs to be a part of the reporting and disclosure considerations connected to stablecoins or other asset-backed coins is how custody services and offerings factor into these requirements. Custody and the reporting of physical assets are well-established under various regulatory frameworks such as the SEC and CFTC, but custodial services and product offerings around crypto assets are still an emerging field of study. Different categories of wallets, which are the platforms and tools by which an investor or user of crypto assets can access these holdings, do not hold cryptocurrencies themselves. Instead, they serve as a portal to the blockchains where these assets are held. Because of this important role of allowing investors and crypto-asset holders to access these assets, wallets of all kinds play an important role in the accounting, reporting, and disclosure dialog.

A wallet can take different forms depending on the use and applications connected to the crypto assets. Yet, a hot wallet, an online portal that allows investors or merchants to access crypto holdings, is probably the most common way an individual or small and medium size enterprise accepting payment in various crypto assets may choose to hold these crypto assets on an exchange such as Coinbase. These funds are then held in an omnibus account, which is an account where different funds from various investors are held in a single location and are not specifically broken out by account holder. This account is similar to how traditional brokerage firms treat funds of investors. Since investor protection or insurance methods are still developing, the treatment of crypto investments as equivalent to traditional investments raises additional concerns. Hacks, breaches, and other thefts that have occurred at platforms such as Binance, Cryptopia, and QuadrigaCX illustrate the risks with storing crypto assets with centralized exchanges in an environment without comprehensive blockchain or crypto-asset insurance policies (Nikhilest 2019; Thompson 2020). Although these considerations are worth examining, other factors also need to be assessed.

If, for example, an individual or merchant chooses to self-custody crypto-asset holdings, this approach would certainly seem like a relevant part of the accounting and disclosure dialog. If crypto assets are held in a wallet controlled by an organization, some sort of disclosure and detailed information pertaining to the functionality of these wallets is needed. Given that hot wallets are the most vulnerable to hacks and breaches, a business or merchant planning to use such a wallet might require additional reporting and disclosure.

Wallet Definitions

The two wallet types most often associated with the using crypto assets on a daily or otherwise periodic basis are hot wallets and cold wallets.

  • Hot wallet: A hot wallet is an online portal that allows individual or institutional investors to access crypto-asset holdings via an online platform or application. The intent of a hot wallet is to imitate the convenience and ease of use that many online portals currently provide. A trade-off associated with this convenience and ease of use is the increased risk associated with being able to access information from virtually any location or on any device. From a custodian perspective, a hot wallet might be initially simpler to establish and implement, but it may require a larger amount of control, security, and disclosure versus other wallet options.
  • Cold wallet: A cold wallet is a component of hardware or other type of physical device that enables investors to access crypto-asset holdings. It is typically treated as an air-gapped asset, which is not connected to a computer or device connected to the internet or other wireless network. Thus, compared to a hot wallet, a cold wallet seems more secure. Even with this increased security, cold wallets have weaknesses, including being at risk to physical damage and being hacked. One specific point that might require disclosure is the policies or steps that have been implemented to examine whether the hardware device has been compromised with malicious code.

No matter what wallet or third party custodial service is used, the organization involved should provide at least some information about how these wallets function and how their policies fit into the broader control framework. As different wallet platforms develop, mature, and become increasingly integrated into how organizations receive, spend, and use crypto assets, these disclosures and reporting requirements will require updating. The specifics of what level of details will be disclosed and reported may vary among organizations. Nonetheless, market participants should be kept abreast of trends and directions around custodial offerings.

Governmentally Managed Crypto Assets

Another pressing issue is how a centrally managed crypto asset should be reported and disclosed. Non-governmental crypto assets, whether they are decentralized and untethered to physical assets or stabilized and supported by an external asset such as the dollar or gold, represent a different category of crypto assets than any of those issued and sanctioned by a central government. Beginning as a byproduct of including a clause in the COVID-19 relief package of 2020, the possibility of a centrally issued and governed crypto assets seems to be gaining traction (Stein Smith 2020). Setting aside the substantive considerations about privacy and access to such a centrally managed crypto asset, the reporting and disclosure of such assets seems relatively straight forward. Assuming these crypto assets are likely to function as advertised and are worth their assigned value, they should be reported at the equivalent currency unit.

Government Crypto Asset Example

If the US government issued a cryptographically secured dollar, this digital dollar could reasonably be expected to be worth an equivalent of a current US dollar. Such a valuation methodology appears to reinforce the previous argument that a different accounting treatment would be needed depending on the specifics of the crypto asset in question. Although the debate about central government issued crypto assets continues to mature and develop, a reasonable assumption is to expect accounting classification and treatment to emerge more prominently over time. Nonetheless, several other considerations are unique to government issued or otherwise centrally managed crypto assets.

  • How is the supply of these digital crypto assets monitored and controlled? In other words, what specific steps should the Treasury Department or central bank take to ensure that the physical and digital money supplies remain in lockstep? Such safeguards may seem abstract, but bifurcation of the money supply could result in a discount or premium being applied to either the physical or digital version of these currency units.
  • From a tax reporting perspective, should any penalties be assigned to those firms using the crypto version of the currency for errors on estimated payments? Since these organizations, assuming some centralized clearing authority, have access to transactions on a continuous basis, accurately estimating the taxes due and payable should theoretically be a simple matter.
  • Specific to disclosure requirements, organizations using the crypto version of currencies should enact appropriate safeguards around these cash equivalents. Physical custody, separation of duties, and other controls connected to physical cash are well-established but still do not always function appropriately. Since crypto-cash equivalents remain so nascent in nature, paying particular attention to these policies as they adapt to crypto assets seems prudent for practitioners. For example, would the bonding process function the same way for employees handling physical cash versus those handling crypto-cash equivalents?

The reporting and disclosure connected to governmentally issued and controlled stablecoins are likely to be simpler and less complicated than other reporting and disclosure. Consequently, the actual implementation and use of centrally and governmentally controlled crypto assets might involve additional reporting and disclosure requirements. Treating and using these proposed governmental crypto assets as currency equivalents also entail complying with the full array of regulations associated with preventing money laundering and other criminal activity. Although treating stablecoins as fiat currency equivalents might seem like a benefit, a stablecoin creates a dual structure of reporting, custody, and disclosure requirements that might not be as beneficial as initially imagined. Ignoring the potential privacy issues that arise from granting a central government access to the financial transactions of the entire population, the technical complexity of implementation should not be understated. As the efforts launched in March and April of 2020 to support the economy demonstrate, even attempting to launch a relatively straight forward small business lending program can be thwarted by the lack of appropriate financial infrastructure or technical expertise (Omeokwe and Hayashi 2020).

Disclosure

Another consideration that should be discussed about crypto-asset accounting is what types of information, if any, should to be disclosed to the marketplace. Clear and enforceable disclosure principles are available for how other types of information should be disclosed, how this information should be reported, and what specific points of information need to be disclosed to the market and regulators. Interpreting and applying these principles to the crypto-asset space is a logical first step in establishing and normalizing similar policies for crypto assets. A simple example, discussed below, focuses on how an organization should disclose and report crypto-asset holdings given the current regulatory ambiguity. Adding to this uncertainty is the global nature of both blockchain and crypto assets, which has led to a patchwork of regulatory and accounting treatments on a global basis. Capital and financial resources may move on a global basis, but every financial instrument – whether crypto assets or not – must comply with the rules and guidelines of the jurisdictions in which they operate. Besides the effort and expense incurred by organizations seeking to operate a global crypto organization, this lack of consistency hinders wider adoption and development.

Accounting Example

Assume that an organization offers customers the option to pay for its goods and services with crypto assets that comply with all applicable regulatory guidelines. During the course of year, customers pay an equivalent of $10 million when making those payments. Since these payments occur throughout the year, no discernible pattern or routine to these crypto asset payments exists. As management prepares the financial statements throughout the year, it needs to address several questions.

  • Should the footnotes include the fair value of the crypto-asset payments at the point in time of the payment, as well as detailed tracking of the changes in valuation of these crypto-asset payments throughout the year? This question also supposes that the organization incorporated these changes in price into the financial statements during the year, but the additional disclosures might, for example, include valuation methodologies.
  • What, if any, of the due diligence that the firm conducted on the developer or company that was building the blockchain should be disclosed or reported in the organization's footnotes? Although this information might be more technical or computer-related information than strictly financial data or information, understanding these components is a critically important piece of information from a disclosure perspective. Since every crypto asset depends on an underlying blockchain, having this information might be pertinent especially if the organization's leadership team changes or otherwise becomes indisposed.
  • Should the levels (e.g., level 1 stocks and bonds; level 2 investments and assets held by insurance companies, private equity, or other pools of private capital; and level 3 the most illiquid of assets that require comparable or other expert valuation efforts) be identified and disclosed? This practice is routine for more widely traded equity and debt instruments but has not been codified or standardized for the reporting or disclosure of crypto-asset information. For example, if certain assets become delisted, have lower than expected trading volume or liquidity, or are negatively affected by broader market forces, how are these events reflected in the disclosures and other data reported to the marketplace? Given the often volatile and fast changing nature of the crypto and blockchain markets, instituting a process for disclosing these changes and information seems prudent.

Besides determining the information that should be disclosed in financial reporting, another issue is to determine where to disclose this information. Including such information in footnotes of the financial statements might follow current best practices, but could be inappropriate given the new and emerging nature of such information. Conversely, since this information might be unrelated to a firm's financial performance in either the current or medium term, including such information within the financial statements might be irrelevant. Instead, a potential home for these disclosures might be in the management discussion and analysis of financial reporting alongside where management has the opportunity to discuss a firm's narrative and direction both now and going forward. Given the lack of consistent and enforceable standards, firms retain substantial flexibility in this area.

Control Disclosures

Another issue concerns the controls necessary for blockchain and crypto assets to operate appropriately. Although additional controls and safeguards may be needed, how to disclose these controls and their impact on the responsibility of management and external experts still remain a work in progress. In the current environment, the roles and responsibilities of different stakeholders, from management to the external assurance and attestation teams, are well-defined and understood by these stakeholders and regulators. Although the management team is responsible for developing and implementing internal controls, the role of external experts is to assess these controls. Since the control environment directly affects the accuracy and validity of the information reported by the organization, a control audit seems reasonable to include as part of a financial audit. A control audit represents the examination and testing of the policies and processes in place to safeguard the information being reported and produced by an organization. Although the responsibility of developing and maintaining internal controls remains with the management team, external attestation and assurance professionals are responsible for testing these controls. This audit can take the form of multiple tests and other processes by which the controls – implemented and maintained by management – effectively create an environment within which data can be reported and communicated accurately. With blockchain implementation continuing to accelerate across industry lines, the control conversation is rapidly moving from a back-burner issue to a top consideration for management teams.

Besides actually developing these controls, a need exists for examining and reviewing the roles of different stakeholders in a blockchain-augmented environment. External auditors or other assurance professionals cannot, without violating independence, construct or otherwise play a role in the development and construction of internal controls. Thus, expecting such a clear delineation between clients and auditors given how quickly and radically blockchain and crypto assets develop might be unreasonable. Maintaining auditor independence remains a core function. In addition, how auditors and other attestation experts interact and engage with clients is important. Thus, these engagements are unlikely to change with the rise of blockchain and crypto assets. Internal control disclosures and reporting already form a portion of the data reported to the marketplace. The following points seem to form the basis for assessing how these data should be disclosed and reported.

  • What types of information associated with controls around blockchain should be disclosed, and should this information be reported alongside or integrated with current control information, or should these data be reported in a separate section?
  • How should external auditors and attestation experts engage with the development, reporting, and testing of controls? All firms are unlikely to have the in-house expertise to develop and implement blockchain controls, so external auditors are likely to be involved to a certain extent.
    • This issue also raises the matter about how to test and report these controls. Since developing and implementing these controls are likely to be a collaborative effort, having a separate set of external experts involved in at least an advisory capacity seems logical.
  • Given the lack of standards and codification around blockchain and crypto assets including the control environment connected to these technologies, should firms disclose the process by which they develop the controls? If this process is to be disclosed, another issue involves the specific information that an organization should make public versus treat as proprietary.

No matter what approach is used around how controls are developed, tested, maintained, and implemented, some level of disclosure is likely to be required. Documentation usually helps pinpoint pain points and areas for improvement. The transparency related to controls may also help improve investor confidence in the reported valuations and accounting for these crypto assets. Highlighted by several recent Service Organization Control related announcements in the blockchain space, the realization of how important establishing comparable and effective internal control policies seems to increasingly evident to market actors (Loveday 2020).

Smart Contracts

Although not specifically an accounting or financial services issue, the importance of smart contracts is difficult to overstate from an accounting and disclosure perspective. A smart contract is a contractual and computer language that has been translated from traditional contracts and embedded or otherwise connected to a blockchain platform to enable automation of certain job tasks or processes. For example, if a stablecoin is to operate effectively as a legitimate alternative to existing fiat currencies, doing so requires smart contracts to play an important role in the stabilization of any given stablecoins. That is, for a stablecoin to function, the smart contracts connecting the crypto asset to the underlying asset are just as important as the crypto asset itself. The disclosure and reporting of these smart contracts seem like a prudent step to take given the fast changing blockchain and crypto-asset space.

Several considerations might be worth disclosing to the public.

  • What function do these smart contracts actually perform? As they relate to stablecoins, smart contracts can function as a stabilizing agent and also play a role in the interoperability part of the conversation. For example, if a firm takes payment in bitcoin and uses several third-party organizations to manage and custody these crypto assets, these third-party applications will be connected using smart contracts.
  • Are the controls over the smart contracts and those connected to crypto assets properly implemented and maintained? Specifically, are the firm's policies able to maintain an appropriate and robust level of control and monitoring over smart contract performance?
  • Does the firm have the correct levels of technical legal assistance, either from internal in-house counsel or external legal advisors? An example might be a footnote or disclosure documenting which law firm is serving in an advisory capacity to the organization about crypto-asset management and smart contact implementation.
  • Which regulatory agency should oversee smart contracts? In other areas of the financial markets, definitive rules and regulations exist about which agency or regulatory body oversees which components of market actors. For example, developing and using smart contracts remain an emerging field.

Although smart contracts are not specifically an accounting issue or consideration, distinctions can be drawn between accounting considerations, reporting disclosures, and what external stakeholders might need to know. Smart contracts are the proverbial glue that connects blockchains as well as connecting them to other technology systems and platforms. Within that context, these systems underpinning crypto assets should be reported and disclosed to external creditors and investors alongside specific accounting information.

Summary and Conclusions

Accounting valuation and reporting guidance connected to crypto assets is a priority for policy makers in the United States and elsewhere. Yet, accounting firms among others have identified and set forth non-authoritative guidance on various issues. When regulators eventually propose guidance, the risk exists that the practices developed and implemented by the private sector may run counter to whatever guidance that comes forth. Nonetheless, individuals and merchants across difference economic sectors and industries must be able to offer some type of advice that realistically reflects market forces to service their customers and clients. As guidance evolves, so will practices. Over time, more consistent policies, reporting, and disclosures are likely to evolve.

Discussion Questions

(1)Explain the primary differences between decentralized cryptocurrencies and stablecoins or otherwise more centralized crypto assets.

(2)Discuss the disclosure implications around crypto assets, smart contracts, and blockchain control issues.

(3)Discuss how the lack of valuation guidance can provide a headwind or obstacle to broader crypto asset adoption.

(4)Identify how a lack of consistent accounting guidance and frameworks for crypto assets might cause confusion for external users.

(5)Explain how an auditor might go about incorporating a smart contract into an existing audit process.
